I N T R O D U C T I O N 
      I, the Chairman of the Department-related Parliamentary Standing Committee on Science & Technology, Environment & Forests,
 have been authorised by the Committee to present the Report on its behalf, present this Eighty-ninth Report of the Committee.  This
 Report deals with the detailed Demands for Grants (2001-2002) of the Department of Science & Technology (Ministry of  Science and
 Technology) (Demand No.68). 
2.  In the meeting of the Committee held on the 30 th March, 2001 the Secretary and other Officers of the Department of Science and
 Technology gave an overview of the various activities of the Department and the Members sought clarifications on various aspects of
 the performance of the Department to enable it to scrutinise the Demands for Grants. 
3.  The Committee expresses its thanks to the Officers of the Department for replying to the clarifications sought by the
 Members and placing before it the required material to enable the Committee to scrutinise the Demands for Grants of the
 Department of Science and Technology. 
4.         The Committee considered and adopted the Report at its meeting held on 18th  April, 2001.
  
NEW DELHI;                                                                                                                               C. RAMACHANDRAIAH,
April 18, 2001                                                                                                                                 Chairman,
                         Committee on Science & Technology,
                          Environment & Forests.

The Department informed the Committee that the allocation was reduced at R.E on the non-plan side by Rs.23.38 crores. The
 reduction was on account of the requirement of 10%cut in the non-plan expenditure (other than salaries) viz., Rs.14.32 crores and
 balance Rs.9.06 crores on account of an assessment of reduced requirements for salaries assessed at R.E. stage.
Asked as to what were the reasons that the non-plan expenditure has been well above the allocation on the plan side and whether
 any steps were being contemplated to contain the non-plan expenditure.  The Department informed the Committee that the high non-
plan budget was mainly on account of the requirement towards “salaries” for which an amount of Rs.286.75 crores was provided in
 B.E. and Rs.276.88 in R.E. of the year 2000-2001.  Out of this, an amount of Rs.135.24 crores related to the salaries of Survey of India
 in B.E. of the year 2000-2001 and Rs.125.30 crores in R.E. of 2000-2001.  The provision for “salaries” also includes the salaries for
 Autonomous Bodies.
Likewise, India Meteorological Department was allocated Rs.93.33 crores in B.E. and Rs.93.49 crores in R.E. of 2000-2001
 towards salaries.
The provision for Technology Development Board (Rs.70 crores in B.E. and Rs.63 crores in R.E. of 2000-2001 and also in B.E. of
 2001-2002) also accounts for a substantial provision.
The Committee notes the useful work being done by all the Departments aforesaid and reductions in non-plan expenditure cannot
 be effected overnight, the Committee would like the Department to see whether any reduction can be brought about in the expenditure
 other than salaries.   At the same time attempt should also be made to see whether any reduction can be brought about in the staff
 strength of these Departments gradually by not filling some of the vacancies arising out of resignations, retirements etc. occurring in
 the normal course.  The Committee would like to make it abundantly clear that it is not in favour of spreading fear psychosis among
 employees by resorting to unpopular measures.
Provision for salaries continues to be the largest element in the non-plan budget for the year 2001-2002 and an amount of Rs.292
 crores has been provided for salaries.

5.   Asked about the increase in allocation to Topographical Surveys in the year 2001 –2002 to Rs.93.10 crores as against Rs.59.89
 crores in B.E. stage and Rs.54.45 crores during R.E. stage of 2000-2001 and the reason for no allocation being made to development
 project surveys, the Department informed the Committee that the marked difference in the B.E. 2000-2001 & B.E. 2001-2002 under
 Topographical Surveys and Surveys of Development Projects was on account of the merger of both minor heads under Topographical
 Surveys.
6.   In order to meet the national requirement, including that of Defence Forces the responsibility of Survey of India was expanded after
 1962 to provide and update topographical coverage on various scales in the entire country.  Accordingly, a large number of
 Topographical Units were raised to complete this task in the scheduled time, keeping in view peace and war and internal security
 duties.  Simultaneously, under the development programmes, the State Governments had projected their mapping requirements to
 Survey of India for major engineering projects such as Steel Plants, Power & Irrigation Projects, etc. In view of the demands of various
 States, Survey Parties were also formed on regional basis for undertaking Extra-Departmental jobs under the caption “Surveys of
 Development Projects”.  There was thus no functional requirement to operate both the heads separately.  The merging of provision of
 “Surveys of Development Projects” in B.E. 2001-2002 into “Topographical Surveys” has been proposed to ensure smooth functioning.
  
7.   The Department also informed the Committee that the marginal increase of Rs.5.00 lakhs over B.E. 2000-2001 in the provision for
 ‘Foreign travel expenses’ was mainly on account of the increased bilateral and multilateral activities under international cooperation

SCIENCE & ENGINEERING COUNCIL (SERC)
8.   The Committee was informed that the SERC mechanism was under operation since the last twenty-five years. The scheme has been
 focusing on strengthening the research infrastructure in the country during the last decade. The new “Fund for the Improvement of
 Science & Technology Infrastructure”(FIST) programme, which has operationalised during the current year, would lay emphasis on
 evolving coordinated programmes in advanced areas through organization of brain storming sessions. The emphasis would be on
 supporting more Research projects in the university sector to tap the expertise available in the universities.  The areas include plant
 sciences, soft condensed matter physics, lasers & quantum optics, boundary layer modeling, crystal engineering, and Earth Sciences
 applications for societal needs, geophysical exploration, Mathematical Sciences etc.
9.   The allocation for Multi-disciplinary Research in Science and Technology (SERC) has been increased to Rs.87.10 crores for the
 year 2001-2002 from Rs.69.50 crore in B.E and R.E of the year 2000-2001. Asked about the reasons for increased allocation, the
 Secretary informed the Committee that the original budget provision in respect of SERC was Rs.75 crores, out of which Rs.7.5 crores
 had been separately shown under provision for North Eastern region and Sikkim. This has been restored to the SERC budget. He
 further stated that the B.E for 2001-2002 includes Rs.85 crores under plan and Rs.2.1 crores under non-plan. The increase therefore is
 only Rs.10 crores under the plan outlay.
10.  The Committee has been given to understand that SERC is one of the Major R&D programmes of the Department,
 Promoting multi-disciplinary research in Science and Engineering providing support to individual research scientists,
 establishing core groups and centers of excellence and setting up national R&D facilities. Further, the SERC has approved a
 large number of important programmes requiring additional funds. In view of the above and also to take care of the increased
 cost of sophisticated equipment, foreign exchange fluctuations, costly consumables and chemicals etc., the Committee
 recommends that the allocation needs to be suitably augmented.
TECHNOLOGY INFORMATION, FORECASTING AND ASSESSMENT COUNCIL (TIFAC)
11.  The Technology Information, Forecasting, and Assessment Council (TIFAC) is a society registered under the Department of
 Science and Technology. The main objectives of TIFAC include generation of Technology Forecasting/Technology
 Assessment/Techno Market survey reports providing technology related information, promotion of technology and evolving suitable
 mechanism for testing of technology, technology transfer and commercialisation as well as patent information.
      TIFAC has brought out over 250 well-researched, specialized reports – both in breath of technologies covered (Agriculture to
 Advanced Sensors) as well as depth (Technology Assessment and Status in India/Abroad, recent/potential markets, R&D opportunities
 etc.)     
      TIFAC reports have covered all the major sectors, which are of relevance to India.  The reports have also focused on specific
 products, processes & on their applications.
      In order to cater to the fast changing technological scenario in India and abroad, TIFAC reports also address the cutting edge and
 frontier technologies, technologies that may take 506 years to mature.
12.  The Department aims speed up implementation of the Technology Vision 2020 Mission projects. The systems approach technology
 aims to increase agricultural productivity. Besides, up gradation of Science and Engineering colleges is also proposed to be taken up.
 Mission REACH aims at creating centers of excellence in selected Departments at par with best available standards with a view to
 available attract industries to solve targeted problem in a time bound manner. The project aims at designing and developing prototypes
 for commercial production.
13.The Committee is of the view that in the wake of globalization and opening up of global markets, new technologies would
 flood Indian markets. Therefore, TIFAC must strengthen its forecasting/assessment of technologies so as to compete with the
 technologies coming from abroad.  Besides, the technologies proposed to be developed should be cost effective. Efforts should
 also be made to make the scientists aware of the need for taking patents. Knowledge about Procedures for applying a patent as
 also other formalities required being completed should be included, if not already available in the Department’s web page
 along with facility for downloading of necessary forms.  The web site should be updated periodically. The information about
 the patents applied must also be made available, if not already available, in the web sites.  Sometimes, the web sites are not
 easily accessible.  This needs to be looked into.
JOINT TECHNOLOGY PROGRAMME
14.  The Committee was informed that in the 9
th plan, four programmes were initiated under the Joint technology Programmes (a) Glass
 Technology upgradation programme and (b) Vision technology (c) Gold Technology upgradation programme and (d) Laser
 applications.

      Under Glass Technology upgradation programme, upgradation of technology, processes, product and applications of special glass
 (optical as well as ophthalmic glass) and consumer glass were initiated; efforts were also being made to develop technologies to make
 the present production process more cost effective and to enable utilization of glass scrap. The programme also seeks to facilitate
 creation of production facilities for ophthalmic glass to meet domestic and global demands; quality auditing and regulation through an
 appropriate law/act prevent production of substandard glass.
      In regard to consumer glass, efforts were focused on developing technologies aimed improving the technology and product quality
 so that the existing units become more productive and efficient .Eco friendly furnaces and improving glass melting pots were also
 developed.  
      Vision Technology programme aims at developing preventive, diagnostic and curative technologies and instrumentation for
 application amongst a large number of patients. It aims to effectively prevent /delay in onset of cataract and to retard the progression of
 cataract. The Gold Technology Programme aims to promote hallmarking activity.  Appropriate instrumentation was being developed
 for accurate assessment of gold content.  Development of abrasion resistant colourless weatherproof clear surface finishes had also
 been undertaken for value addition to the existing products.       
      In Laser application, Laser awareness programme was initiated for educating and making aware the children and population at large
 about the potential of lasers.  An advanced application of lasers in pattern recognition has been  identified  and  equipment for finger
 print  identification was being developed.  This technology would have many applications in Defence, Quality control in industries,
 Robotic vision and Artificial intelligence.
15.  The Committee is of the view that given the size of population and the use of ophthalmic glass, The country must aim to
 achieve self sufficiency in glass manufacture under vision Technology, the time schedule should strictly be adhered to and tests
 should be conducted before they are transferred to be used on patients, as the cases of failure of cataract operations have made
 many patients reluctant in adopting new techniques.  Laser technologies for curing cataract and other eye disorders must be
 strengthened and technologies developed should be available at affordable prices. 
SCIENCE  & TECHNOLOGY COMMUNICATION & POPULARIZATION PROGRAMME
16.  The thrust of the programme is to popularize Science & Technology, stimulation of Scientific and Technological temper among the
 people, take steps to provide support and coordination of Science & Technology popularization activities in the country.
17.  Under the programme Science & Technology for the visually challenged a variety of software and a science magazine for the blind
 in both Braille and audio cassettes and development of kits/teaching and learning aids were to be developed. Department aims to
 promote voluntary blood donation and a special software “Rudhirnet” was developed which would be made available to various blood
 banks. A programme on Environment and sustainable development would continue.
18.  The National Resource Data Management System (NRDMS), it is stated, would concentrate on building specialized problem
 oriented databases and operationalising them for real life planning and administrative decision-making.  It proposes to create new
 NRDMS databases centres for better coverage in states of Tamilnadu, Nagaland, UP and Assam, develop and disseminate spatial data
 management tools for integrated rural development, formulation of new R&D projects in areas of watershed management; land use
 planning, energy planning and infrastructure development. The Department also proposes to undertake studies to identify landslides
 prone areas in North Eastern states for detailed geological and geo-technical investigations.     
      While the Department proposes to continue the on-going programmes, it also proposes to extend contact programmes for school
 children to R&D labs and S&T organizations, visit to industries and S&T establishment and lecture demonstration programme in
 science would to extended to different parts of the country for stimulating creativity amongst children.
      Besides, programmes related to celebrations of National Technology Day would be extended to different states/UT of the country.
      Despite the changes brought out so far in our education system, a large potential work force comprising of students faces a bleak
 future after completion of their university education.  Asked whether any steps were being contemplated, so far as Ministry of Science
 & Technology was concerned, to inculcate scientific temper in them in course of their studies, or for their utilization/deployment for
 research or other productive purposes by identifying certain projects where they could be deployed during their vacation  or on regular
 basis as  part of their  education
system.  The Department was specifically asked whether any attempt has ever been made to study the experience of their countries
 particularly China and whether any assessment has ever made of the gain that would accrue to country by productive utilization of such
 vast potential.
19.  The Department replied that students constitute a large potential work force.  The scientific community has expressed a serious
 concern about the declining interest in pursuing science by students due to lack of adequate job opportunities.  The Ministry of Science
 and Technology was fully seized of this problem and has contemplated various steps in this direction.  The important initiatives taken

20.While the Committee appreciates the work done in the field of Science & Technology Communication and popularization
 programme. The Committee is constrained to observe that our  planners  have not given  much thought  towards utilisation of 
 this  vast  potential
work force.  While the Committee would likely to impress up the DST the urgent need to fully exploit this work force for the
 purpose of Science popularization programme, it should address other Ministries concerned to tap this work forces with a view
 to impart on them a kind of training which would not only benefit the country but would also help them to gainfully utilize
 their facilities for the development of their career.  Some schemes like ‘Earn while you learn’ could also be consideration for
 introduction.
OPPORTUNITY FOR YOUNG SCIENTISTS
21.            Committee was informed that these programmes aim at providing opportunities to young scientists for pursuing research and
 also give enough opportunities for interaction and exchange of ideas. The emphasis would be on supporting more research projects
 with innovative and creative content. It is planned to support about 150 projects in the year.
22.The Committee is of the view that efforts should be aimed at increasing the number of scholarships so that young scientists
 have interest in the scheme.  Besides, the scope of projects sponsored needs to be suitably increased in order to attract more
 and more scientists to the programme.
Societal programmes
23.  Committee was informed that the Department aims at specific programmes for socio-economic uplift of weaker sections of the
 population in rural and urban areas, women, tribal and scheduled castes communities. Initiatives were focused on integrated
 development of villages through Science & Technology intervention; technology parks for women; international cooperation with
 SAARC countries. The Department also carries All India Coordinated Programme on waste recycling and management for
 demonstrating the viable and sustainable technology packages, it plans to take up scientific management practices especially for
 smaller animals as the scheduled caste population was largely involved in rearing the animals.  In addition, work-based occupation
 such as management of Mandi-waste, handloom etc. would be given focused attention.
24.  The Committee was informed that efforts were made in the area of Non-timber forest produce (NTFP), artisan skills, traditional
 agricultural practices and their improvement. A special programme on animal husbandry was proposed for smaller animals. It also
 proposed to sensitize and encourage scientists/NGOs to work with tribal communities.
25.The Committee observes that programmes meant for tribal population should encourage their participation in the national
 mainstream instead of alienating them. The Department should therefore work in coordination with Department of

33.  Himalayan Glaciology programme was aimed at understanding the behaviour of glaciers and their interaction with climate and

INTEGRATED STUDIES RELATED TO GANGOTRI GLACIER
34.  In the recently initiated multi-disciplinary projects related to the Gangotri glacier particularly dealing with remote sensing,
 microwave  remote sensing, isotopic  and chemical studies, palaeo-
climatology, climate change etc for long terms studies, some significant field data has been acquired.  Two more projects dealing the
 monitoring and modeling of melt runoff and microbial-biodiversity and environmental quality studies have been sanctioned.  A brief of
 the progress made under individual project on Gangotri Glacier is given below:   
      (i)            Establishment and operation of mountain meteorological observatory at Gangotri Glacier.
The aim of this project was to establish high altitude observatories at Bhojbasa near Gangotri Glacier and also to establish
 Automatic Weather Stations (AWS) at near snout, ablation zone and accumulation zone.  Under this project, Snow & Avalanche Study
 Establishment (SASE), built a permanent station at Gangotri near Bhojbasa.  The observatory at Bhojbasa has been made functional
 and all weather parameters are recorded twice a day as per WMO standards manually by the trained observers.  Three Automatic
 Weather Stations (AWS) have been established in the area:  Bhojbasa, Kalindipass and Nandaban.  One VHF radio communication link
 has been established between the observatory at Bhojbasa and R.D.C. SASE, Chandigarh.  The communication link was used for
 transmitting manually observed snow and meteorological data to R.D.C. SASE for archival of both manually observed and the
 automatic data.  Attempt is being made to make the data available to all users through internet.
      (ii)      Monitoring and Modeling of Melt Runoff from Gangotri Glacier
The most suitable site for establishing the gauging site was selected near Bhojbasa.  It was noted that the pattern of the river flow

DRUGS AND PHARMACEUTICALS
36.  The Committee has been informed that Research & Development for new drugs is a challenging area of research due to complexity
 of the biological system and disease process. The scheme on drugs and pharmaceuticals research was initiated in 1994-95 for
 promoting R&D in the drugs and pharmaceuticals sector, development of new molecules leading to commercialisable technology
 towards new drug development, giving special thrust to the development of drugs for treatment of diseases prevalent in the Indian
 climatic zone and promoting R&D in all systems of medicines bringing together the scientific expertise existing in the country in
 research institutions and industry on a joint platform in a project mode and establishment of mechanisms and linkages  
so as to facilitate the development of new drugs by the Indian Industry and the Research Institutes.  
37.  The Committee has been informed that the Department would continue its efforts to support collaborative research projects to
 further joint research programmes for drug development in the area of diseases which are of importance to our country i.e.
 Tuberculosis, Cancer, Gastrointestinal disorders like Diarrhoea, Diabetes, Hypertension, Cardio-Vascular disorders and other prevalent
 infectious diseases in particular acute respiratory infections and food & water borne diseases etc. Special emphasis was planned
 towards development of herbal drugs. 
38.While the Committee appreciates that Department of Science and Technology is choosing herbs for development of drugs
 with a view to find a cure for many diseases affecting the society, the Committee is constrained to observe that not much is
 being done in the field of traditional systems of medicines in the country whereas some of the other countries have been in the
 forefront in adopting our system of medicine at mass scale.  It was reported in the media recently that in order to cure the
 injuries of the victims of Chernobyl victims, an Indian System of medicine was found to be very effective.  This paved the way
 for adoption of the Indian system of medicine in Russia.  This is only one example.  Efforts therefore need to be concentrated in
 adopting the traditional systems of medicine at mass scale by setting up laboratories, hospitals etc. 
      Another point which the Committee would like the DST to bear in mind that the chances of bringing the private sector or,
 for that matter the industry on a common platform for research on any other form of collaboration, are indeed remote because
 the industry does not work from a welfare point of view.  Rather profit is its motive.  In fact the Committee is constrained to
 observe that the commercialisation of human sufferings / diseases appears to be becoming the order of the day in private
 hospitals/clinics etc. This trends needs to be discouraged.
The Committee would like to reiterate that it would be indeed futile to merely add drugs to the ones already existing in the
 country.  Efforts should always be aimed to develop drugs that tend to wipe out the diseases and not merely cure them.

 popularization built around natural phenomena like the total solar eclipses of 1995 and 1999.

 level.  Further, at present, Vigyan Prasar is in the process of recruiting scientific and supporting staff to attain its objectives and

Environment and Forests are two vital sectors where the role of the Ce ntral and State Governments is of
a complementary nature, one supple menting the efforts of  the other in preser ving and promoting a
healthy environment and conserving fo rest wealth which is an important  part of the environment. The
forests being spread in different States all over the country and envi ronmental issues being common and
of equal import to all the State, the Union Ministry  of Environment and Forests acts as the nodal agency
at the national level for pla nning, promotion and coordination of environmental and forestry
programmes.

3.   In its two sittings, the Committ ee went into the specifics of the Demands for Grants of the Ministry
and had detailed clarifications from  the Secretary and other officials. In the course of their evidence a
pointed question was raised about the Eighth Plan outlay for the Mini stry and it was explained that
against the projected requirement of  Rs. 4794 crores for the entire Five Year Plan only Rs. 1200 crores
were approved. During the first th ree years of the Plan period th e expenditure already adds up to
approximately Rs. 957 crores . The implication of this  is that for the remain ing two years of the plan
period only a small amount of Rs. 242.5 cr ores will be left with the Mini stry to carry out  its activities
and schemes. But the apprehension of the Committee that in that case, with such a meagre allocation, the
Ministry's activities/projects w ould go haywire was allayed by the Se cretary who clarified that the
Planning Commission has in  general supported the Ministry's outlays assuming th at there is 10%
increase every year in the outlay the Ministry is expected to finish with a plan size of Rs. 1790 crores for
the entire 8th plan period.  
  
The Committee is inclined to accep t the point put forth by him that, ke eping in view the total approved
outlay of 1200 crores of r upees for entire Eighth Fi ve Year Plan for the Mi nistry, the average annual
outlay would have only been within the vicinity of Rs. 240 crores, which is not  the case as the Ministry
has been getting each year much more amount. This allocation of approximately Rs. 300 crores a yea r
on an average for the Ministry does not  appear to be sufficient, if the issues relating to Environment and
Forests are taken into account; but as the Forest s figure in the Concurrent List, considerable
responsibility to provide finances therefor  devolves on the States also. In that context, a valid point was
made by the Secretary of the Mini stry that the Ministry's budget is  just only a part of the total
expenditure on these sectors in the country. While the Committee agrees that the Ministry has been
getting much more per year than what was originally  envisaged in the Eighth Five Year Plan, and this
has to be viewed in the context of allocations made by the State Go vernments, the Committee feels that
this is not a happy situation that even such small annual allocations  have not been utilised by the
Ministry fully. The table in Annexure-II will amply bear this out. No  doubt, the Ministry has given 
reasons for under-utilisation or non-utilisation or excess expenditure and yet the overall picture does not 
look very healthy, though signs of improvement in respect of spending of funds on the relevant
schemes/projects are noticeable during the year 1993-94.  
  
The Committee has also noted that in the Budget Es timates for 1993-94 the Non-plan component of the 
Ministry was just over Rs. 52 crores which was subsequently revised to over Rs. 62 crores, thereby
effecting an increase of 20% but  in the Budget Estimates for 1994- 95 it has been shown as Rs. 58.27 
crores, which represents a reduction  of about Rs. 4crores over that of the previous year. While the
Committee appreciates that the Mi nistry has sought lesser Non-plan  allocation for 1994-95, it fails to 
understand as to what necessitated s ubstantial increase in Nonplan co mponent in the Revise? Estimates 
for 1993-94. The Committee hopes that the Ministry would take due care and confine the Non-plan 
expenditure to the amount as projec ted in the Budget Estima tes for 1994-95 . d the in crease, if any, will 
be confined to the barest minimum.  
  
6.  The Committee has take up se lectively some of the major head s and sub-heads in the Demands fo r 
Grants of the Ministry and the observations of the Committee are given in the succeeding paragraphs.  
  
Major Head '2406'-Forestry and Wildlife

7.  The Committee has observed that an amount of Rs. 218.15 crores (Plan as well as Nonplan) has been 
provided for in the Budget Estimates for 1994-95 for Forestry and Wildlife which include Education and
Training, Research, Survey and Utilisation of Fore st Resources, Forest Cons ervation, Development and
Regeneration, National Afforestation & Eco-Devel opment Programme and Wildlife. This amount is
against Rs. 197.10 crores (Plan and Non-plan) provided             for in the Revised Estimates for 1993-94 
which represents an increase of over 10%.  
              
The Committee has noted that there are a number of plans and schemes in these sectors being carried out
by the Ministry, which have been  explained at some length in the Performance Budget itself.
Notwithstanding the difficulties be ing faced by it at times in bringi ng the concerned States round to a
common point of view on specific issues, the growing pressures on the forests demand a more concerted
approach on the part of the Mi nistry. The Committee was told th at about 220 milli on tonnes of fuel
wood and 250 million tonnes of  green grass are being c ontributed by the forestry  system to rural India,
qnd village industries like Brick a nd Tobacco etc. too depend upon w ood. Besides 80% of the village
medicinal needs is met from forests and about 12 million c.m. of forest timber is used. This works out to
Rs. 13,000crores of removal every year  from forests, but the revenue from the forestry system through
commercial sale is hardly Rs. 1,500 crores. The Co mmittee feels that the Ministry through its R&D
Units should concentrate on devel oping and providing low cost and fu el efficient energy for cooking so
that the dependence of rural peopl e on fuel wood from the forests is  minimised substantially and the
forests have unhindered growth.  
  
The forest policy of the G overnment envisages that 33% area has to be unde r forest cover, and in this
context afforestation and regenera tion of degraded fo rests are quite importa nt. Dr. Swaminathan
Committee suggested that in the Ei ghth Plan the plantation target s hould be25 million hectares at a cost
of Rs. 14,000 crores, but as conceded  by a representative of the Minist ry before the Committee, money
to the tune of such huge proportions may not be available to the Ministr y. The Ministry accordingly
submitted a proposal to raise 18 million hectares of plantations at 9950 crores of rupees initially and this
too was further trimmed down to about 4000 crores of rupees both for Environment and Forest Sectors.
The Ministry was only given Rs. 525 crores for forestry and other related schemes and Rs. 345 crores
were earmarked by the Planning Co mmission for the State sector. This comes to  about 0.9% of the
National Plan \and whatever the Ministry gets, 70% goes towards plantation. Out of an amount o f
Rs.4082crores meant for forestry, both for the Centre and States, in the 8th Plan about Rs. 2800 crores is
meant for plantation and regeneration. This comes to about Rs. 560 crores annually, In the central sector
nine schemes are there, especially for afforestation, but the Committee fe els that in the State Sectors the
schemes for afforestation are not getting the priori ty and attention they sh ould and over the years the
allocation has been showi ng a declining trend. In 1993-94 it has co me down from Rs. 745  crores to Rs. 
676 crores.  
  
Forests are capital assets of the nation and the States do need cent ral budgetary support in this vital
sector. This central budgetary support can also be limited s ubstantially if the Stat es are encouraged to
generate their own funds by utilizi ng forest resources without, in a ny way, contributing to degradation.
In this context the Committee feels that the Ministry  of Environment and Forests can play an effective
role in impressing upon the States to draw upon the e xperience of the State of Madhya Pradesh, which
as told to the Committee is genera ting income from forests to the tune of 400 crore rupees whereas its
forest plan component is just of an amount of 50 crore rupees.  
  
11.  An important component of th e Ministry's Af'forestation Progr amme is tree plantation in a
conventional manner as also through modern methods of aeri al seeding and corelate d with this is the
need for extensive forest survey and strict moni toring of the prescribed targets, Committee has noted
that under the Inte grated Afforestation and Eco-Develo pment Pro jects Schemes. Ph ysical tar get fo r

1993-94 was 64,000 hectares and agains t this achievement urto end of January 1994 has been just
49,377 hectares. Similarly, the Aerial Seeding Scheme lus also failed to  achieve the stipulated physical
target of 30,000 hectares for 1993- 94, as the actual physical achievem ent is just 10,000 hectares. The 
position is not very flattering in respect of Grants-in-Ai d Schemes (for Volunt ary Agencies) whereby 
target achieved is 17 projects as against 35 projects.  
  
12.  The Committee is of the view that any shortf all in achieving the target s results in surrendering o f 
allocated amount unless of course the funds themselv es fall short and there is cost es calation, if the
projects go beyond the periods earmar ked for their comple tion. As' regards Aerial Seeding Scheme it 
was submitted before the Committee that the result s achieved under this sche me have not been that
much satisfactory for various reasons such as lack of interest on the part of some States, non-checking of 
grazing and resistance from the people engaged in making soil fit for seeding because they do not have
employment round the year. Nevertheless, the Minist ry is in the process of  identifying areas like
Chambal ravines of D.P. and M.P.  to bring them under Aerial Seeding Scheme . The Committee feels
that there has not been any major R&D effort on the pa rt of the Ministry in th e field of Aerial Seeding
and whole approach is of  a lackadaisical nature. The Committee,  therefore, urges upon the Ministry to
strengthen R&D in this vital sector to make the Aerial Seeding Scheme more viable and meaningful.  
  
13.  It is of utmost importance that monitoring and evaluation aspects of prescribed targets are taken due
care of and mechanism provided ther efore is suitably strengthened. In this context, the Committee has
observed that in the budge tary estimates for 1994-95 the Plan outlay for monitoring and evaluation o f
schemes formulated under the National Afforestation and Eco Development  Programme (NAEP) has 
been reduced from Rs. 1.5 crore during the previous ye ar to Rs. 75 lakhs. Similarly to carry out such an
important activity as the Forest su rvey, the Ministry has been deferr ing purchase of Digital Cartography
System for the last three years consecutively notwithstanding the fact that allocations therefor have been
made each year in the budgetary system. The explanat ion given by the Ministry is that to operate the
computers at light work stations, the software which is needed is of three kinds and these three kinds
have come up with new versions and now the Technical Evaluation Committee has examined the matter
threadbare and formulated its recommendations. On th at basis the Ministry hopes to acquire the Digital
Cartography System during 1994-95. Sin ce the Ministry proposes to acqui re equipment such as Digital 
Cartography System and other softwares, the Plan outlay for Survey  and Utilisation of Forest Resources
has come down from Rs. 8.5 crores in 1993-94 to Rs. 3.8 crores in 1994-95 and once this equipment is 
acquired, the Ministry may not need any extra money for forest survey etc. In response to a specific
query from the Committee as to wh ether there would be any cost ascalation in purchasing Digital
Cartography System in view of the fact that it has not been acquired by the Ministry despite provision of
budgetary allocation consecutively fo r three years, it was explained th at there will not be any cost
escalation because customs duty has been reduced recently. The Committee was, however, not informed
whether there would be any cost escalation in real  terms in the purchase of the equipment from the
manufacturing country.  
14. Another point raised was what the Ministry wa s doing to prevent deforestation. The submission o f
the Ministry was that during 1980s , 40,000 hectares of land was be ing lost every year, but with
increased Plan allocation, and financial assistance to  the tune of about Rs. 100 crores each year, the
Ministry has been able to contain deforestation to a great extent. The Ministry has been assisting people
to undertake plantation in private lands, Government  Wasteland, etc. and the target is to cover 800
million hectares of land. Seedlings worth Rs. 135 cror es are being distributed all over India at a very
nominal cost and the people are being imparted education in respect of planting the seedlings. Besides, it
is being impressed upon the Planning Commission and the Urban Development Ministry not to sanction
any Plans without considering various aspects of urban forestry.  
  
15.  The efforts of the Central and State Governme nts at afforestation, prev enting deforestation and
extending forest area b y developing wastelands cannot succeed unl ess the critical area of rava ging fires
Page 7 of 149th Report Of Committee On Science And Technology, Environment And forests
7/16/2008http://10.21.217.2/book2/reports/science/9threport.htm

in the forests is tackled on a war footing. A major fire in a forest may cause devastation as recently
happened in the Nagarhole forests. Such fires virtually reduce to naught  years of effort s of Ministry o f
Environment and Forests and the State Forest Departments in just minutes. In the course of the evidence
of the Secretary and othe r officials of the Ministry taken by th e Committee it came to light that in
controlling fires the Mi nistry is still depending upon conventi onal methods such as collecting the
villagers and providing fire fighting tools to them to undertake, the gigantic task of controlling forest
fires. In the Budgetary estimates for 1994-95 a provision of  just 2 crores of rupees has been made fo r 
introduction of modern forest  fire control methods in the country. Even if it be  assumed that this outlay
will be further supplemented by State allocations, s till this amount looks ridi culous when we talk o f
introducing modern methods of fire control. It has come to the notice of the Committee that close on the
heels of a major fire in the Nagar hole forest, another devastating fire  has been caused in vast areas o f
Orissa's Simlipal Wildlife Sanc tuary which went on raging for over 15 days with 'still no signs of its
being controlled. On a total area of  2,200 sq. kms. of the sanctuary at  least 200 sq. kms. was reported to
be in the grip of fire and the loss was expected to run into millions of rup ees. The Committee feels that
forest wealth worth crores of rupees is lost in  fires and accordingly would like to impress upon the
Ministry to examin e whether it could not be worth spe nding a small amount  on employing modern
methods of fire control like sprayi ng chemicals with the help of aeropl anes as is being done in some o f
the advanced countries. Besides, the Committee re commends that law should be made more stringent
with deterrent penalties' for thos e who deliberately set the forest s on fire and cause huge losses o f
national wealth. 
  
16.  Project Tiger is an important Centrally Sponsored Programme in the area of wildlife protection
launched in April, 1973; and for this a budgetary dema nd of Rs. 7.70 crores in th e Plan sector has been
made for 1994-95. This project has now been over 20 years old but the Committee feels that the basic 
objectives of this project have not been achieved in as much as that tiger population in the country has
registered a decline, poaching still continues in menacing proportions and the habitat for tigers seems to
have shrunk in area. The Committe e recommends that an evaluation of  the entire project be undertaken
by a high powered body to make it more meaningful and result-oriented.  
  
Major Head '343S'-Ecology and Environment  
  
            In the Budget outlay for 1994-95 a sum of Rs. 150.74 crores for the Plan sector and Rs. 38.80 
crores for the Non-plan sector has been earmarked. A comparison of these figures with the figures of the
previous year (1993-94) would reve al that there is just an incr ease of Rs. 2.41 crores in the Plan
component whereas there is a decr ease of Rs. 4.47 crores in the Non- plan component. In other words, 
the Plan outlay for 1994-95 in resp ect of ecology and environment is more or less corresponding to the
figures of the previous year. In the sub-head 'C.1 Surveys' under the majo r head of 'Ecology and 
Environment' the Non-plan component for the succe ssive three years has been  more than the Plan 
component, almost double. Confronted on this point, the explanatio n given by the Ministry is that Non-
plan expenditure reflects expenditu re on ongoing activities and Plan expenditure is the expenditure
proposed to be incurred on additi onal activities during a Plan peri od as per approval by the Planning
Commission. Moreover, the expenditure on establishm ent and on maintenance of assets created during
any Plan period are require d to be met out of Non- plan budget in the years subsequent to the Plan 
period. On the basis of the summary of Ministry's activities in the Environmental and Ecology sectors as
given in the Performance Budget, the Committee has come to the view that while these areas ·are 
engaging the attention of the Minist ry, the allocation in real terms do not reflect the magnitude of the
problem. Only a meagre allocation of Rs. 3 crores has been provide d for promotion of common effluent
treatment plants and that too unde r externally aided schemes. The Committee was surprised that even in
this area the progress is very slow and not much headway has been ma de, with the allocated amounts
practically lying unutilised. TheCommit tee feels that the Ministry shou ld initiate more concerted action
to motivate lar ger number of industrial units to go in for effluent treatment plants in lar ger national
Page 8 of 149th Report Of Committee On Science And Technology, Environment And forests
7/16/2008http://10.21.217.2/book2/reports/science/9threport.htm

interest of pollution control.  
  
18.   Though an allocation of Rs. 50.33 crores (both Plan and Non-plan) has been sought by the Ministry 
for prevention of air and water pollution during the year 1994-95, a perusal of the schemes in this area 
does not indicate that any major pr oject is on the anvil to meet the increasing challenge of the
environmental degradation. Th e projected assistance for abatement of pollution is just to the tune of 2
crores and similarly the amount ea rmarked for Hazardous Substance Ma nagement is just 3 crores o f
rupees. There is a need to strengthen the pollution fi ghting agencies which can be achieved only if there
is integrated action bot h by the Central and State Government . The State Governments are perhaps
unable to get actively involved in th is area because either  they are not in a pos ition to give matching
grants or lack pr oper motivation. Most of the schemes launched or contem plated by the Ministry o f
Environment and Forests such as Paryavaran Sudhar Pariyojna are of a peripheral nature and do not
strike at the root of th e problem. The idea behind setting up one Paryavaran Vahini for each identified
district with a view to create environmental awareness and involvement of people through active
participation, reporting of illegal  acts pertaining to forests, wild life, pollution and environmental
degradation is no doubt good, but there a ppear to be many pitfalls in the scheme which is mainly to be
administered through the District Co llectors who are supposed to take  action on the complaints of the
Members of the Vahini. There is an apprehension th at the persons brought on these Vahinis may not be
right sort of persons and the gr ant of Rs. 200 per month to each  Member given through the State
Gove7"nments may be poc keted by the persons who are not doi ng any' worthwhile  service. The
Committee, therefore, feels that while the Paryavaran Vahini Scheme  should be contined  and adequate
funds be made available therefor, there should be strict monitoring in respect of performance of these
Vahinis.  
  
19.   The Committee has observed that quite a substantial outlay of Rs. 350 crores has been provided for
in the Eighth Plan period for Ganga  Action Plan which involves prev ention of pollution of riverGanga
and National River Acti on Plan. However, in view of some dela ys in respect of some schemes relating
to Ganga Action Plan there have been cost overruns. In  the course of the oral evidence of the Secretary
and other officials of the Ministry, the Committee was apprised that the Ganga Action Plan is beset with
problems. For example, in respect  of the Sewage Treatment Plants  at Naini near Allahabad and at
Kanpur, the job is entrusted to a firm which has no t been able to push it through. The problem has been
solved as it has been decided that the work can be completed through other agencies. A point was raised
that frequent power failur es virtually make a sewage  treatment plant inoperationa l as a result of which
over flows are caused in the plants and the polluted water goes into the river defeating in the process the
very objective of the Ganga Action Plan. The Project Direct or of the Ganga Acti on Plan clarified that
there was of course, problem of power failure and the matter has been taken up with the Government o f
Uttar Pradesh .at various levels to ensure unint errupted power supply to the pumping stations. A
Steering Committee has been const ituted for the purpose of finding la sting solution to the problem and
the Governments of Uttar Pradesh a nd Bihar have given posi tive assurances that efforts will be made to
maintain regular power supply to the pumping stations. The Committee feels th at since Ganga Action
Plan is a Centrally Sponsored Sc heme, with Phase I thereof bei ng totally funded by the Central
Government, due emphasis should be laid on infrastructural facilities sothat the Plan makes unhindered
progress without being subject to handicaps of thenature     power failures.  
  
General Observations/Recommendations  
  
20. The Committee feels that in  order to fulfill the task s expected of the Ministry  it is necessary to have
technical personnel with the appropriate experience at the highest level of administration in the Ministry
rather than operate it largely as an administrative Ministry. This Ministry by itse1f cannot be expected to
perform all the major tasks relating to environment a nd forestry, even with th e assistance of related
agencies of the State Government s. The role of the Ministr y is to perform promotional and catal ytic
Page 9 of 149th Report Of Committee On Science And Technology, Environment And forests
7/16/2008http://10.21.217.2/book2/reports/science/9threport.htm

activities that show the way for society to implement meaningful pr ogrammes. For this it is necessary
that the Ministry concerns itself significantly with research and development that will enable it to evolve
practical low cost solutions. This does not appear to be apparent in the perfor mance of the Ministry and
the actuals of the Budget.  
  
21.  The Committee feels that the Mi nistry is engaged in far too ma ny schemes over which the financial
allocations are distributed, this probably leads to sub critical efforts in various  areas. The Committee is
of the view that in the manner in which the progr ammes and activities of the Ministry have been
formulated and are being implemented; there is not any integrated thrust in the direction of sub-stainable 
development.  In this, they will have work out an integrated mix of regulatory & promotional measures,
awareness building in education and close institutional tie-ups with the multiple agencies concerned 
with developmental tasks.

R E P O R T
 
      The Ministry of Environment and Forests is entrusted with the responsibility of planning, promotion and coordination of environment and
 forestry programmes. The activities of the Ministry include conservation and control of pollution, afforestation and regeneration of forests in
 degraded areas, protection and conservation of forests, wildlife and protection of environment.  The tasks are sought to be achieved through
 environmental impact assessment, eco-regeneration, assistance to organisations implementing environmental and forestry programmes, enactment
 of environmental legislation, formulation of environmental policies, promotion of environmental and forestry research, extension, education and
 training to augment the requisite manpower, dissemination of environmental awareness among all sectors of the country’s population.  The
 activities of the Ministry are divided in four major sectors, i.e.
1.       Environment;
2.       National River Conservation Directorate;
3.       Forests and Wildlife; and
4.       National Afforestation and Eco-Development Board.
BUDGETARY ALLOCATION FOR THE YEAR   2001-2002
2.   The Annual Plan 2001-2002 of the Ministry provides for an outlay of Rs.800.00 crore. This includes Rs.80.00 crore earmarked for North
 Eastern States & Sikkim. Out of this, Rs.40.00 crore are for Capital expenditure. Details of outlays, sector-wise, for the current year as also the last

NATIONAL RIVER CONSERVATION PLAN INCLUDING GANGA ACTION PLAN
10.  The Secretary informed the Committee that the Ganga Action Plan (GAP)  referred to in the Comptroller and Auditor General’s Report for the
 year ending March,2000 includes works under GAP Phase-I and Phase-II . The GAP Phase-I, which was started in 1985, has been declared
 completed as on 31.03.2000.  Although two schemes of sewage treatment plants in Bihar are yet to be completed.  The total expenditure incurred
 on this plan is Rs. 452 crore. Pollution abatement works in 25 towns in the States of UP, Bihar and West Bengal have been taken up under    Phase-
I. Under this plan, a capacity of 835 million litres per day (mld) has been created against the target of 873 mld. The total estimated sewage in 1985
 was 1340 mld. Thus, pollution load treated in terms of pollution level of 1985 is about 65%, but in terms of the present pollution level, it would
 amount to about 35% only. Certain problems of operation & maintenance of assets created under GAP Phase I have emerged in Bihar and to some
 extent in Uttar Pradesh. The matter was being constantly pursued with the State Governments concerned at the highest level. These were the major
 reasons for a lower visibility of impact of GAP Phase I on the water quality of river Ganga. However, the water quality monitoring results
 indicated that wherever the pollution abatement works have been commissioned and made functional, the river water quality has shown
 improvement. For example, in 1986 the biochemical oxygen demand (BOD) ranged from  5.5 to 15.5 mg/l in the stretch from Kannauj to Varanasi
 whereas the BOD in this stretch ranged from 1.8 to 6.5 mg/l in 1999.
10.1 As for the GAP Phase II, the programme was approved in 3 stages from 1993 to 1996. A total capacity of about 1861 mld of sewage treatment
 along with allied works was to be created under this Plan. The works of Yamuna Action Plan under GAP Phase II in Haryana ( 12 towns), U.P. (8
 towns) and Delhi were in an advanced stage of completion.
10.2   The Committee observes that for any plan or programme regarding cleansing of rivers of such a magnitude as Ganga, to succeed, it is
 necessary to have a meticulous planning.  Any delay in its execution is bound to result in the plan going awry.  More so, because the parameters
 regarding the size of the population and the extent of urbanization etc., which would have been taken into account at the stage of planning, are
 subject to rapid changes in a country like India.  Hence, timely execution is crucial for such programmes or else we would be back to square one.
10.3 At the same time it is necessary to see whether any alternative effective indigenous technologies can be advantageously used instead of
 draining out vast sums from national exchequer for which no audit may be possible.
10.4 The Committee has been given to understand that a team of experts from Varanasi has devised a method to rid the Ganga of a big chunk of its
 pollutant load, using the inherent energy of the flowing waters and the sun and the filtering properties of the riverbed.
10.5   Banaras Hindu University’s (BHU) Ganga Laboratory has developed the “three gradient theory”, using the river’s sand bed, solar energy and
 the kinetic energy of the water that could prove a vital pollution management tool in cities located along the country’s rivers that are struggling to
 contain water pollution.
10.6   The Committee understands that the system basically filters the inorganic, organic and microbiological pollutant load of the river – usually
 left untreated by sewage treatment plants (STPs) – through the sand piled up on the concave bank or downstream and upstreamofthecity.
 10.7  “The polluted water first flows out of a trickling box – which is a large filter comprising sand and stone layers and then the sand bed.  It then
 mingles with the high velocity zone in the river for a natural course of flow again”.  The problem of pollution is acute between December and July,
 which is the dry season, when the river level falls below 65 meters and the dissolved oxygen also decreases.  But this energizes the sand bed as
 solar radiation converts it into a hot plate to treat a higher quantum of inorganic and microbiological waste.
10.8  The Secretary also apprised the Committee the reasons for delayed implementation of GAP Phase II  which are as under:-
(i)
                    The scheme of National River Conservation Plan of which GAP Phase II is a part, was originally envisaged on 50:50 cost sharing basis between Centre and States.
 However, in view of the difficulties of the State Governments in bringing their 50%  share,  the National River Conservation Authority under the Chairmanship of Prime
 Minister at its 9th Meeting held in July, 1997 converted the scheme into a 100% Centrally Funded Scheme. But the Cabinet approval to this decision could be obtained
 only in November, 1998. During the intervening period of 16 months, the States were not providing their share in anticipation that the scheme would become 100%
 Centrally funded. As a result, the progress of the scheme became very slow.
 (ii)       The convention technologies proposed earlier did not address the problem of bacterial pollution fully. In order to address this issue, a decision was taken in July, 1999 to
 adopt oxidation pond based sewage treatment in all the places. These ponds, although requiring large areas of land were capable of reducing fecal coliform suitably. The
 State Governments could not provided such areas of land in larger towns which account for a major chunk of the capital cost. As a result, the progress of work was
 extremely slow for nearly 18 months.
(iii)
                  Until 1999-2000, grants were released to the State Governments. Transfer of such grants to the implementing agencies were invariably delayed in almost all the States
 for a period ranging from 6-9 months affecting the progress of work adversely.
(iv)                 The quality of preparation of Detailed Project Reports was not up to the mark from a number of States which resulted in significant delays.
(v)                  There were delays in land acquisition.
(vi)                 Decision was taken by the Ministry not to release funds for GAP Phase II in Bihar because the operation and maintenance of assets created under GAP Phase I was not
 satisfactory.
10.9   The Ministry was of the view that most of these bottlenecks have now been resolved and the plan was targeted for completion by 2005. The
 impact of the Action Plan on the improvement of water quality of Ganga and its tributaries can be expected only after its completion.
10.10The Committee observes that the Ganga Action Plan, launched in 1985, with the objective of bringing water quality of  river Ganga and  its

YAMUNA ACTION PLAN
11.  About 1.3 billion litres of untreated sewage is discharged into the river Yamuna in Delhi everyday. This has been revealed by a joint inspection
 report of the Central Pollution Control Board of the Ministry of Environment and Forests and Central Public Health and Environmental
 Engineering Organisation of the Ministry of Urban Development.
11.1 The Yamuna Action Plan was approved by the Government in April 1993 with an approved cost of Rs.509.54 crore. Under this Plan, works
 have been taken up in 21 towns out of which 8 towns are in Uttar Pradesh and 12 towns in Haryana besides Delhi. The Plan includes such works as
 interception & diversion of sewage, sewage treatment plants, low cost toilets, crematoria and river front development. So far, an expenditure of
 Rs.453 crore has been incurred on this Plan. The Delhi component of Yamuna Action Plan was small comprising 2 sewage treatment plants each of
 10 million litres per day capacity and one electric crematorium.
11.2 The Government of National Capital Territory of Delhi was implementing the major part of pollution abatement programme of Yamuna out of
 their own plan funds. 14 additional sewage treatment plants along with allied works are to be constructed under the programme. Out of these, 9
 treatment plants have already been completed and another 5 would be completed by the year 2003. Besides, 15 common effluent treatment plants
 were also to be constructed in order to treat industrial effluents emanating from 21 industrial estates of Delhi. This Project was under
 implementation and would be completed by December 2002.  A number of steps have been taken
by the Government of National Capital Territory of Delhi under the directions of the Supreme Court to close down polluting industries. In pursuance of the directions of a High Powered
 Committee set up under the chairmanship of Member (environment), Planning Commission on minimum flow in river Yamuna, all the riparian states except Delhi have started releasing
 their respective share of water for maintaining 10 cusecs of minimum flow in Yamuna along Delhi. The quality of river water and underground water in the area is expected to improve
 only after all the common effluent treatment plants and sewage treatment plants have been constructed & commissioned and pollution from other industries would effectively be
 monitored and controlled.
11.1     In  Delhi,  out of  16 proposed Sewage Treatment Plants (STPs) along the banks of the  Yamuna, 8 have been completed while 5 were operating. The Committee is
 constrained to observe that despite the Supreme Court orders in  1995  for setting up of STPs, number of treatment plants have not been established. The Committee has been given
 to understand that out of 22 drains discharging effluents into the Yamuna, 20 have not met the water quality standard. Rather the quality of the river water has deteriorated because of
 continuous discharge of domestic and industrial effluents into the river.  It has been further stated that the dissolved oxygen in the river water was nil while the river should contain
 minimum 4 mg/l of dissolved oxygen. The river has 41 mg/l of Biological Oxygen Demand(BoD), which is much higher than the prescribed limit, of minimum 3mg/l.
11.2     The Committee is also of the view that the Ministry of Environment & Forests  in coordination with the State Governments of Uttar Pradesh, Haryana and Delhi should  plan out
 a strategy for augmentation of water resources in the upper stretches of Yamuna and for conserving water both in domestic and irrigation use.

 much still to be done in this area as the phenomenon of cutting of trees, removal of precious timber and mysterious forest fires continues unabated.  The problem cannot be overcome
 unless a consciousness is built among the people that the forests belong to them and they belong to the forests and the feeling of alienation among the tribals and local population
 goes.  The Committee feels that the local population (including tribals) residing in the forest areas should be actively associated with the management of forests and  allowed to share
 the usufructs, without in any way compromising on the preservation of our national forests. If this happens, many of the ills currently afflicting our forests will disappear.  The Ministry
 should devise steps to inculcate among them, a sense of belonging and purpose about the forests. The people performing outstanding work in their area should be suitably rewarded
 and honoured at the appropriate forum.
CONSERVATION AND DEVELOPMENT OF NON-TIMBER FOREST PRODUCE
19.  The centrally sponsored scheme 'Conservation and Development of Non-Timber Forest Produce (NTFP) including Medicinal Plants' has been
 under implementation since 1988- 89. Plantation of NTFPs including medicinal species is promoted under the scheme. 75 projects have been
 sanctioned so far in the Ninth Plan to all States with a total outlay of Rs.99.68 crore. Since 2000-01, special emphasis was also being given for
 rearing of medicinal and bamboo plantations by sanctioning projects under the scheme exclusively for this purpose. An allocation of Rs.22.50
 crore (Rs.16.50 crore for other states + Rs.6.00 crore for N.E. States) has been made for 2001-2002. The committed liabilities in 2001-02 for the
 projects sanctioned so far amount to Rs.23.88 crore.
20.  The Committee observes that it is necessary to diversify the programme under “Conservation and Development of Non-Timber Forest Produce
 (NTFP) including Medicinal Plants”.  More areas needs to be identified for rearing of medicinal and bamboo plantations and steps  taken to carry
 out conservation of medicinal plants found in the forest and protected areas.
INTEGRATED AFFORESTATION AND ECO-DEVELOPMENT PROJECTS
21.  Implementation of afforestation activities in the States through Forest Development Agencies (FDAS) was contemplated on pilot basis during
 2000-01 and 2001-02 to enhance people's participation  in  the  afforestation   programmes  and also  to  accelerate the flow of funds to  the field
 level agencies under the Budgetary Allocation for the Projects Scheme (Central Sector Component) was Rs.1.00 crore in March 2000.   It was  also
  considered  desirable  to  reduce the
number of schemes being operated by the Ministry in the tenth plan by seeking to converge these schemes appropriately.
21.1 Guidelines for the establishment and operation of Forest Development Agencies, on the pattern of DRDAS, were prepared in consultation with
 the State Forest Departments.  The FDAs comprising representation form the local forest protection committees, concerned developmental
 departments, etc were expected to set themselves registered under the Societies' Registration Act. The agencies were chaired by territorial/wildlife
 conservators of forests, territorial/wildlife DFO as member secretary. The FDAs have since been set up in 20 States. In anticipation of the
 establishment of FDAs, and the promotion of afforestation activities in States through these agencies, allocation under the central sector of the
 above scheme was fixed at Rs. 10.70 crore for 2000-01 at the RE stage. 51 projects have been received from 20 States, of which 11 projects have
 been sanctioned to 5 States so far with an outlay of Rs.23.29 crore for the Ninth Plan.  The amount released in the current financial year (2000-
2001) being Rs.10.35 crore. The remaining projects and the new projects expected to be received from other States, are proposed to be sanctioned
 in the next financial year (2001-2002) year keeping in view the regional distribution.  An allocation of Rs.30 crore has been proposed under the
 scheme for 2001-02 for this purpose.

            RED OIL PALM PROJECT-ANDAMAN & NICOBAR ISLANDS FOREST & PLANTATION DEVELOPMENT
 CORPORATION LIMITED
24.During its visit to Andaman & Nicobar Islands the Committee was informed that in order to increase the availability of edible oil in the country, the Government of India decided to
 take up a Red Oil Palm Plantation Project (ROP) in Andamans which is agro climatically similar to Malaysia and Indonesia.  The project was accordingly sanctioned for raising Red Oil
 Palm in 2400 ha. and the project was entrusted to Andaman & Nicobar Islands Forest & Plantation Development Corporation Limited. An area of about 1593 ha has been brought under
 Red Oil Palm cultivation till 1985. In the year 1984 an expert Committee appointed by the Andaman & Nicobar Administration identified about 68,000 ha. of area suitable for Red Oil
 Palm
 cultivation. In view of adverse impact  on  the local  ecology perceived due to  monoculture of  Red Oil Palm
plantations the Government of India put a ban on further plantation of Red Oil Palm from 1986.  The project was thus stopped halfway. Various Project constraints cited were as under:-
 
(a)  Ban imposed by the Government of India in 1986 on further extension of the project;
 
(b)  Ban confirmed by the Island Development Authority in 1994;
 
(c)  Existing size of Plantation in 1593 ha. of land was unviable;
 
(d)  Unviable size of the project would require low investments and hence low productivity and
 
(e)  Large import of edible oils due to import duties resulting in decline in prices.
 
25.1 The Island Development Authority commissioned the Central Agricultural Research Institute(CARI), Port Blair to conduct a study on the
 impact of Red Oil Palm Cultivation on the local ecology in the year 1987.  The Report of CARI, was published in 1996.  According to the report
 cultivation of Red Oil Palm has no significant adverse impact on the local ecosystem. The Report further stated that Little Andaman Island was
 most suitable agro-climatically for cultivation of Red Oil Palm.
26.The Committee notes that on the basis of the Report submitted by the Central Agricultural Research Institute(CARI), Port Blair which conducted a study on the impact of Red Oil Palm
 Cultivation on the local ecology, there has not been any significant adverse impact on the ecology of the Islands.  The report has also pointed out that Little Andaman Island was most
 suitable agro-climatically for cultivation of Red Oil Palm.  The Committee therefore recommends that the Ministry of Environment & Forests should go ahead with the plantation/cultivation
 of Red Oil Palm for extension to 2,400 ha. which was originally sanctioned in 1979 and thereafter to 5,000 ha. so that a full fledged refinery unit could be established in Andaman &
 Nicobar Islands and the Project completed.  This would also provide succour to Andaman & Nicobar Islands Forest & Plantation Development Corporation Ltd., which at present is a
 venture, incurring losses.
27.After considering the Demands for Grants of the Ministry of Environment & Forests and assessing the progress of various programmes and projects administered by it, the Committee
 recommends that the Demands for Grants of Rs. 911.00 crores as sought by the Ministry of Environment & Forests for the year 2000-2001, under Demand No.21  may be approved.
RECOMMENDATIONS/OBSERVATIONS AT GLANCE
1.  The Committee observes that there is need for radical transformation in the attitude of officials concerned with inspection of the level of pollution generated by industrial units.  The
 attitude should be objective, need based and be guided by the need to control the pollution in the interest of present generation as well as posterity.
The Ministry should also prepare an Action Plan for already identified 24 critically polluted areas of the country for improvement of Environment.
 (Para 8.2)
2.   The Committee observes that the national emission standards  introduced by the government are nothing more than the minimum requirement. 
 In the interest of a clean environment there is perhaps a need for more rigid standards.  At the same time there is a need to consider whether any
 particular type of fuel or gas, say CNG alone will result in a clean and green environment.  Whether it is safe to use it?  A decision has to be taken,
 keeping in view the infrastructure available and without causing hardships to commuters and throwing the entire economy out of gear.
(Para 9.1)
3.The  Committee is aware that  the Ministry of Environment & Forests enjoys statutory powers under the Air Act, 1981 and the Environment (Protection) Act to enforce more stringent
 regime of standards with a view to control pollution.  The Ministry should have stepped in the current controversy with regard to use of CNG in public transport and help bring a
 harmonious solution to the problem with a view to control the pollution without causing hardships to any section of the society.
(Para 9.2)
 
4.   The Committee observes that for any plan or programme regarding cleansing of rivers of such a magnitude as Ganga, to succeed, it is necessary
 to have a meticulous planning.  Any delay in its execution is bound to result in the plan going awry.  More so, because the parameters regarding the
 size of the population and the extent of urbanization etc., which would have been taken into account at the stage of planning are subject to rapid
 changes in a country like India.  Hence, timely execution is crucial for such programmes or else we would be back to square one.
(Para 10.2)

6.   The Committee has been given to understand that a team of experts from Varanasi has devised a method to rid the Ganga of a big chunk of its
 pollutant load, using the inherent energy of the flowing waters and the sun and the filtering properties of the riverbed.
(Para 10.4)
 
7.   Banaras Hindu University’s (BHU) Ganga Laboratory has developed the “three gradient theory”, using the river’s sand bed, solar energy and
 the kinetic energy of the water that could prove a vital pollution management tool in cities located along the country’s rivers that are struggling to
 contain water pollution.
(Para 10.5)
 
8.   The Committee understands that the system basically filters the inorganic, organic and microbiological pollutant load of the river – usually left
 untreated by sewage treatment plants (STPs) – through the sand piled up on the concave bank or downstream and upstream of the city.
(Para 10.6)
9.
  “The polluted water first flows out of a trickling box – which is a large filter comprising sand and stone layers and then the sand bed.  It then mingles with the high velocity zone in
 the river for a natural course of flow again”.  The problem of pollution is acute between December and July, which is the dry season, when the river level falls below 65 meters and
 the dissolved oxygen also decreases.  But this energizes the sand bed as solar radiation converts it into a hot plate to treat a higher quantum of inorganic and microbiological waste.
(Para 10.7)
10.  The Committee observes that the Ganga Action Plan, launched in 1985, with the objective of bringing water quality of river Ganga and its
 tributaries to bathing levels , has not been able to achieve its objective till date. GAP Phase-I of the plan is not yet fully complete, even after delay
 of over 10 years. GAP Phase-II is also far behind schedule, and is due to end in December 2001. There are reports of creation of only 13.7% of the
 targeted sewage treatment capacity so far. The assets created under the Scheme suffered serious impairment and often closure particularly in Bihar
 and Uttar Pradesh because of technical flaws in design, problems in land acquisition, contract mismanagement, lack of maintenance and in general
 because of the lackadaisical attitude of the States and their implementing agencies. Technologies adopted by the National River Conservation
 Directorate (NRCD) for construction of Sewage Treatment Plants (STPs) were often questionable inasmuch as they could not adequately address
 the problem of reducing bacterial load in the river to the desired level.  The NRCD has abandoned the crucial activity of monitoring the water
 quality on river Ganga since September, 1999, reportedly for want of funds, and deprived itself of a key instrument of overall performance
 monitoring of the GAP. The Ministry of Environment and Forests needs to seriously review the implementation of the entire GAP and  evolve a
 financing arrangement whereby the States and the implementing agencies develop a more involved stake in creation of assets, their maintenance,
 and their functionality at all times; review and strengthen technical and administrative monitoring to ensure the value for money and assets created
 at great public expense; and facilitate competent technological support for optimum utilization of resources.
(Para 10.10)
 
11.The Committee observes that  Rs. 453 crore has been incurred on the  Plan so far as against the present approved  outlay of Rs. 509 crore and,  a capacity of only  646 mld has
 been commissioned and made functional with the remaining 90 mld capacity yet to be created. The Ministry should consider whether the indigenous methods suggested in the foregoing
 paragraphs could be tried without putting the Ganga Action Plan(GAP) out of gear.
(Para 10.11)
12.In  Delhi,  out of  16 proposed Sewage Treatment Plants (STPs) along the banks of the  Yamuna, 8 have been completed while 5 were operating. The Committee is constrained to
 observe that despite the Supreme Court orders in  1995  for setting up of STPs, number of treatment plants have not been established. The Committee has been given to understand
 that out of 22 drains discharging effluents into the Yamuna, 20 have not met the water quality standard. Rather the quality of the river water has deteriorated because of continuous
 discharge of domestic and industrial effluents into the river.  It has been further stated that the dissolved oxygen in the river water was nil while the river should contain minimum 4 mg/l
 of dissolved oxygen. The river has 41 mg/l of Biological Oxygen Demand(BoD), which is much higher than the prescribed limit, of minimum 3mg/l.
(Para 11.1)
 
13.The Committee is also of the view that the Ministry of Environment & Forests  in coordination with the State Governments of Uttar Pradesh, Haryana and Delhi should  plan out a
 strategy for augmentation of water resources in the upper stretches of Yamuna and for conserving water both in domestic and irrigation use.
