2, O2 and N2 levels in suitable polymeric film packages of desired permeability,
 this offered potential for long distance transportation including export of commercially important fruits such as mango,
 banana, litchi, pomegranate and strawberry as well as important vegetables.
 
38.       In the field of Nutrition supplements for school children, the Committee was informed that   CFTRI has
 developed two nutrients enriched snacks namely nutro biscuits and `suruchi meetha’, a burfi like product, both valuable
 as items for the mid-day meal schemes in schools. 
39.       The Committee reiterates its earlier recommendation that Department should take initiative to impress upon the
 State Governments concerned to waive sales and trade tax so that they reach the maximum population.  The Committee
 also feels that Indian exports especially edible products were not able to compete in international markets due to
 reasons such as unscientific packing which results in leakage or decay of products.  This could be prevented by
 applying best packaging methods.
The Committee appreciates the development of enriched snacks.  Efforts should be made to make available these snacks
 in the schools especially in areas where young students suffer from malnutrition as well as undernutrition.
 
ESTABLISHING GENETICALLY MODIFIED FOODS REFERAL FACILITY
40.       The Secretary informed the Committee that genetically engineered plants were being used for agronomical,
 nutritional, pharmaceutical and industrial applications. Although the use of Genetically Modified Organisms (GMOs)
 have the potential to offer real benefits in agricultural practice, the concerns being expressed were mainly on food
 quality, nutrition and health safety. In India several GM crops were under various stages of trials, such as Mustard,
 Tomato, Cabbage, Cauliflower, Cotton, Brinjal etc. So far there were no mandatory regulations for the addition of
 GMO in foods. Considering the large number of GMOs in development, combined with the increasing number of
 GMOs coming to the market, it has become necessary to establish a centre of excellence for testing of GM foods.  The
 Department therefore proposed to set up a state-of-art analytical laboratory for GMO testing,
41.       The Committee is of the view that adequate nutritional and toxicity studies should be conducted before the
 introduction of genetically modified foods in the market.  All the same it should be left to the farmers/users whether to
 adopt these keeping in view their tastes & preferences.
HEALTH CARE, DRUGS & PHARMACEUTICAL
42.       It has been stated that allergy related disorders such as asthma, rhinitis were on the rise in the developing
 countries especially in India due to diverse reasons. These diseases were acquiring dimension of an epidemic resulting
 in huge cost to public health and the economy. Asthma alone affects around 15% of the Indian population and in the
 four metropolis the incidence was placed as high as 30%. Genes and environment both played a very important role in
 this disease. Environment contributed in precipitating the disease due to the increased exposure to sensitizing allergens
 and reduced stimulation of the immune system.
In course of his presentation before the Committee the Secretary, DSIR informed that even though a clear understanding
 of the cellular and molecular mechanisms of this allergic disease was lacking, a group of scientists at the Indian
 Institute of Chemical Biology (a unit of CSIR), Kolkata, developed ASMON, an Aryurvedic medicine for the relief and
 remedy of Asthma (Bronchial), a plant based product known to be used by the people over the centuries.    Bronchial
 asthma patients of all ages could take this medicine safely.  Working on the inhibition of arachidonic acid oxidation by
 the preparation, it has been proposed as an anti-leukotriene asthma medicine.  Elaborating  Asmon, he  said, it inhibits
 oxidation of the arachidonic acid in an ex vivo
blood assay system wherein the blood cells were stimulated by calcium ionopher or known stimulator to enhance their
 oxidative activity.  Asmon helps to control asthma symptoms including the acute breathing problem arising out of
 bronchial asthma.  Asmon offers asthma patients a new treatment option to enhance the control of their asthma by
 inhibiting the oxidation of Arachidonic acid.
43.       The Secretary further stated that the technology had been transferred to M/s Herbo Chem Pvt. Ltd., Kolkata.

 20,000 bottles per day and 5,000 capsules per day which could not cope with the demand.  He accepted the fact that

 under an agreement gave the company exclusive rights.  The Secretary, however, informed that by July, 2002 a new
 plant would be angulated and a better version Asmon plus would also be launched.
44.       The Committee is happy to note the success of the herbal drug Asmon, but is constrained to observe that the

45.       This sector was served by four laboratories of CSIR viz Central Building Research Institute, Roorkee, Structural
 Engineering Research Centre, Madras, Structural Engineering Research Centre, Ghaziabad and Central Road Research
 Institute, New Delhi besides six other laboratories RRL Bhopal, Central Electrochemical Research Institute (CECRI),
 Central Glass and Ceramic Research Institute (CGCRI), NEERI, NGRI and Central Fuel Research Institute (CFRI),
 were also, to some extent engaged in research on the materials used in construction.  R&D programmes were being
 pursued on development of alternate building construction materials which utilized wastes, economise on energy and
 were eco-friendly; functional planning, construction, maintenance and rehabilitation of structures; and development of
 earthquake cyclone resistant structures.  The Committee has been informed that Fly ash bricks, tiles from ferro-chrome
 and other industrial wastes, multiblend cement formulations and polymer modified cementitious (PMC) tiles were in
 the process of being developed by the various laboratories of the Department. However, the Secretary, in the course of
 his presentation, before the Committee stated that there was no large scale usage of these fly ash bricks because
 conventional bricks were cheaper.
46.       The Committee observes that the quality and cost of construction were two important requisites in the field of
 construction. It is necessary to develop low cost alternatives which the private sector alone can do.  But the technology
 therefore had to be developed & transferred to that sector by our laboratories/institutions after extensive research.  The
 laboratories etc. should therefore be geared up to develop cheaper & durable alternatives.
 
INFORMATION DISSEMINATION & PRODUCTS
47.       Realising the inevitable explosive growth in the IT sector and knowledge based society powering the twenty first
 century, CSIR laboratories have evolved strategies to derive the benefits from the rich data and information base
 generated and from the updated domain knowledge they possessed.  A Unit for R&D on Information Products (URDIP)
 was setup specifically for this purpose.  Also Indian National Scientific Documentation Centre (INSDOC) & National
 Institute of Science Communication (NISCOM) have changed the mode of delivery of their services from the printed to
 the electronic / digital format.  A Unit for R&D on Information Products (URDIP) was setup at Pune to convert the
 dispersed and non-digital databases of CSIR to merchandisable electronic information products.  Gaining by the
 experience of turmeric & neem the emphasis was to first bring out in digital form, traditional knowledge in the health
 domain.  A multimedia laboratory has been established.   The unit has started its operation, from the new premises. It
 devised and put out a multimedia format in two CDs on ‘Health Heritage’ incorporating both traditional knowledge
 from Sanskrit classics and the modern information made available through systematic scientific and patent research. 
 Another CD titled ‘Patenstate’ was a data base of full text of CSIR patents granted between 1991-95.
48.       The Committee notes the development with satisfaction.

 Technology Management Education in India have been completed.
Studies on Technology Status of Vegetable Dyes Industries in the Country.  Technology status of Guar Gum based
 industries and Status of Technology Management Education in Select Countries were in progress.

52.       The National Information System for Science & Technology (NISSAT) commenced its operations in 1977 with
 the objective of organizing information support facilities for a customer base largely dominated by people engaged in
 research and academics.  In pursuance of the national efforts in liberalisation and globalization of the economy,
 NISSAT reoriented its programme activities in order to be useful to a wider base of clientele in diverse subjects. 
 Besides, establishing the internal linkages between the information industry, its promoters and users, NISSAT has been
 making efforts to establish a bridge between information resource developers and users in India and other countries.

 Dissemination.  It has established VIGYAN Server of Indian Science & Technology and initiated action for the

R E P O R T
            The Ministry of Environment & Forests is concerned with the planning, promotion and co-ordination of environment and
 forestry programmes in India. The important activities of the Ministry incorporate conservation and control of pollution, afforestation
 and regeneration of forests in degraded areas, protection and conservation of forests and wildlife and protection of environment.
 These tasks are sought to be achieved by the Ministry through environmental impact assessment, eco-regeneration, assistance to
 organizations implementing environmental and forestry programmes, enactment of environmental legislation, formulation of
 environmental policies, promotion of environmental and forestry research, extension, education and training to augment the requisite
 manpower, dissemination of environmental information international cooperation and creation of environmental awareness among all
 sectors of the country’s population. The major activities of the Ministry are spread over four major sectors, i.e.
(a)
    Environment;
(b)   National River Conservation Directorate;
(c)    Forests and Wildlife and
(d)   National Afforestation and Eco-Development Board.

MAJOR SCHEMES OF THE MINISTRY
WILD LIFE PROTECTION
8.         The Ministry in reply to a Question, apprised the Committee that “Poaching and illegal trade in wild animals”, has become a
 lucrative trade because of increasing demand for various wildlife products across our borders. The pecuniary gain from the illegal
 trade was very high. The prices fetched by some of the wildlife products in the clandestine international markets were as follows:
(i)         Tiger bone        - US $2425/Kg.
(ii)        Rhino horn        - US $1150/ Kg.
(iii)       Musk               - US $50,000/Kg.
(iv)       Ivory                - US $ 400/Kg.
8.1       There were reasons to believe that routes and conduits of illegal wildlife trade were largely the same as those for smuggling of
 narcotics, arms, gold and other commodities. The masterminds running these operations operate either from Metro cities or areas
 quite far from the forest areas.
8.2       During its visit to Andaman & Nicobar Islands the Committee was apprised of poaching and smuggling of sea cucumber and
 other marine products by Vessels from Myanmar, Indonesia, Thailand and other neighbouring countries. There were reports of large
 scale felling of trees in Diglipur and Mayabunder Islands by old revenue settlers and encroachers as well. One of the reasons
 attributed to this was existence of ineffective enforcement infrastructure. Therefore, the Committee recommends that the Ministry
 should create necessary enforcement infrastructure both within protected areas and outside protected areas to prevent poaching.
8.3       The Committee was apprised of various measures taken by the Central Government to control poaching and illegal trade in
 wild animals and its derivatives as follows:
(i)
      Central Bureau of Investigation have been empowered under the Wild Life (Protection) Act, 1972 to apprehend and
 prosecute wildlife offenders. Anti- poaching efforts were being coordinated with INTERPOL.
(ii)    Ministry of Home Affairs has written to all the State Governments to lend a helping hand to the field formations to curb

9.         The Committee believes that the “Wild Life (protection) Act, 1972”, is a comprehensive Act. The provisions regarding
 punishment for violation of the Act are quite stringent. However, these do not appear to have been enforced effectively because of
 the inadequacy of field formations both in number and in terms of efficiency in detection of wild life crime and successful
 prosecution. Intelligence gathering infrastructure is more or less absent. The problem appears to have been further compounded by
 the ban on filling of vacant posts and the tardy flow of funds to the field level.
9.1       The Committee recommends that the Ministry should take up immediate steps in co-ordination with various State
 Governments at the highest level to fill up all the vacant posts at the field level and provide the enforcement staff with adequate
 mobility, communications network and sophisticated arms.
9.2       The Committee notes with concern that a number of policy recommendations are yet to be considered by the Union
 Government.  For example, the recommendation of the Subramaniam Committee for the Prevention of Illegal Trade in Wildlife has
 been lying with the government since 1994.  The Ministry should examine the Report in right earnest and devise a policy for
 conservation –– both for scientific or participatory management.
Bt. COTTON  & ISSUES RELATED THERETO
10.       In India, Cotton was grown on approximately 9 million hectare of land, highest in the world, accounts for about 20% of the
 world acreage.  India stands 3
rd in the lint production, producing only 319 kg/ha lint yield compared to the world average of 603
 kg/ha.  Cotton is highly susceptible to insects and consumes over 50% of the total insecticides used in the country.  India spends
 nearly Rs.1,200 crores worth of pesticides for controlling various pests of cotton.  Approximately, 60-70% of the pesticides are used
 only for control of the dreaded pest namely bollworm against the world average of 30%.  It is estimated that in India about 20-30% of
 the productivity of cotton is lost due to the damage of insect pests.
10.1     In genetically engineered foods, genes from bacteria, viruses, other plants or animals are inserted into crops such as corn,
 canola, soyabeans, potatoes, tomatoes, squash, and papayas to achieve favourable characteristics including higher yield, faster
 ripening, pest control and herbicide tolerance.   Similarly,  Transgenic Bt. Cotton is a  technology that has been proposed as
an alternative to overcome the problem of bollworm, reduction in pesticide use and improving the environment.
10.2     A gene from the soil borne bacterium Bacillus thuringiensis   has been introduced into the cotton plant.  This gene encodes a
 protein, Cry1A (c)  that has specific insecticidal properties to control bollworms.  This gene was transformed into cotton plants by
 M/s. Monsanto, USA and M/s. Maharashtra Hybrid Seeds Co. Ltd. (Mahyco), Mumbai (in which Monsanto has a 26 per cent
 stake)  has introduced it into Indian cotton germplasm by traditional breeding methods.  This transgenic cotton on which cotton pests
 namely bollworm feeds, interferes with the digestive tract of insect and kills it.  The new plant has no effect on other insects or pests.
10.3     Studies like gene flow, aggressiveness and cross-ability with wild near relatives of cotton, conducted with transgenic cotton
 revealed that the possibility of gene flow in nature becomes negligible and therefore there is a least chance of effecting the
 biodiversity and less chance of possibilities of cross pollination in nature.  The toxicity and allerginicity studies conducted on birds,
 fish, mammals including ruminants (goats, cows and buffaloes) on Bt. Cotton established that it is as safe as non-Bt. cotton has no
 impact on non-target insects and on bio-flora.  The Bt. cotton hybrids were further characterized for the absence of the Terminator
 gene and confirmed that these hybrids are not having any terminator gene sequences.  Composition analysis of Bt. Cotton showed
 that it is comparable with non-Bt. cotton. Contained limited field studies and large sale field studies in farmers’ fields and also in
 ICAR system indicated that Bt. cotton showed distinct agronomic advantage over non-Bt. cotton.
10.4     The economic benefit of Bt. cotton is estimated to be substantial when compared to current practices of cotton cultivation. 
 Significantly higher benefits are expected to be derived from the yield savings of the Bt. cotton in addition to savings in the cost of
 pesticides.  The farmers are expected to gain 50% to 70% of the economic benefits generated from the technology. Small farmers are
 more likely to adopt this technology as they do not have to spray every 3 to 4 days and 20 to 25 times.
10.5     According to various News reports over 4,000 hectares in Gujarat, and 190 hectares in just one district of Andhra Pradesh,
 Karimnagar, are under Bt cotton production.  There are reports that the Karimnagar plantation is intended for seed production, which
 will be used for plantation in some 80,000 hectares next year in the Kharif season.
10.6     In India today, clearance of a GMO goes through two Committees: Review Committee on Genetic Manipulation (RCGM) of
 the DBT, and the Genetic Engineering Approval Committee (GEAC) of the Ministry of Environment & Forests.  On 26.3.2002, the
 GEAC of Ministry of Environment & Forests had examined the data generated on Bt. cotton and had cleared three Bt. cotton and
 hybrids for commercial cultivation with certain conditions.

OLIVE RIDLEY TURTLE AT GAHIRMATHA BEACH IN ORISSA
12.       The issue of large scale Olive Ridley Turtles being killed by the Fishing Trawlers has attracted the  attention  for   quite  
 sometime and the Committee   too  has  noted   with   concern.
According to various news reports, experts have long established that turtle excluder devices (TED) are the only known way to reduce
 turtle casualty.  A turtle excluder device is a simple grid like instrument made of steel, aluminum or iron.  It has interspaced bars and
 a flap made of net attached to it, which allows the turtle to escape, while allowing fish to pass through between the bars into the bag
 of the trawler net. 
13.       The Committee is of the view that the non-usage of TEDS is turning the Gahirmatha beach in Orissa into the largest graveyard
 for turtles. Although, the use of turtle excluder devices (TEDS) has been made mandatory in the State, but trawler operators continue
 to flout norms with impunity.  The Ministry of Environment & Forests should take-up this issue on priority basis in coordination with
 the State Governments and take steps to strictly enforce the usage of turtle excluder devices (TED).
TAJ PROTECTION MISSION
14.       The Committee was informed that there were ten ongoing schemes, which were to be completed during this year’s budgetary
 support of Rs. 25.00 crores but as the funds are provided by Union and State Government of Uttar Pradesh on matching basis i.e.
 50:50 basis, there exists every likelihood of delays in completion of Projects.
14.1     According to News reports, the Taj continues to reel under the onslaught of suspended particulate matter (SPM) and sulphur
 dioxide (SO2), despite the closure of polluting units in its vicinity from December 31, 2001,.  According to the latest data of the
 Archaeological Survey of India (ASI), the SPM was 286.3 microgrammes per cubic metre on December 10, 2001.  But on January 9,
 2002, even after the closure of all industries, the SPM level was as high as 522.8 microgrammes per cubic metre.  Likewise, the SO2

15.       The Committee is of the view that the levels of both the pollutants might not have come down due to the pollution load of the
 Mathura Oil Refinery.  The rise in SPM and SO2 levels has also been caused because of the heavy vehicles going via Agra.  The
 Ministry should also examine recommendations of the Vardarajan Committee, appointed by the Supreme Court to look into Taj
 pollution, which remain unimplemented while chalking out various programmes under the Taj Protection Mission.
VEHICULAR POLLUTION CONTROL MEASURES
16.       The Committee is aware that as regards the use of CNG as a transport fuel with special reference to public transport in the
 National Capital Region, the Supreme Court in continuation of its order dated 28
th July 1998 delivered a landmark ruling on April 5,
 2002, after an exhaustive deliberation with the parties concerned.  According to the order, all public transport vehicles would now
 run on CNG in Delhi.  Another marked difference was other polluted cities such as Lucknow, Pune and Jodhpur finding mention in
 the verdict, with the Supreme Court suggesting that they, too, switch over to CNG for running their public transport. The Court has
 chalked out a clear-cut strategy wherein 800 diesel buses would be phased out every month in the city from May 2002 onwards
 against a corresponding installed production capacity of 1100 CNG buses.
16.1     The apex court’s verdict is a sharp departure from its earlier approach of setting a deadline for the government and expecting it
 to comply with the order.  Emphasis was laid this time on making “public health”, the core issue through the application of the
 ‘precautionary principle’ and by getting into the ‘polluter pays’  principle.  The Supreme Court has also imposed
a stiff penalty on diesel bus operators who, in defiance of the Court’s earlier order, have continued to run their vehicles on the
 polluting fuel.  A fine of Rs.500 per bus per day was being charged from April 6 2002.  This will be hiked to Rs.1000 from May 6
 until there is a complete shift to CNG.  The Supreme Court has also slapped a penalty of Rs.20, 000 on the Union government for
 repeatedly seeking modification of its order.
16.2     The “polluter pays principle”, is adopted as an underlying economic code for environmental policy.  According to it the
 polluters were liable to take steps to prevent in advance, or at least reduce, any inconveniences rising from their activity.  They were
 also responsible for any damage they cause to the environment.  The principle fixes the accountability of industries for the pollution
 they generate.  It emphasizes the fact that the costs of measures to prevent, control and reduce damage resulting from pollution
 should be borne by the polluter.  The principle does not mean one can pay for pollution and purchase the environment.
17.       The Committee is of the view that the Ministry of Environment & Forests have adequate powers under section 5 of the Air
 Act, 1981, and the Environment (Protection) Act to enforce more stringent standards for pollution at hot spots.  Apart from the
 instance of 1997, when it notified the first ever fuel quality norms, the Ministry has never made its presence felt.  It has never
 discouraged the use of diesel by the Indian auto sector.  There has thus been no show of commitment or initiative on the part of the
 Ministry.
17.1     The Ministry of Environment & Forest’s 1997 white paper on pollution in Delhi is little more than a common position of all
 the other Union government agencies concerned, such as Ministry of Industry, Ministry of Surface Transport and Ministry of
 Petroleum and Natural gas.  It does nothing more to push for CNG than propose government tradition of making toothless but
 politically correct suggestions.

17.2     The Committee is of the view that Environmental regulation through Courts has serious drawbacks. Judicial intervention is
 most effective in correcting bureaucratic conduct when it is selective and surgical, but in significant environmental litigations such as
 the Ganga Pollution Case, the Vehicular Pollution Case and the Taj Trapezium Case the administrative agency – the Ministry of
 Environment & Forests has been reduced to preparing only knee-jerk responses to judicial orders. The Committee believes that
 despite more than a decade of judicial activism, there is no evidence to show that the Pollution Control Boards, Department of
 Forests or the Ministry have become institutionally stronger, or more capable of discharging their responsibilities today.         
17.3     The Committee is aware of the Supreme Court’s orders on April 5, 2002 regarding plying of all public transport vehicles on
 CNG in Delhi being implemented by concerned agencies but at the same time the Committee is constrained to note the sad plight of
 commuters who continue to suffer. As a result of the judicial pronouncement and the consequent steps taken by the Government, the
 commuters continue to suffer with no immediate steps in sight being taken by the government to address their problems.  On the
 other hand transporters seem to be bent upon to exploit them by over charging and making their journeys uncomfortable and costlier. 
 The Traffic Police as the Press reports suggest, are exploiting the situation by forcing the operators to grease their palm.  The
 Committee feels that the Apex Court should have foreseen these realities before pronouncing an order.
FOREST CONSERVATION, DEVELOPMENT & REGENERATION
18.       Members have raised the controls of large areas of densely forested regions in the country by Naxalites on more than one
 occasion in the Committee. In these forested areas, the state and forest administration dare not enter. Naxalites use the growing
 alienation of tribal people against forest laws to gain ground. They build check dams where governments cannot because of
 restrictive forest conservation laws. They secure tribal rights over non-timber forest produce and dispense quick justice — at
 gunpoint. There are also massive financial gains for the Naxals in looting state forests. Poachers to timber mafia and protection
 money from paper industry, all contribute to their "revolution". According to reports by ensuring people’s access to forest and
 distributing forestlands for cultivation, today Naxalites have established parallel governments and nearly 10.03million hectares (mha)
 of forests in the country are under the control of Naxalites.
18.1     According to the 1999 Forest Survey Report ,  over 0.4 mha of forests in the country were under encroachment — 60 per cent
 of which were in the Naxalite-affected areas and in  almost all the Naxalite-affected districts, forest loss has been attributed to
 encroachment due to ‘local disturbances’.
18.2     In a meeting with the Standing Committee on Developments of  Meghalaya Legislative Assembly the Committee was
 apprised of the imposition of   an interim ban on felling in forests on December 12, 1996. Having India’s one-fourth of forests, the
 seven states are worst affected as a large chunk of their population earns its livelihood from forests. The ban has come at a time when
 the region was losing 31,700 hectares every year, mostly due to the government and timber traders’ nexus. It also made the ban
 conditional: by putting in place a sustainable way of using the forests. The proposal makes sense for a region, where traditional
 village institutions control and manage 80 per cent of forests.  For a region that largely depends on forests for economic and
 livelihood survival, the ban has come short of a death sentence. The economic loss is unimaginable, particularly for poor forest
 dwellers that form a majority in the seven states — Arunachal Pradesh, Mizoram, Nagaland, Assam, Tripura, Manipur and
 Meghalaya.
18.3     The Supreme Court has observed that till date, a clear definition of forests is not given in the existing legal instruments —
 Forest Conservation Act (FCA), 1980, Forest Conservation (Amendment) Act, 1988, and the Indian Forest Act, 1927. Under Section
 2 of the FCA forests have been defined as "reserved forest, protected forest or any area recorded as forest in the government record".
 The court also stated that forest should be understood according to its dictionary meaning — "a large area of land thickly covered
 with trees, bushes, etc". Then it ordered every state to form an expert committee, which would identify forests, irrespective of class or
 ownership; all wood-based industries and assess the sustainability of forests. The ruling also reinforced the formulation of rules
 before any felling was resorted to. Though private plantations and social forestry programmes, were excluded from the ban in the
 first ruling, the court brought these areas in the ambit of the ban in its next ruling.
18.4     State governments have been slow in formulating the working plan, mandatory for carrying out felling and as a result only 14
 per cent of the plans have been completed in the last five years and some states still do not have a single working plan in place.
 Manipur and Mizoram did not have even a single working plan in place till October 2001. Similarly in Nagaland, where timber is the
 main source of livelihood for local people, the state formulated working plans for just 0.1 per cent of forests This is despite Ministry
 of Environment & Forests setting up a regional centre in Shillong for easy access.
18.5     The Supreme Court have not been happy the way governments were trying to frustrate the implementation of the ban. 
 Therefore on February 18, 2002, the Supreme Court slapped a fine of Rs.5,000 on the Union government for not framing a
 comprehensive scheme regarding forestland approved for deforestation. Similarly, state governments too were being pulled up for
 misguiding the court.
18.6     Another area of conflict is the Wildlife (Protection) Act of 1972, which also has attracted the attention of the Committee. The
 Act of 1972, amended in 1991, prohibits human intervention in national parks, and allows limited intervention in sanctuaries. There
 are about 550 of these today, covering more than 4.3 per cent of the country’s geographical area. The Wildlife (Protection) Act of
 1972 hangs like a Damocles’ sword for the thousands of people living in or around protected forests.  Some of the Communities
 living near the Protected areas and deprived of human intervention are shown here under in the Table (Table- 8).

18.7     Another area of conflict is in Gadchiroli district in the State of Maharashtra. The major cause of conflict in Gadchiroli is over
 “forest produce”. The Maharashtra government's ordinance, issued on 10 December, 1997, has made provisions for transfer of
 ownership of minor forest produce (MFP) to panchayats. But several impediments have been mentioned an accordance with the
 Indian Forest Act, 1927. These include exclusion of the ownership of land and trees in the panchayat areas, exclusion of national
 park and sanctuaries and adherence to the rules laid in the working plan. The exclusion of tendu and bamboo has become a highly
 emotive issue for the villagers.  Several villages have already stopped extraction activity even though they stand to lose wages, which
 they earn from extraction work. e.g. the case of Ballarpur Paper Mill which has already paid royalty to the government.
19.       The Committee is of the view that the Supreme Court order merely seeks to  enforce the law laid down by the government.
 Ban on felling of trees is permitted under the Forest Conservation Act, 1980 but only after a working plan has been approved by the
 Union Ministry of Environment and Forests.  However, hardly any state appears to have implemented the provision. The order was
 being misinterpreted to bureaucratise forests. Since the order asks for a clear definition and identification of forest, some state
 governments have taken this as an opportunity to gain control over large areas that remain ‘unclassified’  even  today in  the 
 Northeast.  Forest officials, who  wanted  to do away  with
‘unclassified’ forests, see this as a chance to alienate local people by claiming ownership, which were otherwise under the control of
 the community.
19.1     The Committee observes that forests in the country continue to be the victims of apathy and inadequate management in the
 country.  Besides, the categorisation of forests into reserved, protected and village forests, which are essentially administrative
 categories, does not help in their growth.  The “State of the Forest Report”, does not give a detailed classification of India’s forests,
 the percentage of natural or pristine and plantation areas, which would be of interest and use to both environmentalists and wood
 based industry. The neglect of forests has resulted into loss of produce with reported smuggling by mafias, fires – which are termed
 deliberate. This has affected their growth as it discourages participation of the people.  While tribals in some parts of the country
 have a right to enter the forests and take a part of the produce, mainly wood, for meeting their bonafide requirements, it appears to
 the Committee that this has not helped in the growth of forests because the denser the forest, the more is the alienation — tribal
 people are refused entry into forests; they cannot cultivate land they believe is theirs. It is simple. People want livelihood through
 forest but government wants control over forests.  The Committee therefore feels that it is time the forests are taken out completely
 from the bureaucratic control and managed by direct participation of the people preferably through cooperatives.  There is thus a need
 to take a dynamic initiative for the management of the forests so that the objectives of the forest policy could be met with direct
 involvement of the people in the management and growth of forests.
20.       The Committee was informed that people could collect Tendu leaves and minor forest produce for their livelihood under the
 State regulations in which they could sell some produce directly and some to the Government agencies. The people have been
 granted rights to collect minor forest produce from Scheduled Areas under Panchayat (Extension to Scheduled Area) Act, 1996. The
 Ministry of Environment & Forests has already written to the various State Governments to take necessary action in this regard.
21.       The Committee further observes that the Forest (Conservation) Act is only regulatory in nature and has enough flexibility to
 meet the development needs of the State Government.  Therefore, there is no need to amend the Forest (Conservation) Act. 
 However, there is a need to re-examine issues under the Indian Forest Act, 1927 so that it takes care of the definition of forests.
SUNDERBAN MANGROVES
22.       The Committee was informed that the “Sunderban Mangroves” are the most extensive mangroves in the country and form the
 largest single mangrove of the world.  The area occupies 1434 sq. kms, which includes 578 sq. kms of dense mangroves, and 856 sq.
 kms of sparse mangroves.  It occupies 44% of the total mangrove area of the country.   The salient features of the Sunderban
 biosphere reserve include:
(i)
                  It has the  largest floral and faunal diversity and tiger population.
(ii)                It is selected as a World Heritage Site and a Biosphere Reserve in the Global Network of UNESCO.
(iii)               It is the home of several endangered, threatened and endemic floral and faunal species and acts as a fish nursery and
 supports coastal fisheries along Bay of Bengal and Indian Ocean. It provides protection to the inland habitations
 against fury of cyclones and acts as a sink for the mega metropolitan pollutants.
22.1.    The Sunderbans is represented with 26 species of mangroves covering 14 genera and 11 families and 34 species of mangrove
 associates covering 28 genera and 18 families. 
22.2.    Taking into consideration the ecological and economic significance of mangroves in Sunderbans and the threats faced by these
 mangroves, Government  has identified this area for intensive conservation and management under the Scheme on Conservation and
 Management of Mangroves and Coral Reefs since 1987.  The main objectives of the management action plan for conservation of
 Sunderban mangroves include:

(i) Restoration of the unique mangrove ecosystem of sunderban and conservation of its biodiversity.
(ii)                Development of sustainable, economic, social activities of the population living in the Sunderban biosphere reserve
 so as to reduce pressure on the mangrove areas.
(iii)               Facilitate research, monitoring, education and training to perpetuate the achievements made and integrate the same
 with the management.
22.3     Under the “Scheme on Conservation and Management of Mangroves and Coral Reefs” the Ministry extends financial
 assistance to Government of West Bengal for conservation of mangroves in Sunderbans.  The Ministry considers management Action
 Plans prepared by the State Government.  The main activities include survey and demarcation, aforestation and regeneration of
 mangroves, protection measures, eco-development activities and educational awareness related to conservation of mangroves.  The
 Ministry has released an amount of Rs.220.37 lakhs to the Government of West Bengal under IXth Five Year Plan for
 implementation of management action plan on Sunderban mangroves. 
22.4     The Committee was apprised of the major threats to “Sunderban mangroves”, which include exploitation of the mangrove
 forests due to human pressure, conversion of mangrove areas for agricultural purposes, dwindling of fisheries and loss of flora and
 fauna including endangered species.  Lack of fresh water is another major problem  with extreme violent winds and erosion of banks
 which are unfavourable factors. The natural threats include acid sulphate soil, effect of pollution, sedimentation and erosion and
 embankment constructions. Another problem is the  trans-boundary migration of Tigers. 
23.       The Committee is of the view that the entire Sunderbans is one eco-system and for wild animals,  physical boundaries have no
 relevance.  The tigers move in their entire home range, irrespective of these boundaries.  If the food availability is improved and
 habitat is better managed, the home ranges get reduced and trans-boundary migration gets minimised.  However, in the interest of the
 long term conservation of Sunderbans, the Ministry of Environment & Forests should devise Management Plans which may involve
 joint effort of  India and Bangladesh. 
BIOMEDICAL WASTE MANAGEMENT
24.       The Committee was apprised of the inherent dangers in improper management of Bio-medical wastes and therefore the
 Committee impressed upon the need to promote awareness and train para- medical and supporting staff.
25.       The Committee recommends that the Ministry should co-ordinate with the State Governments / State Pollution Control Boards
 (SPCBs) to ensure that Bio-medical waste generating units are set up along with the treatment facilities and they obtain authorisation
 from the SPCBs.
JHUM/SHIFTING CULTIVATION
26.       The Secretary informed the Committee that as per estimates, about 10 million ha. of forest areas have been subjected to
 Jhum/Shifting cultivation. Shifting cultivation is practiced in tribal dominant areas mostly in the North-Eastern States where it
 accounts for most of the forest degradation. The increase in the population of Shifting Cultivators and declining productivity of forest
 soils have resulted in the Shifting Cultivation cycle shortening from about 20 years to 4 years. Such intense farming on poor quality
 soil has made the system ecologically fragile. The National Forestry Action Programme prepared for next 20 years clearly
 incorporates the objectives defined in the National Forest Policy, 1988 to control the Shifting Cultivation practice through  following
 measures:
·
        Alternative avenues of income
·        Suitably harmonised with the right land use practices
·        By propagating improved agricultural practices
·        Social forestry and energy plantations
27.       The Committee believes that the National Forest Action Programme in respect of shifting cultivation needs to be rationalised
 by Settled Cultivation with tree farming under various agro-forestry systems. Rationalisation of Shifting cultivation should be
 approached in a holistic manner, covering the socio-cultural and economic aspects and issues relating to the land tenure.

R E P O R T
 
      The Chairman, Rajya Sabha in pursuance of the rules relating to the Department-related Parliamentary Standing
 Committees, referred* the Water (Prevention & Control of Pollution) Cess (Amendment) Bill, 2000**, as introduced in the
 Lok Sabha on 15 th December, 2000 and pending therein, to the Standing Committee on Science & Technology,
 Environment & Forests for examination and Report.
2.   The Water (Prevention & Control of Pollution) Cess Act, 1977 provides for “the levy and collection of a cess on water
 consumed by persons carrying on certain industries and by local authorities, with a view to augment the resources of the
 Central Pollution Control Board and the State Pollution Control Boards for the prevention and control of water pollution
 which were constituted under the Water (Prevention & Control of Pollution) act, 1974”.  The existing rates of water cess
 were revised in 1991, because the responsibility and workload of the pollution control boards had increased considerably
 and the funds available with these Boards were not adequate for the overall commitments involving heavy financial
 liabilities. The Government disburses the water cess so collected to the pollution control boards/committees according to
 criteria prescribed by the Government.
3.   The Water Cess Act, 1974 lists the rates of cess applicable for various types of water consumption in Schedule II.  This
 Schedule was amended in 1991 affecting an increase in the rates.  The Schedule– II is again being amended by the current
 amendment to augment further the resources of the Boards. The proposal is to further enhance the existing cess rates
 approximately three fold.
4.   Prior to this amendment, the Water (Prevention & Control of Pollution) Cess (Amendment) Bill, 1995 was introduced in
 the Parliament on 1
st June 1995 to enhance the cess rates.  The Bill was referred to the Department related Parliament
 Standing Committee on Science and Technology, Environment and Technology for review.  The Committee after
 discussing with various concerned agencies recommended the following:
(i)                  Cess on water used for domestic purposes need not be increased.
(ii)                Cess need not be levied on the use of water by hydel power generating units.
(iii)               All industries which use water and cause pollution may be covered under theWater Cess Act for levying cess. 
 For this purpose, the Ministry may examine Schedule 1 of the Water Cess Act comprehensively.
      However, the Bill lapsed due to dissolution of the 10 th Lok Sabha.  Later, a fresh exercise to introduce the Bill was
 started and subsequently the Water (Prevention & Control of Pollution) Cess (Amendment) Bill, 2000 , based on the
 recommendations aforesaid, was introduced in 2000.  The Bill envisages enhancement of cess rates (approximately three
 times) specified in Schedule II and deletion of Schedule I enlisting 16 categories of industries for the purpose of levying
 cess.  After the amendment, the Act would apply to all industries, which consume water and discharge trade effluents. 
 However, the cess rate for domestic purpose category has not been enhanced and the Bill excludes the hydel power units
 from its purview.

STATEMENT OF OBJECTS AND REASONS
 
The Water (Prevention and Control of Pollution) Cess Act, 1977 was enacted to provide for the levy and collection
 of cess on water consumed by industries and local authorities with a view to augmenting the resources of the Central and
 State Pollution Control Boards for the prevention and control of water pollution which were constituted under the Water
 (Prevention and Control of Pollution) Act, 1974. The existing rates of water cess were revised in 1991 because the
 responsibility and workload of the Pollution Control Boards expanded considerably with the rapid expansion of industrial
 and other economic activities causing pollution and affecting the environment. The present rates of water cess are
 inadequate for the purpose of meeting the financial requirements of the Central and State Pollution Control Boards. There is
 need for enhancing the resources of the Boards to enable their effective functioning for protecting and improving the
 environment. It is also expected that the rationalization of the cess rate structure will induce discipline and economy in the
 use of water.
2.         Further, the State Boards are inter alia entrusted with various responsibilities including the enforcement of the Water
 (Prevention and Control of Pollution) Act, 1974. The responsibilities of the State Boards are expected to grow further as
 economic activities in the industrial and transportation sectors expand. Besides, it is necessary that the water cess rates
 should motivate consumers towards water conservation by making industries pay more for increased use of water. This is
 necessary because water is gradually becoming a scarce natural resource. Accordingly, the cess rates are being revised and
 the applicability of cess is being extended to all categories of industries, which consume water more than the prescribed
 minimum water quantity level and discharge sewage or trade effluents. However, cess is proposed to be abolished on the
 hydel power units.
3.         The Bill seeks to achieve the above objects.

The Report of the Committee deals with the Action Taken by the Department of Science & Technology on the recommendations
 contained in the One Hundred-Second Report of the Department-related Parliamentary Standing Committee on Science &
 Technology, Environment & Forests on the Demands for Grants (2002-2003) of the Department of Science & Technology which was
 presented to the Rajya Sabha on 7th May, 2002.  There are Twenty-three recommendations in the  Report of the Committee. Action
 Taken notes on the recommendations of the Committee was received from the Department on 5th August, 2002.
On scrutiny of the Action Taken notes as received from the Department of Science and Technology, the Committee finds that all
 the Twenty-three recommendations have been fully implemented. 
The Committee’s recommendations, action taken thereon and comments of the Committee on the action taken by the Department
 of Science and Technology are given in the succeeding paragraphs: -
 
BUDGETARY ALLOCATIONS
Recommendation
The Committee would like that the Department should make an effort to reduce the non-plan expenditure by way of generating
 the Internal Extra Budgetary Resources (IEBR) through training programmes and transfer of technology to the industry etc. so that
 Department would not depend solely on budgetary allocation.
(Para 8)
Action taken by the Department
The Recommendation of the Committee has been noted.
Comments
The Committee notes the reply.
SCIENCE AND ENGINEERING COUNCIL (SERC)
Recommendation 
The Committee notes with satisfaction the increased allocation for SERC. The Committee feels that there should be a periodic
 review of the Programmes in order to avoid wasteful expenditure.
(Para 13)
Action taken by the Department
The Science and Engineering Research Council (SERC) is an apex body through which the Department of Science and
 Technology promotes R & D programmes in newly emerging and frontier areas of science and engineering. The council is composed
 of eminent scientists, technologists drawn from various Universities / National Laboratories and industries, SERC supports various
 types of activities which include project support to scientists, core groups and centres of excellence, national research facilities and
 training programmes and fellowships.
The performance of the R & D activities is continuously monitored through various Programme Advisory Committees (PAC) and
 Monitoring Workshops. Specific evaluation of sanctioned projects is performed by different core groups composed of identified
 experts. In addition, high value projects are continuously subjected to on-site monitoring by experts in the field. These rigorous
 monitoring mechanisms generate development of appropriate models and methodology for the improvement of the field and avoid
 wasteful expenditure.
 
Comments
The Committee notes the reply.
 
OPPORTUNITY FOR YOUNG SCIENTISTS
Recommendation 
The Committee observes that very few talented students are motivated to come forward to take-up R&D as career. It is necessary
 that efforts should, therefore, be made not only to increase the number of schemes/projects, the schemes should also be innovative
 and students should be provided with the state of art laboratory facilities and expert care should be provided to encourage them to test
 their ideas. In case there is dearth of ideas, suggestion could be invited from all & sundry and a list could be drawn up to keep it
 handy for those who need it.
(Para 15)
 
Action taken by the Department
Development and nurturing of manpower for R&D has been the focus of new initiatives taken by the Department recently. The
 launch of fellowship schemes such as the Kishore Vaigyanik Protsahan Yojana, DST-JNC Student Summer Research fellowship etc.
 aim at identifying students at 10+2, under-graduate and post-graduate level and providing them placement in labs under an expert and
 with state-of-the-art facilities, in order to inculcate a motivation for taking research as a career. In addition to these schemes, other
 complimentary programmes such as FAST Track Scheme for Young Scientists, SERC Visiting Fellowship, integrated Science
 Olympiad Programme, Contact programme, SERC Schools etc. also facilitate in providing a thrust for motivating students in science
 discipline as well as the faculty.
 
Comments

NATIONAL ACCREDITATION BOARD FOR TESTING AND CALIBRATION LABORATORIES (NABL)
 
Recommendation 
The Committee feels that the large-scale food and drug adulteration can be prevented only if sufficient number of food and drug
 testing laboratories are available in all major cities. Besides that training of staff involved in testing and calibration processes about
 the new standards is necessary for better results.
(Para 22)
Action taken by the Department
National Accreditation Board for Testing & Calibration Laboratories is a voluntary programme. The majority of Food and Drug
 Testing Laboratories is under Ministry of Health and Family Welfare and the same Ministry has been conducting awareness
 programme on NABL Accreditation for these laboratories. NABL training on Quality System Management and Internal Audit for

 laboratory personnel is regularly conducted. Considering the recommendation of the Committee, a letter is being sent from Secretary,
 Department of Science & Technology to Secretary, Health and Family Welfare communicating the recommendations of the
 Parliamentary Standing committee on Science and Technology, Environment and Forests.
 
Comment
The Committee notes the reply.  However, it would like the Department to pursue the matter with the Ministry of Health &
 Family Welfare as contaminated food and spurious drugs are a cause of concern and a reason for many diseases and sometimes
 resulting in  death.  As such, High Quality Standards in laboratory are required to be maintained. The Laboratories should be
 equipped suitably.
 
PATENT FACILITATING CELL
Recommendation
The Committee is of the view that Patent Facilitating Cell should be reorganized into a vibrant nodal and referral agency for
 developing countries in Asia and Africa which could provide consultancy services for industry, universities, R&D institutions,
 government, NGOs and individuals, databases, video and multi-media products, undertake and support research and futuristic studies
 on IPR related topics. Besides, efforts should be made to develop Patent Facilitating centres at state levels in State S&T Councils,
 universities, colleges; industry association for easy access to IPR related information at the local level.
(Para 25)
Action taken by the Department
Patent Facilitating Centre (PFC) has been recognized by some countries as a possible model for them to create IPR awareness and
 provide support to their scientific community for protecting their inventive work. The countries like Bangladesh, Indonesia, Sri
 Lanka and Namibia have already had consultation with PFC under different programmes. The country like Mauritius have also
 shown interest for utilizing the services of PFC. Most of these actions have emanated from S&T collaborations/S&T dialogue with
 these countries. This activity will continue to grow and it is proposed to strengthen this activity during the 10
th Plan and budget for
 the same is being requested.
PFC has already set up 10 Patent Information Centres in the States of Punjab, Rajasthan, Sikkim, Manipur, Gujarat, West Bengal,
 Uttar Pradesh, Andhra Pradesh, Himachal Pradesh and Madhya Pradesh. Steps are being taken to set up similar Centres in the
 remaining States and Union Territories preferably with the cooperation of State S&T Councils. The budget provisions for the same
 are being made during the 10
th Plan.
 
Comments
 
The Committee notes the reply.
 
DRUGS & PHARMACEUTICALS RESEARCH
Recommendation 
 
The Committee observes that given the recent scare of anthrax and reappearance of plague in some parts of India efforts must be
 renewed to counteract these diseases. With its traditional knowledge the country can perform pioneering role in tackling these
 diseases.
(Para 30)
Action taken by the Department
The recommendation of the committee is noted. Accordingly emphasis will be given inter-alia on anthrax and plague in the two
 National seminars that Department has sanctioned on traditional medicines viz. on Ayurvedic medicine at Banaras Hindu University,
 Varanasi during November 2002 and on Siddha medicine at Tamil University, Thanjavur during December 2002. The participants of
 this seminar will be from leading R&D/Academic institutions involved in traditional medicines. The seminar will also be discussing
 indepth the strength of Ayurvedic/Siddha Medicines in tackling many tropical diseases of relevance to our country.
 
Comment
The Committee notes the reply.
 
DRUGS & PHARMACEUTICALS RESEARCH
 
Recommendation 
 
The Committee is constrained to note the snail’s pace in the development of herbal medicines when they have the potential to cure
 dreaded diseases like AIDS & Cancer besides the diseases like Diabetes, Hypertension etc. Not only the herbal medicines, there is
 need to open big hospitals based on the Indian System of medicines. The Committee is given to understand that the Indian System of
 medicine notably ayurveda did miraculous healing to the victims of chernobyl  disaster. This lead the Russians to take more interest
 in this system of medicine so much so that they evinced interest in the learning of the system. Likewise the United States of America
 is reported to have set up a very big hospital in one of its states based on the Indian System of medicine. If it really be so, it is indeed
 unfortunate we have not used our system of medicine in such a big way to set up hospitals of that scale. The Committee feels it is
 time Government thinks over the matter irrespective of the fact whether Department of Science & Technology is individually

Under Drugs and Pharmaceuticals Research Programme, research projects related to development/standardization of herbal drugs

A novel oligospirostanoside from Asparagus racemosus  Novel process for the preparation of ‘Asavas’ and ‘Arishtas’ range of

 medicines viz. on Ayurvedic medicine at Banaras Hindu University, Varanasi during November 2002 and on Siddha medicine at
 Tamil University, Thanjavur during December 2002. The participants of this seminar will  be from leading R&D/Academic
 institutions/Industries involved in traditional medicines. These seminars will also be discussing in depth the strength of
 Ayurvedic/Siddha Medicines in tackling many tropical diseases of relevance to our country.
The department has noted the observations of the Committee emphasizing the use of Indian system of medicine by way of setting
 up large scale hospitals. Since the service/setting up of hospitals falls within the mandate of Ministry of Health and Family Welfare,
 Department of Indian System of Medicine and Homeopathy (ISM&H), the DST will interact intensively with Department of ISM&H
 to set up hospitals with adequate facility based on Indian system of medicines in the country. This will further help the Department in
 carrying out R&D efforts within the country.
 
Comments
The Committee notes the reply.
 
TECHNOLOGY INFORMATION, FORECASTING AND ASSESMENT COUNCIL (TIFAC)
 
Recommendation 
            The Committee is of the view that effective technology transfer process to industry may also help in challenging the
 technologies coming from abroad. Besides, the technology transferred to the industry is to be cost effective and also retain certain
 safeguards to prevent industry from exploiting the research.
(Para 34)
Action taken by the Department
The department has taken effective steps in smooth transfer of technology to industry and also to make it cost effective. Under the
 technology related programme on Drugs and Pharmaceuticals, industry association is ensured right at the inception of the
 programme. The department contributes towards financial requirements of the institutions and in this manner the
research programme is subsidized to the industry. Industry is given the first option to commercialize the technology.
The department under the programme on Home Grown Technology implemented by TIFAC, also provides financial assistance for
 technology upgradation to the industries. The financial assistance is provided on very soft terms in order to make the technology cost
 effective. Similarly, the newly created Technology Development Board which is under the administrative control of the department
 also provides loan on soft terms to industries to commercialize the technologies.
Comments
The Committee appreciates the steps taken by the department and hopes that effective and adequate safeguards have been initiated
 to prevent the industries from misusing the funds/loans made available to them.
 
SPECIAL COMPONENT PLAN FOR SCHEDULED CASTE
Recommendation 
The Committee notes with satisfaction the programme undertaken for the benefit of weaker sections of the society. The
 Committee desires that the benefits of these programmes should reach the large population living in rural areas and smaller towns
 who might be unaware of these programmes.
The Committee feels that effective coordination should be established with other Departments who are involved in similar
 activities to prevent overlapping of schemes.
(Para 37)
Action taken by the Department
The focus of initiatives under Science & Society programmes during the 10
th Five Year Plan has been further sharpened. In order
 to ensure replication of successful models of technological intervention, it is proposed to involve development departments of the
 Centre as well as those in the States/Union Territories in assessment of proposals, monitoring of progress and evaluation of impact.
 The Expert Committees, which guide the programmes, have been reconstituted with representatives of other departments, which are
 involved in similar activities.

Recommendation 
The Committee would like the Department to consider starting more such programmes which should lead to development, self
 employment and income generation of women and other weaker sections of the society. The Committee recommends that special

(Para 41)

Several initiatives are proposed to promote vigorously efforts of applying science & technology for creating opportunities the area
 of self-employment and income generation amongst women and weaker sections of the society. Women technology parks being set
 up through this Ministry and through the Department of Women & Child Development in different states will amongst other

The Committee notes the reply.
 
VIGYAN PRASAR
Recommendation 
The Committee is of the view that the young generation should be encouraged to take up the study of science through easy-to-do
 practical and other innovative ways, incentives, ‘earn while you learn’ schemes etc. to help build scientific temper.
(Para 45)
Action taken by the Department
A short term (5 days) module has been developed to train middle school science teachers in the use of low and no-cost activities
 for teaching fundamental concepts of science. Resource persons are being trained who in turn will help in skill development of
 teachers. A series of activities for senior students are being developed which will encourage innovation and creativity under the
 initiative ‘Rise of Modern Indian Science’. This will be a nation wide programme.

The Committee notes the reply with satisfaction.  However, it feels that each programme should be emphasised to develop skills

VIGYAN PRASAR
Recommendation 
The Committee is also of the view that use of HAM radio should be popularized in regions/areas prone to natural disasters and
 this can be done if in schools training of HAM radio’s taken up as an extra curricular activity.
(Para 46)
Action taken by the Department
HAM sets have proved useful during the relief and rescue operations following any natural disasters. Training programmes to
 popularize HAM radio among school students through science clubs will be given a thrust during the 10
th Five Year Plan period.

The Committee notes the reply.
 
 
NATURAL RESOURCES DATA MANAGEMENT SYSTEM (NRDMS)
Recommendation 
The Committee observes that even though the country has made technological advances there are frequent cases of landslides. In
 order to prevent this, it is necessary to have a complete hazard zonation map clearly demarcating landslide prone areas similar to the
 one
for earth quake prone areas. Besides GIS data received form GRAM ++ should be utilized for the agricultural development.
(Para 48)
Action taken by the Department
Under NRDMS, a sub-programme on Landslide Studies is operational over the last one decade. DST had supported more than
 dozen projects for preparation of landslide hazard zonation mapping in parts of Himachal Pradesh, Garhwal and Kumon Himalaya,
 North Eastern States, Western Ghats and Nilgiris Hills. In addition to this, close interaction has been made with the other central
 agencies like Department of Space and Geological Survey of India who have also done landslide hazard zonation mapping as their
 in-house R&D activities. DST has also constituted an Expert Committee to oversee the R&D activities. Further, efforts are being

106th Report

 made to identity the gap areas where landslide hazard zonation mapping has not been done. During Current Financial Year, five
 R&D projects on Landslide Hazard Zonation were supported under ‘Jai Vigyan Mission’ Project on “Natural Disaster Mitigation”.
 The LHZ mapping will be carried out in part of North Eastern States. Apart from this, DST has initiated site specific studies to
 investigate and analyze various surface and sub-surface parameters responsible for landslides. Efforts are also being made for
 monitoring of critical landslides areas, development of suitable site specific control measures and dissemination of emerging
 technologies/training to the potential users.
 
Comments
            The Committee feels that hazard zonation maps prepared should be made available to the district administration and other
 agencies who can take proper precautions by enacting laws of construction which conform to quake resistant models to prevent loss
 of life and property caused due to land slides.

Recommendation 
The Committee hopes that joint research projects in areas of Mutual interests in new emerging areas like genomics, nano
 technology and implementation technology would help both the countries to forge bonds of friendship between the two countries.

(a)  The Indo-US S&T Forum has already organized a joint workshop between India & US in Nano Technology at Santa Barbara
 U.S.A. in November, 2001. Eight scientists from India participated in this workshop on emerging area of Nano fabrication and
 technology.
 
(b)  In the field of genomics, an exploratory team of our US scientists visited various laboratories in Delhi, Bangalore and
 Hyderabad during April, 2002 and thereafter has agreed to hold a joint workshop in functional genomics in India during early 2003

(c)  In the field of information technology, the Governing Body of this Forum has decided to support joint workshop on e-security
 and distance learning. The workshop plan is under preparation by the Ministry of Information Technology for submission to the

The Committee notes the reply.
 
NATIONAL CENTRE FOR MEDIUM WEATHER FORECASTING (NCMRWF)
Recommendation 
The Committee feels that the thrust of weather forecasting should be on its accuracy. The Committee observes that Department
 should consider enhancing the spatial resolution, range and accuracy of forecasts and advisories by constantly improving forecast
 models with use of available satellite data and techniques.
(Para 54)
 
Action taken by the Department
India Meteorological Department (IMD) is solely responsible for issuing weather forecast in different time-space scales. Since
 1988, IMD has been successfully using 16 parameteric power regression model for issuing Long Range Forecast of South West
 Monsoon rainfall for the entire country as a whole.
For day-to-day weather forecast IMD is equipped with adequate infrastructure. Concerted efforts are being made to enhance the
 forecasting capabilities of IMD by constantly updating the resources/technology so that improved and more reliable weather
 forecasts/warnings/advisories could be provided to various user agencies. Recently, Quasi-Langrangian Model has been
 operationalised for tropical cyclone forecasting. It is providing higher resolution outputs and is assimilating the necessary satellite
 derived information. A new workstation “ORIGIN-200” has been commissioned at IMD Hqrs. It has enhanced our capabilities to run
 numerical models whose output for 24 hrs. forecast is now available within 2 hrs. after submission of the input data.
 
Comments
The Committee is of the view that the predictions made for monsoon should be precise and accurate. All efforts of the Department
 should be geared to making the forecasts accurate.

Recommendation 
The Committee appreciates the work being done by the Department for rebuilding and Rehabilitation of Quake victims of Gujarat.

financial agencies like Housing Urban Development Corporation (HUDCO) / National Housing Bank (NHB) etc. for providing low

The Committee notes the reply with satisfaction.
 
SURVEY OF INDIA
 
Recommendation 
 
The Committee feels it is time that Survey of India thought of diversifying its activities. Apart from preparing and bringing out
 political & physical maps of the country, it should endeavour to bring out maps of tourist interest of National Highways, towns and
 cities to meet the local needs.
(Para 58)
Action taken by the Department
 
Survey of India has been bringing out the following special series of maps of tourist interest in addition to topographical, political
 and physical maps of the country.
 
(a)  Trekking maps viz. Badrinath, Badri-Kedar, Gangotri-Yamnotri, Kullu Valley, Kumaon Hills, Route map of J&K and Shimla
 Hills.
(b)  Route map from Rishikesh to Badrinath, Kedarnath.
(c)  Chandigarh and its environs, Delhi and its environs.
(d)  Motoring map of India and Motoring Atlas.
(e)  Hill ranges & Rivers.
(f)   National Parks and Sanctuaries.
 
In the meantime, SOI has also taken up updation of maps of some of the selected cities/towns using IKONOS imageries and

 highways are also being taken up for compilation from the existing digital map data. Preparation of one such map of the state of
 Uttaranchal is already allotted to one of our Digital Centres.
 
Comments
 
The Committee notes the reply.  However, it would like the department to take up similar activities in other parts of the country
 particularly Northeast and Western ghats where these trekking maps could be used to tap the  potential of tourism.

Recommendation 
 
The Committee expresses its concern over delay in commissioning of Doppler Radars which are needed for accurate weather
 forecasting. Besides, In India occurrence of cyclones is a regular feature every year, the Commissioning of Digital Cyclone Warning
 Dissemination System (DCWDS), should be given a priority. The Committee would appreciate if these could be installed before the
 beginning of Monsoon Season.
(Para 60)
Action taken by the Department
 
The Doppler Weather Radar (DWR) at Chennai has already been commissioned on 21
st February, 2002 and working
 satisfactorily. The print out of radar products from this DWR are regularly being sent to various users on E-mail. The DWR at
 Kolkata has been installed. Test observations are being taken regularly. It is likely to be commissioned in July, 2002. The Third

SEISMOLOGY
 
Recommendation 
 
The Committee has been given to understand that exact prediction of earthquakes has not been possible so far. Nevertheless, the
 Committee feels that attempts should be made to use all technological advances available to unravel the mysteries which the Nature
 has so far not permitted the mankind to penetrate into. Perhaps the day might not be far when the Mother earth might relent and
 impart some insight to human beings about its fury expressed through earth quakes. The Committee therefore feels that efforts should
 continue in that direction.
(Para 65)
Action taken by the Department
 
An Expert Group has been set up by DST under the Chairmanship of Prof. V. K. Gaur, Distinguished Professor, IIA to prepare a
 comprehensive document as well as to identify priority projects for implementation under the mission mode project. The first
 meeting of this group was held on May 21
st, 2002 and discussed the various issues. Apart from the several recommendations, it was
 agreed to establish multi-parametric geophysical observatories at a few selected locations in the country. The proposed observatories
 will house the various geophysical instruments, including magnetometer, gravitymeter seismograph, GPS resistivity meter, Gas
 emanometers and ULF/VLF equipments. The data collected by these instruments may help in possible correlation of precursory
 phenomena with the earthquake occurrence.

 Maharashtra, where sizable quantity of Bamboo is produced, have not been included in the Mission. Besides, the Quality of Bamboo

The recommendations of the Committee in respect of the proposed National Mission for Bamboo Applications have been noted.

 Development which was presented/laid to both Houses of Parliament on 7
th May, 2002.  There are fifteen recommendations
 contained in One Hundred-first Report of the Committee. Action Taken notes on the recommendations of the Committee
 were received from the Department  on 27
th August, 2002.
The Committee’s recommendations, action taken thereon and comments of the Committee on the action taken by the
 Department of Ocean Development are set out in the succeeding paragraphs: -
 
BUDGETARY ALLOCATION
 
Recommendation
 
The Committee observes that there were major variations in the budgetary allocations and their utilization.  The non-
utilisation of the allocation meant less or reduced activities of the Department.  The Committee is not happy with the reasons
 advanced by the Department for the non-utilization of funds which includes delay in transfer of foreign consultation, change
 of priorities, delay in initiating discussion with the neighbouring countries, non approval and uncertainty of elements.  The
 Committee feels that the Department should have foreseen these difficulties before asking for budgetary allocation and
 should have evolved suitable mechanism to monitor the budgetary proposal and its allocations.
(Para 7)
Action Taken by the Department
 
Regarding the major variations in the budgetary allocations and their utilization, all  efforts will be made to minimize
 such variations.  In respect of National Institute of Ocean Technology where there has been an increase in the actual as
 compared to the BE, the main reason was on account of the additional requirement of the OTEC project.  For this, all
 necessary approvals including for the supplementary demand for grants was taken.
 
ICMAM (World Bank assisted project) Rs. 3.11 Crore
 
The tasks relating to collection of data for ICMAM Plan of Goa and Gulf of Kachchh could not be initiated in 2000-2001
 as more time was taken to finalise the contracts. The Integrated Coastal and Marine Area Management programme being a
 World Bank assisted project, approvals needed to be taken from both government and the world Bank. Since there was
 variance in opinions there was delay in awarding the contracts. Hence the entire funds could not be utilized in the financial
 year under mention. Further, the savings are also on account of reduction in the scope of work in the foreign consultancies.
 
PMN-Unmanned submersible Rs. 4.09 crore
 
The project on the development of a unmanned submersible was approved by the EFC at an estimated cost of Rs. 18.28
 crores. At the time of approval, the Department had a proposal in hand from an institute (EDBOE) under Russian Academy
 of Sciences to develop the equipment/vehicle in technical collaboration with National Institute of Ocean Technology
 (NIOT). Later on, it was felt that it could be better to explore possibilities of technical collaboration from other sources and

 an effort in that direction was made. All  this resulted into delay in starting the project and hence the entire provision kept
 for the project had to be surrendered.
 
Oceanographic Survey – Continental Survey – Continental Shelf –Rs.. 43 crore
 
The unspent balance in relation to the continental shelf programme is on account of various factors. It may be noted that
 Delineation of Outer Limits of Continental Shelf is the international programme and India is expected to gain about 1
 million square km of area in the sea based on the supporting scientific data. The data acquisition is based on the Scientific
 and Technical Guidelines of the Commission on the Limits of Continental Shelf. The issue of the guidelines were delayed
 by the UN Commission on the Limits of Continental Shelf which was beyond the control of Department of Ocean
 development. The scientific and technical guidelines were received towards the end of calendar year 1999 and various
 parameters of the project such as the quantum of work, technical parameters and their specifications, area of operation, types
 of survey and survey requirement were worked out keeping in mind the guidelines as well as the national interest.
Further the Department kept major provision of the programme in the budget for the year 2000-2001 as the work was
 required to be completed on priority basis due to fast approaching last date of submission of claim in June 2005. Later on,
 somewhere towards middle of the year 2000, it was learnt that the extension of the last date for submission of claim is being
 considered and Department felt that it would be appropriate to slow down the pace of ground work and watch for
 development at international level. Thus, the efforts of the Department were diverted towards detailed examination of the
 guidelines, specification of surveys, and inter-departmental and international dialogues instead of taking up the surveys for
 which the budget provision was made. Hence the provision kept for the survey work was surrendered.
 
Comments
 
The Committee has observed that the budgetary support has been surrendered regularly at the end of each financial year
 without spending the single paise by the Department as the project undertaken were not completed for which budgetary
 allocation was sought. Although it is true that the completion of the project was beyond the control of the Department.  In
 this connection Committee would like to suggest that 50% of budgetary allocation should be surrendered at R.E. stage
 instead of holding of budgetary allocation for the full year, if possible.
 
COASTAL RESEARCH VESSELS
 
Recommendation
 
The Committee commends the efforts being made by the Department in utilising the services of two vessels.  However,
 in view of decommissioning of existing vessels after another 10 years, it is time to plan for acquiring new vessels which can
 cater to shallow water survey, data buoy maintenance and provide a platform for various coastal and deep ocean activities
 and other requirements which could reasonably be foreseen in the years ahead. The new vessels would not only serve as a
 platform for the programmes envisaged in the Tenth plan but also serve as a utility vessel which might augment the capacity
 requirements for programmes on the marine living and non-living resources.
(Para 10)
 
Action Taken by the Department
 
Noted.  The Department has proposed for a new research vessel in the Xth Plan to be used as a platform for its various
 technology development activities and to augment the capacity requirements for its scientific programmes.
 
Comments
 
The Committee notes the reply.  However, it would like the Department to see that the plan for the acquisition of a new
 research vessel is implemented in a time bound manner.
 
POLAR SCIENCE (ANTARCTIC RESEARCH) PROGRAMME
 
Recommendation
 
The Committee is of the view that in addition to on-going programmes in various domains of polar sciences, National
 Centre for Antarctic Ocean Research (NCAOR) should also initiate cutting-edge experiments in such frontier areas as
 assessment of biotechnological potential of Antarctic microbes, biodegradation of organic wastes using microbial

 consortium and productivity and ecosystem dynamics in the Antarctic lakes.  It should also envisage initiating meaningful
 logistics operation with other countries which could lead to operational and financial cooperation.
(Para 16)

 and long term scientific programmes including frontier areas such as assessment of biotechnological potential of Antarctic

 operations with other countries are also being explored.

While the Committee notes the reply, it would like sustained efforts on the part of Department to review the performance

Recommendation
 
The Committee observes that the efforts of the Department to monitor pollution in the coastal areas need to be continued

 diffusion and dispersion characteristics.  Besides, the stations for collection of near-shore samples must be planned with a
 view to reflect the pollution load that was occurring there and the data collected should be processed and forwarded to State
 Pollution Control Boards for taking remedial measures.
