Bt. COTTON & ISSUES RELATED THERETO
Recommendation
            The Committee feels that a satisfactory system of assessing the risks associated with the release of genetically modified (GM) plants; micro organisms, animals and marine
 organisms into the environment must be evolved.  Certain grey areas still exist in the field of genetically modified foods, particularly for people who have food allergies, because they
 are neither subjected to tests nor controlled.  There is thus a need to adopt a cautious approach.
(Para 11)
Action taken by the Ministry
In order to contain possible hazards to environment from the release of Genetically Modified Organisms, the Ministry of Environment and Forests (MoEF) has notified  in December
 1989, the ‘Rules for the manufacture, use, import, export and storage of hazardous Micro-organisms/Genetically Engineered Organisms or Cells, under the Environment (Protection)
 Act (EPA) 1986.These Rules are being implemented through a three tiered mechanism:
Institutional Biosafety Committees (IBSCs) at the institutional  level.
Review Committee on Genetic Manipulation (RCGM) in the DBT
Genetic Engineering Approval Committee (GEAC) in the MoEF
The Government is following a policy of case by case approval of transgenic crops. Introduction of any new technology requires careful evaluation and long term sustainable benefits.
 Extensive Rules and guidelines have been framed for evaluating environmental and health safety aspects of genetically modified organisms. Any company involved in the use of
 genetic engineering techniques has to obtain approval of the Review Committee on Genetic Manipulation (RCGM) for conducting testing under laboratory conditions and confined
 field conditions. Thereafter approval of GEAC is required for large scale field trials and introduction to environment.
The Ministry of Health & Family Welfare has set up an Expert Committee on Genetically Modified (GM) Foods, to inter-alia:
suggest the structure and capacity required for regulating GM foods in this country from the point of view of consumer health;
identify the parameters on which risk assessment, if any, is required to be done for GM food – both imported and domestically produced and to spell out the modalities for doing so;
advise the Government on risk assessment issues relating to GM foods and to undertake review of such products, where considered necessary.
Further  action  would  be  taken  in  accordance  with  the  recommendation  of  this Committee as and when received.

OLIVE RIDLEY TURTLE AT GAHIRMATHA BEACH IN ORISSA
Recommendation
The Committee is of the view that the non-usage of Turtle Excluder Devices (TEDs) is turning the Gahirmatha beach in Orissa into the largest graveyard for turtles.  Although, the use
 of TEDs has been made mandatory in the State, but trawler operators continue to flout norms with impunity.  The Ministry of Environment and Forests should take-up this issue on
 priority basis in coordination with the State Governments and take steps to strictly enforce the usage of turtle excluder devices (TEDs). 
(Para 13)
Action taken by the Ministry
            Although the use of Turtle Excluder Device has been made mandatory requisite but adequate number of these devices are not available in the market.  Central Institute of
 Fisheries, Nautical Engineering and Training, Cochin has finalized the design of Turtle Excluder Device. 
The Institute at present is involved in the process of popularizing the design of the Turtle Excluder Device and improving its availability. Meanwhile, Fisheries Department of Orissa is
 ensuring that the trawlers which have procured Turtle Excluder Devices use them regularly.
Comments
            The Committee feels that there should be an emphasis on data collection and monitoring programmes to gather information on the nature and magnitude of threats to the turtle
 population.  Besides, the installation of TEDs should be made mandatory on all boats and the development of these devices should be done on priority basis.
           
TAJ PROTCTION MISSION
Recommendation
            The Committee is of the view that the levels of both the pollutants might not have come down due to the pollution load of the Mathura Oil Refinery.  The rise in SPM and SO2
 levels has also been caused because of the heavy vehicles going via Agra.  The Ministry should also examine recommendations of the Vardarajan Committee, appointed by the
 Supreme Court to look into Taj Pollution, which remain unimplemented while checking out various programmes under the Taj Protection Mission.
(Para 15)
Action taken by the Ministry
            The annual average level of SO
2 was as high as 21ug/M3 in 1991, which has come down to 10 ug/m3. The annual average level of NOx was as high as 12 ug/M3 in 1991, which
 has come down to 9 ug/m3. The annual average level of SPM was as high as about 515ug/M3 in 1991, which has come down to about 351 ug/m3. It would be pertinent to point out
 that even the background levels of SPM assuming the complete absence of industrial, vehicular and SPM emitting from the domestic activity, would be above the prescribed levels of
 70ug/m
3. These are due to certain natural conditions that are prevailing in the vicinity such as proximity of the Thar desert in Rajasthan, agricultural activity such as tilling, &
 ploughing and  barren land coupled with blowing winds, pollen of crops, and flowering plants which contribute to the levels of SPM. The low humidity prevalent in this region also
 promotes formation of SPM. One of the most effective economical and useful approach for control of environmental pollution is by tree plantation.  The forests have been described as
 the "green lungs" of the earth.  The project has envisaged plantation in 1244 hectares of land. Plantation has already been completed in 1015 hectares of land. Action has been taken, as
 directed by the Supreme Court for pollution control in the Mathura Refinery and other sources of pollution. 10 schemes have been taken up by the U.P. State Government with funding
 from the Central and the State Governments for control of pollution in the TTZ Area for protection of the Taj Mahal from the environmental pollution. Besides these, the State
 Government is also formulating some more schemes for implementation under the Center-State financing for the protection of the Taj Mahal.  Mathura Refinery has taken various
 pollution control measures viz. setting up of hydro cracker unit and various other devices by which the pollution load from the Refinery has come down .  The Refinery has made an
 investment of Rs. 700.00 crores for technological up gradation/ pollution control equipment for the reduction of SO
2.   As per CPCB report the refinery emits 250-350 kgs./hr. of SO2
 against the prescribed standard of 450 kg/hr.  Attempt has been made by the UP State Government to control the emission  from the  vehicular transportation via  Agra on  National
 and State Highways.  The  Agra bye-pass has been  widened up to 4.70 metres  which act as an alternative route for the transportation of vehicles from Delhi to Gwalior.   
            In response to the Supreme Court's order of 3
rd August, 1995, the Ministry of Environment and Forests, in consultation with all the stakeholders including the State
 Government of Uttar Pradesh, prepared various schemes for the protection of the Taj Mahal. These schemes were submitted to the Supreme Court after the detailed examination of the
 NEERI and Vardharajan Report. The Planning Commission, in consultation with the State Government allocated an amount of Rs.600 crores on a 50:50 per cent (Centre-State)
 matching basis to implement various schemes relating to protection of the Taj Mahal. A separate cell to oversee the progress of the Schemes for which allocation was made by the
 Planning Commission and on behalf of the Central and State Governments, a Mission Management Board (MMB) has been constituted under the Chairmanship of Chief Secretary,
 UP. The Ministry of Environment and Forests has vide Notification S.O. No.350 (E), dated 17.5.1999 constituted an Authority known as the Taj Trapezium Zone Pollution
 (Prevention and Control) Authority for monitoring the implementation of various projects undertaken under Taj Protection Mission Scheme. The Mission Management Board
 submitted schemes, as mentioned in Para 14 for the environmental protection of the Taj Mahal.

VEHICULAR POLLUTION CONTROL MEASURES
Recommendation
            The Committee is of the view that the Ministry of Environment & Forests have adequate powers under section 5 of the Air Act, 1981, and the Environment (Protection) Act to
 enforce more stringent standards for pollution at hot spots.  Apart from the instance of 1997, when it notified the first ever fuel quality norms, the Ministry has never made its presence
 felt.  It has never discouraged the use of diesel by the Indian auto sector.  There has thus been no show of commitment or initiative on the part of the Ministry.
(Para 17)
Action taken by the Ministry
            For control of vehicular pollution, the Ministry of  Environment and Forests has played a major coordinating role with the concerned Ministries and its associated
 bodies/organizations including the Ministry of Road Transport & Highways, the Ministry of Petroleum and Natural Gas and the Ministry of Heavy Industry & Public Enterprises for
 up-gradation of automobile technology, supply of improved quality fuel, expansion of urban public transport systems and promotion of integrated traffic management.
            In 1991, for the first time the emission norms for motor vehicles were notified by Ministry of Environment & Forests under the Environment (Protection) Act, 1986. The
 progressive stringent emission norms known as Bharat Stage I and II norms akin to Euro I and II have been notified under the Motor Vehicles Act, 1988 by the Ministry of Road
 Transport & Highways, for which this Ministry played a major role being the member of the standing committee for emission legislation.  Euro I norms were made effective in the
 entire country from 1.4.2000 for all categories of vehicles.  The more stringent Bharat Stage II norms for four wheelers were made effective in Delhi, Mumbai, Kolkata and Chennai in
 a phased manner where the increasing air pollution is attributed to automobile population boom.
            The Ministry notified specification of fuel (Petrol as well as diesel) for emission related parameters on 2
nd April, 1996 commensurate with Euro I norms.  Unleaded petrol has
 been introduced in Delhi, Mumbai, Kolkata and Chennai from 1.4.1995 and only unleaded petrol is being supplied in the entire country from1.2.2000.  Diesel with 0.25% sulphur
 content (maximum) was introduced in metros from 1.4.1998 and only this quality diesel is being supplied in the entire country from 1.1.2000.  Ministry of Environment & Forests has
 also notified specification of 2-T Oil for  2 & 3 wheelers and is effective in the entire country from 1.4.1999.  Only pre mixed 2T Oil is supplied in Delhi from 31.12.1998.  Petrol and
 diesel with 0.05% sulphur content (maximum) has been introduced from 1.4.2000 in Delhi, from 1.1.2001 in Mumbai and from 1.7.2001 in Kolkata & Chennai.  Petrol with 1%
 Benzene maximum is made available in the NCT of Delhi from 1.11.2000 and from 1.1.2001 in Mumbai.  Petrol with 3% Benzene maximum is made available in Kolkata and
 Chennai from 1.4.2000.
            Further, keeping in view the environmental health effects attributed to emissions from diesel driven vehicles, the Government has taken various measures to discourage the use
 of diesel by the Indian auto sector. These include the following:
Promotion of CNG, LPG and Propane as auto fuel as contained in the action plans prepared by the Ministry of Environment and Forests.
Adoption of CNG as auto fuel and notification of emission norms for CNG driven vehicles under the Motor Vehicles Act, 1988 (administered by the Ministry of Road Transport &
 Highways ) which is effective from 9.2.2000.
Adoption of LPG as auto fuel and notification of emission norms for LPG driven vehicles under the Motor Vehicles Act, 1988 (administered by the Ministry of Road Transport &
 Highways) which is effective from 24.5.2001.
Fiscal incentives for promoting the use of CNG, LPG and Propane as auto fuel by extending custom duty concession for CNG, LPG and Propane kits and its parts.
Comments
            While the Committee notes the reply of the Ministry it observes that despite the efforts made by the Ministry the magnitude of the problem contains to be enormous and metros
 like Delhi have become a place unfit to live because of the choking smoke engulfing over them.  The efforts to remedy the problem need to be accelerated.
Recommendation
            The Ministry of Environment & Forest’s 1997 white paper on pollution in Delhi is little more than a common position of all the other Union government agencies concerned,
 such as Ministry of Industry, Ministry of Surface Transport and Ministry of Petroleum and Natural gas.  It does nothing more to push for CNG than propose government tradition of
 making toothless but politically correct suggestions.
(Para 17.1)
Action taken by the Ministry
            Keeping in view the increasing environmental pollution, the Ministry of Environment and Forests (MoEF) has prepared a white paper on Pollution in Delhi with an Action Plan
 in 1997 after having a series of interactive meetings with concerned Government agencies, NGOs, experts and citizens, with the objective of defining a plan of action to combat
 pollution.  Action plan also emphasizes planning and development of infrastructure to mitigate pollution.   Apart from the activities outlined in the action plan, specific measures
 relating to control of vehicular pollution have been particularly emphasized by the Ministry of Environment and Forests in its deliberations with various Government and NGOses on
 the subject of control of pollution in Delhi.  These include adoption of clean fuel such as CNG as an auto fuel and conversion of commercial taxis and public transport vehicles on
 CNG mode.
            White Paper also envisages measures for control of pollution in Delhi from other sectors as well i.e., water, solid waste management, industrial, noise, institutional and planning
 aspects, public participation and general awareness etc.
            Apart from several steps taken for control of vehicular pollution as given in para 17 above, the Ministry of Environment and Forests has made efforts/coordination activities
 with the Nodal Ministries / Agencies to adopt and use CNG as auto fuel in Delhi.  These include:
Environment Pollution (Prevention and Control) Authority (EPCA) for the National Capital Region was constituted by the Ministry for improving the quality of environment and
 preventing, controlling and abating environment pollution.

All commercial/transport vehicles which are more than 20 years has been phased out after 2.10.1998, 17 to 19 years old vehicles has been phased out after 15.11.1998 and 15 and 16
 years old vehicles has been phased out after 31.12.1998.
More than 8 years old buses (diesel drive) are not allowed to ply on Delhi except on clean fuels from 1.4.2000.
Entire city bus fleet (diesel driven) has been asked to convert to single fuel mode on CNG from 31.3.2001.
All pre 1990 autos and taxis were ordered to replace them with new vehicles on clean fuels by 31.3.2000.
For successful implementation of expansion of CNG project in Delhi, Indraprastha Gas Limited (IGL)-a joint venture company of Bharat Petroleum Corporation Limited and Gas
 Authority of India Limited was incorporated in December 1998.
When the IGL was incorporated in Delhi there were only 9 CNG stations one station on IGL land and the remaining 8 stations on oil company’s existing petrol pumps.  IGL has setup
 86 additional CNG stations in record time of 3 years with an investment of more than Rs. 220 crores.  Ten stations are exclusively dedicated to DTC depots.  The CNG sale is 4.55
 lakh kg/day in June, 2002 from the CNG outlets (27 Mother stations, 13 on line station, 26 Daughter-Booster stations and 29 Daughter stations).
As on April, 2002 there are 53, 479 vehicles including 4463 buses are plying on CNG mode.
From 6
th April, 2002 diesel driven buses are permitted to ply only after depositing the requisite costs.  Rs. 17,03,50,500/- (Rupees Seventeen crore three lakh fifty thousand and five
 hundred only ) has been realised as cost from diesel buses.
As on 4
th July, 2002, 4286 diesel buses has been phased out from Delhi.
 
Comments
            The Committee notes the reply.
Recommendation
            The Committee is of the view that Environmental regulation through Courts has serious drawbacks.  Judicial intervention is most effective in correcting bureaucratic conduct
 when it is selective and surgical, but in significant environmental litigations such as the Ganga Pollution Case, the Vehicular Pollution Case and Taj Trapezium Case the administrative
 agency – the Ministry of Environment & Forests has been reduced to preparing only knee-jerk responses to judicial orders.  The Committee believes that despite more than a decade of
 judicial activism, there is no evidence to show that the Pollution Control Boards, Department of Forests or the Ministry  have become institutionally stronger, or more capable of
 discharging  their responsibilities today. 
(Para 17.2)
Action taken by the Ministry
            Section 5 of the Environment (Protection) Act, 1986 empowers the Central Government in the Ministry of Environment and Forests to issue directions in writing to any person,
 officer or authority  for the purpose of implementation of the objective of the EP Act namely, protection and improvement of environment and for matters connected therewith.  These
 directions include the power to direct (a) the closure, prohibition or regulation of any industry, operation or process; or (b) stoppage or regulation of the supply of electricity or water
 or any other service.
            The powers under Section 5 of the Environment (Protection) Act, 1986 have been delegated by the Ministry to the Central Pollution Control Board, State Pollution Control
 Boards and Pollution Control Committees and State Governments to issue directions to the polluting units for compliance with pollution control norms.
            The State Pollution Control Boards and Pollution Control Committees issue directions under section 33 A of the Water (Prevention and control of pollution) Act, 1974 and
 Section 31 A of the Air (Prevention and control of pollution) Act, 1981 to the polluting units for compliance with the pollution  control norms.  The  Central  Pollution  Control  Board
 issue  directions  under section 5 of the Environment (Protection) Act, 1986 to the polluting units for compliance with the pollution control norms.  The Central Pollution Control
 Board also issue directions under section 18 (1)(b) of the Water (Prevention and control of pollution) Act, 1974 and / or the Air (Prevention and control of Pollution) Act, 1981 to the
 State Pollution Control Boards and Pollution Control Committees for enforcement of pollution control norms. 
            The Central Pollution Control Board has issued 447 directions to various polluting industries for compliance with pollution control norms under section 5 of the Environment
 (Protection) Act, 1986.  The Central Pollution Control Board also issued 747 directions under Section 18(1)(b) of the Water (Prevention and control of pollution) Act, 1974 and/or the
 Air (Prevention and control of pollution) Act, 1981 to the State Pollution Control Boards and Pollution Control Committees for enforcement of pollution control norms.
            The State Pollution Control Boards/Pollution Control Committees have taken legal action against the defaulting industries.  About 5677 cases have been filed under the Water
 (Prevention and Control of Pollution) Act, 1974 and about 1667 cases have been filed under the Air (Prevention and Control of Pollution) Act, 1981.
            For strengthening of the Pollution Control Boards/Committees for effective implementation of Environmental Laws, the following steps have been taken as per the Coimbatore
 Charter resolved in the Conference of State Environment Ministers held during 29-30 January, 2001 at Coimbatore.
Induction of academicians, legal professionals etc, in the Boards/Committees.
Appointment of multi-disciplinary staff.
Training of Personnel.
Streamlining of consent/authorization procedures.
 Formulation of annual action plans
Preparation of State of Environment Reports.

Recommendation
            The Committee is aware of the Supreme Court’s orders on April 5, 2002 regarding plying of all public transport vehicles on CNG in Delhi being implemented by concerned
 agencies but at the same time the Committee is constrained to note the sad plight of commuters who continue to suffer.  As a result of the judicial pronouncement and the consequent
 steps taken by the Government, the commuters continue to suffer with no immediate steps in sight being taken by the government to address their problems.  On the other hand
 transporters seem to be bent upon to exploit them by over charging and making their journeys uncomfortable and costlier.  The Traffic Police as the Press reports suggest, are
 exploiting the situation by forcing the operators to grease their palm.  The Committee feels that the Apex Court should have foreseen these realities being pronouncing an order.
                                                                                                                                (Para 17.3)
Action taken by the Ministry
            As per the Supreme Court’s Order on April 5, 2002 regarding plying of all public transport vehicles on CNG in Delhi, 800 diesel buses are being phased out every month.  The
 Government of National Capital Territory of Delhi (GNCTD) has equipped Delhi Transport Corporation (DTC) with a new fleet of 2130 CNG buses and it has been decided to
 purchase another 1000 CNG buses.  At the same time a number of buses are switching over to the CNG mode.  As on 23.6.2002, the total number of CNG buses plying on Delhi roads
 are about 5687.  State Transport Authority (STA) has already announced allotment of State carriage (Route) Permits for 1088 buses to ply on routes of their choice.  In addition, a

 scheme.
            Cases / instances of overcharging coming to notice are being dealt under the respective provisions of the Motor Vehicles Act. 
Comments
            While lthe Committee notes the reply, it observes that there is too much shortage of CNG Buses with DTC in the capital particualrly in trans yamuna and far flung colonies and
 the commuters continuing to suffer at the hands of privte transporters.
 
FOREST CONSERVATION, DEVELOPMENT & REGENERATION
Recommendation
The Committee is of the view that the Supreme Court order merely seeks to enforce the law laid down by the government.  Ban on felling of trees is permitted under the Forest
 Conservation Act, 1980 but only a working plan has been approved by the Union Ministry of Environment and Forests.  However, hardly any state appears to have implemented the
 provision.  The order was being misinterpreted to bureaucratise forests.   Since the order asks for a clear definition and identification of forest, some state government have taken this
 as an opportunity to gain control over large areas that remain ‘unclassified’ even today in the Northeast.  Forest officials, who wanted to do away with ‘unclassified’ forests, see this as
 a chance to alienate local people by claiming ownership, which were otherwise under the control of the community.
 (Para 19)
Action taken by the Ministry
            According to Forest (Conservation) Act 1980 diversion of any forest land for non forest activity, its assignment by way of lease to private persons or removal of vegetation
 thereupon requires approval of the Central Government under the provision of Section 2 of the Forest (Conservation) Act 1980.  The category under which forests fall have no
 relevance as far as application of this section of Forest (Conservation) Act 1980 is concerned.
            The directions of the Supreme court that every forest is worked according to a Working Plan basically goes in the favour of tribals because they continue to get access to the
 usufruct like, fuel, fodder, fruits, seeds, etc on a sustained basis.
It is submitted that out of 620 Working Plans remaining Working Plans are also in the process of preparation and sanction of the schemes for infrastructure support to the Forest
 Department would go a long way to expedite the process.
 Comments
            The Committee notes the reply.
Recommendation
            The Committee observes that forests in the country continue to be the victims of apathy and inadequate management in the country.  Besides the categorization of forests in
 reserved, protected and village forests, which are essentially administrative categories, does not help in their growth.  The “State of the Forest Report”. Does  not  give a detailed
 classification of India’s forests, the percentage of Natural or pristine and plantation areas, which would be of interest and use to both environmentalists and wood based industry.  The
 neglect of forests has resulted into loss of produce with reported smuggling by mafias, fires – which are termed deliberate.  This has affected their growth as it discourages
 participation of the people.  While tribals in some parts of the country have a right to enter the forests and take a part of the produce, mainly wood, for meeting their bonafide
 requirements, it appears to the Committee that this has not helped in the growth of forests because the denser the forest, the more is the alienation – tribal people are refused entry into
 forests; they cannot cultivate land they believe is theirs.  It is simple.  People want livelihood through forest but government wants control over forests.  The Committee therefore feels
 that it is time the forests are taken out completely from the bureaucratic control and managed by direct participation of the people preferably through cooperatives.  There is thus a
 need to take a dynamic initiative for the management of the forests so that the objectives of the forest policy could be met with direct involvement of the people in the management
 and growth of forests.
(Para 19.1)

Action taken by the Ministry
            Forest cover of the country is assessed biennially since 1987 by Forest Survey of India with the help of satellite data.  The result of the assessment are published as ‘State of
 Forest Report’.  The assessment is done on the basis of reflectance from the forest as per growth of the crown and its chlorophyll content which is broadly classified in three classes
 i.e. dense forest       ( 40% and above density),  open forest (between 10 to 40% density) and mangroves forest which have characteristic tone, texture and unique ecological functions. 
 The technology do not permit to give the extent of natural or pristine forests in the country.  However, latest State of Forest Report, 1999 gives details about the total cumulative
 plantation area in various States on the basis of Reports compiled by the Ministry from the information furnished by the State Governments. 
            The JFM Programme of the ministry has strong presence in the tribal areas and around 12 lakhs (of the total 28 lakhs) tribal families in the management of forest through 63000
 JFM Committees covering an area of 14 mha of forests.  The programme has empowered people to manage the forests by themselves through village level institution.
Comments
            The Committee observes that the provision of the Forest (Conservation) Act, 1980 should not be invoked to alienate the people who had been living in the forests for a long
 time.  The Committee reiterates that with the active participation of the local people, the forest laws can be better implemented.
            Though the Committee feels that Governments move to alienate the tribal people is against their right to livelihood.
Recommendation
            The Committee further observes that the Forest (Conservation) Act is only regulatory in nature and has enough flexibility to meet the development needs of the State
 Government.  Therefore, there is no need to amend the Forest (Conservation) Act.  However, there is a need to re-examine issues under the Indian Forest Act, 1927 so that it takes care
 of the definition of forests.
                                    (Para 21)
Action taken by the Ministry
            The revision of India Forest Act, 1927 is under active consideration of the Ministry in which various directions of the Hon’ble Court have been examined.  Comments of
 various Ministries on the draft of the Indian Forest Act are under active examination of the Ministry.
Comments
            The Committee notes the reply.
 
SUNDERBAN MANGROVES
Recommendation
            The Committee is of the view that the entire Sunderbans is one eco-system and for wild animals, physical boundaries have no relevance.  The tigers move in their entire home
 range, irrespective of these boundaries.  If the food availability is improved and habitat is better managed, the home ranges get reduced and trans-boundary migration gets minimised. 
 However, in the interest of the long term conservation of Sunderbans, the Ministry of Environment & Forests should devise Management Plans which may involve joint effort of India
 and Bangladesh.
(Para 23)
Action taken by the Ministry
            An umbrella project covering Sundarban both in India and Bangladesh addressing conservation issues and the stake holder communities is being launched.  This project is titled
 ‘Biodiversity Management in Sundarbans’ and is funded by UNEP/UNDP.  The project has an ecosystem approach and would lead to an integrated Conservation Development Project
 for Sunderbans in both States.  GEF fund would be leveraged for the project.
Comments
            The Committee is happy to note that both India and Bangladesh are working together to protect the eco-system and Biodiversity of Sunderban.  However, the Committee feels
 that as the deterioration of Sunderban affects both countries, there should be a workable and coordinated approach to be followed in order to save Sunderbans.
BIOMEDICAL WASTE MANAGEMENT
Recommendation
            The Committee recommends that the Ministry should co-ordinate with the State Governments / State Pollution Control Boards (SPCBs) to ensure that Bio-medical waste
 generating units are set up along with the treatment facilities and they obtain authorisation from the SPCBs.
(Para 25)
Action taken by the Ministry
            The Committee has suggested that the Ministry should co-ordinate with State Government/State Pollution Control Board (SPCBs) to ensure that all Biomedical Waste
 generating units obtain authorization and set up treatment facilities.  The Ministry of Environment  & Forests has constituted a Steering Committee to examine the issues pertaining to
 the implementation of Bio-medical Wastes (Management and Handling) Rules, 1998 & amendments thereof.  A meeting of the Steering Committee is being held on 24 July 2002 in
 which, inter-alia, the status of implementation of the Rules including issuing of authorizations, setting up of common treatment facilities for the benefit of small hospitals, etc., would
 be reviewed.  Depending on policy decisions taken in the meeting, the mater would be pursued with the State Governments and State Pollution Control Boards.

R E P O R T
 
The world over environmental degradation has assumed alarming proportions.  Concerns for preservation of
 environment constitute the defining feature of our age.  Our first Prime Minister Pandit Jawaharlal Nehru while
 remaining a moving force behind the establishment of heavy industrial enterprises and hydroelectric projects had also
 articulated the needs for protection of environment.  In a letter to the Chief Ministers on 15 August, 1957 he observed,
 “I should like to refer to something which I think is rather important and which, perhaps, has not received much
 attention.  We want to exploit as well as conserve our natural resources. Sometimes the desire to exploit them outruns
 discretion and we forget the part of conservation.” He further added, “We have many large scale river valley projects
 which are carefully worked out by our engineers.  I wonder however, how much thought is given before the project is
 launched, to having an ecological survey of the area and to find out what the effect would be on the drainage system or
 to the flora and fauna of that area.  It would be desirable to have such an ecological survey of these areas before the
 project is launched and thus to avoid the imbalance of nature.”  Establishment of the Ministry of Environment and
 Forests in 1985 as the nodal Ministry in the Government for the planning, promotion, coordination and overseeing the
 implementation of various schemes relating to environment and forests remained at the heart of our efforts to
 effectively address the challenges of the deteriorating environmental situation.  While the Ministry is entrusted with the
 responsibilities of conservation and survey of flora, fauna, forests and wildlife, its functions and jurisdiction also
 encompass numerous other activities such as promotion of afforestation, regeneration of degraded areas, prevention and
 control of pollution and overall protection of environment.  By assessing the impact of developmental projects on the
 environment, by extending assistance to organizations engaged in implementing environmental and forestry

ENVIRONMENTAL PROTECTION OF TAJ MAHAL
10.       The Committee was informed that in pursuance of directions of the Apex Court , Ministry of Environment &
 Forests has taken up the    work of Environmental Protection of the Taj Mahal. The work will be implemented through
 State Government of Uttar Pradesh and Ministries concerned.  The work also involves making of a green belt around
 the Taj Mahal. It is proposed that from  Tenth Plan onwards, the scheme would be expanded to cover other important
 Heritage sites.
11.       The Committee was apprised that ten projects under the Taj Protection Mission Programme which aims at
 improving electric supply, water supply, solid waste management, roads of Agra city were approved and are at different
 stages of implementation.  To reduce and contain pollution, construction of a by-pass for diverting the vehicular traffic
 is also being implemented.   Besides these ten projects, seven other priority projects as recommended by the Mission
 Management Board constituted under the Programme, are also being considered. These include a Heritage Corridor in
 the Taj Trapezium Zone, Automatic Air Monitoring Station, Hazardous Waste Secured Land-fill site for Agra &
 Mathura, common treatment facility for treatment of biomedical waste at Agra, creating public awareness in the Taj
 Trapezium, etc.  The EFC Memo of these projects has been circulated and will be finalized soon.  The Mission
 Management Board, Central Pollution Control Board and the Ministry are regularly monitoring the progress of
 implementation of the projects formulated under this scheme.  The annual average level of Sulphur Dioxide has come
 down from 23mg/m3 in 1992 to 4.5 mg/m3 in 2002 and SPM level from 438 in 1992 to 385 in 2002.  The Nitrogen
 Oxide level has increased from 15mg/m3 in 1992 to 21.7 mg/m3 in 2002.   It has been observed that hydrogen sulphide
 which generate from the swamp of river Yamuna is causing more damage to the Taj.
12.       The protection of the Taj Mahal has been a major priority and constant efforts are required to save the
 monument. The Committee feels that concerted effort should be taken for the protection of the Taj which suffered
 substantial damage due to pollution. The Committee recommends that instead of involving multiple agencies for the
 protection of Taj, a constituent body be formed which would be responsible for coordination with all allied agencies,
 supported by a strong legal framework for effective implementation of the policies undertaken.

 standards by preventing pollution load reaching the river by undertaking works like (i) interception & diversion works

14.       Under this scheme, polluted stretches of major rivers have been identified for sewage collection and treatment. 
 At present, 153 towns have been considered under the National River Conservation Plan (NRCP), out of which 74
 towns are located on Ganga, and 21 on Yamuna.  This project was started with 100 per cent funding by the Centre. 
 However, given resource constraints, states have to share 30 per cent of the cost during the Tenth Plan.
15.       The first River Action Plan was taken up in 1985 under the NRCP as the Ganga Action Plan (GAP) to improve
 the water quality of the River Ganga.  An amount of Rs.452 crores has been spent on the GAP Phase-I.  The entire
 funding has been provided by the Central Government.  It was initially expected that programme would be completed
 in 6-7 years.  However, it has been delayed considerably due to land acquisition problems, court litigation and lack of
 experience in implementing a programme of this nature and magnitude. The work under NRCP, including that of GAP
 are expected to cost Rs.3780.00. Till January, 2002, Rs.1,295 crores has been spent on the scheme.  About 45 per cent
 of the cleaning of the Ganga has been completed.  However, overall progress is poor because of delays in land
 acquisition and slow pace of work by municipal corporations.
16.       GAP Phase-I,  launched in 1985,  was completed on 31.3.2000 at  a total cost of Rs.452 crores, although two
 projects of sewage treatment plants in Bihar have not been completed so far due to problems of litigation on the land
 proposed for these facilities.  Under this plan, a sewage treatment capacity of 865 million litres per day (mld) has been
 created which will become 882 mld against the target of 873 mld after the remaining two sewage treatment plants are
 completed in Bihar.  This will account for about 35% of the pollution load presently reaching the Ganga.
17.       The Committee was informed by the Ministry that despite the problems of operation & maintenance (O&M) of
 assets created under GAP Phase-I the water quality of the river has shown improvement over the pre-GAP period water
 quality.  It is seen that in 1986, the Bio-Chemical Oxygen Demand (BOD) which is an indicator of pollution of river
 water quality was ranging from 5.5 to 15.5 mg/I in the critical stretch of Ganga from Kannauj to Varanasi.  As against
 this, the value of BOD in 2002 in the stretch of Kannauj to Kanpur was ranging from 1.2 to 4.9 mg/I and that of
 Allahabad to Varanasi from 2.5 to 3.8 mg/I.
18.       In the year 2000, fifteen years after the implementation of the Ganga Action Plan, the Norwegian Institute for
 Water Research, after analysing the Ganga water observed that water of Ganga is polluted with concentration of
 Chemical Oxygen Demand twice as high and the concentration of chrome a thousand times higher compared to
 untreated sewer in Norway. On the occasion of Makar Sankranti (14
th January, 2003) and Mauni  Amavasya (1st
 February, 2003) some group of  sadhus protested strongly about the pollution of Ganga at Sangam caused by discharge
 of industrial effluents from factories upstream  of Kanpur. Secretary, Ministry of Environment and Forests discussed
 the matter with the Chairman, UPPCB and directed that punitive action should be taken against the defaulting
 distilleries and industrial units which created the situation and report compliance.
19.       Since Ganga Action Plan Phase-I did not cover the pollution load of Ganga fully, GAP Phase-II, which includes
 river Ganga and its major tributaries viz. Yamuna, Gomti and Damodar was approved in stages between 1993 and
 1996. It covers pollution abatement  works in 95 towns spread over 7 States viz.  Uttar Pradesh, Haryanan, Delhi,
 Uttaranchal, Bihar, West Bengal and Jharkhand.  The present approved cost of GAP Phase-II is Rs.1499 crores against
 which an expenditure of Rs.763.30 crores has been incurred so far.  The quantity of waste water to be treated under
 GAP Phase-II is about 1860 mld out of which a capacity to treat 728 mld has been created under Yamuna Action Plan
 Phase-I on account of completion of works in Haryana, Uttar Pradesh and Delhi funded by Japan Bank for International
 Cooperation (JBIC).  It may be mentioned that six towns in Haryana and eight towns in U.P will have facilities for
 treatment.  Works in the six additional towns in Haryana which are not covered under the  JBIC assistance are in
 different stages of implementation.
20.       The Committee was informed that the operation and maintenance of various pollution abatement works
 constructed under GAP Phase-I and GAP Phase-II is the responsibility of the respective State Governments as
 committed by them.  However, adequate funds are not being provided in time by all the state Governments including
 the UP government for O&M.   This matter is being constantly pursued with them, as a result of which of UP
 Government has provided Rs.10.70 crores recently to UP Jal Nigam for O&M.  They have also promised that in future
 funds would be regularly provided for proper O&M of assets created under the river action plans.

22.       The Committee observes that for any plan or programme regarding cleaning of rivers of such a magnitude as
 Ganga, to succeed, it is necessary to have a meticulous planning.  Any delay in its execution is bound to result in the
 plan going awry.  More so, because the parameters regarding the size of the population and the extent of urbanization
 etc., which would have been taken into account at the stage of planning, are subject to rapid changes in a country like
 India.  Hence, timely execution is crucial for such programmes or else we would suffer severe consequences of
 contamination of our rivers on the banks of which our civilization began and flourished.
23.       The Committee is constrained to observe that even after nearly two decades of  Ganga Action Plan (GAP)-I, the
 pollution levels at various places in the River has more or less remained the same. It is seen that every programme
 failed to achieve its stipulated objectives and proved ineffective. The Committee feels that a strong administrative will
 is needed to implement such plans.
24.       The Committee recommends that punitive action should be taken against the defaulting distilleries and industrial
 units which are responsible for the problem. The Committee also recommends that a programme to monitor the
 performance should be introduced and it should be reviewed quarterly.  The Committee also feels that the non-
availability of funds in the Tenth Plan would become a major constraint to effectively address the problem of cleaning
 rivers.  The Committee has been apprised that the Ministry of Environment and Forests has written a letter to the Prime
 Minister to augment  the Tenth Plan outlay to undertake the remaining works of river pollution in Ganges.  The
 Committee observes that efforts for cleaning of our rivers must not be restrained by lack of availability of funds.

GENERAL OBSERVATION
36.       The Committee is of the view that the present status of the river cleansing programme is not satisfactory and
 under these circumstances it would not be possible to achieve the target of clearing all the rivers by 2007.  All the
 phase-wise programmes need to be monitored and the Measure of Performance (MOP) should be introduced to review

37.       In a recent article written jointly by Shri Nitin Desai of the UN Department of Economic and Social Affairs; 
 Mark Malloch Brown of UN Development Programme; Klaus Toepffer of UN Environment Programme; Koichiro
 Matsuura of UNESCO, Anna Tribaijuka of UN-Habitat; Carlo Bellamy of UNICEF and Hans Van Ginkel of UN
 University the following has been written which has a bearing on the cleaning of our rivers.
“There are signs of hope.  Up until the middle of the last century many of the rivers on continents like North America
 and Europe and especially those running through big industrial areas were so polluted that they were classed as “dead”. 
 Some were so polluted that the water could be used as ink, and noxious gases, bubbling up from their depths, could be
 ignited by a match.  Today after billions of dollars of investment in water treatment and agreements with industry on
 effluents, fish are again spawning and migrating to their upper reaches through these now relatively clean estuaries and
 tributaries.  The Thames in Britain was officially declared a dead river half a century ago, save for a few mud worms. 
 Today some 120 species including migrating salmon can be found.”
38.       The Committee therefore feels that efforts at the government and community levels must be redoubled to clean
 our rivers.

 body shampooing (vii) frolicking   (viii) acceptance of donations into the rivers (ix) obscenity (x) discarding or cleaning
 of garments (xi) beating and swimming across.  The Committee recommends that many of these can be incorporated by

40.       The Wildlife Sector provides assistance to the State Governments for the development of National Parks &

 financial assistance to 20 additional Protected Areas during 2003-04.  For species conservation programmes like Project
 Tiger and project Elephant, enhanced allocations are required for infrastructure, habitat improvement, anti-poaching
 drives and mitigating man-animal conflicts.  Wildlife Institute of India has been allocated an additional grant of Rs.1
 crores for completing unfinished works.

 been constituted under the Project Elephant initiated in 1991.  These projects have not only benefited the main species
 but have led to the amelioration of eco-systems and this is reflected in re-vitalization of aquifers and security to the
 range of floral and faunal diversity.  The estimated population on cardinal species is:
            Tiger                Over 3,500
            Elephant           Over 27,000
            Asiatic Lion      Over 300
            Rhinoceros       Over 1,700

 5% of the total area of our country.  Outside the Protected Areas, the anti poaching infrastructure is weak and the wild
 animals are thus vulnerable to poaching. Moreover the budgetary support has been inadequate to meet even the basic
 minimum needs of this sector.

53.       In view of the steady depletion of forest resources and increasing deforestation, the Committee is of the view

 programme. In the absence of any direct benefit and sufficient authority for the local community, there would be very
 little incentive for them to participate in any activity of the Ministry. Therefore, the Committee recommends that the
 Joint Forest Management (JFM) programme should be vigorously pursued by involving women and tribals to protect
 and regenerate degraded forests. Moreover non-timber forest produce should also be properly regenerated, harvested,
 processed and marketed for improving the economy of forest-dwellers.

INDUSTRIAL AND HAZARDOUS WASTE
66.       Hazardous waste includes sludge contaminated with heavy metals, wastes from paints, dyes and organic
 chemical units and highly acidic and alkaline wastes.  The major hazardous waste generating industries are petroleum
 and petro-chemicals, pharmaceuticals, pesticides, paint and dyes, fertilizers, inorganic chemicals and general
 engineering industries etc.  The presence of toxic chemicals in solid/liquid effluents from industries and other activities
 leads to ground water contamination. 
67.       The Committee was informed that at present, around 7.2 mt of hazardous waste are generated in the country, out
 of which, according to one estimate, 1.4 mt re recyclable, 0.1 mt to be incinerated and 5.2 mt to be disposed on land. 
 The hazardous waste of 5.3 mt would  require about Rs.1,600 crores a year for treatment and disposal at an estimated
 rate of Rs.3,000 tonne.  In addition, land required for disposal will be around 1km   taking a depth of 4 m and density of
 disposal as 1.2 tonnes/m3.
68.       The Committee was also informed that the Water Act, 1974  and Air Act, 1981 were not sufficient to regulate
 the disposal of hazardous waster and has called for the formulation of the Hazardous Waste Management and Handling
 rules, 1989.  Since then, efforts to make an inventory of hazardous waste were initiated. The initiatives taken in this
 direction are:
Estimate of the hazardous waste inventory in various States and identification of disposal sites based on environment
 impact assessment.
CPCB has prepared a ready reckoner to provide information on the source of the hazardous waste, their characteristics
 and the methods for recycling and disposal.
Training programmes have been organized to deal with hazardous waste management.
Import of hazardous waste containing toxic metals like beryllium, selenium, chromium, thallium, pesticides etc. have
 been restricted on the recommendations of an Expert Committee.
Export and import of waste containing cyanide, mercury and arsenic have been prohibited since December 1996.
The import of waste oil and metals such as brass, zinc and lead for processing to recover resources is fully regulated by
 the Ministry of Environment and Forests.
69.       Though the Committee appreciates the efforts being taken by the Ministry for handling of industrial & hazardous
 waste, it proposes that parameters to assess the impact of measures adopted should be evolved to enable the country to
 know their effect vis-à-vis the money being invested in this highly important programme.  It is hoped that the
 Department shall be able to let the Committee know of the nature and periodicity of such monitoring.

 facilities and infrastructure to facilitate research and training of manpower. The Environmental Research Programme
 specially deals with problems related to air, water and soil pollution and development of suitable cost effective
 technology for abatement of pollution load in the environment .  Emphasis is given on development of eco-friendly, 
 biological and other interventions for prevention of pollution and development of strategies/technologies, instruments
 etc.  Many projects have been taken for development of biodegradable plastics. Besides, emphasis has been laid on the
 development of clean technologies.  Many studies have been undertaken to reduce the impact of mining on
 environment. Waste recycling and resource recovery from waste along with development of eco-friendly and cleaner
 technology are given due priority.
74.       To strengthen the system of forestry research in India, the Indian Council of Forestry Research and Education
 (ICFRE) is entrusted to undertake, aid , promote and coordinate forestry research and its application; function as a
 clearing house for research results and information; and disseminate technology.  ICFRE imparts forestry education and
 is developing forestry curricula at various levels to accelerate the pace of research and to provide expertise in different
 fields of forestry research.  Universities providing forestry education are being given grants-in-aid for strengthening
 their infrastructure and technical capabilities.  Opportunities are also being provided for furthering the academic
 advancement of foresters/scientists/academicians in the field of forestry.
75.       During the year 2003-04 a budgetary provision of Rs.17.00 crores in plan side and Rs.0.02 crores in non-plan
 side has been made.
76.       The Committee recommends  that talented persons may be encouraged with remunerative schemes and attractive
 pay scales to do research on environment issues.  Besides, Ministry should also consider introducing research
 scholarships to school leaving students in order to motivate them to join frontier areas of research in the field of
 environment.  These initiatives may help in accelerating the pace of environmental research for the development of a
 strong knowledge base and its application for society at large. Efforts should also be made to include environment as a
 formal subject in the schools / professional management courses.
77.       The Committee observed that the organisations like Botanical Survey of India, Zoological Survey of India and
 other organisation under the control  of Ministry of Environment and Forests should be given more autonomy in
 implementing their plans.

 awareness and training.  Therefore, it recommends that such programmes may be started for educating and sensitizing
 people about environmental issues and making them conscious about their own roles in protecting nature and

NATIONAL FOREST COMMISSION
79.       The constitution of National Forest Commission has been notified on 7.2.2003 by the Ministry of Environment
 & Forests and Wildlife Sector with the following terms of reference:
Review and assess the existing policy and legal framework and their impact in a holistic manner from the ecological,
 scientific, economic, social and cultural viewpoint.
Examine the current status of forest administration and the forestry institutions both on all India and State level to meet
 the emerging needs of the civil society.
Make recommendations indicating policy options for achieving sustainable forest and wildlife management and
 development, bio-diversity conservation and ecological security.
Suggest ways and means to make forest administration more effective with a view to help to achieve the above policy
 options.
Establish meaningful partnership and interface between forestry management and local communities including tribals.
80.       The Commission will work under the administrative control of the Ministry of Environment & Forests and will
 be given funds from the budget of the Ministry for its smooth functioning.
81.       For effective implementation of the policies and programmes of the Ministry the Committee feels that instead of
 bureaucrats more and more technocrats and scientists should be associated.
82.       An absurd implementation of a rule to conserve the seacoast from pollution was brought to the notice of the
 Committee.  The Construction of toilets along the sea coast is prohibited by rule.  Not even mobile toilets are permitted.
 The result is that people defecate along the beaches thus leading to stink & high pollution on thebeaches.  This rule
 evidently  needs to be reviewed immediately. The objective is to prevent  pollution of beaches and not just enforce the
 rules rigidly thus defeating the very objective.
83.       The Committee was informed about toilets on the Goa beaches.  It was informed that funds have been released
 for the construction of toilets from the MPs funds but permission has not been granted to construct them.  The
 Committee therefore recommends that immediate action may be taken in this regard and construction of toilets should
 be permitted to maintain cleanliness of beaches. Alternatively mobile toilets in sufficient numbers should be placed on
 all beaches of the country where people throng in large numbers.

 of various important programmes and projects administered by it, the Committee recommends that the budgetary
 allocation of      Rs.1124.59 crores, as sought by the Ministry of Environment & Forests for the year 2003-04, under
 Demand No.  29, may be approved.
SUMMARY OF THE RECOMMENDATIONS
1.         The Committee recommends that at R.E. stage curtailment of funds for the Ministry may be avoided so as to
 enable  the smooth and unhindered implementation of programmes  and policies of the Ministry.  The Committee also
 recommends that the programmes and policies may be effectively and substantially implemented at the ground   level
 so as to get the desired result.
(Para 7)
2.         The protection of the Taj Mahal has been a major priority and constant efforts are required to save the
 monument. The Committee feels that concerted effort should be taken for the protection of the Taj which suffered
 substantial damage due to pollution. The Committee recommends that instead of involving multiple agencies for the
 protection of Taj, a constituent body be formed which would be responsible for coordination with all allied agencies,
 supported by a strong legal framework for effective implementation of the policies undertaken. 
(Para 12)
3.         The Committee observes that for any plan or programme regarding cleaning of rivers of such a magnitude as
 Ganga, to succeed, it is necessary to have a meticulous planning.  Any delay in its execution is bound to result in the
 plan going awry.  More so, because the parameters regarding the size of the population and the extent of urbanization
 etc., which would have been taken into account at the stage of planning, are subject to rapid changes in a country like
 India.  Hence, timely execution is crucial for such programmes or else we would suffer severe consequences of
 contamination of our rivers on the banks of which our civilization began and flourished.
(Para 22)
4.         The Committee is constrained to observe that even after nearly two decades of  Ganga Action Plan (GAP)-I, the
 pollution levels at various places in the River has more or less remained the same. It is seen that every programme
 failed to achieve its stipulated objectives and proved ineffective. The Committee feels that a strong administrative will

(Para 23)
5.         The Committee recommends that punitive action should be taken against the defaulting distilleries and industrial
 units which are responsible for the problem. The Committee also recommends that a programme to monitor the
 performance should be introduced and it should be reviewed quarterly.  The Committee also feels that the non-
availability of funds in the Tenth Plan would become a major constraint to effectively address the problem of cleaning
 rivers.  The Committee has been apprised that the Ministry of Environment and Forests has written a letter to the Prime
 Minister to augment  the Tenth Plan outlay to undertake the remaining works of river pollution in Ganges.  The
 Committee observes that efforts for cleaning of our rivers must not be restrained by lack of availability of funds.
            Tests of pollution levels to be carried out in the presence of 2 to 5 Members of the Standing Committee.  In the
 light of rusty red water at Sangam at Prayag in February 2003, the degree of decrease in pollution of Ganga looks
 unreal and question arises as to the spots that are chosen to test the waters.
(Para 24)
 
6.         The Committee is deeply perturbed to note that the Yamuna water at Delhi continues to be stinking and dirty.  It
 notes with concernthat  waste is still dumped in the Yamuna river through drains. The Committee notes with anxiety
 that cleaning of sewerage has become erratic and the functioning of the sewage treatment plants have been stalled due
 to frequent power cuts or some other reason.  These STPs cannot afford to be dysfunctional  for even a minute and the
 Committee would like to knowthe arrangements for captive power gensets.  It also noted with concern about the lack of
 public awareness and public participation in the cleaning of rivers. The Committee is, therefore, of the view that the
 cleansing of Yamuna has to go beyond cosmetic measures like removal of slums along the banks and greening of
 banks. Perhaps the more concrete solution is to prevent the drainage wastes from entering  the river and to ensure the
 increase of the flow of  fresh water. The Committee would also like to know if the Delhi Government/Central
 Government have obtained an extension of time from the Supreme Court  for compliance of its order which was to be
 implemented by 31.3.2003 or are the Governments responsible for non-compliance, therefore, committing  contempt of
 the Supreme Court. 
(Para 34)
7.         The Committee is also of the view that the Ministry in coordination with the State Government of Uttar Pradesh,
 Haryana and Delhi should plan a strategy for augmentation of water resources in the upper stretches of the Yamuna and
 for conserving water both for domestic and irrigational purposes. 
(Para 35)
8.         The Committee is of the view that the present status of the river cleansing programme is not satisfactory and
 under these circumstances it would not be possible to achieve the target of clearing all the rivers by 2007.  All the
 phase-wise programmes need to be monitored and the Measure of Performance (MOP) should be introduced to review
 the cleaning activities.
(Para 36)
9.         The Committee therefore feels that efforts at the government and community levels must be redoubled to clean
 our rivers.
(Para 38)
10.       Our rivers have been revered throughout ages. Our tradition invested divinity with our rivers.  Pages of our
 mythologies show as to how norms were prescribed to keep the water of the Ganges clean.  The Committee observed
 that the Bramhanda Purna prohibited thirteen actions to maintain the purity of the Ganges. Some of these are (i)
 defecations (ii) ablutions (iii) discharge of waste water (iv) throwing of used floral offerings (v) rubbing of filth (vi)
 body shampooing (vii) frolicking                (viii) acceptance of donations into the rivers (ix) obscenity (x) discarding or
 cleaning of garments (xi) beating and swimming across.  The Committee recommends that many of these can be
 incorporated by the Ministry in their norms for prohibiting activities to keep the Ganges clean.   
  (Para 39)
11.       The Committee is happy to note that at present, there are 27 tiger reserves covering an area of 0.38 lakh sq km in
 17 States. However, there is need to strengthen anti-poaching camps, mobile squads, capacity building of frontline staff
 in intelligence gathering and detection and successful prosecution of cases. Necessary infrastructure in this regard has
 to be strengthened. About one lakh sq km area is covered under the Project Elephant. But the

Committee is constrained to observe that there has been considerable increase in human-elephant conflict and crop
 raiding by elephants. Therefore, the main thrust in the Tenth Plan should be on protecting existing elephant habitat from

12.       Shortage of water in forest areas due to drought or any other reason compel animals to enter the villages to
 quench their thirst. In the process they destroy the crops and kill people. The Ministry normally gives compensation to
 the affected persons. The Committee feels that the way of compensation is not the solution to the problem. The

13.       In view of the steady depletion of forest resources and increasing deforestation, the Committee is of the view
 that the active and willing participation of local communities is necessary for the success of any forest regeneration
 programme. In the absence of any direct benefit and sufficient authority for the local community, there would be very
 little incentive for them to participate in any activity of the Ministry. Therefore, the Committee recommends that the
 Joint Forest Management (JFM) programme should be vigorously pursued by involving women and tribals to protect
 and regenerate degraded forests. Moreover non-timber forest produce should also be properly regenerated, harvested,
 processed and marketed for improving the economy of forest-dwellers.
(Para 53)
14.       The Committee recommends that the rural people, particularly, women and the tribal community have an
 intimate knowledge of forest products, their species, their growth characteristics, utility, medicinal value, etc.  They are
 also well informed about the species that need to be planted in a given locality to satisfy specific requirements of fuel,
 fodder, timber, and other non-wood forest products.  This knowledge should be utilized under the JFM for the larger
 cause of environmental protection and benefit of the community.  The progress made in measurable terms should be
 reported to Parliament in the Department’s Annual Report on the successof JFM scheme on these specific points. This
 will be an important step for empowerment of these people. There is also need to give thrust to it during the Tenth
 Plan.  However, its strengths and weaknesses need to be identified.
(Para 54)
15.       The Committee was given to understand that one of the goals of the Ministry is to increase the forest cover of the
 country upto 25% by 2007 and 33% by 2012. The Committee appreciates the goal set out by the Ministry but is of the
 view that a blanket approach should not be adopted in this regard. Some States already have a forest cover in excess of
 33% and complain about hampering of development activities due to thick forest cover. Therefore, the policy of
 increasing forest cover should be implemented only in those states which are short of the stipulated target so that a
 balanced proportion of forest cover can be maintained in all parts of the country. 
(Para 55)
16.       The Committee has noted that there was a programme in the 1980s when women used to do social forestry and
 grow and supply seedlings for which they were paid. The Ministry has withdrawn this scheme and given it to forest
 contractors. The Committee recommends that it should be restored to woman Self Help groups.
 (Para 56)
17.       The Committee notes that active involvement of people in the development of the forestry sector has to be
 further strengthened.  The destruction and depletion of forests will not only lead to loss of our vegetation but will also
 result in widespread deterioration of environment with fatal consequences to the very existence of all forms of life. 
 There is, however, much to be done in this area as the phenomenon of cutting of trees, removal of precious timber and
 forest fires continues unabated.  The problem cannot be overcome unless a consciousness is built among the people that
 the forests belong to them and they belong to the forests and the feeling of alienation among the tribals and local
 population goes.  The Committee feels that the local population (including tribals) residing in the forest areas should be
 actively associated with the management of forests and allowed to share the its products,
 without in any way
 compromising the preservation of our national forests.  If this happens, many of the ills currently afflicting our forests
 will disappear.  The Ministry should devise steps to inculcate among them a sense of belonging and commitment to
 forests.  People performing outstanding work in their area should be suitably rewarded and honoured at an appropriate
 forum.
(Para 60)
18.       The Committee also recommends that the vacancies of forest guards needs to be filled immediately in order to
 strengthen the manpower requirements of the forest Department to enforce forest protection at the ground level.
(Para 61)

INTRODUCTION

 Environment & Forests, having been authorised by the Committee to present the Report on its behalf, present this One
 Hundred-Thirteenth Report of the Committee.  This Report deals with the detailed Demands for Grants (2003-2004) of
 the Department of Scientific & Industrial Research (Demand No.81).
2.         In the meeting of the Committee held on the 24 th March, 2003 the Secretary and other Officers of the Department
 of Scientific & Industrial Research gave an overview of the various activities of the Department and the Members sought
 clarifications on various aspects of the performance of the Department to enable it to scrutinise the Demands for Grants.

R E P O R T
            Long years back while fighting for freedom Mahatma Gandhi, the father of our nation had conjured up a vision of
 India studded with research laboratories for the service of her people.  Establishment of the Council for Scientific and
 Industrial Research in 1942 was a landmark event in our quest for using science and technology, for national
 reconstruction.  During sixty years of its existence it has emerged as one of the largest R&D organizations in the world for
 scientific and industrial research.  In spite of budgetary constraints and many other bottlenecks the CSIR has striven to
 achieve excellence in promoting and applying science for nation building.  Responding to the new challenges of our
 society, economy and international environment it has now remained in the forefront of forging science-business
 partnerships.  It is now awake to the new norms of competition and innovation and is moving towards the path of self-
financing by generation of its own funds.  After the formation of a separate   Ministry of Science and Technology on
 January 4, 1985 the Department of Scientific & Industrial Research became part of this Ministry.  Business allocated to
 this Department under the Notification is: All matters concerning the Council of Scientific and Industrial Research
 (CSIR), National Research Development Corporation (NRDC), Central Electronics Limited (CEL), National Information
 System on Science and Technology (NISSAT), Registration and Recognition of R&D Units, Matters relating to
 UNCTAD and WIPO, National register for foreign collaborations, the Creation of a pool for temporary placement of
 Indian Scientists and Technologists and  National register of Scientific Manpower.

COUNCIL OF SCIENTIFIC & INDUSTRIAL RESEARCH
4.         The Council of Scientific and Industrial Research (CSIR), an autonomous organization with its 38 laboratories and
 fifty outreach, centers has recently completed sixty years of their existence. CSIR has emerged as a scientific institution
 which has been highly acclaimed inside and outside India.  It aims at achieving global excellence with local relevance; it
 symbolizes a culture that links science with society through technology , industrial manufacture, and dissemination of
 scientific temper among people.
5.         The Committee was informed that during the Ninth Five Year Plan, CSIR had effected wide spread changes to
 meet the challenges of economic reform, introduction of new industrial and trade policies and liberalization of economy.
 It also effected a reorientation of its programmes with the aim to make CSIR more responsive and move towards a self
 sustaining R&D institution. The cardinal feature of the Ninth Five Year Plan was the White Paper on CSIR focusing on its
 Vision and Strategy. Some of the reform process effected relate to re-engineering of the organizational structure; linking
 research to market place; mobilizing and optimizing the resources base; creating conducive and workable infrastructure
 and investing in high quality science that would be a harbinger of future technologies.
6.         As a result, CSIR stands today amongst the finest publicly funded scientific industrial research establishments of
 the whole world. As the nation’s strongest holder of intellectual property rights (IPR), it leads the way in protecting
 traditional knowledge strength while adding to the new IPR capital.   CSIR today ranks second amongst the major PCT
 applicants from developing countries at USPTO.
7.         CSIR has also promoted excellence in science and is the only S&T organization which had nurtured and supported
 human-tech from 16 to 65 years of age through numerous schemes on human resource for scientific research.  CSIR’s
 mission is to provide scientific industrial R&D that maximizes the economic, environmental & societal benefits for the
 people of India.
8.         The detailed functions assigned to the Council are:
      i.            Promotion, guidance and coordination of scientific and industrial research in India, including the institution
 and financing of specific researches;
      ii.            Establishment or development and assistance to special institutions or departments of existing institutions for
 scientific study of problems affecting particular industries and trade;
      iii.      Establishment and award of research studentships and fellowships;
      iv.            Utilization of the results of the researches conducted under the auspices of the Council towards the
 development of industries in the country and the payment of a share of royalties arising out of the development of

9.         The Committee was informed that the guiding principle for CSIR during the Tenth Five Year Plan would be to
 provide scientific industrial R&D that maximizes the economic, environmental and societal benefits for the people of
 India and accordingly, the Tenth Five Year Plan of CSIR and the Annual Plans have been formulated keeping in mind 8%
 growth rate envisaged by the Planning Commission and Government policy to invest 2% of GDP on Science &
 Technology. 
10.       CSIR seeks to foster the organizational values of: Excellence in science; Global competitiveness in technology
 based on high science; Local relevance in tune with socio-cultural and economic ethos of the people; and Innovation
 ranging in all the spheres of activities from science to technology and from management to financing.  These principles
 coupled with detailed analysis on strength, weakness, opportunities and threats carried out by CSIR laboratories were
 taken into consideration in deriving the opportunities for CSIR in the market place as well as for socio-economic
 development.
11.       The other factors which has bearing on CSIR programmes for the Annual Plans are: Responsibilities on CSIR
 arising out of International Intellectual Property Rights arena; continuous training and re-training of CSIR staff;
 advancement of knowledge through enlarging the scope of fellowships to trans-disciplinary areas and supporting basic
 research that dovetails with its own requirement and expansion of S&T to proliferate CSIR technologies to the masses.

14.       When the Department was asked by the Committee as to how the enhanced budgetary allocation would be helpful
 to promote its activities, it informed that the enhanced allocation of Rs.95.48 crores (Rs.80 crores plan and Rs.15.48
 crores under Non-Plan) would be helpful in meeting the demands of higher expenditure as successful concepts move
 towards commercialization/field implementation stage.  In the Tenth Plan, CSIR has focused attention on programmes of
 National Laboratories under the three categories viz. (i) continuously building & refurbishing competence at globally
 competitive level, skills and competency, in all scientific areas; (ii) taking up in house projects with well defined
 objectives, deliverables, time frame; and (iii) performing contract R&D for industry and other users to deal with problem
 through expertise gained over the years.  Accordingly, some well focused programmes/projects were identified and
 formulated with a view to synergising the competencies developed in laboratories and getting them implemented in a
 network mode.
15.            Explaining the reasons for reduction on allocation in R.E stage last year the Department informed that the
 projects, after formulation, were sent to the Planning Commission for “in-principle” approval.  This procedure took time
 as apart from coordination within CSIR laboratories, formal letters of approvals were also needed from participating
 concerned ministries before the “in principle” approval of Planning Commission could be obtained.  Thus, due to resource
 constraints and the delays in obtaining the “in principle” approval from the Planning Commission, the progress of
 expenditure was not commensurate with allocations. Finance ministry effected a cut of Rs.65 crores under the plan
 scheme at RE stage.
NATIONAL LABORATORIES
16.       CSIR today has a network of 38 Laboratories and 50 field stations/extension centres/regional centres located all
 over the country that undertake R&D in various S&T areas and disciplines. The extension and regional centres have been
 established to reach  out to the diverse users and disseminate knowledge and information on R&D capabilities, techniques
 and technologies developed by the National laboratories of CSIR.
17.       The Committee was informed that CSIR in the Tenth Five Year Plan (TFYP) would seek to further broaden and
 strengthen this trend and undertake more of its activities in the project mode by networking and alliancing on a Team
 India basis. The programmes of National Laboratories have been further categorized sectorally under the following
 sectors: Aerospace; Biology and Biotechnology; Chemical; Earth Resources and Natural Hazards Assessment; Ecology &
 Environment; Electronics and Instrumentation; Energy; Food & Food processing; Health Care, Drugs & Pharmaceuticals;
 Housing & Construction; Information Dissemination and Products; Leather; Materials, Metals, Minerals and
 Manufacturing and Rural Development so as to enable and facilitate an easy alignment with the overall ‘National
 Planning process’. The areas of thrust in these categories have been identified through interactions with various national
 agencies, government departments, industry associations and potential clients keeping in view the strengths and
 capabilities in the CSIR laboratories and the external opportunities. 
18.            Projects of the Tenth Five Year Plan have been evolved, over a period of one year, through interactive and
 repetitive consultations with the Steering Committee on S&T, Working Group for Tenth Five Year Plan, Sectoral
 Subgroup of the Working Group, Research Councils of the respective National Laboratories.  The evolution of the
 Projects, thus, has gone through a great deal of churning of vast S&T expertise available in the country and also in the
 concerned departments/agencies of the Government.
19.       When the Committee asked the Department whether they have identified any core areas for research activities for
 which an increased allocation for national laboratories have been sought the Committee was informed that CSIR has
 formulated programmes to be implemented in Network and Mission mode during the Tenth Plan.  The emphasis is on
 synergising the core competencies available at various laboratories.  The core areas identified include genomics &
 proteomics, integrative biology, herbal preparations for global positioning, bioinformatics, green technologies,
 nutraceuticals & nutragenomics, new approach to drug development, specialty materials, waster minimization through
 new routes, advanced manufacturing technologies, nano technology etc.
