National S&T Human Resource Development
22.       The Committee was informed that CSIR has initiated schemes to attract brightest of youth to science education and
 R&D as a career viz. CSIR Programme on Youth for Leadership for Science (CPYLS) and Shyama Prasad Mukherjee
 (SPM) Fellowships at school level & post graduate levels respectively. Through them CSIR provides support to higher
 institutions of learning on S&T.  It also supports research schemes for the development of science and technology in the
 country. It also provides fellowships and associateships for pursuing research by scholars.
23.       It will establish fellowships in trans-disciplinary areas.  In a calculated manner it will support researchers to come
 out of the areas where there are limited opportunities and challenges and enable them to rise to the new problems and
 opportunities offered by ever widening of scope of science and technology.   Since research scholars hardly seek
 opportunities for self employment and entrepreneurship they end up looking for employment opportunities in government
 R&D establishments.  CSIR would make efforts to inculcate a spirit of entrepreneurship   among research scholars to
 establish their own R&D enterprise through appropriate motivation, skills development and venture financing.  It also
 aims at enlarging CPYLS to attract bright school leaving children.
24.       The Committee was informed that CSIR would continue to upgrade extra mural human resources in diverse
 disciplines of S&T by providing appropriate fellowships in transdisciplinary areas. The Shyama Prasad Mukherjee awards
 were introduced to promote creativity and nurture talent at postgraduate level of science.
25.       The Committee reiterates its earlier recommendation made in 86
th Report that there is a need for reviewing and
 strengthening /revamping the existing S&T support systems in the universities and other educational institutions. The
 Committee is of the view that an agreement be reached with various financial institutions for providing loans to those
 research scholars for setting up their own enterprises.
Intellectual Property & Technology Management (IP&TM)
26.       CSIR today occupies the number one position in Indian & Foreign patent filings.  CSIR would stress to maintain its
 number one position of patent holder in India. It would create electronic/digital databases on CSIR’s IP & knowledge base
 holdings. It would also build capacity to defend and initiate action against patent infringement for which it could refurbish
 the skills and knowledgebase of those engaged in the IPR game and also advise policy makers appropriately.
27.       CSIR has been on the forefront of filing & managing IPR since its inception.  However a massive programme of
 education and skills acquisition on diverse aspects of IPR, innovation and technology management was mounted at the
 commencement of the Ninth Plan Period only. As a result most of the CSIR scientists are now IPR and R&D business
 savvy and literate.   The earlier operating slogan of CSIR 'patent, publish and prosper has since been enlarged to 'patent,
 publish, peddle and prosper" so as to derive value from the IPR portfolio. The laboratory-wise patent progress is given in
 the Annexure-II.
28.       The Committee was informed that It was CSIR that initiated the action with the US PTO for the re-examination
 and revocation of the patent granted on turmeric as a wound healing agent. This was followed by meticulous and
 strenuous efforts in compilation of voluminous scientific data. Finally it resulted in  successful revocation of the US
 Patent. This demonstrated CSIR's capabilities to understand the complex techno-legal-issues of IPR both defensively and
 aggressively and reassure the Indian public and policy makers of India's capacity and capability to meet the challenges of
 globalization and WTO.  Thereafter,  CSIR  have  globally  pioneered  the concept of
According ‘Traditional Knowledge' due recognition and privileged position in the IPR domain. Traditional Knowledge

INFRASTRUCTURE RENOVATION & REFURBISHMENT
35.       The Committee was informed that in 1997 CSIR was amongst the first to plan for V-SAT connectivity to all its
 laboratories.  It was established to some limited extent; however, the delays in implementation and the radical changes in
 communication set-up since then have made it imperative that it be upgraded into an efficient internet.  CSIR has been
 advising and assisting other organisations to take up computerization and the use of information technology but it has not
 benefited fully from the revolution, except in isolated pockets.  Thus the organizational benefits of the radical gains in
 productivity brought about by IT have not yet been realised.   The IT Task Force has also enjoined that  every
 organization devote  2 % of its outlay on IT. In order to inculcate an IT
 
Culture in the system, it would be assigned a driving role.  Internet connectivity to all the laboratories will be sought
 through a national level ISP including VPN solutions to establish a CUG (Closed User Group), high speed, satellite-based
 communication network, interconnecting around 100 nodes: Hqs & 39 labs and 50 field Centres to provide an “on-line”
 Management Information System (MIS) for: R&D Project management System; Technology Management System;
 Intellectual Property Management System, Human Resource Management System, Financial Accounting & Management
 System; Investment Management System.
36.       When the Committee asked the Department as to how the infrastructure renovation & refurbishment is different
 from the scheme on modernization undertaken during the ninth five year plan it was informed that in Infrastructure
 renovation & refurbishment emphasis was on renovation and refurbishing of infrastructure facilities  (e.g. old buildings,
 old electrical wirings, etc.) whereas in modernization the emphasis was on the modernization and upgradation of
 equipment and R&D facilities.
37.       The Committee asked the department to find out as to why adequate steps were not taken to improve the
 infrastructure for laboratories. It was informed that CSIR infrastructure was built or acquired more than thirty years ago
 and some of the laboratories like the CDRI, CFTRI, CSMCRI etc. are housed in palaces, which are centuries old.  The
 premises were converted into laboratories by carrying out only small renovations.  Most of the laboratories are thus not
 suited for modern day R&D especially in terms of Good Laboratory Practices, standardization of facilities as per ISO
 standards, NABL requirements for accreditation and certification, IT connectivity through LAN, WAN etc. Also many of
 them today are at a stage of dilapidation and pose safety hazards.  Most laboratory buildings need strengthening of
 foundations and roofs, revamping of electrical wiring and substations, better communications connectivity, lifts etc.  The
 38 CSIR Laboratories and 50 field centers are to be renovated and refurbished. Accordingly, the new scheme specifically
 dedicated to renovation & refurbishing has been initiated and an outlay Rs. 100 crore is placed during TFYP.
38.       The Committee feels that the state-of-art infrastructure / laboratories are extremely important to further augment
 and enrich our capabilities in the fields of science and technology so as to face the increasing challenges thrown up by
 intense research activities in many scientific and technological institutions across the globe.  The infrastructure should be
 seen as a strategic national resource and funding should be given on a continuing basis to maximize their effectiveness,

TECHNOLOGY PROMOTION, DEVELOPMENT AND UTILIZATION PROGRAMME
39.       The Committee was informed that Technology  Promotion, Development and Utilization Programmes has been
 formulated by merging some of the ninth Plan schemes as per the recommendation of the planning Commission under
 zero base budgeting exercise. The Schemes are: Research and Development by Industry  (RDI); Programme  Aimed at
 Technological Self-reliance (PASTER) and Scheme to Enhance the Efficacy of Transfer of Technology (SEETOT) .
a)   Research and Development by Industry  (RDI)
      The component scheme on Research and Development by Industry (RDI), deals with all activities relating to
 recognition of in-house R&D units in industry and non-commercial Scientific and Industrial Research Organizations,
 fiscal incentives and  other  mechanisms and  initiatives  towards  supporting  and  encouraging  the  R&D efforts  of 
 industry.  There  were 1175  in-house  R&D units  in Industry having valid recognition by DSIR as, on 31 December
 2002.
b)   Programme Aimed at Technological Self-reliance (PASTER)      
            The component scheme on Programme Aimed at Technological Self-Reliance (PATSER) aims at catalyzing and
 supporting activities relating to technology absorption, adaptation and demonstration including capital goods
 development, involving industry and R&D organizations.  Under this scheme   research, development, design and
 engineering projects for absorption and up-gradation of imported technology as well as development and demonstration of
 new and improved technologies are supported.  While DSIR support has been catalytic and partial, the bulk of the
 financial contribution in any project has been from the industry. These projects cover products and processes in various
 important industries such as metallurgy, electrical & electronics, instrumentation, mechanical engineering, earth moving
 & industrial machinery, chemicals, explosives and drugs & pharmaceuticals. A distinctive feature of PATSER funding is
 that many of the programmes also involve Govt. research laboratories or IITs, IISc. or Universities as partners along with
 the industrial companies concerned. 
40.       Under PATSER, about 74 projects are in progress and these have considerable commercial potential for products/
 processes. PATSER projects have strengthened the linkages with more than 25 national research laboratories/ institutions.
 The Committee was informed that during the 10
th Plan Department would further enhance its efforts to strengthen
 industry’s linkages with CSIR and other research labs. It aims at networking with other funding schemes such as
 Technology Development Board, Home Grown Technology Programme of TIFAC and other financial institutions. 
 Department has interacted with other ministries for identification of technology development projects. More such

59.       The Committee was informed that as a result of rapid urbanization and industrialization most Indian cities have

 statistics also indicate that respiratory infections and chronic illness are becoming wide spread among the urban

ESTABLISHMENT OF GENETICALLY MODIFIED FOODS REFERRAL FACILITY (GMFRF)
83.       The advancement in modern agricultural biotechnological R&D has led to development of diverse novel food
 crops.  These have been designed to possess unique nutritional characteristics.  Such crops are being increasingly used in
 food processing without proper labeling. The market is flooded with imported processed foods without specifying their
 content of GM component. At present there is no referral facility in the country for detection and analysis of GM foods
 and their safety as well as nutritional aspects. Hence they propose to establish such a facility in CFTRI, which will also
 network with ITRC and CCMB under the CSIR umbrella.  In the market many irradiated foods and food products are
 available. They are erroneously confused with GM foods by consumers. It is also believed that radiation brings about
 changes at molecular levels in the food. It is very important to distinguish irradiated food from GM food because
 irradiation constitutes the cheapest method of food preservation. Therefore the proposed facility will also develop
 methods for distinguishing irradiated foods from GM foods.  The facility will be a referral centre for the nation and will
 boost export of foods and food products based on their declared absence or presence of the GM component.
84.       The new Centre has a short term as well as long-term objectives. The short-term objectives include: to develop and
 standardize appropriate detection procedures for identification of GMOs in raw, processed and complex foods using DNA
 and protein based methods;  to establish a single robust method for accurate quantification of GMOs in raw and processed
 foods; to Validate  methods with Certified Reference Materials (CRM) for suitability and certainty; to  develop sampling
 plans to ensure adequacy of testing; to document time  tested procedures, practices on a sound scientific basis so as to
 ensure their replicability in other testing laboratories; to develop database containing data on GM foods worldwide; to 
 evaluate safety of GM food in the light of  Allergenicity, physico chemical stability toxicity,  to establish  a GMO
 germplasm preservation centre and maintain a culture collection of microorganisms used in Indian traditional foods.
 Long-term Objective would be to evolve the GMFRF as the reference centre for the South East Asia.
85.       The Committee notes with satisfaction that the Department has taken an important step by establishing this unique
 centre, which would monitor the quality and content of G.M. food.  The Committee feels that such a referral centre is
 necessary for checking the activities of those who flout laws related to the import of G.M. food and target those who trade
 in such foods without proper trials and approvals.
86.       The Committee observes that innovative ideas on scientific aspects not only come from urban educated people but
 also from persons who are not educated and who hail from rural areas.  Scientific discovery of excellence gives rise to
 technological innovations of excellence.  The Committee therefore recommends that the Department should create special
 awards for uneducated people who apply their genius in scientific fields and make important discoveries.  There is also
 need for publicity about the quality testing facility so that people at large avail of it.
NATIONAL SCIENCE AND TECHNOLOGY HUMAN RESOURCE DEVELOPMENT
87.       The Committee notes with concern the lack of interest on the part of students for science education.  Many
 prominent scientists in their write-ups in the media have also sounded alarm bells in this regard.  In fact the total
 allocation for the year 2003-2004 for the programme ‘Research Schemes, Scholarships and Fellowships’ is Rs.57 crores
 as against Rs.55.65 crores in B.E. and Rs.54.94 crores at R.E. for the year 2002-2003.  Such a marginal increase was a
 cause of concern for the Committee.  It wanted to know from the Department as to how such marginal enhancement of
 funds would attract young scientists/students to pursue science education.
88.       The Department in its reply stated.
            The scheme on National S&T Human Resource Development comprising Research Schemes, Scholarships and
 Fellowships and Scientists Pool has been provided with a budgetary allocation of Rs.61 crores (Plan Rs.7 crores; Non
 Plan Rs.54 crores) during 2003-04, which is higher by Rs.1.35 crores than B.E. 2002-03.  This enhanced outlay would
 permit CSIR to initiate new schemes for the Tenth Plan but will not permit it to meet the total requirements of the desired
 number of scholarships being presently envisaged.  The additional requirement of Rs.16 crores is mainly due to the
 upward revision of the amount of scholarship/fellowship and associated emoluments and contingencies effective from
 1.8.2002.  In addition, CSIR envisages increasing the number of fellowships and scholarships to encourage young
 scholars to pursue science.
This additional requirement could not be fully provided at the time of pre-budget discussions by the Ministry of
 Finance.  Analysis since then indicates that number of scholarships and their seeker are continuously increasing.
89.       The Committee feels that the amount is not at all enough for developing human resources for science and

            Interest and awareness among students for science and technology has to be sustained.  The Committee feels that,
 Science Cafes, in the pattern of Cyber Cafes, may be opened in different localities and educational institutions.  Exposure
 to scientific works and activities in such cafes would encourage the youth of our country to show more interest in science. 
 The Committee strongly recommends that some time (at least five minutes) may be allocated in the chaupal    programme

REGIONAL CENTRES OF EXCELLENCE
90.            Different parts of our country is endowed with variety of resources.  For instance while Rajasthan is replete with
 marbles and precious stones, North-East has enormous amount of bamboo and leather.  There is a feeling that CSIR has
 not opened adequate number of institutes to exploit these resources.  Therefore the Committee strongly feels that Regional
 Centres of Excellence on Technology may be established in different regions to develop those resources.  This will also
 go a long way in fostering the team-India spirit which the CSIR is now making the central strategy for pooling our talents
 and abilities for the advancement of our country.
PROMOTION OF SCIENTIFIC TEMPER
91.            Evolution of human civilization from steam age to the age of biotechnology is indeed fascinating and exciting. 
 While human capability is expanding through science and technology, the attitude and outlook of people do not change
 correspondingly.  Enormous technological strength without a scientific and humane approach would create imbalances in
 as well human personality and society at large.  To enable our scientists to file their patents we teach them patent literacy. 
 It is important for their success in the age of competition and innovation.  Even more important is to promote scientific
 temper among our people.  The Committee has been focussing  its attention on this issue.  Swami Vivekananda regarded
 modern science as a manifestation of the real religious spirit, for it sought to understand truth by sincere effort.  Pandit
 Jawaharlal Nehru in his book “The Discovery of India” wrote that the future would witness an increasing alliance between
 science and humanism producing what he called scientific humanism.  Our country is witnessing a counter revolution
 which is reviving outmoded practices and rituals.  This rising tide of counter revolution can be reversed by promoting
 scientific temper.  It is heartening to note that the Council for Scientific and Industrial Research is a vital source of science
 and technology for national societal missions which combine technology with a human face. The Committee recommends
 that the CSIR, while pursuing the challenging goal of becoming a self-financing R&D institute must remain committed to
 promote scientific humanism among our people.
92.       After considering the Demands for Grants of the Department of Scientific & Industrial Research and assessing the
 various programmes and projects administered by it, the Committee Recommends that the Demands for Grants of
 Rs.1136.41 crores, as sought by the Department of Scientific & Industrial Research for the year 2003-2004 under,
 Demand no.81 may be approved.
SUMMARY OF THE RECOMMENDATIONS
 
1.         The Committee appreciates the Department for carrying out research in many frontier areas of science and
 technology.  It notes with satisfaction the laudable claim of the CSIR that science is one of the areas which can bring
 leadership and meet the kind of objectives that India has set for itself.  However, it is of opinion that the Department
 should make efforts to raise funds from Industry by successful transfer of technologies. There is also a need for wider
 dissemination of technologies so that there is a greater interface between Industry & R&D laboratories.   
(Para 21)
2.         The Committee reiterates its earlier recommendation made in 86
th Report that there is a need for reviewing and
 strengthening /revamping the existing S&T support systems in the universities and other educational institutions . The
 Committee is of the view that an agreement be reached with various financial institutions for providing loans to those
 research scholars for setting up their own enterprises.
(Para 25)

3.         The Committee commends the Department for emerging as a pioneering institute to achieve number one position
 in Indian & Foreign patent filings.  The Committee hopes that Department would maintain its position.  Earlier Basmati
 rice was patented and some NGOs filed PIL in courts to activate the Government for appropriate action.  The Committee
 hopes that CSIR will remain vigilant in future to safeguard our age old indisputable rights on our traditional knowledge.
(Para 30)
4.         The Committee observes that although CSIR initiates  good works in various fields for the development of our
 country and indeed the mankind, these accomplishments have not been made known to the people.  It notes with
 satisfaction that efforts are being made to establish CSIR brand equity among the public.  To reach out to the people for
 making them aware of the important role played by CSIR publicity through electronic and Print Media, must be made. 
 Even the organization of exhibitions in rural areas displaying activities of the CSIR must be made for the benefit of our
 people.  
            The Committee has been given to understand that due to personal efforts of one of its Members the Minister of
 Information & Broadcasting has approached the Minister of Science & Technology to find out as to how the Ministry of
 I&B  could be use for providing publicity to the scientific and technological programmes.  The Committee also
 understands that the Minister of I&B has also extended all cooperation in this regard.  The Committee therefore
 recommends that the Director General of CSIR must seize this opportunity and assist the Minister of Science &
 Technology to send out the plans for giving wide publicity to its various programmes and activities.  
(Para 34)
5.         The Committee feels that the state-of-art infrastructure / laboratories are extremely important to further augment
 and enrich our capabilities in the fields of science and technology so as to face the increasing challenges thrown up by
 intense research activities in many scientific and technological institutions across the globe.   The infrastructure should be
seen as a strategic national resource and funding should be given on a continuing basis to maximize their effectiveness,
 improvement and relevance for our scientific community.  The infrastructure should also be developed keeping in view
 the future advances in science & engineering.  The Committee also feels that high speed internet access facility be
 established as vast amount of scientific data is available on the internet. This will enable our scientists to have faster
 access to scientific data bases
(Para 38)
6.         The Committee feels that the merging of these programmes would not in any way effect the importance of these
 schemes and that they would continue to do the commendable work of transfer of technology for commercial
 exploitation.  The Committee also feels that such efforts of the CSIR would further encourage the entrepreneurship among
 our scientists and contribute towards technological self-reliance.   However the Committee recommends that greater
 attention must be paid by the CSIR to ensure that our industrial enterprises take necessary and important steps for
 augmenting their contributions to R&D.  Our expenditure for R&D as percentage of G.D.P. has fallen from 0.98 during
 1958-59 to 0.8% during 21
st Century.  Out of it 80% is contributed by the government and only 20% comes from
 industry.  In all most all the developed countries contribution to R&D as percentage of GDP is 3%.  Out of it industry
 contributes 80% and the government only 20%.  Our vision is to make India a developed country by the year 2020.  While
 the Committee strongly recommends that at least during the first quarter of the tenth five year plan contribution to R&D
 as percentage of GDP must target at 1% and the percentage contribution of industry to it must rise substantially.  In the
 age of innovation and competition, it is appropriately said that “real temples of India have to be industry”.  For this to
 happen their contribution to R&D has to be bolstered.  Money spent in R&D is not an expenditure but an investment for
 the future.  It is also important that the know-how is sold to industry on competitive bids to extract the best return.
 (Para 41)
7.         The Committee notes that the activities of the CSIR is broad based and wide-ranging.  It has taken laudable steps to
 augment R&D facilities in industry. It is important that such facilities are further enhanced and bolstered by the industries
 themselves to augment their scientific and technological abilities so that they stand on their own for upgrading their
 knowledge base.  It would also enable them to successfully compete in the national and international arena.  In the age of
 geo-economics research and development will only open new vistas of technological innovations and help our industries
 to successfully meet the challenges of the present and future.  The Committee recommends that CSIR must redouble its
 efforts to realize this objective in practice and in full measure.  The Committee observes that closer coordination among
 research laboratories should be obtained for producing better products which would eventually be disseminated among the
 people who are the end users of such products.

 between scientific laboratories and industrial establishments for transferring technologies.  However, the Committee feels
 that a lot needs to be done to reach out to our people living in rural area.  In fact it is aptly said that rural areas are thirsting
 for science and technology. By developing appropriate technology for rural areas and transferring them for the benefit of
 our people a silent revolution can be  ushered    in for improving the living conditions of our teeming millions.
            The Committee poignantly observed that we have yet to produce a prototype of a modern bullock cart for our
 framers that could be more sturdy, far less strenuous for the bullock as well as passengers, distinctly faster & safer on
 roads.  Director General of CSIR, in one of his interviews, some time back had observed that  “I do not believe that
 indigenous science and technology, barring very few notable exceptions, has contributed as much to economic
 development as one would have desired”.  Therefore it recommends strongly that more attention must be given to produce
 appropriate technologies for use  in rural areas, the Committeestrongly feels that the living and working conditions of our
 people living in thousands of villages across the country have to be improved by making their hut roofs fireproof and
 longer-lasting.  Besides, it emphasizes that their hygienic conditions have to be improved so as to ensure them proper
 sanitation and better atmosphere for prevention of diseases.  Therefore the Committee recommends that appropriate
 technologies may be used in rural areas for achieving these objectives. 
(Para 57)
10.       The Committee notes with satisfaction that the National Research Development Corporation, through transfer of
 technology and other activities have earned Rs.33.51 lakhs (slightly over 3 million).  In a country of India’s size profit of

 pace so that greater revenue generation is ensured.  Only after achieving  this we can realize the goal of making CSIR less
 dependent on government funds.  The Committee further recommends that transfer of technology in areas such as
 defense, nuclear energy, biotechnology, aerospace, electronics and computer should be such that it takes care of the
 problems of obsolescence.  
(Para 58)
11.       The Committee feels that all pollution monitoring devises should be site specific as the causative agents in different
 areas are diverse and every anti-pollution process must have measurable parameters to Monitor its efficacy. The
 Committee observes that pollution in the country has become acute and it is being seen as a challenge to the scientists to
 come up with new scientific tools to monitor and review the existing health based ambient quality standards. The
 Committee observes that the department should coordinate with Pollution Control Boards in various states so that
 effective action is taken to sharply curb & finally prevent pollution in the country.
            As far as the presence of arsenic content in water is concerned the Committee was informed that Bangladesh has
 developed some technology to rectify it.  The Committee recommends that CSIR may study that technology with a view
 to adopting it for our country’s benefit. 
(Para 61)
12.       The Committee is pained to note that the percentage of Asthma patients of all ages has risen sharply.  It is
 assuming dimensions of a wide spread public health disaster.  There is a need to create awareness about the symptoms of
 the disease for early detection and cure. The research should focus on the medicines, which are affordable to all classes in
 society.  The publicity of the medicine already discovered by the CSIR is grossly inadequate. Special attention needs to be
 focused in allergic Asthmas.
(Para 65)

R E P O R T
 
INTRODUCTION
One of the most exciting and spectacular developments in the recorded history of mankind is the exploration of
 space and application of space technology for solving the complex social, economic and environmental problems
 confronted by mankind.  Since ancient times infinite space fired the imagination of Indians and their minds soared high to
 unravel its mysteries.  In more modern times pioneers of India's space programme considered space research and space
 technology as essential and indispensable for national reconstruction. While space technology has emerged as a proven
 means of successfully transforming society in a cost effective and limited time frame, the investment involved has
 prompted skeptics to question its relevance. Dr. Vikram Sarabhai the founder of our space programme when asked about
 the necessity of India venturing into such high profile scientific quest against the background of our resource crunch and
 social and economic backwardness had said,
There are some who question the relevance of space activities in a developing nation... we are
 convinced that if we are to play a meaningful role nationally and in the community of nations, we must
 be second to none, in the application of advanced technologies to the real problems of man and society
 which we find in our country. 
2.         One of the first astronauts of the USA John Glenn who subsequently  became a Senator justified the huge
 expenditure on space programmes by saying "Every dollar we put into the space programme gives us seven dollars worth
 of new technology".  In 1995 while delivering the annual K. R. Narayanan Oration, established by the Australian National
 University, Professor U. R. Rao, former Chairman of the Space Commission focused on the theme “Space Technology
 for  Sustainable Development in Asia” and stated that space technology could transform stagnant societies within less
 time and money.
3.         Today India is nothing short of a role model in space research and application  of space technology for

ONE HUNDRED-FOURTEENTH REPORT
file:///C/Users/user/Desktop/pri/Committee%20on%20S%20and%20T,%20Env.%20and%20Forests/114threport.htm[29-08-2018 16:24:49]
 transforming and improving our social, economic and environmental conditions and for reaching the "the high peaks of
 development in the fields of science and technology". 
4.         During four decades of India's space programme which commenced with the formation of the Indian National
 Committee for Space Research in 1962 our country has reached many milestones and scaled unprecedented heights in
 applying space technology for nation building.  Beginning with the launch of the first sounding rocket from Thumba
 Equatorial Rocket Launching Station in November 1963 the Indian Space Programme has progressed with many restraints
 imposed on it and is rightly described as "Success under Embargoes".
5.         The Indian Space Research Organisation (ISRO) was established in 1969 under the Department of Atomic Energy. 
 The Government of India gave a fillip to the space activities by formally setting up the Space Commission and the
 Department of Space (DOS) in June 1972, and bringing ISRO under DOS.  The primary objective of DOS is to promote
 the development and application of space science and technology for the socio-economic benefit of the nation.  The
 programme is executed through ISRO, National Remote Sensing Agency (NRSA), Physical Research Laboratory (PRL),
 National Mesosphere-Stratosphere-Troposphere Radar Facility (NMRF), North Eastern-Space Applications Centre (NE-
SAC) and other agencies.  The Antrix Corporation, a wholly owned Government  company,  which was established in
 1992, is  engaged
in commercial marketing of space products and services.  The establishment of space systems and their utilization are
 coordinated by national level committees, namely, the INSAT Coordination Committee (ICC), Planning Committee of
 National Natural Resources Management System (PC-NNMS) and Advisory Committee on Space Sciences (ADCOS). 
 Five Regional Remote Sensing Service Centres (RRSSC) help in undertaking remote sensing application projects relevant
 to the region.
6.         The Secretariat of DOS and the Headquarters of ISRO are located at Antariksh Bhavan in Bangalore.  Programme
 offices at ISRO Headquarters coordinate the overall programmes like satellite communication, earth observation, launch
 vehicle, space science, space-industry coordination, disaster management   support, international cooperation, publications
 and public relations, budget and economic analysis and human resources development.
7.         The Indian space programme was initially directed towards demonstrating the efficacy of space systems for
 national development through development of experimental satellites, launch vehicles and conduct of application
 experiments.  While the Satellite Instructional Television Experiment (SITE), was conducted during 1975-76, the Satellite
 Telecommunication Experimental Project(STEP), was conducted during 1977-79. These were the two important steps
 undertaken in this direction to gain experience in the use of satellite for developmental communications and domestic
 telecommunications.
8.            Simultaneously, space hardware was developed for experimental missions which would ultimately lead to
 indigenous operational space systems.  Aryabhata, the first  Indian satellite launched in April 1975, provided experience
 in design, fabrication and operation in space of a satellite system.  It was followed by two experimental remote sensing
 satellites, Bhaskara-1 and Bhaskara-2, launched in June 1979 and November 1981, respectively.  The Bhaskara satellites
 gave hands-on experience in building and operating space-based remote sensing system.  APPLE (Ariane Passenger
 Payload Experiment), an experimental communication satellite launched in June 1981, besides, enabling continuation of
 telecommunication experiments that had earlier been conducted under STE provided inputs in orbit raising and in-orbit
 maintenance of a geo-stationary satellite.  India’s first satellite launch vehicle, SLV-3, was launched successfully on July
 18, 1980.
9.         The experiments and demonstrations of the 70’s were consolidated to evolve operational space systems.  In this
 direction, over the years, India has established two operational space systems – the Indian National Satellite (INSAT)
 System providing services for telecommunications, TV broadcasting and meteorology including disaster warning support
 and the Indian Remote Sensing Satellite (IRS) System for resource monitoring and management.  The Polar Satellite
 Launch Vehicle (PSLV) is well proven through six successive successful flights. The successful launch of the first
 developmental flight of Geosynchronous Satellite Launch Vehicle, GSLV-D1, in 2001 was a major land mark in the
 Indian space programme making India the sixth country in the world to demonstrate capabilities for launch of geo-
stationary satellites of INSAT type.
10.       The constellation of Indian Remote Sensing Satellites comprises of five satellites including India’s first
 oceanographic satellite (IRS-P4).  They, besides, provide data worldwide, through a network of international ground
 stations serve as  a  main  stay of the  National Natural Resources Management System (NNRMS).  The Vital applications
 such as identifying zones which could yield ground water, suitable locations for recharging water, monitoring command
 areas estimating crop areas and yields, assessing deforestation, mapping urban areas for planning
purposes, delineating ocean areas with higher fish catch potential and monitoring of environment are being pursued

 actively by users with the space based data.  In the field of space communication and meteorology, the INSAT system,
 currently consisting of four satellites, viz, 2DT, 2E, 3B and 3C, is one of the largest domestic communication satellite
 systems in the world.  METSAT, a satellite exclusively for meteorology, was launched in September 2002.  It has been
 renamed after Kalpana Chawla, the Indian born space scientist, who lost her life after the space shuttle Columbia
 disintegrated during its return journey to earth.    INSAT contributes significantly to a variety of services in
 telecommunications and television broadcasting including meteorological observations, disaster communications, distance
 education, telemedicine and training.  The Department of Space has taken initiatives to pilot a Satellite Communication
 Policy in 1997 paving the way for the use of INSAT capacity by private users.  The new Satellite Communication
 (Satcom) Policy has also opened the possibilities for private Indian Satellite Systems in India.  A comprehensive Remote
 Sensing Data Policy on acquisition and distribution of satellite remote sensing data from Indian and foreign satellites for
 civilian users in India has been formulated and approved by the Government which ensures that users are not denied
 access to valuable satellite data for developmental purposes.
11.            Significant  scientific investigations are being carried out in the fields of astronomy, atmospheric sciences and
 long term climatic research using satellites, balloons, sounding rockets & ground instruments.  The Indian space
 programme has played a critical role for our industrial sector for augmenting their capabilities.  A strong bond with
 academic institutions exists through extensive research partnerships.  Unique organizational systems have been evolved in
 the national space programme for fulfilling diverse functions like development, operations and applications of complex
 space systems.  The space programme has enabled significant technology growth in multiple disciplines as spin-off
 benefits.
12.       Indian capabilities in space thus represent a wide spectrum of expertise ranging from the conceptual design to
 building and operating a variety of space systems, which are matched only by a few nations in the world.  In view of these
 multiple dimensions and capabilities, India is recognised as a leader in application  of space technologies.  The end-to-end
 capability in space for vital application in communications, broadcasting, meteorology and natural resource information,
 which are of direct relevance for national development, has secured India a unique place in the International community. 
 The diverse roles of space technology/services in various fronts – social, commercial, economic and strategic – have made
 the space systems an important component of our national infrastructure.

(a)    Fourth generation INSAT-4 satellites (INSAT-4A/4B) to augment the INSAT system capacity with Ku band and C

(b)   Radar Imaging Satellite (RISAT) with active microwave sensor which provides all-weather capability for acquiring the
 data on natural resource management applications.
(c)    Advanced satellites for Oceanographic studies (Oceansat-2) and Resource management applications (Resourcesat-2)
 to ensure continuity of data for the users.
(d)   Advanced Geosychnronous Satellite Launch Vehicle GSLV Mk III capable of launching 4T satellite into GTO, the
 first launch of which being targeted for 2007-08.
(e)    PSLV and GSLV Continuation programmes to meet the launch requirements of 10th plan.
(f)     Development of multi-wavelength Astronomy Satellite ASTROSAT.
(g)    Development of GSAT-3 (Edusat) and GSAT-4 satellites to be flown on GSLV.

INSAT
18.       INSATis a multipurpose satellite system for telecommunications, broadcasting, meteorology and search & rescue
 services.  Commissioned in 1983, INSAT is the largest domestic communication system in the Asia-Pacific Region.  It
 now comprises of five satellites – INSAT-2DT, INSAT-2E, INSAT-3B, INSAT-3C and METSAT – with a total capacity
 of over
hundred transponders in C, Extended C and Ku-bands. Besides it has got meteorological instruments.
19.       It carried twenty four transponders – twelve operating in the normal C-band frequency, six in Extended C-band and
 six in Ku-band.  Nine of the twelve normal C-band transponders provide expanded coverage and the remaining three have
 India coverage beam.  All the extended C-bands as well as the Ku-band transponders have India coverage beam.  INSAT-
3A also carried a Ku-band beacon.
20.       For meteorological observation, INSAT-3A carried a three channel Very High Resolution Radiometer (VHRR)
 with 2 km resolution in the visible band and short wave infrared bands providing a spatial resolution of 1 km.  A data
 Relay Transponder (DRT) operating in UHF band is incorporated for real-time hydro meteorological data collection from
 unattended platforms located on land and river basins.  The data is then relayed in extended C-band to a central location.
21.            INSAT-3A also carried another transponder for Satellite Aided Search and Rescue (SAS & R) as part of India’s
 contribution to the international Satellite Aided Search and Rescue programme.
22.            INSAT-3A is launched by European Ariane-5 Launch Vehicle into a Geosynchronous Transfer Orbit (GTO)
 with a perigee of 200 km and an apogee of 35,980 km.  The satellite is manoeuvered to its final orbit by firing the
 satellite’s apogee motor.  Subsequently, the deployment of solar array, antennae and the solar sail is carried out and the
 satellite is commissioned after in-orbit checkout.
23.            INSAT-3A is the third satellite in the INSAT-3 series. INSAT-3B and ISNAT-3C were launched in March 2000
 and January 2002 respectively by the Ariane launch vehicle and both the satellites are now providing regular service. 
 INSAT-3A is to be located at 93.5 deg east longitude in the geostationary orbit and was launched by Ariane-5 launch
 vehicle of Arianespace in the early hours of April 10, 2003 (as per IST), from Kourou in French Guyana.
24.       The Committee congratulates the Department for the successful launch of the INSAT-3A and records its

25.       In its maiden test flight on April 18, 2001, GSLV successfully placed a 1540 kg experimental satellite, GSAT-1,
 into Geo-synchronous Transfer orbit.  GSLV is a three-stage vehicle, 49 m tall and weighing 401 tonne at lift-off.
26.       The second test flight, GSLV-D2, is planned in the first half of 2003.  A major milestone during the year towards
 the improvement of GSLV capability was the successful testing of the up-rated version of the liquid propellant Vikas
 engine.  The up-rated version develops higher chamber pressure than in the current version.  This new engine uses UH25
 (a mixture of unsymmetrical Di-methyl Hydrazine and hydrazine hydrate) as fuel and nitrogen tetroxide as
oxidizer.  The new engine has the potential to increase the payload capability of GSLV by about 150 kg in the Geo-
synchronous Transfer Orbit (GTO) and the GSLV-D2 can carry a mass of 1,800 kg in GTO.
27.       All mission related studies/simulations including trajectory design, payload optimization configuration of flame jet
 preventor, thermal analysis, etc, for the second test flight, GSLV-D2 have been completed during the year.
GSLV Mk-III Project
28.       The development of an advanced version of ISRO’s Geo-synchronous Satellite Launch Vehicle, known as GSLV
 Mk-III, which will have a capability to launch four tonne satellites into GTO, was approved during the year.  The
 development is expected to take about six years.  GSLV Mk-III will be a three-stage vehicle with a 110 tonne core liquid
 propellant stage and strap-on stage with two solid propellant motors, each, with 200 tonne propellant.  The upper stage
 will be a cryogenic stage with a propellant loading of 25tonne and will be 42.4 m tall.  The payload fairing will have a
 diameter of 5 metre and a payload volume of 100 cubic metre.
29.       During the year, plans for S-200 motor production, static test and vehicle integration facilities, earth storable and
 cryogenic propellant storage and servicing facility and range instrumentation systems for GSLV Mk-III have been
 completed.  L-110 realisation plan has also been prepared.  C-25 engine and stage development plan, hardware realization
 plan and schedules have also been prepared.
30.       The objective of this Project is to develop a Launch Vehicle capable of launching 4 tonne class communication
 satellites in to GTO. The GSLV Mk–III project was approved in May 2002 at an estimated cost of Rs.2498.00 crores, and
 envisages development of a number of technologies which include 200 tonne solid stage booster, 25 tonne cryogenic
 engines, cluster of two vikas engines as core booster, vehicle characterization, etc. Realisation of the vehicle is targeted in
 about 6-7 years.
31.       The Committee was deeply appreciative of the sincerity of purpose prevailing in the Department and hopes that
 GSLV Mk-III would open new areas of industrial participation including private capital investments.
METSAT (KALPANA-1)
32.            KALPNA-1 is the first in the series of exclusive meteorological satellites built by ISRO. Earlier, meteorological
 services were combined with telecommunication and television services in the INSAT system.  This meteorological
 satellites are named after the Indian born American astronaut Dr. Kalpana Chawla, who died on February 1, 2003 in the
 US Space Shuttle Columbia.  KALPANA-1 is a precursor to the future INSAT system that will have separate satellites for
 meteorology and telecommunication & broadcasting services.  This will enable large capacity to be built into INSAT
 satellites, both in terms of transponders and their radiated power, without the design constraints imposed by
 meteorological instruments, which are also expected to become heavier with advanced features.
33.       For meteorological observation, KALPANA-1 carries a Very High Resolution Radiometer (VHRR) capable of
 imaging the Earth in the visible, thermal infra-red and water vapour bands.  It also carries a Data Relay Transponder
 (DRT) for collecting data from unattended meteorological platforms. KALPANA-1 will relay the data sent by these
 platforms to the meteorological Data Utilisation Centre at New Delhi.  Such platforms have been installed all over the
 country.
34.       At the time of launch, KALPANA-1 weighed 1060 kg, which included about 560 kg of propellant.  The propellant
 carried by Kalpana-1 was mainly required to raise the satellite from the Geosynchronous Transfer Orbit to its final
 Geostationary Orbit.  KALPANA-1 is located at 74 deg. East longitude. 
35.       The main objective of METSAT is to support the India Meteorological Department (IMD) in ensuring
 meteorological data and weather imageries on a continuous basis.  The sanctioned cost of the project is Rs.75.00 crores. 
 (DRT).  Satellite was successfully launched on September 12, 2002, on-board PSLV-C4 and the performance of the
 satellite is satisfactory. 
36.       The Committee hopes that with the launch of METSAT, the input for climatic/numeric weather prediction model
 studies would be better and this would improve the quality of prediction for accurate weather forecasts.

GRAMSAT Pilot Projects (GPP)
37.       The GRAMSAT Programmes is an initiative to provide communication networks at the state level, connecting the
 state capitals to districts and blocks.  The networks provide computer connectivity, data and TV broadcasting for applications
 in E-governance, national resource information system, development information, tele-conferencing, disaster management,
 telemedicine and distance education.   The status of implementation of the GPP in various states is as follows:
Madhya Pradesh:  The network comprising the terminals installed under TDCC and JDCP with hub and studio at Bhopal, is
 already functioning.  The nodal agency is MPAA/Govt. of Madhya Pradesh.  In Gujarat the network is operational with hub
 at Gandhinagar.  More than 360 ITPs have been conducted.  In addition, the network is also utilised for connecting the
 engineering colleges on a daily basis.  The nodal agency is RESECO/Govt. of Gujarat.  In Karnataka the network is
 operational with uplink facility at Mysore.  The ITPs are presently being conducted from Mysore.  In Andhra Pradesh, the
 Government has set up an integrated satellite network (Mana TV) for the purpose of distance education, healthcare and rural
 development.  The network is operational with the hub at Hyderabad.  In Orissa the ITPs are being conducted regularly using
 a  Fly-Away Terminal (FAT) located at Cuttack.  More than 110 ITPs have been conducted.  The network is proposed to be
 upgraded with studio and hub.  The nodal agency is ORSAC/Govt. of Orissa.  In the North Eastern Region twelve Direcet
 Reception Sets (DRS) have been installed at selected locations in the NE states.  The network will soon be made operational
 by NE-SAC.  In Rajasthan a pilot DRS network covering 17 locations of Jhalwad and Baran districts was inaugurated in
 September, 2002.  The total network proposal for the entire state is under planning.  The network proposals for Andaman &
 Nicobar Islands, Himachal Pradesh, Chhatisgarh and Jharkhand are being studied.
38.       The Committee hopes that by the end of the 10
th Plan period the GRAMSAT programme would cover all the rural
 areas of India.  The Committee also hopes that local bodies, district offices and all those involved in planning at the rural
 level would be given the data for their use. Since we have constitutionally guaranteed 33% reservation for women in
 Panchayat bodies the Committee recommends that special focus should be given to women’s development issues through
 GRAMSAT. Lest all this effort goes waste the Committee strongly urges the government to launch a scheme to equip every
 village of the country with the equipment necessary to utilise the service that will be given through GRAMSAT.

SPACE CAPSULE RECOVERY EQUIPMENT
41.       Space Capsule Recovery Experiment (SRE) envisages development of 500 kg recoverable capsule.  It is intended
 to develop and demonstrate technologies related to conducting microgravity experiments in space, recovery from orbit
 through re-entry into earth’s atmosphere and recovery of the capsule on sea or land. It is proposed to be launched along
 with a passenger through one of the forthcoming launches of PSLV into polar sun-synchronous orbit during 2004/05.  The
 main objective is to carry out micro-gravity experiments in orbit and demonstrate technology of de-boost from orbit for
 re-entry and recovery from sea using floatation system.  Development of basic technologies needed for future Reusable
 launch Vehicles (RLV) is also envisaged.
42.       SRE capsule has four major hardware: aero-thermo structure (ATS), spacecraft platform, declaration and flotation
 system and micro-gravity payloads.  Two micro-gravity experiments – Quasi crystal growth experiment and biomimetic
 material synthesis experiment have been selected. 
43.       The design and development work of SRE is progressing well. The spacecraft design has been completed and the
 procurement action for components and materials has been initiated. The aerothermal studies and the wind tunnel test are
 in progress.  The detailed design for deceleration and flotation system and the recovery module are nearing completion
 and several ground tests like airdrop test, lid plate ejection test, water impact test, etc. for design validation have been
 conducted. The microgravity experiments to be conducted onboard have been identified and the work related to the
 development of experimental packages have also been initiated. The launch of the SRE onboard PSLV-C7 is planned for

ISRO-GEO SPHERE BIOSPHERE PROGRAMME
44.       Global climate change is of great concern to the world scientific community UN and many others.  Realising the
 importance of scientific studies to arrive at specific migration strategies for the Indian sub-continent, the Department
 initiated the ISRO Geosphere-Biosphere Programme 10 years back which has contributed significantly in understanding
 various issues related to climate change using space-based and convention systems.  This programme encompasses the
 study of land-air-ocean interaction, past climate, changes in atmospheric composition, aerosols, carbon cycle, bio-mass
 estimation, bio-diversity and other related areas of scientific investigation.  The ISRO-GBP is aimed at using maximum
 data from ISRO’s own satellites.  Data from balloon-borne experiments are also used for studying the climate change
 processes.
45.       ISRO-GBP contributed significantly to Indian Ocean experiments (INDOEX-I) during 1998-1999.  Investigation
 on the aerosol distribution and spatial variability of AOD using the network of observations is continuing.  Satellite
 observations of the regional aerosol loading, aerosol transport and the clear sky aerosol rediative forcing over the oceanic
 areas around the Indian subcontinent are being carried out.  The studies  are being made on the impact of El Nino related
 south Asian forest fires on the regional aerosol distribution over the Indian Ocean.
46.       The Committee hopes that the ISRO-GEO sphere programme would be helpful in predicting, the arrival of
 monsoon with greater precision. It also hopes that the programme would be useful to study the recent phenomenon like
 Asian Brown cloud. 
LUNAR MISSION
47.       In order to promote space exploration, discussions had been held under the auspices of Indian Academy of
 Sciences and Astronautical Society of India to study the feasibility of undertaking an unmanned Lunar Mission.  These
 studies were primarily related to definition of possible scientific objectives, conceptualization of mission including the
 spacecraft and the feasibility of using Indian launch vehicles to place a spacecraft into lunar orbit.  Based on the inputs
 from discussions, ISRO has set up a Lunar Mission Task Force, to study the various possibilities for undertaking a
 scientific mission to the moon.  The National Task Force has submitted its report.  After considering various options, the
 team has recommended that it is feasible to launch a lunar polar orbiter at an altitude of 100 km using the existing
 PSLV/GSLV capabilities of ISRO.  The main objective of such a mission would be to realize the technological goal for
 planetary missions.  In addition, the first lunar mission may have the following scientific objectives:
(i)
                 Preparing a 3-dimensional atlas (with a high spatial and altitude resolution of 5-10m) of regions of
 scientific interest on the moon.
(ii)                Chemical mapping of the entire lunar surface for exploring elemental abundance of Mg. Al, Si, Ca, Fe and
 Ti with a spatial resolution of abut 10km and distribution of high Z elements such as 222Rn, U, Th, etc,
 with a spatial resolution of about 20 km on the lunar surface. At present, the report of the Task Force
 (Study Group) is being examined for further action.
48.       In reply to the Committee Question whether the Department has any plans to send the man to the moon in the near
 future the Committee was informed that the Department of Space has no immediate plan for sending a manned expedition
 to the Moon. However some studies are being carried out to explore the possibility for launching an unmanned lunar
 probe in the near future.
49.       ISRO had constituted a Lunar Mission Study Task Force for considering and making an assessment of the possible
 configuration and feasibility of taking up such a mission. The task force has submitted its report identifying the potential
 scientific objectives of the mission, the payload options, the spacecraft configuration, the launch vehicle requirements and
 the mission related aspects.
50.       In order to review and formulate the recommendations on the Indian Mission to Moon programme based on the
 study group report, Chairman, ISRO/Secretary, DOS has convened a peer review meeting in the first week of April 2003.
 The feedback and recommendations of the review meeting would be used for deciding the further course of action.
51.       The Committee notes with satisfaction that our Space programme is progressing and generating momentum of its
 own to boost the confidence of our space scientists.   These missions if completed successfully will help our space
 programmes take great strides and bring glory to the entire nation.

TELEMEDICINE
75.       The Committee was informed that  telemedicine is an emerging area where there is a lot of scope to successfully
 apply space technology.  Most of the States are interested to adopt telemedicine practices to extend medical facilities to
 people inhabiting remote and inaccessible areas.  Doctors are showing keen interest to offer their services to patients
 through telemedicine. Tele-medicine mainly consists of customized medical software integrated with computer hardware,
 along with medical diagnostic instruments connected to the commercial VSAT (Very Small Aperture Terminal) at each
 location, which is turn, is linked to a super specialty hospital through satellite.  The medical records of the patient like
 medical images and outputs from medical devices are sent to the specialist, who in-turn study them, diagnose and advice
 on the course of treatment through videoconference with the doctor or a paramedic at patient’s end.  The
specialist could even guide the junior doctor at the patient’s end during a surgery.  Thus the patients in distant and rural
 areas can avail timely consultations of specialists without the ordeal of travelling long distances and spending a large
 amount of money.
76.       DOS undertook tele-medicine demonstrations with the involvement of selected super specialty hospitals located in
 major cities and smaller health centres in remote areas during the year.  They include Tele-medicine links between Port 
 Blair and Car Nicobar and Chennai benefiting the inhabitants of Andaman & Nicobar Islands,  Kavaratti in Laksha
 Dweep linked to Cochin and Karnataka tele-medicine project connecting a specialty hospital for heart care in Banagalore
 with District Hospital at Chamrajanagar and a rural hospital at Sargur in H D Kote taluk.  Apart from these, telemedicine
 facilities were set up in remote areas like Tripura, Assam and Leh. 
77.       The Committee commends the Department for bringing high quality medical care to patients transcending the
 barriers of geography, distance, time and costs.  It believes that this can be a boon for countries like India where the
 majority population lives in remote areas without access to even basic health care.   The Committee however hopes that
 the poor quality of internet/telephone services will not come in the way of effective functioning of telemedicine services.
78.       The Committee also hopes that in the next few years there will be telemedicine kiosks throughout the length and
 breadth of suburban and rural India. It is hoped that the government scheme to provide such kiosks will go hand in hand
 with the spread of telemedicine facility.

 equipment, mode of interaction with state Governments, role of NGOs/HAMs, maintenance schedule, etc.  The various
 follow up actions have been identified for implementing the system.
84.            Airborne Survey Facility: To meet the information needs of disaster mitigation in terms of flood-plain zoning
 and damage assessment, an airborne survey facility is planned to be set up in NRSA, consisting of Airborne Laser Terrain
 Mapping system (ALTM) and Digital Camera.  Actions have been initiated to procure suitable systems.
85.       Digital Database Creation: One of the critical requirements to provide spatial information on floods and other
 disasters is the availability of digital database.  A Technical Committee has worked out the database requirements in terms
 of themes, spatial scale, updating cycle, methodology and priority districts.  Based on these inputs, a major project has
 been formulated to create digital database for selected districts in five states on a priority basis.  The project is being
 carried out with support from RRSSC’s, State Centres and NRSA.  Work for nine districts in Assam has been completed.
86.            International Charter on Space & Major Disasters:   As a follow-up to signing the international Charter on Space
 & Major Disasters, which was initiated by major space agencies in August 2001, ISRO is taking several steps to
 participate in the Charter effectively.  Personnel were identified from various ISRO Centres to support the Charter.  After
 successful completion of the Qualification Exercise in August 2002, ISRO has been operationally integrated to the
 Charter.  For realizing this goal, necessary capacity building measures such as digital database creation, close contour data
 using airborne laser terrain mapper, airborne Synthetic Aperture Radar development, querry shell development, etc. have
 been initiated.  Besides coordination with the user departments have been further strengthened.
87.       The Committee feels that the remote sensing data is not being used to its full potential. With regard, to the
 landslide hazard zonation, the Committee feels that standardized landslide inventory maps would be helpful. Besides,
 accurate slope stability studies  may be made by using space technology so as to understand the possible locations where
 landslides could occur.  The Committee feels that special attention should be given to North-East and Uttaranchal where
 landslides during rainy season block roads for days together. An internet image transferring system may be of help for
 local bodies and relief agencies for emergency response in affected areas.
NATIONAL NATURAL RESOURCES MANAGEMENT SYSTEM
88.       When the Committee asked the Department to explain the higher allocation of Rs.54.80 crores on National Natural
 Resources Management system for  the year 2003-04 and the activities
planned or proposed to be carried out with the enhanced budgetary support, the Department replied that the proposed
 increase during BE 2003-04, is primarily towards the new activities identified in the 10
th five year plan such as the
 periodic conduct of Natural Resources Census (NRC) and establishment of the National Spatial Data Infrastructure
 (NSDI) in the country as well as for Large Scale Mapping activities.
89.       The inventory and the monitoring of the natural resources of the nation on a periodical basis planned under the
 Natural Resources Census is expected to lead to the generation of a ‘State of the Country’s Environment Report’. The
 NRC will also lead to the identification of Natural Resources Hotspots that are a cause for concern and which need urgent
 conservation / management actions.
90.       The NSDI at the national level is envisaged as a spatial data infrastructure encompassing various national map
 holdings of survey agencies and also satellite images and would, thus, be a standardised national repository of spatial

92.       The North Eastern Space Applications Centre (NE-SAC) aims to provide developmental support to the region by
 undertaking projects in remote sensing and satellite communications.  The Space application activities undertaken by NE-
SAC include Deforestation study of Sonitpur District in Assam, Bamboo resource mapping for Meghalaya, Erosion hazard
 assessment in catchment area of Umiam Hydel Project, Meghalaya , Decision support system for early warning of
 outbreak of Japanese Encephalitis in Dibrugarh District, Assam , Forest working plan preparation for East Assam Forest
 Circle, Brahmaputra river channel changes study to identify stable river islands (char) and locations for flood control
 measures, Providing flood inundation coverage map in near real-time for damage assessment, Identification of areas for
 extending cashew nut crop in East Garo Hills District of Meghalaya under Technology Mission for Integrated
 Development of Horticulture in NER, Supporting the development of the database on National Resource Information
 System (NRIS) which will be an important tool for developmental planning in the region, Installation of Data Receiving
 Systems (DRS)  in selected places for experimental telecast of programmes on the development of the region, Connecting
 Guwahati Medical College Hospital to All India Institute of Medical Sciences (AIIMS), New Delhi through the satellite
 for telemedicine services (nearing completion).
93.       The Committee appreciates the Department for undertaking projects in the North-East, which merits concentrated
 attention. The Committee hopes that bamboo resource mapping, erosion hazard assessment etc would cover the whole of
 the Northeast so that the data could be used for meaningful  planning for development.
94.       The Committee is of the view that India is emerging as a water stressed country with millions of  its  people 
 without  access to safe drinking water.  The Committee deeply
Appreciates that the Department has applied Space Technology to prepare 1500 maps in respect of six States for the
 purpose of ground water exploration.  While the Committee notes that the Department is mapping for few of the States it
 recommends strongly that such efforts of the Department must be extended to all States, giving special priority to those
 which have been severely affected by drought and shortage of rainfall.
95.       The Committee notes that the Department is proposing to prepare National Resource Information System in Nine
 states.  Earlier the Department had set up such a system in 30 districts in different States.  The Committee recommends
 that such systems beestablished as soon as possible in all the States of the country to enable the Government, people and
 larger civil society to have access to such information for national development.
96.       The Committee takes note of the large-scale developmental activities undertaken by the Government agencies
 throughout the length and breadth of the country.  The Committee feels that Space Technology should not only be used as
 an input and a strategy for development but also for monitoring the developmental work.  Therefore, the Committee
 strongly recommends that the application of space technology should be made an integral element in assessing and
 monitoring the success and effectiveness of various developmental schemes being implemented in the country.  The
 Committee feels that the Governments both at Union and State levels must take the help of the Department in making this
 possible.  The States need to be educated about the potential available in this direction through the efforts of  the
 Department of Space.

R E P O R T
           
Oceans have played a critical and decisive role in our history. Numerous invasions of India through land frontiers never
 turned our country into a colony. We fell to that status only when mastery of our seawaters was lost. Oceans,
 particularly the Indian Ocean is assuming importance in shaping the world order. In the 19
th century, Admiral Mahan
 of the United States of America, had predicted:
“Whoever controls the Indian Ocean dominates Asia.  This ocean is the key to the seven seas.  In the twenty first
 century the destiny of the world will be decided on its waters.”
Not only from the strategic point of view but also from the point of view of our very survival and development we will
 increasingly depend on oceans, particularly the Indian Ocean in the centuries ahead.
“Oceans sustain nearly half of all life on earth and provide us with vital resources.  They are a source of food, energy,
 commerce, medicine and recreation…. They shape our weather and link us to other nations.  In the twenty first century,
 we will look increasingly to the oceans to meet our every day needs.”
This declaration formed the cornerstone of the convention on the Law of the Sea and Oceans Conference held in 1998, a
 year that was designated as the U.N. Year of the Ocean.
2.         Recognising the importance of oceans for our all round development on a sustainable basis, the Department of
 Ocean Development was created in July, 1981 within the Cabinet Secretariat directly under the charge of the Prime
 Minister.  In March, 1982 it became a separate Department and has since been functioning as a nodal Department for
 organizing, coordinating and promoting ocean development activities in the country, in line with the Ocean Policy
 Statement of 1982. The national level R&D laboratories, educational institutions and industries assist the Department in

115TH REPORT
file:///C/Users/user/Desktop/pri/Committee%20on%20S%20and%20T,%20Env.%20and%20Forests/115threport.htm[29-08-2018 16:25:50]
 carrying out its multi-disciplinary plans and programmes. Marine research and capacity building are key areas of the
 Department to promote basic research in marine science for self-reliance.  The activities of the Department are targeted
 towards scientific research and technology development with orientation towards its applications and harnessing ocean
 resources.  The Department has also the mandate for international programmes arising out of international obligations
 and bilateral and multilateral cooperative ventures to create technological capacity building and human resources
 development for self-reliance.
3.         The Department witnessed a phenomenal growth with manifold expansion of its activities during the 9
th Five
 Year Plan period, involving a plan outlay of Rs.510.62 crores.  A wide range of subjects and activities introduced
 during the 9
th Five Year Plan period included Ocean Thermal Energy Conversion (OTEC), Assessment of the Marine
 Living Resources, Integrated Coastal and Marine Area Management, Ocean Observation and Information Services,
 Delineation of Outer limits of Continental Shelf, etc.  They were directed towards development, dissemination and use
 of Ocean Science and Technology for socio-economic benefit of the country, with the active participation of a large
 number of national research laboratories, academic institutions etc.  In addition, two autonomous institutions, viz.,
 National Centre for Antarctic and Ocean Research (NCAOR) at Goa and Indian National Centre for Ocean Information
 Services (INCOIS) at Hyderabad were established under the Department for carrying out and implementing
 programmes in the areas of Polar Science; and Ocean Observation and Information Services, respectively.  For
 implementation of the Environment Management Capacity Building project and the related infrastructure, R&D and
 training programmes, the Integrated Coastal and Marine Area Management (ICMAM) Project Directorate was
 established in Chennai, jointly funded by the International Development Association and the DOD.  The Sagar
 Sampada Cell of Kochi was renamed as a “Centre for Marine Living Resources and Ecology” for implementing the
 programmes relating to Assessment of Marine Living Resources in the Indian EEZ.  Some of the major achievements
 include the development and successful testing of a seabed mining system at a depth of 410m of Tuticorin in Tamil
 Nadu coast, as a forerunner to the development of deep sea mining system for operation at 6000 m water depth;
 deployment of 12 Met Ocean Data Buoys along the Indian coastline for collection and dissemination of oceanographic
 data on real time basis; establishment of Ocean Science and Technology Cells in 8 different disciplines for human
 resource development and capacity building in Ocean Science and Technology.
4.         The Vision statement highlighting the Perspective Plan 2015 of the Department was formulated and released
 during this year (2002-03).  The following objectives have been set by the Department in the Vision Statement for the
 coming decades :
i)          Promoting ocean science, supporting technology development and strengthening observations, so as to
 continuously improve our understanding of local and remote processes.
ii)         Modelling sustainable uses of the coastal zone and reliably predicting extreme events, for the socio-economic
 benefits of the coastal population.
iii)         Understanding the influence of the ocean on the monsoons and contributing to the capability to forecast it.
iv)        Strengthening programmes in the southern Ocean and Antractica that offer unmatched opportunities to study
 planet earth in its pristine state.
v)         Mapping ocean resources and evolving guidelines for proper stewardship so that they are sustainably utilized
 with minimal environmental impact.
vi)        Developing reliable and safe deep sea technology that permits man to understand, quantify and harness ocean
 resources.
vii)        Partnering Indian Ocean neighbours in mutually beneficial programmes.
viii) Creating awareness in stakeholders about the complex functioning of the ocean and the inherent limits to the
 predictability of ocean processes.
ix)        Creating an Ocean Resource Commission as a national framework so that national efforts on ocean resource
 issues are effectively coordinated.
5.         The following programmes of the Department have been reoriented and revamped during the 10
th Five Year
 Plan:
Polar (Antarctic) Science
Marine Living Resources
Marine Non-Living Resources
Marine and Coastal Area Management
Ocean Observation & Information Services
Marine Research and Capacity Building

POLAR SCIENCE (ANTARCTIC RESEARCH) PROGRAMME
9.         The objectives of the Antarctic Research Programme are to identify and initiate programmes of scientific and
 economic significance besides establishing infrastructure.  The Antarctic Research Progamme has been designed to
 take advantage of the unique location and environment of the icy continent for understanding the key global processes
 which are manifested and controlled by this polar cap.  Antarctic is a pristine and natural laboratory, which enables the
 scientists to study, detect and monitor global phenomena, such as the atmospheric patterns and ocean circulations. 
 Glaciological and geophysical research provides a clue to the geological history and evolution of the earth.  In addition,
 Antarctica provides a singular platform for conducting studies on solar terrestrial interaction, adaptation of organisms,
 including human beings in the cold land isolated conditions.  The XXII scientific expedition with 48 members was
 launched successfully from Cape Town, South Africa on the 10
th January, 2003.  This expedition will carry out
 research in the fields of atmospheric, geological, biological, environmental, medical and engineering sciences and
 global change.
10.       The Committee was informed that the during the year 2003-04, preparatory exercise is proposed to be initiated
 of identifying the location of a second permanent Indian station in Antarctica, replacing “Maitri”.  With this year’s
 allocation of Rs.24.00 crores, the Department proposed to augment the research facilities at Indian Antarctic Station
 and also to actively undertake research in the Southern Ocean Oceanography area.
11.       The success of the Antarctic Programme and sustained capabilities in Antarctic science and logistics prompted
 the Department to establish the first polar research lab of the country at Goa namely the National Centre for Antarctic
 Ocean Research (NCAOR) in 1998 which is responsible for carrying out all the activities relating to Antarctic
 expeditions. The research on polar science and expeditions to Antarctica was being planned, executed and launched
 annually on behalf of DOD by the Centre.  The Centre has a specific R&D mandate in the realm of polar science and to
 coordinate and launch Indian Antarctic expeditions.  The Centre has a unique laboratory for low-temperature research
 on ice cores retrieved from Antarctica and the Himalayas.  It would also have the facility for the application of remote
 sensing techniques aimed at understanding the sea-ice-atmosphere interaction in the Polar Regions.  It would also have

of-the-art experiments in accordance with the long-term science strategy for the Antarctic expeditions.

 excellence of our scientific and technological capabilities beyond the frontiers of our country. The study and research
 undertaken during Antarctic expeditions have produced a repository of data and information which are of immense
 importance not only for India but for the entire world. Pursuing this mission as part of the mainstream of the
 international endeavour to explore the icy continent has made invaluable contribution to promote international
 understanding. The Committee, therefore, feels that the Antarctic programme should not be allowed to suffer for want

 composition and ice-cover in Antarctica.
