 in Antarctica.
POLYMETALLIC NODULES (PMN) PROGRAMME
17        Robert Heilbroner in his book ‘An Enquiry into the Human Prospects’ pointed towards a bleak future for
 humans in the process of approaching finite resources of the earth.  Later he did modify his assessment.  He wrote “I
 would like to take a more hopeful view of the mineral resources problem.  This is because I did not know when I wrote
 the book of the possibility of mining the seabed for mineral nodules which are estimated to exist in the order of
 hundreds of billions of tons”.
17.       The above paragraph indicates the potentiality of the oceanic world in terms of the sources of energy. 
 Manganese nodules of the deep seabed today have revolutionised the expectations of the industrialized countries.  The
 commercial exploitation, in the near future, of this nodule will not only provide the much needed scarce minerals but
 also change fundamentally the international mining market and its allied fields.  This will help the nations who have got
 technological superiority to explore and exploit the deep seabed.  Therefore, India has taken steps to extract
 Polymetallic nodules from the deep seabed. 
18.       The Polymetallic Nodules Programme (PMN Programme) is a national programme with international
 commitments which envisages eventual exploitation of the nodules from the allotted 1,50,000 sq. km. mine site in the
 Central Indian Ocean Basin. The programme consists of four components-Survey & Exploration of Polymetallic
 Nodules in the Central Indian Ocean Basin (CIOB); Environmental Impact Assessment studies at CIOB; Technology
 Development for mining of nodules;  and  Technology  Development  for  extraction of  metals from  nodules. The
 work related to Survey and Exploration was mainly directed towards assessing relative concentration and quality
 characteristics of nodules as well as seabed topography.  Demarcation of grade of nodules in the Central Indian Ocean
 Basin was one of the main objectives.  Design and development of mining system has been re-oriented so that the
 intermediate applications of the technology could be achieved before developing the ultimate system for a depth of
 6,000 m.  Towards this design, development and testing of mining nodule complex has been undertaken. 
19.       The Committee was informed that a joint collaborative programme between NIOT, Chennai and Experimental
 Design Bureau of Oceanological Engineering (EDBOE), Russia, for design and development of unmanned
 submersibles capable of operation up to 6,000 m was likely to be taken up soon in pursuance of a MoU signed between
 DOD and Russian Academy of Sciences. Besides, a continuous demonstration pilot plant of 500 kg/day capacity for
 extraction of Copper, Nickel and Cobalt from nodules was set up at Hindustan Zinc Limited (HZL), Udaipur.  An
 Environmental Impact Assessment (EIA) monitoring cruise is also proposed during 2003-04 as a part of continuing
 studies in the pioneer area for assessing the impact of the simulated mining at deep seabed at the site of nodules
 occurrence.

22.       The Committee hopes that the periodical review of the Polymetallic Nodules (PMN) Programme would continue
 to be undertaken to adopt new technologies in view of the fast changing technologies.  This project has tremendous
 potential in supplying adequate minerals for the benefit of our economy.
23.       The Committee recommends that efforts to extract polymetallic manganese nodules from the deep seabed be
 assessed from the point of view of its impact on the ocean environment.
 24.      The Committee hopes that data generated from the R&D activities of the Department for extraction of
 manganese nodules could be studied in depth with the ultimate objective of designing a commercial plant.
DRUGS FROM SEA
25.       World wide researchers believe that oceans hold the key to a whole range of new drugs for chronic pain,
 epilepsy and Parkinson’s disease.  The current attempt to reap a chemical harvest from the seas is just a continuation of
 the bio prospecting that the big drug companies have been doing in jungles for the past few decades.  The National
 Project on Drugs from Sea is a multi-institutional project aiming at developing potential drugs and chemicals from the
 marine flora and fauna. This project has led to identification of five marine organisms showing potent activity as anti-
diabetic, anti-viral, anti-fungal, anti-cholesterol and spermicidal agents for developing new drugs. The exploratory
 attempts will be continued in an intensive manner during the 10
th plan period. The Department has fostered the search
 for novel drugs from the sea and will continue to encourage these activities, supporting extensive bioassay guided
 screening programmes.  The emphasis will be on following aspects:
Extension of inventory of organisms with bioactive potential.
In-vitro synthesis molecules recognized for their bioactivity.
Development and application of novel screening programmes for bioactivity.
Explore and understand at levels ranging from genes to organisms, unique properties of the production of novel
 compounds.
Understand interactions between organisms and their habitats.
26.       An amount of Rs.2.50 crores has been allocated for 2003-04 for the programme Drugs from Sea as against
 Rs.2.00 crores allocated both at B.E. and R.E. stages of 2002-03. The enhanced allocation would strengthen the
 facilities for bioactivity screening and regulatory pharmacological and toxicological analysis of the promising
 compounds. Lead compounds for anti-diabetic and anti-cholesterol have been identified. The anti-diabetic lead has
 completed the toxicity test and clinical trials will be continued. For anti-cholesterol compound, toxicity test is proposed
 to be undertaken. In order to continue the exploratory activities for identification of bioactive compounds having the
 properties of anti-fungal, anti-cancer, spermicidal, etc., it is proposed to intensify the survey and screening activities for
 which an additional amount of Rs.50.00 lakhs is needed. The amount will be used to enhance instrumental and other
 analytical facilities in the institutes involved in the programme.
27.       The Committee notes with satisfaction that under the Drugs from Sea Programme the Department has done
 commendable work.  The Committee trusts that the Department would continue the exploratory work relating to
 collection, identification and bio-evaluation of the marine flora and fauna from the Indian Coastal waters for the
 purpose of extracting drugs.
28.       The Committee is of the view that possibly from marine resources some medicines could be extracted which
 otherwise are not available at present to treat some of the diseases affecting mankind.   Therefore, the Committee

COASTAL OCEAN MONITORING AND PREDICTION SYSTEM (COMAPS)
29.       Under the Coastal Ocean Monitoring and Prediction System (COMAPS) Programme, the Department of Ocean
 Development had taken up scientific monitoring of pollution at different locations. The programme aimed to assess the
 status and likely trends in coastal marine environment quality and contribute directly to the development of strategies
 for maximising the economic benefits derived from the intelligent and sustainable use of marine environment and
 resources. The programme had been continuing since 1991 for monitoring the level of various marine pollutants and its
 impacts on marine fauna and flora of the country. The data collected under the programme was made available to the
 Pollution Control Boards and periodically discussed with them. Any significant increase in pollutants at a particular
 location was brought to the notice of the Central Pollution Control Board for control as well as remedial actions.  The
 main objective of the Programme was to constantly assess the health of India’s  marine environment and indicate areas
 that needed immediate and long term remedial action.  Data on 25 environmental parameters were being collected at 82
 locations last year with the help of nine R&D institutions.  The Programme along with the modeling component would
 be continued during 2003-04. An allocation of Rs.2.00 crores has been sought for carrying out the activities under the
 programme for the year 2003-04
30.       At present the Department is monitoring pollution levels at 82 locations in our coastal waters and brings data to
 the notice of Central Pollution Control Board as well as concerned State Pollution Control Boards for mitigative
 measures. Enormous efforts are made to collect data through the coastal research vessels, i.e., Sagar Purvi and Sagar
 Paschimi. The data generated under this programme is reviewed periodically in the presence of Member Secretaries of
 Coastal Pollution Control Boards who are permanent members of the Steering Committee of the programme.
 Development of GIS based database is a continuous process as the data is collected on a long-term basis. As far as
 monitoring activities of the Department are concerned, the present projection of Rs.2.00 crores is sufficient for 2003-04
 at the B.E. stage.
31.       The Committee recommends that the Department may augment its ongoing Coastal Ocean Monitoring and
 Prediction System to regularly monitor the condition of the coastal waters and adjoining areas. 
MARINE RESEARCH AND CAPACITY BUILDING
32.       The objectives of the programme are to foster the concept of stewardship through education, training and human
 resource development and increasing awareness at all levels. The activities proposed in the programme include
 promotion of research under the basic categories of marine ecology, marine biology, marine microbiology, marine
 benthos, coastal marine culture systems, marine geology/geophysics and ocean engineering & underwater robotics. 
 Besides the ongoing programme of award of fellowships to students for pursuing higher studies in
 academic/educational institutions in various disciplines of ocean science and technology, organizing exhibitions and
 fairs to create awareness among the public on the oceans would continue.
33.       The Scientific Research and Technology Development programmes for exploration and sustainable use of the
 marine resources are multi-disciplinary and multi-institutional.  Basic research and developments are required in a wide
 spectrum of areas to gain adequate knowledge and expertise.  Required infrastructure and trained personnel are
 essential for successfully implementing different programmes.  There is need for effective interaction between R&D
 institutions, academicians and industries.
34.       The Department has been implementing this programme with a view to encouraging research in the newly
 emerging and frontline areas of Marine Chemistry, Marine Biology and Microbiology, Coastal Zone management,
 Marine Archaeology, Exploration and Exploitation of Marine Resources, etc. to finance infrastructure facilities in
 Universities / Institutions / Organizations etc., and to generate special Manpower in the Ocean Sector.
35.       Asked about the efforts being made by the Department for disseminating information about its research activities
 and achievements to the masses, it informed the Committee that the awareness campaigns aim to spread scientific
 knowledge among school children and masses about our oceans. By organising exhibitions, trade fairs, seminars,
 conferences, workshops etc. the Department aims at promoting awareness about our oceans among our people.  Senior
 officers of the Department also actively contribute to this awakening by giving interviews/ programmes on the national
 media, i.e., television, radio, newspapers and magazines. Furthermore training programmes, quiz shows for children,
 audio-video presentations on the Department and its attached offices/institutions help spread knowledge on the oceans.
 A television series on ocean related activities is being telecast on the national channel. A bimonthly newsletter
 "WISTA: Ocean Wealth" for disseminating information on oceans and activities of DOD and other related aspects is
 being published.
36.       For strengthening ocean research centres in coastal universities, the Department is emphasising on quantum
 jump in our approach towards the ocean.  To achieve that purpose the Committee recommends that the Department

COASTAL RESEARCH VESSELS
37.       Two research ships ORV Sagar Kanya and FORV Sagar Sampada have been carrying out oceanographic surveys
 for the exploration of non-living and living resources in the Exclusive Economic zone (EEZ) and beyond, around
 Indian Ocean region since 1984.  These vessels were being utilised for multi-disciplinary research on the physical,
 chemical, geological and biological aspects of the Indian Ocean.  The vessels were also engaged in campaigns for
 validating satellite oceanographic data, assessment of marine living resources and for various technology demonstration
 activities. The vessels facilitate systematic collection of samples and immediate analysis of the mandatory parameters
 like nitrate, phosphate etc. for the Coastal Ocean Monitoring  & Prediction   System  (COMAPS) programme.   Both   
 the   vessels   are equipped with sophisticated scientific facilities for onboard analysis and navigational equipments
 alongwith communication facilities. In order to strengthen the programme on monitoring of marine pollution along the
 coastal waters of the country and to promote research on near shore phenomena, the two vessels do sampling at desired
 locations of the transects identified for potential hot spots. The National Institute of Ocean Technology, Chennai
 through its Vessel Management Cell is maintaining these vessels. During the year 2003-04 an allocation of Rs.5.00
 crores has been earmarked for the programme.
38.       These vessels are being used for pollution monitoring under the Coastal Ocean Monitoring and Prediction
 System (COMPAS) programme of the Department and also Integrated Coastal and Marine Area Management
 programme.  These have completed 56 cruises for 15 institutions along the west and east coast of India.  The ship time
 is being effectively utilized by engaging the vessels for various programmes and preventive and periodical maintenance
 was ensured for trouble free functioning of onboard equipment and machineries.  During the cruises, these vessels
 undertook CTD, ADCP observations, dreadging, water  sampling and plankton net operations.  In addition  the cruises
 participated in the Marine  Archaeological findings at Gulf of Cambay and Multibeam sonar survey at Ennore and
 Haldia ports.  Public sector undertakings and corporate agencies like IGCAR, ONGC utilised the service of these
 vessels.
39.       Both the Coastal Research Vessels have been plying in east and west coast for pollution monitoring since 1996
 and have been conducting experiments in close coordination with the COMAPS participating institutions. The grant
 projected is for regular running, maintenance of vessels, upkeep and upgradation of scientific equipments. Since they
 are of regular nature, the expenditure is expected to be at the same level with slight increase in running and
 maintenance expenditures and decrease in the equipment upgradation and purchase. Hence, the projected level of
 expenditure i.e. Rs.5.00 crores can sustain the activities.
40.       The Committee observes that the Coastal Research Vessels(CRVs), with the participation of scientists of other
 related institutions, should cruise frequently to monitor pollution and do other multidisciplinary work.
INTEGRATED COASTAL AND MARINE AREA MANAGEMENT (ICMAM)
41.       The Integrated Coastal and Marine Area Management (ICMAM) programme focuses on development of
 expertise in ICMAM oriented activities and dissemination of knowledge gained by the users like coastal states through
 organized training programmes; developing capabilities in the coastal states and UTs for adoption of ICMAM through
 training; creating a base for human resource development in the fields of ICMAM and ensuring sustainable
 development and management of the ocean resources and enforcement of rules and regulations for regulation of ocean
 related activities in the ocean zone to make Indian oceans clean and productive.
42.       The programme has two components, namely (i) Capacity building and (ii) Development of Infrastructure for
 R&D, Survey and Training for ICMAM.  The capacity building component is being funded by the International
 Development Association containing the activities, namely (i) Development of Geographic Information System (GIS)
 for 11 critical habitats in the coastal and marine Areas in India (II) Determination of Waste Assimilation Capacity at
 selected estuaries along coastal areas of India, (iii) Development of Guidelines for Environmental Impact Assessment
 and (iv) Preparation of Model Integrated Coastal and Marine Area Management Plans.  Under the component on
 infrastructure, training, laboratories and other facilities have been established in the NIOT Campus, Chennai.  The
 determination of Use Classification for Coastal/Waters and no impact zone for selected habitats like coastal lakes and
 mangroves were in progress.
43.       The enhanced allocation of Rs.5.50 crores for ICMAM programme for 2003-04 is 10% over and above the
 previous year’s (2002-03) allocation of Rs.5.00 crores. The additional allocation of Rs.0.50 crores is for creation of

INTERNATIONAL COOPERATION
44.       The objectives of the Department through this programme is:
to contribute and participate effectively in all the international/bilateral organizations, meetings, conferences,
 committees etc. with a view to projecting India’s role in ocean development activities
to exchange information and expertise in different aspects of ocean science & technology between the Department and
 its organizations and other countries, for upgrading knowledge and for fostering technical cooperation.
45.       The Committee was informed that a MoU was signed between the Government of India and the Republic of
 South Africa in 2002 for promoting Antarctic cooperation. In the same year Indian and Russian delegations visited each
 other’s countries to study the subject of Gas Hydrates and related technologies. Another delegation, from America,
 visited India in February, 2003 to discuss a bilateral project proposal on ‘Ocean Observation for the Indian Ocean  and
 Assessment of Data Available’ and ‘Greenhouse Gas Measurements’. Besides, the Department has entered into MoUs
 with countries such as  Chile, Argentina, Peru, South Korea, Portugal, Germany, etc for conducting experiments related
 to basic and advanced research in the field of Oceanography/ Ocean Sciences.

 Intergovernmental organizations/bodies such as Antarctic Treaty System, SCAR, Council of Managers of National
 Antarctic Programmes (COMNAP)/Standing Committee on Antarctic Logistic Operation (SCALOP), CCAMLR, IOC,
 Regional Seas Programme, International Sea Bed Authority and International Tribunal on Law of the sea (ISBA),
 IBPIO/DBCP etc.
47.       The Committee notes that India is a signatory to the Ocean Charter which is not a legal entity, but which
 stipulates that all nations shall act in unison to protect the oceans.  India being a major maritime country in the Indian
 Ocean rim, it has a greater responsibility to take initiatives for bringing together all littoral countries for the
 development, protection and conservation of oceans.  The Committee notes with trepidation the observation of Dr. R.
 Sengupta, renowned oceanographer, “Of the three greatest water bodies, the Atlantic, the Pacific and the Indian Ocean,
 the latter was the cleanest.  But that is history now”.  The Committee therefore recommends that India must take a lead
 to protect its own interests and the interests of developing countries vis-a-vis their oceanic resources.
OCEAN OBSERVATION & INFORMATION SERVICES (OOIS)
48.       Recognizing the need to operationalise the oceanographic services in the new areas of Science & Technology,
 the Department has implemented the Ocean Observation and Information Services (OOIS) programme from the
 beginning of the 9
th Plan.  The objective of the Programme is to provide ocean information services for various
 applications in the ocean section.  OOIS is structured  around four major  themes  namely,  Ocean  Observing 
 Systems,  Ocean  Information
Services, Satellite Coastal and Oceanographic Research (SATCORE) and Indian Ocean Modelling & Ocean
 Dynamic(INDOMOD).

 bathythermographs (XBT), current meter arrays and tide gauges, and designed particularly for acquisition of real-time
 sea surface, meteorological and upper oceanographic parameters from the coastal and deep waters.  Validation of the
 satellite sensors has also been undertaken using the sea truth data generated under this programme.  The Data Buoy
 Programme was initiated in 1996 with partial financial assistance from Norwegian Agency for Development (NORAD)
 and National Institute of Ocean Technology (NOIT) has been entrusted with the responsibilities for deployment,
 operation and maintenance of the data buoys.
50.       The Ocean information service envisages generation and dissemination  of ocean data/data products on an
 operational basis.  The 14 National Marine Data Centres will be continued under the Ocean Information & Services.A
 dedicated centre “Indian National Centre for Ocean Information Services (INCOIS)” started functioning at Hyderabad
 from 1999 for  efficient development and dissemination of data products.   INCOIS is involved to synthesis, generate,
 promote, provide and coordinate various endeavours in the field of ocean sciences, ocean observations, satellite
 oceanography, and ocean information and advisory services.  INCOIS has a vision to emerge as a knowledge and

NATIONAL INSTITUTE OF OCEAN TECHNOLOGY
55.       The National Institute of Ocean Technology (NIOT) was established in November, 1993 as a registered society
 under the administrative control of the Department of Ocean Development with a view to developing technology in the
 ocean sector. The main aim of NIOT is to develop and  promote  technology  in mission  mode  for  specific  purposes 
 in  ocean  related  areas. The multifarious activities of NIOT are carried out as in-house technology development
 programmes and field demonstration projects. Initially NIOT’s spectrum of activities includes the four core mission
 activities i.e. Ocean Energy, Deep Sea Mining, Coastal and Environmental engineering and Marine Instrumentation.
 Subsequently, NIOT was also entrusted with the operation & maintenance of two CRVs by establishing a  Vessel
 Management Cell in 1996 and National Data Buoy Programme in 1997. In 1998-99, one more project on Island
 Development was added to the activities of NIOT and renamed as Ocean Science & Technology for Islands. NIOT is
 also entrusted to undertake Hi-tech consultancy service in ocean related activities.  During 2003-04, the major
 activities, ongoing as well as new, undertaken by NIOT are testing of 1MW Ocean Thermal Energy Conversion
 (OTEC) Plant, design of mining system for depth upto 6000 m, preparation of Environmental Impact Assessment (EIA)
 guidelines for Coastal Ocean management, development of Under Water Marine Instruments and calibration of the
 same and continuing the project on enhancement of Marine Living Resources. For the project Ocean Science &
 Technology for Islands, NIOT has already made a headway in enhancement of marine living resources in the island
 groups by taking up technology development for breeding, rearing and fattening lobsters to begin with. The facilities
 both at the Island groups and at the mainland have been augmented for this purpose. It is proposed to expand the
 activities under this programme to other marine organisms on selective basis and also to coordinate the implementation
 of all the programmes of the Department in the island groups for the benefit of the island community.
56.       The Committee was informed that the budgetary allocation for the National Institute of Ocean Technology
 (NIOT) has been kept at Rs.25.00 crores as against last year's allocation of Rs.23.40 crores. The increase in allocation
 was caused due to new activities on Marine Archaeology under the Coastal and Environmental Engineering Group and
 inclusion of Ocean Science and Technology for Islands Programme as part of the core Mission Programmes of NIOT.
 Feasibility studies for establishment of 5 MW OTEC plant is being implemented during the year 2003-04 by the
 Department in pursuance of the recommendation made by the Committee in its 101
st Report.
57.       The Committee reiterates its earlier recommendation to the Department to build energy plants of higher capacity
 as it feels that this might be cost effective in the long run and lessen the dependence on fossil fuel for power generation.

14.       The Committee recommends that in order to improve Oceanography services, the Department should strengthen
 the observation platforms.  The moored buoy network should also be augmented to improve generation of data useful
 for the Coastal and off shore developmental activities.  The Department should also process the data collected from
 Array for Real-time Geotropic Oceanography (ARGO) Floats for obtaining temperature and salinity profiles from the
 Indian Ocean to study the long-term climate and Monsoon variability.
 (Para 52)
15.       The Committee observes that the Department should monitor the performance of the Indian National Centre for
 Ocean Information Services (INCOIS) for efficient dissemination of ocean data and data products to user communities
 on a regular basis.
(Para 53)
16.       The Committee recommends that the Department should take initiatives in setting up information kiosks in the
 coastal states to facilitate the dissemination of data/data products to user communities.
 (Para 54)
17.       The Committee reiterates its earlier recommendation to the Department to build energy plants of higher capacity
 as it feels that this might be cost effective in the long run and lessen the dependence on fossil fuel for power generation.
(Para 57)
18.       The Committee hopes that such activities of the Department yield good results.  The Committee strongly feels
 that the allocation for the Department for this area must be substantially enhanced. 
(Para 59)
19.       The Committee has been recommending for a Research Vessel for the Department and therefore notes with
 satisfaction that the proposal for such a vessel has been approved in principle by the Planning Commission.  The
 Committee recommends that this proposal be implemented as soon as possible to enable the Department to do its
 important work in ocean development.
(Para 65)
20.       The Committee strongly recommends that all the new projects proposed by the Department should be taken up
 on a time bound basis.  The Committee also strongly recommends that sufficient allocations be made for the successful
 completion of these projects.
(Para 67)
21.       After considering the Demands for Grants of the Department of Ocean Development and assessing the progress
 of various important programmes and projects administered by it, the Committee recommends that the budgetary
 allocation of Rs.199.33 crores, as sought by the Department for the year 2003-2004, under Demand No. 65, may be
 approved.

#          Nominated w.e.f. 7th April, 2003.
INTRODUCTION
 
            I, the Chairman of the Department-related Parliamentary Standing Committee on Science & Technology,
 Environment & Forests, having been authorised by the Committee to present the Report on its behalf, present this One
 Hundred-Sixteenth Report of the Committee.  This Report deals with the detailed Demands for Grants (2003-2004) of
 the Department of Biotechnology (Ministry of Science and Technology) (Demand No.82).
 
2.         In the meeting of the Committee held on 1
st April, 2003 the Secretary and other Officers of the Department of
 Biotechnology gave an overview of the various activities of the Department and the Members sought clarifications on
 various aspects of the performance of the Department to enable it to scrutinise the Demands for Grants.
 
3.         The Committee expresses its thanks to the Officers of the Department for replying to the clarifications sought by
 the Members and placing before it the required material to enable the Committee to scrutinise the Demands for Grants
 of the Department of Biotechnology.
 
4.         The Committee considered and adopted the Report at its meeting held on 29
th April, 2003.
 
 
NEW DELHI;
April  29 , 2003
 
 
 
C. RAMACHANDRAIAH,
Chairman,
Parliamentary Standing Committee on
 Science & Technology, Environment & Forests.
       
 
R E P O R T
 
            Focus on biology has brought about a paradigm shift in the understanding of human life and the entire
 ecosystem.  The hallmarks of the second half of the 20
th century were the discovery of double helix, DNA structure,
 transfer of genes from one unrelated organism to another and the sequencing of human genome.  Much before all these
 path-breaking scientific activities were undertaken, Pandit Jawaharlal Nehru had written, with rare far sightedness in
 the Discovery of India.  “Perhaps new developments in biology……… and other similar sciences and the interpretation
 of biology may help man to understand and control himself more than he has done in the past”.  While 20
th century was
 the age of physical sciences, the 21st century has been perceived as the century of biology.  India, with its vast
 biological resources is poised to reap rich harvests in the century of biology.  Establishment of the Department of
 Biotechnology is a significant step in that direction.
2.         Biotechnology as a branch of modern biology is hardly two decades old and it is the fastest growing branch of
 modern science.   It is rapidly becoming the cornerstone of industrial development and leading us to the brink of bio-
industrial revolution.  In fact, we are now in biotech century and our way of life is likely to be more fundamentally
 transformed in the decades to come. The present day definition of biotechnology is the application of scientific and
 engineering principles to the processing materials by biological agents to produce goods and services.  The applications
 of biotechnology are so wide that virtually every industry including pharmaceuticals, textiles, aquaculture, chemicals,

116TH REPORT
file:///C/Users/user/Desktop/pri/Committee%20on%20S%20and%20T,%20Env.%20and%20Forests/116threport.htm[29-08-2018 16:26:51]
 household products, manufacturing, environmental cleaning, food processing and forensics, are using such technology. 
3.         Biotechnology is emerging as a major player for enhancing the food productivity, nutritional status, sustainable
 utilization of biological resources, prospecting of new molecules and genes, identification and characterization of
 biological wealth, development of new vaccines, diagnostics and drugs, pollution abatement through biotechnological
 route, waste recycling, etc.  Bioinformatics and human resource development have given rich dividends in terms of
 highly skilled and trained human resource available in the country and a strong information network being utilized by a
 large number of scientists. The Department of Bio-technology under the Ministry of Science & Technology was set up
 in February, 1986 to give a greater impetus to the development of biotechnology in the country.  The objectives of the
 Department include development of products and processes and technologies whose large scale applications would
 result in societal and economic benefits.
4.         The main responsibilities of this Department are :
To evolve integrated plans and programmes in Biotechnology.
Identify, specific programmes of Research and Development and oversee related research and manufacturing activities
 for biologicals.
Identify, set up and support centres of excellence for research and development in biotechnology and ensure proper
 dovetailing of these activities with national priorities.
To act as a screening, advising and approving body of Government with regard to import and transfer of new
 technologies for the manufacture of biological and biotechnological products.
To evolve safety guidelines for biotechnology research, development and manufacturing in India.
To act as the Central agency for the import of genetically manipulated/modified materials, culture cells, specimens,
 tissues and biotech products including DNA and RNA of any type and for promoting their production in the country.
To serve as the inter-ministerial and inter-agency nodal point for all specific international, bilateral and multilateral
 research and development collaboration in the area of biotechnology and act as the nodal point for all technology
 transfers in the area of biotechnology.
For manufacturing and application of cell-based vaccines.
To evolve programmes of human resource development in the area of biotechnology.
To act as the administrative department for autonomous institutions
Serve as the authorised Department of the Government in respect of legislative Parliamentary requirements in all areas
 mentioned under Allocation of Business for the Department.
5.         The biotechnology programmes are being implemented through a number of autonomous and statutory
 institutions and Universities to which assistance is provided by the Department by way of grants-in-aid.  The
 Department is also looking after the work relating to the International Centre for Genetic Engineering and
 Biotechnology (ICGEB).  The autonomous institutions established by the department under Societies Registration Act,
 1860, include: National Institute of Immunology (NII), New Delhi, National Centre for Plant Genome Research, New
 Delhi, National Centre for Cell Science (NCCS), Pune, Centre for DNA Finger Printing and Diagnostics, Hyderabad,
 National Centre for Plant Genome Research, New Delhi, National Brain Research Centre, New Delhi, Institute of
 Bioresources and  Sustainable Development (ISBD), Imphal, Institute of Life Sciences, Bhubaneshwar.  A Public
 Sector undertaking namely, the Bharat Immunologicals and Biologicals corporation Ltd. (BIBCOL), Bullandshahr is
 engaged in manufacturing Oral Polio Vaccine (OPV) and other immunologicals under Prime Minister’s Technology
 Mission on Immunization, with a view to achieving self-sufficiency in manufacturing of Oral Polio Vaccine (OPV).
6.         The major programmes /projects to be taken up during 2003-04 include: six new P.G. teaching programme in
 regions not represented, NMR facility at Indian Institute of Chemical Biology (IICB) Kolkata, upgradation of some of
 the major bioinformatics centres as centres of Excellence for undertaking advanced research and postgraduate
 education; collaborative mutli-institutional research projects on functional genomics of rice, biotechnology for
 improvement of semi-arid crops; post harvest biotechnology for improved shelf life, nanobiotechnology, development
 of cocktail diagnostic molecular tools for infectious diseases, drugs through combinatorial chemistry and high
 screening throughput, basic research on diarrheal diseases, sequencing and molecular typing of infectious agents,
 neurodegenerative diseases, edible vaccines and contraception mission programmes on h
erbal
Products development, new generation vaccines, vaccines research and development, food and nutritional security,
 bioenergy and biofuels, genomics, oncology, advanced research in stem cell biology, the genomic sequencing of
 microbes relevant to India, establishment of bio-villages, international collaborations as per agreements and work plans
. The proposals for establishment of biotech parks, biotech incubators and other centralized facilities specially from
 State Governments will also be taken up.

116TH REPORT
file:///C/Users/user/Desktop/pri/Committee%20on%20S%20and%20T,%20Env.%20and%20Forests/116threport.htm[29-08-2018 16:26:51]
7.         Keeping in view the above programmes, recent trends and international developments, the Department had
 projected a requirement of Rs.450.00 crores for the year 2003-04 to the Planning Commission. However, an allocation
 (plan side) of Rs.260.00 crores has only been provided. During the year 2002-03, the plan allocation at B.E. and R.E.
 stages was Rs.225.00 crores and Rs.205.00 crores respectively. The enhanced allocation for 2003-04 will primarily be
 utilized on new programmes/initiatives. Functional genomics, vaccines and plant based products will be a priority.
8.         The Committee was informed that one of the recurring problems of the Department is the shortfall of the non-
plan budget. Recurrence of such problems on year to year basis, the Committee was apprised,  has created a compelling
 situation for the autonomous bodies whereby they had to cut down from plan funds to pay salaries to the scientists. The
 Committee is constrained to note that scientific institutions engaged in research in frontier areas of science have to
 confront such a situation. The additional requirement of the Department for non-plan expenditure is to the tune of
 Rs.5.00 crores. The Committee, therefore, recommends that sufficient funds may be provided to the Department to
 overcome this problem. It further underlines that the Departments dealing with science and technology should be
 accorded priority for allocation of funds  and  if  necessary,   special  provisions  may  be  made  for  them  so  that they
 do not face such problems.  Biotechnology era is waiting to dominate the World  economy in the next twenty years. 
 Investment in this field is not commensurate with the potential of this branch of Science.

 and utilization, societal development and biotech industrial growth.

 as Tenth Plan proposals. These programmes aim at enhancing the knowledge base and generating highly skilled human
 resource, nurturing leads of potential utilityby emerging bioscience enterprises areas of agriculture, health care and the
 environment and bringing bio-products to the marketplace for generation of wealth, import substitutions, export
 promotion and technological self sufficiency. The emphasis would be on excellence and relevance for socio-economic
 progress. Agricultural Biotechnology programmes such as rice genome sequencing, development of pest and disease
 resistant varieties, nutritionally rich crops, virus free tissue culture plants, improved biofertilisers and biopesticides will

 Committee consisting of experts from research institutions, universities, industry and NGOs does the same exercise.

PLANT TISSUE CULTURE
17.       Tissue culture is an important tool of biotechnology which can be used to improve the productivity of planting
 material through enhanced availability of identified plant stock with desired traits.  The main object of the programme
 is to develop protocols for regeneration of economically important plant species covering Forest Trees, Horticulture and
 Plantation Crops.  Plant Tissue Culture technology is being used for mass multiplication of elite forest species and also
 for producing large quantities of planting material with desired characteristics.   The shortage of biomass and the
 increasing gap between supply and demand due to the mounting population pressure necessitated the mass propagation
 of trees through Tissue Culture.  The tree species identified cover a wide spectrum including trees of desert and arid
 zones, tropical and temperate zones.  DBT has supported programmes on priority crops to increase productivity per unit
 area by developing a strong R&D component concentrating on the production of high yielding and improved varieties
 and fresh methods of multiplication of elite plus trees.
18.       The Committee was informed that during 2003-04 the ongoing efforts in R&D programmes on tissue culture
 protocol standardization would continue for the identified priority crops.  Protocols for in vitro production of Saffron
 and Kalazira will be refined and scaled up.  Studies will continue for complete technology development for coffee, tea,
 spices, apple and citrus.  The Network programmes on Apple and Citrus will be launched and the germplasm will be
 characterized.  The certified virus free plants would be field planted and evaluated.  The novel orchid hybrids produced
 will be evaluated based on commercial parameters and an effort will be made to take these hybrids for commercial
 production.  Field demonstration of tissue culture raised Black pepper will be taken up in all identified sites.
19.       The Committee was apprised that under Plant Tissue Culture, 20 regeneration protocols have been developed
 and a molecular diagnostic kit for detection of Bunchy top Virus in Banana is in use at present.  The Micropropagation
 Technology Parks are serving as a platform for transfer of proven technologies and training in tissue culture.  So far,
 6.5 million plants have been produced and planted in 7500 hectares in 17 States.  Technologies for 10 species have
 been transferred to the industry.  A satellite park has been setup in North-East for popularization of technology and
 production of planting material for the region.  In addition, five Regional Hardening Units in different States are
 functioning well.
20.       The Committee is of the view that efforts should be made to make use of the tissue culture and floriculture
 technology in rural areas. Additional incentives should be given to persons willing to work in these areas.

 modern biology including data banks of genetic importance published literature, patents and other information of
 scientific and commercial value.  It also aims to provide necessary infrastructural support for modern research in
 biology involving computationally intensive analysis.  The network consists of 11 Distributed Information Centers

 institutions like International Centre for Co-operation in Bio-informatics (ICCB), a UNESCO based funded bio-
informatics programme and is also linked with EMB net, as well as international legume-data base and information
 services (ILDIS).  Educational and training activities in bio-informatics will also form part of the scheme.  National Jai
 Vigyan Mission on Mirror Sites for Genomic Research to establish four major databases have progressed well. These
 projects are being pursued at Indian Institute of Science, Bangalore; University of Pune; Jawaharlal Nehru University
 and Institute of Microbial Technology, Chandigarh.  New projects for establishing Centres of excellence in bio-
informatics will be taken up.

 institutions/universities.  Each centre of the network has built up Bioinformatics resources in their specialized areas in
 the form of databases, software packages for application to Biotechnology and Molecular Biology, which are shared by
 the researchers in the country.  Towards the development of molecular modelling and simulation studies in

 Though, there is an increase in the number of DNA fingerprinting cases by 20-25% every year, the Centre can sustain
 the thrust of its activities with the same allocation of the budget. 
59.       CDFD has constructed a laboratory complex on a 13 acre plot of land given by the Government of Andhra
 Pradesh at Gandipet. The construction of laboratory has been completed and the contract for services, interior work,
 furnishings landscaping, etc. will be awarded soon .It is expected that CDFD will move to its own complex before the
 end of this year. Initially, the cost of the building of the CDFD was estimated at Rs.3.63 crores and as per the revised
 cost estimate, it amounts to Rs.13.55 crores. The cost revision in the building is primarily because of construction of
 separate research complex.  CDFD was earlier supposed to be a small centre working on DNA fingerprinting for which
 it was proposed to be housed in the land adjoining the IICT campus, Hyderabad with the main building area of only

60.       While the Committee notes with satisfaction the contributions of the Centre to forensic medicine and wildlife

National Brain Research Centre (NBRC)
61.       The National Brain Research Centre (NBRC), an autonomous body of the Department, was registered as a
 society in June 1999. The mandate of the Centre is to undertake basic research to understand brain function in normal
 health and disease and establish linkages with national/international organizations involved in neuroscience research. It
 would not only have infrastructure facilities and a coordinated multi-disciplinary team of scientists working in the
 frontier area of neuroscience but also to support and network the existing groups in the country. Thus, the centre would
 act as National Apex Centre for Brain Research to promote neuroscience research. NBRC has been recently recognized
 by UGC as deemed university for  post graduate education in neurosciences.  The centre would continue research work
 on basic brain function, disorders, imaging and neurosciences and neuroinformatics and human resource development.
 Construction of the phase II of the campus will also be undertaken.
62.       An amount of Rs.16 crores was proposed for 2003-04 to carryout research activities of NBRC and to execute
 Phase-II of the center. However, outlay has been scaled down to Rs.11 crores as the Phase-II proposal of the NBRC is
 under consideration. EFC memo has been circulated for the comments of the concerned Ministries/Departments. The
 outlay will be suitably adjusted   upwards  after the  EFC is  approved  and  in  accordance  with  the  budget 
 provisions.  During the last year NBRC has initiated new research activities in areas like computational neuroscience,
 system and cognitive neuroscience and understanding gender differences in pathogenesis of neuro generative disorders
 and theoretical neurobiology. Functional Micro-array facility for neuro-genetic disorders has also been established. 
 Further, the centre has already initiated projects in the frontier area of research, which includes Stem Cell Research,
 Developmental neurobiology and basic research towards understanding of neurological and psychological disorders.
 The NBRC has been accorded the status of Deemed University.
63.       The Phase-I construction of its permanent campus at Manesar has been completed ahead of time without any
 time and cost overrun and laboratories of the centre have been shifted from its interim facility at Gurgaon to Manesar. 
 At present, the NBRC is functioning from its new campus. EFC for Phase-II has been circulated and construction is
 expected to be completed by March, 2007.   
64.       The Committee notes with satisfaction the research activities undertaken at the National Brain Research Centre
 (NBRC). 
65.       Moreover, in order to inform Medical Colleges and concerned Departments of Neurology about the research
 findings of the NBRC, the Department should undertake activities in a networking manner with the existing
 neuroscience groups/institutions in the country and promote multidisciplinary research in neuroscience. 
National Center for Plant Genome Research (NCPGR)
66.       TheNational Centre for Plant Genome Research (NCPGR) is mainly working to understand the structure,
 expression and function of genes and their arrangement on plant genomes and their manipulation to breed improved
 varieties of food and industrial crops for high yields of better quality products.  The Centre is pursuing projects on
 functional and application genomics of chickpea (pulse) and Catharanthus roseus (important medicinal plant),
 development of nutritionally enhanced potato, tomato with reduced oxalate contents and tolerant to fungal infections,
 improvement of protein contents in rice, sweet potato and cassava  Lathyrus sp. (Khesri Dal) free of neurotoxin.  The
 Centre is also engaged in human resource development in the core-areas of plant molecular biology, genetic
 engineering and genome analysis by way of imparting   advanced training at pre-and post-doctoral levels. 
67.       The Committee was informed that the building of NCPGR is under construction.  Out of budgetary  allocation of
 Rs.7.00 crores for the year 2002-2003, approximately      Rs.4.5 crores is meant for building construction.
68.       The Committee endorses the vision of the Department to make agriculture sustainable by using biotechnology.
 To get better yields, we need plants and methods of cultivation which will be in harmony with biodiversity and eco-
system and therefore will not bring down the fertility of land and kill useful animals, pests and weeds. This objective
 can be achieved by, among others, changing plant characteristics through genetic modification. The Committee
 impresses upon the Department to work with full vigour to realise this objective. Prof. M.S.Swaminathan, one of the

 leading figures who spearheaded green revolution in our country, has said that green revolution can become ever green
 revolution by making it pro-nature, pro-poor and pro-women. Therefore, the Committee emphasizes that the

MEDICAL BIOTECHNOLOGY
69.       Medical Biotechnology has come to the centrestage with spectacular advances in biology. This is due to a
 number of emerging and re-emerging infections requiring development of suitable diagnostics and therapeutics. Several
 events at the international biotech scene such as the rise of genomics era, stem cell research and bioinformatics have
 percolated down to the national biotechnology scene with a large number of scientists galvanized to reap the benefits.
 The Department of Biotechnology has continued its efforts for the development of suitable diagnostics, vaccines,
 therapeutic and better drug delivery systems.
70.       The objectives of the medical biotechnology programme are:
Development of suitable diagnostics for early detection of major communicable & non-communicable diseases.
Development of new generation vaccines for prophylaxis and therapeutic use.
Development of newer and alternate drug delivery system.
Production of important biological and bioactive molecules using suitable expression systems and modern fermentation
 technology.
Programme support for creation of infrastructures in newer areas of biotechnological research.
Transfer of prototype technologies to suitable industries for refinement, upscaling and commercialization.
To develop multi centric programme on stem cell biology.
71.       During the year 2001-2002, 12 prototype diagnostics/other technologies relating to medical biotechnology
 discipline have been transferred to industry for refinement, up scaling and commercialization. The diagnostic
 technology relating to ELISA system to measure Alpha feto protein levels in pregnant women is ready for launching. 
 During the year 2002-2003, after an interactive discussion meeting with industrial entrepreneurs, three entrepreneurs
 have agreed to take up three systems to diagnose pulmonary and extra pulmonary tuberculosis. In addition, the
 industries have joined hands with the Department to develop prototype/candidate vaccine for Malaria, Rota Virus and
 DNA Rabies Vaccine.
72.       Medical biotechnology and health care areas lay emphasis on molecular diagnostics, genetic vaccines, molecular
 characterization of pathogens, new drug targets and new drug delivery systems relating to viral, bacterial and parasitic
 infections.  Also, major programmes have been implemented in the areas of cervical and oral cancers, stem cell
 biology, development of products and processes, development of products and processes, development of advanced
 infrastructure and expertise.  Currently, about 115 R&D projects are under implementation and during the reporting
 period, 165 papers have been published in national and international journals from these projects.  Four patent
 applications have been filed and industrial partners for several diagnostics technologies have been identified for
 upscaling and commercialization.
AGRICULTURE BIO-TECHNOLOGY
73.       The department is supporting three main types of research activities under the scheme; R&D projects in priority
 crops, multi-institutional projects and plant molecular programmes in certain institutions/universities.  The multi-
institutional project involves interaction amongst a number  of  institutions  with  well  defined  objectives.  The project
 on  (a)  the  development  of transgenic crops – cotton, rice, mungbean and tomato resistance to biotic stresses deal with
 cotton bollworm CLCV, in rice – RTSV and RTVV, in mungbean MYMV and in tomato TMV (b) the project on
 molecular characterization and field trials of mustard transgenic for hybrid seed production and low – till cultivation is
 being pursued by three institutions.  The project involves studies on characterization of male sterility/restoration lines
 and improvement of technology, testing of male sterile lines and the identify homozygous barstar the storer liens and    
 (c) development of varieties with durable resistance to leaf and stripe rust using molecular marker technology in wheat. 
 This project deals with validation of genetic stocks for documented genes conferring seed and adult plant resistant to
 leaf rust and stripe rust, identification of molecular markers for important gene and pyramiding important APR and
 seed resistance genes in common cultivars.
INTERNATIONAL COOPERATION
74.       The allocation for the International Cooperation has been increased to Rs.8.00 crores for the year 2003-04. The
 budget was enhanced for implementing the on-going commitments and new initiatives.  Several new bilateral
 programmes have been initiated with countries like Denmark, Mauritius, Brazil and Sudan.    New programmes are
 being identified with UK, Norway, Chile and Mongolia.  Ongoing programmes have been expanded with countries like
 USA, Germany, Sri Lanka, Israel, Syria, Myanmar, Russia, Belarus and Switzerland. There are proposals to establish
 Indo-ASEAN Biotechnology Network, Asian biotechnology consortium, and India – Singapore Joint Biotechnology

 Park in association with Ministry Of External Affairs. Indo-Russian centre for biotechnology will be fully operational.
75.       The Committee was informed that International cooperation is pursued for R&D work with the most advanced
 countries for mutual benefit.  It also helps in implementation of national R&D programmes and to open up avenues for
 collaborative interaction in advanced areas leading to transfer of technologies / knowledge into the country.  The
 activity has already resulted in training of large number of young scientists. A diagnostic to identify Sea food pathogens
 was developed and transferred to Industry under Indo-German Programme.  Further, three new genes responsible for
 cerulean cataract were identified.  Under Indo-US collaboration, cellulose sulphate and polystyrene sulphonate
 preparations were developed as vaginal anti-microbial contraceptives.  Technologies were developed for treatment of
 waste water from textiles.  Under Indo-Swedish programme, integrated approaches have been developed for prevention
 of heavy metal leaching from the over burdened heaps of iron, copper and zinc mine spoil dumps. Techniques have
 been standardized for micro-propagation of tree species etc.  There are several leads already available for technology
 development under bilateral programme with Switzerland such as molecular markers specific to rust disease resistance
 in wheat; field testing of bio-pesticides formulation for management of insects of pulses; a phytoremediation protocol
 for remediation of pesticide contaminated soils; a biosensor for detection of pesticide residue in soil and water;
 regeneration and transformation protocols of chickpea for insect resistance and a bioremediation protocol for pesticide
 degradation. Gene constructs, reagents, protocols, sophisticated equipment, tools and techniques have also been made
 available to Indian laboratories through joint R&D projects. Several interactive workshops and seminars have added
 value to the knowledge base. Financial support from some of these collaborations to the Indian laboratories is about
 Rs.20 crores.
 
EXPEDITIOUS CLEARENCE OF PROJECTS SUBMITTED BY THE DEPARTMENT
76.       The Committee was apprised that the proposals submitted by the Department are subjected to periodic review
 and assessment by different agencies including the Planning Commission. The Department further stated that it
 remained ever ready to subject itself and its activities to scrutiny. However, it informed the Committee that time taken
 for review of its projects is too long and therefore comes in the way of its expeditious implementation. While pursuing
 research in the field of science, the Department has to constantly innovate to remain abreast of the ever-evolving
 activities of the scientific community across the globe. Delay in clearing a project, therefore, will throw a spanner in the
 wheel of scientific progress which the Department is carrying forward within a limited budget, to fulfil the objectives
 set before them in a goal oriented and time bound manner. Therefore, the Committee strongly recommends that all the
 proposals of the Department must be cleared expeditiously and within a set time frame.
BUDGET PROPOSALS AT R.E.STAGE
77.       The Department informed the Committee that the reduction of its budget at the R.E. stage causes a lot of
 problem in resetting its priorities. It prepares its plan as per the budget proposals and accordingly prepares its schedule
 of activities. Time taken to re-do the priorities due to cut in R.E. stage is not less than three or four months. Such re-
planning for scientific projects deviates the Department from the set objectives. The Committee is constrained to note
 that such problems are confronted by the Department.
Professor G. Padmanabhan, the UNESCO Professor in Biotechnology Department of Biochemistry, Indian Institute of
 Science, Bangalore in an important article “Contrary to reports, India has not missed the biotech bus” has written about
 the budget requirements of biotechnology which is revealing:
“A single funding agency in the USA has a Rs.4,000 crores budget for genomics. In India, all the funding agencies
 together can mobilise about Rs.100 crores a year for research in this area. It is interesting to note that the country can
 still come up with new drugs, vaccines and diagnostics within this limited budget. If India plays its cards right, it can
 hope to become a world leader in modern vaccine manufacturing, since MNCs are not interested in this field due to
 poor economic returns. All that is needed is a commitment on the part of the Government to ensure availability of the
 committed amount for the next five years, release of grants in time, a mechanism for quick clearance of clinical trials to
 convert the results of the laboratory into commercial products”.
78.       Determination and will of the scientists to achieve the goal which is comparable to international standards and
 within a limited but committed fund is indeed heartening. The Committee, therefore, recommends that the budgets for
 all the Departments dealing with science and technology including that of the Department of Biotechnology may not be
 reduced at the R.E. stage.

 of such knowledge.  This rich reservoir of such resources must  be  understood  scientifically  and safeguarded.  The

1.         The Committee was informed that one of the recurring problems of the Department is the shortfall of the non-
plan budget. Recurrence of such problems on year to year basis, the Committee was apprised,  has created a compelling
 situation for the autonomous bodies whereby they had to cut down from plan funds to pay salaries to the scientists. The
 Committee is constrained to note that scientific institutions engaged in research in frontier areas of science have to
 confront such a situation. The additional requirement of the Department for non-plan expenditure is to the tune of
 Rs.5.00 crores. The Committee, therefore, recommends that sufficient funds may be provided to the Department to
 overcome this problem. It further underlines that the Departments dealing with science and technology should be
 accorded priority for allocation of funds  and  if  necessary,   special  provisions  may  be  made  for  them  so  that they
 do not face such problems.  Biotechnology era is waiting to dominate the World  economy in the next twenty years. 
 Investment in this field is not commensurate with the potential of this branch of Science.

REPORT
Indian tradition of pursuing science and science related activities dates back to thousands and thousands of years. 
 After we attained independence the Government accorded top priority to science and scientific research.  Prime Minister
 Jawaharlal Nehru described our planning process as nothing but science in action.  He declared that “It is science alone
 that could solve the problems of hunger and poverty”.   In spite of resource constraints India’s success in the fields of
 science and technology is spectacular.
To give a direction to the promotion of Science and Technology the Department of Science and Technology was
 established with the primary objective of promoting new areas of Science and Technology and to play the role of a nodal
 department for organising, co-ordinating and promoting S&T activities in the country.  The mandate given to DST
 include, among others:
Ø      Formulation of policy statements and guidelines on S&T
Ø      Promotion of new areas of scientific research
Ø      Co-ordination of inter-departmental S&T efforts
Ø      Support basic and applied research in universities and other institutions
International S&T Co-operation

Ø      Catalyzing S&T interaction in societal programmes, and entrepreneurship development

BUDGETARY ALLOCATION
4.         The Department of Science and Technology has been allocated Rs.1176.12 crores (Rs.790.00 plan and Rs.386.12

The increase in Plan provision of 2003-2004 as compared to R.E 2002-2003 is mainly due to increased allocations
 for Research & Development support – up from Rs.210.00 crores to Rs.215.00 crores; outlay for Technology for Bamboo

FUND FOR IMPROVEMENT OF S&T INFRASTRUCTURE IN UNIVERSITIES AND OTHER HIGHER
 EDUCATIONAL INSTITUTIONS (FIST)
           
7.         The Committee was informed that the objective of this initiative is to strengthen R&D infrastructure in the
 Academic/Research Institutions. It would identify active University/Academic Departments through a peer review
 mechanism including on-site visits and the funding would be done at two levels.   The scheme would provide basic
 infrastructure and facilities for promoting R&D in new and emerging fields of S&T which would also help in attracting
 fresh talent in such Departments.  The proposals supported under the programme would be monitored annually or bi-
annually through an appropriate mechanism.
8.         It was informed that they also plan to invite fresh applications from the prospective Departments/Centres of the
 Universities/academic institutions sometime in July-August 2003 for supporting under the Program and an allocation of
 about Rs.35-40 crores required to extend support to the freshly recommended proposals in year 2003-04.
            The progress of departments who have received the support under the Programme will also be monitored   &
 reviewed by visit of the Expert Member along with the Presentation by the department.
9.            Financial support to the 25 Proposals under Level – II category has also been provided.  Support is also extended
 for continuation of already supported cases in both levels I & II for remaining Equipment grants, Networking &
 Computational facility, Infrastructure Facility and Maintenance and to carry out these activities so far about Rs.35 Crores
 have been utilized.
10.       The Committee notes with constraint that the quality of infrastructure available in our Universities and research
 laboratories for pursuing scientific research is not upto the  mark.  Lack of interest on the part of students to go for science
 education is indeed alarming.    The Department is taking steps to encourage young scientists to pursue serious scientific
 work.  The Committee notes with concern the decline of the quality of our research papers.  There is an urgent need to
 take concerted efforts to arrest this trend to give new dynamism and momentum to Indian science.   
SCIENCE & TECHNOLOGY FOR WOMEN
11.       Women form a very important part of the national scientific workforce.  Indian science requires induction of more
 women scientists and technologists to improve the quality of science and its application towards national development.
 Women face special problems due to their
duties towards motherhood and family and, most of them, suffer “break in their careers” due to these responsibilities.  
 There has been a long-felt need to have special schemes to revive their professional careers.
12.       The Committee was informed that through the scheme ‘Science and Technology for Women’ support is provided
 to time bound action-research projects designed to reduce drudgery, provide newer opportunities for income generation
 based on local resources, address problems pertaining to women’s health and nutrition including occupational health. 
 Successful technology packages are then replicated to field test the model through coordinated programmes.  The
 Department also provides support for the setting up of rural Women’s Technology Parks to showcase technology
 packages relevant to the area, provide technical and entrepreneurial training to women and interface with S&T institutions
 to address specific problems faced by women.
13.       The Government of India, in keeping with its commitment towards welfare and empowerment of women, has come
 up with a special and innovative new scheme which  envisages support to woman scientists, with or without a break in
 career, to pursue science in all its aspects and encourage them to continue in the scientific profession and also to
 contribute towards application of science and technology to societal development.  Approximately 100 scholarships a year
 will be awarded in the specialized subject areas. It is also interesting to report that the women scientists have showed an
 overwhelming response for the scheme. Approximately 5000 women scientists have already approached the department
 for support under this scheme.
14.       Women Scientists Scheme will provide opportunities to women scientists and technologists between the age group
 of 30-50 years.  Under this scheme, women scientists will be provided attractive financial support to pursue research in
 frontier areas of science and engineering, on societal problems requiring S&T intervention and for receiving training for
 possible self-employment in S&T related services sector.
15.       The Women Scientists Scheme (Part-B) to encourage women scientists to take up research on societal problems

REPORT
file:///C/Users/user/Desktop/pri/Committee%20on%20S%20and%20T,%20Env.%20and%20Forests/117threport.htm[29-08-2018 16:27:52]
 was also widely advertised and about 150 applications have been received.  An Expert Committee has also been set up
 which is screening the proposals.              The Women Scientists (Part-C) designed to prepare women scientists to
 undertake self-entrepreneurship has also been advertised and the selection process is on. 
16.       The Committee appreciates the Department for launching a new Scheme for women and hopes that with the
 introduction of the Scholarships, the contribution of women to science & technology would increase.   The Committee
 recommends that the Department may specially focus on rural women.  The aim should also be to tap the potential of
 women in smaller towns who because of lack of financial support  or infrastructure do not pursue science studies.
SPECIAL COMPONENT PLAN FOR SCHEDULED CASTES
17.       The Department informed the Committee that a special plan was undertaken with a view to promoting research,
 development and adaptation of technology for improving the quality of life of the economically weaker sections of
 scheduled castes in urban/rural areas; to encourage scientists & technologists to apply their knowledge and expertise to
 the needs of
economically weaker scheduled caste communities, specially in rural areas and to promote activities such as workshops,
 publications, jathas, etc.
18.       The Department further informed that based on the past experience gained during implementation of projects they
 propose to encourage and develop coordinated programme on scientific rearing of smaller animals and poultry birds and
 management of organic waste.  Some of the exclusive artisanal trades such as carcass collection and processing, footwear
 making, masonary, etc.  will be accorded priority and at the same time individual projects on creating awareness,
 developing the capability of SC community as also the training programme will also continue.   It is also proposed to
 undertake projects on alternative vocations in the SC pockets where chances of income generation and creation of
 employment are dwindling.  Entrepreneurial skill development will be an important input in our efforts.  Motivated
 engineers and scientists from community poly-techniques and engineering colleges will be encouraged to contribute to
 finding of technical solutions to urban SC populations.
19.       When the Committee wanted to know about the activities undertaken under this scheme it was informed that the
 Department encouraged S&T Institutes & NGOs to undertake innovative and adaptive tasks for the benefit of tribal/SC
 communities.  Broad areas of activities included innovative technology development and functional capability/skill
 development and training in technology areas such as sustainable agriculture, agro-forestry, cover management, natural
 resources regeneration, health, water, medicinal plants, artisanal sector, animal husbandry, post harvest technologies in the
 rural sector and new income generating programmes in the urban sector.  Apart from individual projects on research
 development and adaptation of relevant technologies, coordinated programmes based on the outcome of pilot
 development projects were initiated for large-scale field testing and demonstration.    The scheme is being restructured to
 avoid possible overlap with schemes being implemented by other Departments/agencies.
20.       The Committee hopes that this programme would aim at providing alternate vocation as well as additional income
 to these communities.  The programmes should also aim at uplifting their social status.  These communities mostly are not
 aware of these programmes.   By giving due publicity to such programmes the Department can reach out to the lowest 
 rungs of these communities and sensitise them about the benefits of such schemes for improving their living conditions
 and for their empowerment.   The I & B Ministry is willing to cooperate in the direction and it should be tapped without
 delay.
PATENT FACILITATING CENTRE (PFC)
21.       The Committee was informed that Patent Facilitating Centre has been engaged in many activities related to
 intellectual property rights (IPR) with an objective to introduce patent information as a vital input in the process of
 promotion of R&D programmes; provide patenting facilities to scientists and technologists of the country for Indian and
 foreign patents on a sustained basis; keep a watch on developments in the area of IPR and make important issues known
 to policy makers, scientists, industrialists and others  create awareness and understanding relating to patents and the
 challenges and opportunities in the area; undertake study and analysis of policy related and operational matters emanating
 from the TRIPs agreement and other agreements under the World Trade Organisaton and to act as a focal point in this
 matter within DST.

THE PHARMACEUTICALS RESEARCH AND DEVELOPMENT SUPPORT FUND (PRDSF)
40.       The emerging economic, trade and intellectual property scenario, nationally and internationally, necessitates a
 qualitative change in the industry, to drive Indian pharmaceutical industry away from manufacturing only known drugs to
 discovering and commercializing new molecules. The availability of trained scientific manpower of high quality, S&T
 infrastructure, accumulated knowledge of traditional medicinal system and large bio-diversity of our country offer a great
 opportunity to our industry. However, at present, most Indian drug firms, due to their small size compared to international
 operators and limited resources, are not in a position to invest in a viable new drug development programme. At the same
 time, several Indian academic institutions and national laboratories have established impressive infrastructure and
 developed excellent expertise in selected areas of drug development.
41.       The Committee was informed that the scheme aims at enhancing capabilities of the Indian drugs and
 pharmaceutical industry towards development of new drugs by synergising the strengths of publicly funded R&D
 institutions and the Indian Pharmaceutical drug industry for discovery and introduction of new drugs and practices in all
 systems of medicine.
42.       During the tenth plan the Department has a provision of Rs.150 Crores for the Pharmaceuticals Research and
 Development Support Fund (PRDSF).   This is the corpus fund.  The interest earned from this fund will be used for the
 purposes of supporting Research & Development (R&D) Programmes and setting up of the National facilities for
 furthering R&D activities in the country.  Since the interest on this corpus will be accrued only after a year, an initial
 budgetary support of Rs.10 crores has been provided for sustaining various activities during the financial year 2003-2004. 
 It is proposed to constitute a Drug Development Promotion Board to administer the fund.
43.       It was stated that under this scheme financial support would be provided to national labs and academic institutions
 for joint research programmes conceived by the industry and public funded R&D institutions. The broad objectives of this
 programme include: Development of new molecules and practices for diseases prevalent in the Indian climatic zone by
 bringing together the scientific expertise existing in the country in research institutions and industry; Promote R&D at any
 stage of development in all systems of medicine including alternative system of medicines and Creating state-of-the-art
 infrastructure facilities at par with international standards for the benefit of the Indian Industry and other users.
44.       The existing ongoing Plan Programme on Drug and Pharmaceuticals Research will be merged with this new
 activity.  The broad objectives of this fund are: -
1.         Funding research in all the systems of medicine in particular development of new molecules, natural products
 including plant, mineral and animal based preparations, development of new drug delivery systems,       application of
 genomics/proteomics and development of key chemicals/reagents used in drug research.
2.         To create an enabling infrastructure for promotion of R&D at all stages including clinical research.

 observes that the benefits of research and development in this field have not reached the  people who are engaged in

 suitable for cutting bamboos which are harder than the ones in foreign countries from where such instruments are
 obtained.  The Committee, therefore, strongly recommends that the Department should design instruments, as soon as
 possible, which would be useful for the varieties of  bamboos found in different parts of our country.  The Committee also
 recommends that the Department should coordinate with the Indian Plywood Industries Research Institute at Bangalore,
 an autonomous body with the Ministry of Environment & Forests, for conducting research and training programmes on
 bamboo related activities.   The Committee also suggests that the Department may explore the possibilities of
 collaborating with China with a view to exchanging and sharing ideas and experiences related to making of bamboo
