 better yields, we need plants and methods of cultivation which will be in harmony with biodiversity and eco-system and,
 therefore, will not bring down the fertility of land and kill useful animals, pests and weeds.  This objective can be achieved by,
 among others, changing plant characteristics through genetic modification.  The Committee impresses upon the Department to
 work with full vigour to realise this objective.  Prof. M.S. Swaminathan, one of the leading figures who spearheaded green
 revolution in our country, has said that green revolution can become ever green revolution by making it pro-nature, pro-poor
 and pro-women.  Therefore, the Committee emphasizes that the Department while focusing on biotechnology should also
 harness social forces for making our agriculture sustainable.
(Para 68)
Action Taken by the Department
 Biotechnology interventions have the potential to enhance the yield level, increase resistance/tolerance to biotic and
 abiotic stresses, reduce pesticide use thereby making cultivation of crops eco-friendly and improve nutritional quality.  The
 department has supported a major multi-institutional project on development of transgenic crops (rice, cotton, mungbean and
 tomato) resistant to biotic stresses.  Similarly, some R&D projects are also being supported in this direction.  Another project on
 salinity and dehydration stress tolerance in rice has been supported recently. The project would ultimately result in raising of
 rice transgenic employing candidate genes for resistance against salinity/dehydrations stress.   In an attempt to solve the
 problem of malnutrition in rural areas, a multi-institutional coordinated programme to enhance quantity/quality of protein and
 micronutrients in important food crops viz. rice, cassava and sweet potato has also been supported.
Comments
The Committee notes with satisfaction Biotechnology based projects towards making agriculture sustainable and hopes 
 that awareness will be generated among the rural masses for popularizing such projects.
EXPEDITIOUS CLEARANCE OF PROJECTS SUBMITTED BY THE DEPARTMENT
Recommendation
The Committee was apprised that the proposals submitted by the Department are subjected to periodic review and
 assessment by different agencies including the Planning Commission. The Department further stated that it remained ever ready
 to subject itself and its activities to scrutiny.  However, it informed the Committee that time taken for review of its projects is
 too long and, therefore, comes in the way of its expeditious implementation.  While pursuing research in the field of science, the
 Department has to constantly innovate to remain abreast of the ever-evolving activities of the scientific community across the
 globe.  Delay in clearing a project, therefore, will throw a spanner in the wheel of scientific progress which the Department is
 carrying forward within a limited budget, to fulfill the objectives set before them in a goal oriented and time bound manner. 
 Therefore, the Committee strongly recommends that all the proposals of the Department must be cleared expeditiously and
 within a set time frame.
(Para 76)
Action Taken by the Department
The issues related to clearing of projects by other departments and Planning Commission have been taken up at highest
 level and the same has been streamlined.
Comments
The Committee notes the reply with satisfaction and further suggests that the Department should pursue the matter with
 the highest decision-making body so that the objectives of clearing of various projects can be achieved with an immediate
 effect.
BUDGET PROPOSALS AT REVISED ESTIMATES STAGE
Recommendation
The Department informed the Committee that the reduction of its budget at the R.E. stage causes a lot of problem in
 resetting its priorities.  It prepares its plan as per the budget proposals and accordingly prepares its schedule of activities.  Time
 taken to re-do the priorities due to cut in R.E. stage is not less than three or four months.  Such re-planning for scientific projects
 deviates the Department from the set objectives.  The Committee is constrained to note that such problems are confronted by the
 Department.
Prof. G. Padmanabhan, the UNESCO Professor in Biotechnology, Department of  Biochemistry, Indian Institute of
 Science, Bangalore in an important article “Contrary to reports, India has not missed the biotech bus” has written about
 the budget requirements of biotechnology which is revealing:
“ A single funding agency in the USA has a Rs.4,000 crores budget for genomics.  In India, all the funding agencies
 together can mobilize about Rs.100 crores a year to research in this area.  It is interesting to note that the country can
 still come up with new drugs, vaccines and diagnostics within this limited budget.  If India plays its cards right, it can

 hope to become a world leader in modern vaccine manufacturing, since MNCs are not interested in this field due to poor
 economic returns.  All that is needed is a commitment on the part of the Government to ensure availability of the
 committed amount for the next five years, release of grants in time, a mechanism for quick clearance of clinical trials to

Determination and will of the scientists to achieve the goal which is comparable to international standards and within a

 R.E. stage.
(Para 78)

The matter is being pursued with Ministry of Finance, Government of India.

USE OF TRADITIONAL KNOWLEDGE
Recommendation
India is rich with traditional knowledge.  Our people with centuries of experiences have emerged as practitioners of such
 knowledge.  This rich reservoir of such resources must be understood scientifically and safeguarded.  The Committee was
 informed by a Member that Ganga Jal, Gou Mutra and Gober have anti-bacterial properties.  It was also told that Gober is
 radiation resistant.  It was told that when hospital wastes were treated with layers of Gober for five months, it was found that all
 bacteria, toxin and poison had been neutralised.  Therefore, the Committee recommends that steps must be taken by the
 Department to explore the anti-bacterial properties of Ganga Jal, Gou Mutra and Gober, specially the effectiveness for treating
 hospital waste.
(Para 79)
Action Taken by the Department
The Department has noted the recommendations of the Committee on Ganga Jal, Gou Mutra and Gobar. At present, there
 are no specific projects in these areas. However, other agencies like Council for Scientific and Industrial Research (CSIR) have
 conducted investigations and experimentations on the utilities of the above-mentioned products. Similarly, Ministry of Health &
 Family Welfare and Ministry of Environment and Forest are implementing projects/programmes on regulation and treatment of
 hospital waste in which the department is not directly involved. However, in future, if any such proposal is submitted to the
 department, it will be considered on scientific merit.
Comments
        The Committee feels that the department should initiate efforts on its own with regard to exploring the anti-bacterial
 properties of Ganga Jal, Gou Mutra and Gobar.

NEW DELHI;
January 23, 2004
C. RAMACHANDRAIAH,
 Chairman,
 Parliamentary Standing Committee on 
 Science & Technology, Environment & Forests.
 
 R E P O R T
The Report of the Committee deals with the Action Taken by the Department of Space on the recommendations
 contained in the One Hundred-fourteenth Report of the Department-related Parliamentary Standing Committee on Science &
 Technology, Environment & Forests on the Demands for Grants (2003-2004) of the Department of Space which was presented
 to both Houses of Parliament on 2 nd May, 2003.  There were twenty-one recommendations contained in One Hundred-
fourteenth Report of the Committee. Action Taken notes on the recommendations of the Committee were received from the
 Department on 5th September, 2003.
The Committee’s recommendations, action taken thereon and comments of the              Committee on the action taken by
 the Department of Space are set out in the succeeding paragraphs: -
INSAT SERIES
Recommendation
The Committee congratulates the Department for the successful launch of the INSAT-3A and records its appreciation for
 the abilities and talents of our scientists who have further enhanced the glory of our nation through this splendid performance.
 The Committee hopes that the other satellites in the INSAT series would be launched as planned without any cost escalation.
(Para 24)
Action Taken by the Department
After the launch of INSAT-3A on April 10, 2003, the spacecraft has been commissioned in orbit and put to operational
 use. The next satellite, INSAT-3E, is also now ready for launch. The spacecraft has been transported to the launch site French
 Guyana and the launch is scheduled for the third quarter of 2003. The work on INSAT -3D, an advanced meteorological
 satellite and also the last satellite in the INSAT -3 series, is in progress and the launch is targeted for 2004-05 onboard India's
 GSLV. The work on fourth generation INSAT-4A & 4B satellites has also begun. No cost escalation is foreseen in INSAT
 satellites at present.
 
Also, GSAT-2, an experimental communication satellite, was successfully launched on the second developmental flight
 of GSLV (GSLV-D2) on May 8, 2003 from the Satish Dhawan Space Centre, Sriharikota. GSAT-2 has augmented the INSAT
 capacity with four C-band, two Ku band and One Mobile Satellite Service transponders.
Comments
The Committee congratulates the Department of Space and scientists of ISRO for the successful launch of GSAT-2 and
 expresses its best wishes for the success of all the future programmes.
DEVELOPMENT OF CRYOGENIC ENGINES
Proven abilities of our scientists have now to be used to develop the cryogenic technology which has been subjected to
 many experiments. The Committee feels that the indigenous development of cryogenic engines is critical to the development of
 our own geostationary satellite launch vehicles. It express full faith on our space scientists and hopes that they will accomplish
 the mission.

(Para 24)
Action Taken by the Department
ISRO has made considerable progress related to the development of our indigenous cryogenic stage for use on Geo-
synchronous Satellite Launch Vehicle (GSLV). The first two-engine hardware have undergone a total cumulative ground hot test
 firing duration of 4000 seconds. These tests have given confidence for the normal performance of the engine. Preparation for
 the stage test is in progress and stage tankages have been moved to the test stand for various tests before conducting the first hot
 test planned this year. The first set of flight version tanks have been realized. Based on a success-oriented schedule, it is planned
 to make a test flight of the indigenous cryogenic stage during 2004-05. The work on development of a higher thrust cryogenic
 engine (C-25) has also been initiated as a part of GSLV Mk III project.
Comments
The Committee appreciates the progress in the development of the indigenous cryogenic engines. However, it hopes that
 the progress in the development of higher thrust cryogenic engines (C-25) would be initiated as per schedule so that the projects
 like Mission to Moon, envisaged with cryogenic engines are not delayed.
GRAMSAT PILOT PROJECTS (GPP)
Recommendation
The Committee hopes that by the end of the 10
th Plan period the GRAMSAT programme would cover all the rural areas
 of India. The Committee also hopes that local bodies, district offices and all those involved in planning at the rural level would
 be given the data for their use. Since we have constitutionally guaranteed 33% reservation for women in Panchayat bodies, the
 Committee recommends that special focus should be given to women's development issues through GRAMSAT. Lest all this
 effort goes waste the Committee strongly urges the government to launch a scheme to equip every village of the country with
 the equipment necessary to utilize the service that will be given through GRAMSAT.
(Para 38)
Action Taken by the Department
GRAMSAT programme envisages provision of satellite transponders for developmental communications including
 education and training, health, women & child development, Panchayati Raj functionaries etc. Under GRAMSAT Pilot Projects,
 such networks have already been established in Madhya Pradesh, Gujarat, Karnataka, Andhra Pradesh, Orissa, Goa and
 Rajasthan. The developmental programmes broadcasted under the network by State Governments address the women
 development issues also. In fact, the impact evaluation of the GRAMSAT network in Jhabua district of Madhya Pradesh
 indicates that the backward and tribal communities of the region, especially women are the main beneficiaries of the
 GRAMSAT programme. Work has already been initiated to build a satellite - EDUSAT (GSAT-3) -dedicated for spreading
 education and training at all levels covering a large area of the country including North East through a satellite based network.
Comments
The Committee observes that steps may be taken to cover all the states, particularly the hill states by the next phase of
 GRAMSAT project and hopes that EDUSAT satellite would cover wider regions.
LAUNCH VEHICLE INFRASTRUCTURE
Recommendation
The Committee commends the Department for making significant progress in completion of second launch pad and
 hopes that it would be ready for commissioning by the end of this year without any further delays.
(Para 40)
Action Taken by the Department
The Second Launch Pad is now ready to receive PSLV and the activities related to mock-up trials have been initiated.
 The Second Launch pad will be ready to receive     GSLV by end of the year after completing the installation and
 commissioning of           Cryo processing facilities.
Comments
The Committee hopes that the second launch pad would reduce our  dependence on foreign launching pads and besides,
 India could  offer its launching services to other countries.
 
ISRO-GEO SPHERE BIOSPHERE PROGRAMME
Recommendation
The Committee hopes that the ISRO-GEO sphere programme would be helpful in predicting, the arrival of monsoon with

 greater precision. It also hopes that the programme would be useful to study the recent phenomenon like Asian Brown cloud.
(Para 46)
Action Taken by the Department
ISRO-GBP focuses on the issues related to characterisation of parameters responsible for climate change. The
 programme is guided by an inter- agency expert group drawn from premier institutions in the country like Indian Institute of
 Tropical Meteorology, National Institute of Oceanography, India Meteorological Department, Centre for Atmospheric Sciences
 of Indian Institute of Science, National Physical Laboratory, IITs and several other Universities.
ISRO-GBP studies on "Regional Climate Modeling" contribute to enhance our understanding of monsoon. The Aerosol
 Radiation Budget studies and the special campaigns on aerosol measurements by land and Ship based cruises will facilitate the
 study of Atmospheric Brown Cloud (hitherto Asian Brown Cloud) phenomena.
Comments
The Committee notes the reply.
SPONSORED RESEARCH
Recommendation
The committee recommends that apart from initiating the research projects in the academic institutions, the Department
 should develop a mechanism for constant monitoring of the performance of the projects to ensure their timely completion.
(Para 56)
Action Taken by the Department
The ISRO Sponsored Research Projects (RESPOND) are carried out at the Academic Institutions such as Universities,
 Colleges, National Institutions, IITs, Research laboratories under the supervision of experts at ISRO Centres. The Department
 has established a well-structured review system as below to monitor the progress of these research projects.
(a)        Each project has been assigned with a Focal Point (Expert) from the ISRO Centre who will interact with the
 project on a timely basis to ensure smooth progress of the project work. At the end of every year, the project
 submits an annual progress report which is reviewed by the Focal Point and other experts at ISRO Centres before
 recommending further renewal (continuation) of the project and release of grants for the next year.
(b)        Since last 5 years, ISRO has initiated an additional review mechanism, the Annual RESPOND Review meetings
 at ISRO Centres, where an exclusive ISRO Committee constituted and chaired by Director of each ISRO Centre
 will review the progress of the Projects and make suitable suggestions and mid-course corrections on the project
 work to ensure satisfactory completion of the project within the project period.
Comments
The Committee notes with satisfaction the initiatives taken by the Department for  review of the progress of  sponsored
 research projects.
 
TECHNOLOGY TRANSFER
Recommendation
The Committee appreciates the efforts made by the Department for transfer of technologies to the Industry; however, the
 Committee recommends that the Department should acquire patents of the technologies transferred to prevent exploitation. The
 Department should assess such technology transfers from the commercial point of view and generate the maximum revenue out
 of it. The Committee notes with satisfaction that the Department is bringing in more and more participation from industry in
 conducting the space programme. The Committee hopes that through greater transfer of technology, participation of industry
 will be further broadened.
(Para 62)
Action Taken by the Department
ISRO/DOS has been pursuing a Technology Transfer (TT) policy that has enabled the commercialization of ISRO
 developed technologies through Indian industries. Adequate measures are being taken to safeguard ISRO's interest through
 filing of appropriate patents, copyrights and trademarks. The technology transfer mechanism established by ISRO has resulted
 in more than 255 technologies being  licensed to the Indian industries in the small, medium and large scale sectors. Efforts are
 being made to widen the avenues and scope for industry participation with a view to maximally utilize the industrial capability
 and expertise.

Comments
The Committee notes the reply.
 
INTERNATIONAL COOPERATION
Marketing of Space Services & Products
Recommendation
The Committee feels that India's expertise in space technology can be further shared with many other developing
 countries. The Department should explore opportunities for launching of more satellites and marketing of remote sensing data to
 many other countries.
(Para. 73)
Action Taken by the Department
ISRO has set up a Scheme "Sharing of Experience in Space (SHARES)" under which training in different applications of
 space science, technology and applications is provided to scientists from developing countries. Another important initiative in
 this direction is the establishment of the Centre for Space Science and Technology Education for Asia and the Pacific (CSSTE-
AP) affiliated to United Nations which offers specialized training in Remote Sensing & Geographical Information System,
 Satellite Communications, Satellite Meteorology, Global climate & Space / Atmospheric Studies and more than 300 scholars
 from about 40 developing countries have been benefited from this Centre.
The Department through Antrix Corporation (ANTRIX), the commercial wing of the Department of Space has mounted
 efforts towards promoting the market for launch services and marketing of remote sensing data to global customers. Concerted
 efforts have been made by contacting a number of potential customers in Europe (Germany, Sweden, Italy etc.), Canada etc., for
 provision of launch services, though the geo-political constraints play a dominant role in the global launch services market. On
 the marketing of remote sensing data, discussions have been held with international customers in South Africa, Yemen, Ecuador
 and Algeria etc., for the reception and dissemination of IRS data. Efforts are also on to provide value added services to
 Mauritius in the area of land Information System (LIS). Preliminary proposals have been submitted to the customer in this
 regard.
Comments
The Committee notes the reply.
Development of low cost technologies 
Recommendation
The Committee feels that intense competition is on to capture the limited market of space industry and India can innovate
 design concepts for small as well as large payloads and by doing so can offer competitive prices to the interested countries for
 availing of India's technologies. The Committee recommends that the Department may explore the possibility of developing low
 cost space technologies which would be useful to developing countries.
(Para 74)
Action Taken by the Department
The Department with its unique expertise in space application, spacecraft and launching has been exploring the
 possibility of end-to-end services, which can be useful to developing nations.
With the GSLV capability improving to launch satellites of weight higher than 2000 kg; Department of Space is planning
 to launch satellites compatible with indigenous launchers and catering to the emerging markets such as DTH, TV broadcasting,
 long distance thin route communications, Ku-band satellites with multiple beams, Ka- band Regenerative payload etc. are being
 planned to develop low-cost space technologies suited to developing countries, Discussions are under way for providing
 satellite based communication systems for Vietnam, Malaysia etc.
Further, the concept of developing micro-satellites with appropriate payloads has been developed along with the Anna
 University, which also provides opportunities to develop low cost based technologies that could be of relevance and use to the
 developing countries.
Comments
The Committee notes the reply.
 
TELEMEDICINE
Recommendation

            The Committee commends the Department for bringing high quality medical care to patients transcending the barriers of
 geography, distance, time and costs. It believes that this can be a boon for countries like India where the majority population
 lives in remote areas without access to even basic health care. The Committee however hopes that the poor quality of internet /
 telephone services will not come in the way of effective functioning of telemedicine services.
(Para 77)
Telemedicine Kiosks
Recommendation
The Committee also hopes that in the next few years there will be telemedicine kiosks through the length and breadth of
 suburban and rural India. It is hoped that the government scheme to provide such kiosks will go hand in hand with the spread of
 telemedicine facility.
(Para 78)
Action Taken by the Department
The telemedicine technology demonstration projects have been operating in the State of Karnataka, Andhra Pradesh,
 Kerala, UT of Andaman & Nicobar and Lakshadweep Islands, Jammu & Kashmir including Ladakh, Assam, Sikkim and
 Tripura etc., connecting 27 hospitals (10 super speciality hospitals, 17 district/medical college hospitals) providing specialist
 consultation to remote hospitals located at rural and inaccessible areas.
The telemedicine system consists of customized medical software integrated with the diagnostic instruments like EGG,
 X-ray scanner which will be connected to VSAT for connectivity with the satellite. Similar VSAT and the medical software
 exists at the specialist end for viewing and analysis of the medical information. The tele-consultation and treatment are provided
 during the video conferencing between the patient end hospital and the specialist end.
The concept of a Tele-medicine Kiosk co-located with Information Kiosks can provide only limited Tele-medicine
 services out of different alternatives. Appropriate option in terms of technology, location, etc., which would maximize the Tele-
 medicine benefits to the remote areas will have to be adopted by implementing agencies.
Comments 
The Committee appreciates the Department’s projects under telemedicine system and feels that by expanding
 telemedicine facilities the objective of access to health care could be realized. The big hospitals in the States of Uttar Pradesh,
 Madhya Pradesh, Rajasthan, Orissa and Bihar should also be linked with telemedicine projects as maximum poor people are
 living in these States.
 
 
DISASTER MANAGEMENT SUPPORT (DMS)
Recommendation
The committee feels that the remote sensing data is not being used to its full potential. With regard, to the landslide
 hazard zonation, the Committee feels that standardized landslide inventory maps would be helpful. Besides, accurate slop
 stability studies may be made by using space technology so as to understand the possible locations where landslides could
 occur. The Committee feels that special attention should be given to Northeast and Uttaranchal where landslides during rainy
 season block roads for days together. An Internet image transferring system may be of help for local bodies and relief agencies
 for emergency response in affected areas.
(Para 87)
Action Taken by the Department
Remote sensing data usage is coordinated under the auspices of the National Natural Resources Management System
 (NNRMS) with active involvement of various Central/State agencies as well as private entrepreneurs and academia. India is one
 of the very few countries in the world, which has effectively integrated remote sensing applications with developmental
 planning at various levels. However, considering that it is still a continuing process and there are newer applications and
 services in the light of advancement in technologies, the Department continues to spread the awareness through appropriate
 training and education programmes, which should enable further enhancement of remote sensing data usage in the future.
Initiatives have already been taken on landslide hazard zonation studies in the North East and the Uttaranchal. A network
 based information transfer and access system towards helping local bodies and relief agencies for emergency response in
 affected areas is being worked out.
Comments
The Committee notes the reply.

 NATIONAL NATURAL RESOURCES MANAGEMENT SYSTEM (NNRMS)
Recommendation
The Committee is of the opinion that a periodic census of the available natural resources would help assessing the
 utilization of such resources so as to formulate a plan for sustainable development.
(Para 91)
Action Taken by the Department
The NNRMS has identified the conduct of a Natural Resource Census (NRC) in the country as a major national activity
 from 10th Plan onwards. As pre-investment activity for the National Mission of NRC, a proto-type exercise has been taken up
 in 12 districts of the country. The Proto-type will generate national mapping standards for NRC and also help operationalise the
 mechanisms of the national mission. After completing the Proto-type activity during the year, the national programme on NRC
 will be initiated.
Comments
The Committee hopes that the National Mission on NRC would be taken up in all the districts of the country so that
 realistic census on the natural resources is drawn up for effective development planning.
NORTH EAST SPACE APPLICATION CENTRE
Recommendation
The Committee appreciates the Department for undertaking projects in the Northeast, which merits concentrated
 attention. The Committee hopes that bamboo resource mapping, erosion hazard assessment etc. would cover the whole of the
 Northeast so that the data could be used for meaningful planning for development.
(Para 93)
Action Taken by the Department
The Department through its North Eastern Space Applications Centre (NE- SAC) has initiated many remote sensing
 application projects covering the whole North East for providing inputs for developmental planning of the region.
Comments
The Committee hopes that the inputs provided by North East Space Application Centre would help in finalizing projects
 for industrial and agricultural development of the region.
Ground Water exploration
Recommendation
The Committee is of the view that India is emerging as a water stressed country with millions of its people without
 access to safe drinking water. The Committee deeply appreciates that the Department has applied Space Technology to prepare
 1500 maps in respect of six States for the purpose of ground water exploration. While the Committee notes that the Department
 is mapping for few of the States, it recommends strongly that such efforts of the Department must be extended to all States,
 giving special priority to those, which have been severely affected by drought and shortage of rainfall.
(Para 94)
Action Taken by the Department
The Department has been working with the Department of Drinking Water Supply (Ministry of Rural Development),
 Government of India towards providing inputs to the Rajiv Gandhi National Drinking Water Mission (RGNDWM) for the
 purpose of ground water exploration as well as recharge. The Department will work closely with the RGNDW to extend the
 above activities to other States as suggested.
Comments
The Committee would like the Department to evolve an effective monitoring mechanism with Department of Drinking
 Water Supply (Ministry of Rural Development) to see the programme succeeds.
National Resource Information Systems
Recommendation
The Committee notes that the Department is proposing to prepare National Resource Information System in Nine States.
 Earlier the Department had set up such a system in 30 districts in different States. The Committee recommends that such
 systems be established as soon as possible in all the States of the country to enable the Government, people and larger civil
 society to have access to such information for national development.
(Para 95)

FUND FOR THE IMPROVEMENT OF S&T IN FRASTRUCTURE IN UNIVERSITIES AND
OTHER HIGHER EDUCATIONAL INSTITUTIONS (FIST) 
Recommendation 
            The Committee notes with constr aint that the quality of in frastructure available in ou r
Universities and research laborator ies for pursuing scientific resear ch is not upto the mark. Lack o f
interest on the part of students to go for science education is indeed alarming.  The Department is taking
steps to encourage young scientists  to pursue serious sc ientific work.  The Committee notes with
concern the decline of the quality of  our research papers.  There is an  urgent need to take concerted
efforts to arrest this trend to give new dynamism and momentum to Indian science. 
(Para 10)
Action taken by the Department 
            The Scheme ‘Fund for Improvement of S&T In frastructure in Univ ersities and Highe r
Educational Institutions’ was initiated in the year 2000 to address these concerns.  The scheme has so far
identified and supported about 460 Departments at various universitie s and related higher educational
institutions in the country.  The supports are mainly provided for st rengthening of infrastructure and
equipments, acquisition of comput ation networking facilities, mode rnisation of library, providing good
quality teaching material, enha ncement of research facili ties in this departments.   While majority of the
Departments supported so far are now  in the process of acquiring thes e facilities, a few departments
have already acquired the same.   Towards monitoring and reviewing of  the progress, these departments
have now submitted the Technical Progress Report, which are being evaluated along with the visit of the
sites by the area Experts. 
In 2003-04, the fresh proposals re ceived from the prospective Departments/Centres of the 
Universities and related acad emic institutions are be ing processed for consideration of support in the
current financial year. 
Comments 
The Committee feels that the Department shoul d monitor and supervise the Technical Progress
Report to evaluate the performanc e of the schemes being implemente d to prevent the misuse of the
funds made available under the schemes. 
 SCIENCE & TECHNOLOGY FOR WOMEN 
Recommendation 
            The Committee appreciates the Department fo r launching a new  Schemes for women and hopes
that with the intr oduction of the Scholarships, the contri bution of women to science and technology
would increase. The Committee recommends that the Department may specially focus on rural women. 
The aim should also be to tap the pot ential of women in smaller towns who because of lack of financial
support of infrastructure do not pursue science studies.   
(Para 16)
Action taken by the Department 
            The response to the Women Scientists Sche me has been overwhelming. The screening o f 
applications by high-level  Expert Committee is currently in progr ess. Special consideration is being
given to women who have faced women-s pecific and location-s pecific problems in pursuing science

            In the first year there has been a very encouraging response from  women scientists from rural
areas and small towns.  This focus will be maintained in future also.  
Comments 
The Committee notes the position a nd would like the Department to take steps to provide current
information on careers, training, scie nce and scientific policies to wo men through universities, colleges
etc. Apart from this there is a need to take initiatives to increase the men to women ratio in science and
engineering fields.  The Committee al so suggests that the special cons ideration which is being given to
women scientists should be given wide publicity in print and audio-visual media. 
SPECIAL COMPONENT PLAN FOR SCHEDULED CASTES 
Recommendation 
            The Committee hopes that this pr ogramme would aim at  providing alternate vocation as well as
additional income to these communities.  The pr ogrammes should also aim at uplifting their social
status.  These communities mostly are not aware of these programmes.  By giving due publicity to such
programmes the Department can reac h out the lowest rungs of thes e communities and sensitise them
about the benefits of such schemes for improving their living conditions and for their empowerment. 
The I & B Ministry is willing to cooperate in the direction and it should be tapped without delay. 
(Para 20)

being attempted through various innovative programmes with sciences and technology intervention such
as functional capability development, skill upgradation training, etc.  Regarding publicity a dialogue has
already been initiated with Pr asar Bharati although th is is a not a major bottleneck since the
interventions are designed and implemented by scient ists and technologists in  academic and research
institutions.  
Comments 
The Committee would like the Department to evol ve an effective monitoring mechanism to see that
the benefits of the programme reach the targeted community. 
PATENT FACILITATION CENTRE 
Recommendation 
            The Committee notes that patent  literacy will promote grea ter awareness and knowledge among
people and enable them to make informed choices.  To safeguard  our germplasm and traditional
knowledge and to assert our ri ght to own our genetic divers ity knowledge about patenting is
indispensable.  Patenting of Haldee and Basmati abroad a nd our successful fight against those patents is
a clear pointer towards adopting greater vigilance for protecting our biodivers ity.  The Committee
recommends that the Department ma y augment its own efforts in this  regard and give due publicity to
such activities for the benefit of scientists, resear chers and the general public.   After all to save ou r
traditional knowledge we will not only depend on scie ntific community but also on women, rural fol k
and people and individuals. 
(Para 25)
Action taken by the Department 
            The Department will augment its efforts in creating awareness about Intellectual Property Rights
(IPR) among scientists and researcher s.  Attempts are also being ma de to create awareness in schools
and general public.

        The Committee notes with satisf action that attempts are being made to create awareness in
schools and among general public about  intellectual property rights.  The committee would like the
Department to provide support to th e scientific community for protect ing their inventive work and take
steps to setup Patent Facilitation Centre (PFC) in all States and Union Territories. 
 JOINT TECHNOLOGY PROGRAMME 
Recommendation 
            While the Committee notes with sa tisfaction that the Department is engaged in producing and 
applying, technologies for the all ro und development of India it reco mmends that special focus may be
given on the issue of producing clean  and eco-friendly technologies fo r sustainable development of ou r
country.  Increasingly, we have to follow the path  of eco-friendly industrial revolution.  For ou r 
sustainable development eco-friendl y industrial revolution seems to be  a necessity.  Therefore, the
Committee recommends that the Department must  concentrate its attent ion towards producing such
technologies which will be consistent with ecology and industrial development.

Action taken by the Department 
The recommendation is noted and this Departme nt would give special focus on producing clean
and eco-friendly technologies for sustainable development. It may be pertinent to mention here that DST 
has already initiated activities in th e line of clean and eco-friendly tec hnologies in the area of alternate 
fuels for substitution of diesel by the non-edible oil from karanj seed s, promotion of pollution control
technologies for cupola, rice shelling and brick kiln  industry, clean disposal of arsenic and fluoride
sludge, plastic waste disposal using plasma pyrolysis technology, use of micro hydel for powe r
generation in hilly and plain terrain etc.. Concerted efforts are be ing made by the department to develop
technologies in the field of sensor s for detection of LPG and CNG leak ages and also for instrument and
systems development for eco-friendly industrial development. 
Comments 
The Committee feels that the technologies developed should be disseminated to industry and end
users at the earliest for the wider acceptance. 
TECHNOLOGY FOR BAMBOO PRODUCTS 
Recommendation 
            The committee was informed that while some of  the national centres of excellence in India
possess rich expertise in bamboo technology, the knowledge flow to the industry has not come up to the
desired level. As such it is high time to bring the technology sourcing avenues and industries fo r
technology development, transfer and commercialization. Thus the aim is to undertake a programme at
the national level which could impa rt a significant boost to the usage of bamboo, promote specialized
products for commercialization and would generate good employment opportunities. 
(Para 33)
Action taken by the Department 
To bring together technology sourcing avenues and industrie s for technology development,
transfer and commercialization, and to provide a si gnificant boost to the usage of bamboo and its value
added products, a major initiative has been ta ken in the form of Na tional Mission on Bamboo
Applications (NMBA). Th e task of implem enting the Mission has been en trusted to the TIFAC, an
autonomous organisation under Depa rtment of Science & Technolo gy. The Mission has been devolved
to provide a new impetus and direction to the bamboo sector by seeking to:

(i)               Develop and promote environment friendl y value added bamboo based products,

(ii)                Promote innovative design capabilities, fabricati on techniques & testing

(iii)               Improve industry-lab-user linkages and effect inter-institutional / industry interaction
(iv)              Provide financial assistance for risk mi nimization towards new product and market

(vi)              Empower people at the gra ss root level encompassing fa rmers, artisans and othe r

The Committee expresses its sa tisfaction with the progra mmes being conducted for the

While the Committee appr eciates the Department for launchi ng the scheme for Technology fo r

that the Departme nt should design instruments, as soon as possible, which would be useful for the

added products.

(IPIRTI), Bangalore has taken up an exercise to develop validat e and document process technology fo r
manufacture of bamboo composite boa rds, from sympodial bamboo of commercially significant species
available in India to be able to offer techno-economic packages of support to prospective entrepreneurs.

THE PHARMACEUTICALS RESEARCH AND DEVELOPMENT SUPPORT FUND (PRDSF) 
Recommendation 
            The Committee commends the Department for re orienting its strategy to produce molecules fo r 
production of drugs so that it can meet the challenges of product patent arising out of the enforcement of
intellectual property rights from December, 2004.  Wh ile the Committee notes that the Department has
earmarked Rs.150 crores as corpus  fund for pharmaceutical research and development, it recommends
that the benefits derived from the funds provided by the Governme nt of India should be utilized
correctly.  The Committee was told that many multin ational corporations coul d help in pharmaceutical
research and development.  The Committee noted with anguish and pain that most of the pharmaceutical
formulation developed under the exemptions given by the Government of I ndia is taken by the
multinational corporations to their head offices abroad and patented th ere and marketed as international
brands and at international rates.  The Committee was agonized to know that such formulations are
produced by Indian scientists and with the help of Indian tax paye rs’ money and yet the benefits are 
reaped by the multinational drug companies who sell the products at a price wh ich most of the Indians
cannot afford.  The Committee, therefore, strongl y recommends that such technology or formulation
produced by Indian scientists must be patented in India before these are transferred or taken abroad.  The
Committee further recommends th at patenting of such formulat ions in India should be made
compulsory.  The Committee notes  the alarming trend of multina tional companies manufacturing even
Ayurvedic products, branding them and selling them with a high co mmercial pitch.  The Committee
recommends that all out efforts must be made to  reverse this trend and safeguard our traditional
knowledge from appropriation by foreign agencies.

 having been authorised by the Committee to present the Report on its behalf, present this One Hundred-Twenty Fifth Report of the
 Committee. This Report deals with the detailed Demands for Grants (2004-2005) of the Department of Science & Technology (Demand
 No.83).

 Technology gave an overview of the various activities of the Department and the Members sought clarifications on various aspects of the
 performance of the Department to enable it to scrutinise the Demands for Grants.

 placing before it the required material to enable the Committee to scrutinise the Demands for Grants of the Department of Science &

Report
 
India is a land of one of the oldest civilizations of the world with rich cultural heritage, thriving economy and civic life. It has
 been a fountainhead of ancient knowledge and wisdom. The traditions of Science & technology in India are over 5000 years old. The
 resurgence of science in India came as an offshoot of the Nationalist Movement, towards the end of 19th century and the early decades of
 the 20 th century. Since 1947 a renaissance was witnessed with the emergence of India as a politically independent nation and as it
 pursued a programme of employing modern Science and Technology for national development. A few exceptionally talented and
 committed scientists and teachers of that period laid the solid foundation of Indian science by their zeal, dedication ad sacrifice. 
2.         Post independence, conscious efforts were made to enhance and modernize the scientific infrastructure in the country by
 establishing a series of national laboratories, institutes of advanced technical education, universities etc. Science & Technology inputs
 are made an intrinsic part of the planning process and development strategies. Many institutions were created soon after independence to
 promote basic research and technological progress.
3.         As a result of these pragmatic policies, India has turned from a largely agrarian society to a highly industrialized country today.
 Due to systematic exploitation of Science & Technology for socio-economic development and scientific innovations, the country has
 been successfully transformed from a food starving country at the time of independence to a food-surplus nation.
4.         To give direction to the promotion of Science & Technology in the country the Department of Science & Technology was
 established with the primary objective of promotion of new areas of Science and Technology and to play a role of a nodal Department

16.       The Department has a mandate to provide earthquake information to the country.  The India Meteorological Department (IMD)
 which is a part of Department of Science & Technology maintains the National Seismological Network in the country.  During the last
 few years several important projects have been implemented.

Brahamputra plains) with state-of-the-art robust earthquake monitoring systems for fine scale mapping of the earthquake hazard areas and
 ascertaining the seismogenic sources.  The proposal also envisages deployment of strong motion accelerographs and dense network of
 GPS.

 bamboo based products, practices, technology & processes, including wood substitutes.

                        DRUGS AND PHARMACEUTICALS
                        29.       The Committee was informed that the Department recognizing the profound influence of R&D on the prospects
 and opportunities for the growth of the Indian Drug Industry initiated the scheme on Drugs and Pharmaceuticals Research
 in 1994-95 for promoting Industry-Institutional Collaboration R&D in drugs and pharmaceuticals sector. The programme
 aims at enhancing capabilities of institutions and the Indian Drugs & Pharmaceuticals Industry towards development of
 new drugs in all systems of Medicine.  The specific objectives of this scheme are:
            To synergise the strengths of publicly funded R&D institutions and Indian Pharmaceutical Industry in developing drugs in areas of
 national relevance.
            To create an enabling infrastructure, mechanisms and linkages to facilitate new drug development.
            To stimulate skill development of human resources in R&D for drugs and pharmaceuticals.              
30.       The Committee was informed that during the current year, the Department plans to continue efforts to support collaborative
 research projects leading towards drug development in the area of disease which are of importance to our country like Tuberculosis,
 Leprosy, Malaria, Gastro-intestinal disorders like Diarrhoea, Diabetes, Hypertension, Cardiovascular disorders, Skin disorders like
 Leucoderma, Psoriasis and other prevalent infectious diseases. Besides, development of new drug delivery systems and Veterinary drug
 development a total number of sixteen proposals were considered for financial support during the year. Ten proposals were
 recommended by the Expert Committee for funding including nine Industry-Institutional collaborative research proposals and one
 National facility.
31.       Three new collaborative projects have already been sanctioned after signing of agreements and are related to development of a
 novel herbal ectoparasiticidal product ( a veterinary product), Study of safety and efficacy profile of “Kodiveli”-a siddha medicine in use
 for the management of rheumatoid arthritis and development of a novel controlled/sustained release formula for cardiovascular &
 inflammatory diseases.
32.       Besides, seven proposals are likely to be sanctioned during the year, are related to development of novel TB vaccine candidates,
 Designer Polymers for Tailored Oral Drug Delivery systems, study of molecular mechanism of action of Cardoguard and its efficacy in
 the regression of ventricular hypertrophy, Efficacy and Safety evaluation of a Siddha medicine HIVS-2003 for HIV/AIDS, Development
 of herbo mineral and plant based disease oriented immuno-modulator formulations, increase efficacy of herbal medicines and
 standardization and modernization of ayurvedic/herbal formulations using modern techniques.
33.       The emerging economic, trade and intellectual property scenario, nationally and internationally, necessitates a qualitative change
 in the industry, to drive Indian pharmaceutical industry away from manufacturing only known drugs to discover and commercialize new
 molecules.  The availability of trained scientific manpower of high quality, S&T infrastructure, accumulated knowledge of traditional
 medicinal system and large bio-diversity of our country offer a great opportunity to our industry.  However, at present, most Indian drug
 firms, due to their small size compared to international operators and limited resources, are not in a position to invest in a viable new
 drug development programme.  At the same time, several Indian academic institutions and national laboratories have established
 impressive infrastructure and developed excellent expertise in selected areas of drug development. 
34. The Committee observes that most of the drugs developed or available in markets for diseases like malaria, tuberculosis etc. are no
 longer effective as the disease parasites has become resistance to drugs, and this poses a challenge to the scientific community to develop
 more effective drugs. The Committee recommends that Department to look at the repository our traditional medicine which may have
 answers to many of the challenges.

REPORT
 
 
The Department of Scientific and Industrial Research (DSIR) is a part of the Ministry of Science and Technology
 with the mandate of indigenous technology promotion, development, utilization and transfer. Establishment of the Council
 of Scientific & Industrial Research in 1942 was a landmark event in our quest for using science and technology for national
 reconstruction.
 
2.         The primary endeavour of DSIR is to encourage industry to increase their share in country’s R&D expenditure,
 support a larger cross section of small and medium industrial units to develop state-of-the art globally competitive
 technologies of high commercial potential, catalyze faster commercialization of lab-scale R&D, enhance the share of
 technology intensive exports in overall exports, strengthen industrial consultancy & technology management capabilities
 and establish user friendly information network to facilitate scientific & industrial research in the country.  It also provides a
 link between scientific laboratories and industrial establishments for transfer of technologies through National Research
 Development Corporation (NRDC) and facilitate investment in R&D through Central Electronics Limited (CEL).
3.         The above objectives are sought to be achieved through the following during Tenth Plan:
(i)
                    Technology Promotion, Development and Utilization (TPDU) Programmes.
(ii)                  National Research Development Corporation (NRDC)
(iii)                 Central Electronics Limited (CEL)
(iv)                Council of Scientific and Industrial Research (CSIR)
 
4.         Other activities assigned to the Department are:
(i)
                  Matters relating to International R&D collaboration involving industrial companies and industrial R&D
 centres.
(ii)                International Cooperation/Collaboration agreements with other countries relating to industrial R&D with the
 concurrence of the Ministry of External Affairs.
(iii)               Matters concerning domestic technology, particularly the promotion of ventures involving the
 commercialization of such technologies other than those under the Department of Science & Technology.
(iv)              Matters relating to Technology Trade including exports of Technology and Technical Consultancy Services,
 in close cooperation with the Ministry of Commerce.
(v)                Matters relating to technical, engineering and management consultancy organizations and services.
 
5.         The Department of Scientific and Industrial Research in the Ministry of Science and Technology provides the
 administrative link between the Government of India and the CSIR Society.
COUNCIL OF SCIENTIFIC & INDUSTRIAL RESEARCH
6.         The Council of Scientific and Industrial Research (CSIR), an autonomous organization with its 38 laboratories and
 fifty outreach, centers has recently completed sixty years of their existence. CSIR has emerged as a scientific institution
 which has been highly acclaimed inside and outside India.  It aims at achieving global excellence with local relevance; it
 symbolizes a culture that links science with society through technology, industrial manufacture, and dissemination of
 scientific temper among people.
7.         The detailed functions assigned to the Council of Scientific & Industrial Research (CSIR) are as follows:
(i)
                  Promotion, guidance and coordination of scientific and industrial research in India, including the institution and
 financing of specific researches;
(ii)                Establishment or development and assistance to special institutions or departments of existing institutions for
 scientific study of problems affecting particular industries and trade;
(iii)               Establishment and award of research studentships and fellowships;
(iv)              Utilization of the results of the researches conducted under the auspices of the Council towards the development
 of industries in the country and the payment of a share of royalties arising out of the development of the results
 of researches to those who are considered as having contributed towards the pursuits of such research;
(v)                Establishment, maintenance and management of laboratories, workshops, institutes and organizations to further
 scientific and industrial research and to utilize and exploit for purposes of experiment or otherwise any discovery
 or invention likely to be of use to Indian industries;
(vi)
              Collection and dissemination of information in regard not only to research but also to industrial matters
 generally;
(vii)             Publication of scientific papers and journals; and

(viii) Any other activity or activities to promote generally the objectives of the Department.
8.         CSIR has been striving to perform these functions in accordance with the priorities laid down in Five Year Plans and
 perceived needs of the nation from time to time.
9.         The Committee was informed that during the Ninth Five Year Plan, CSIR had effected wide spread changes to meet
 the challenges of economic reform, introduction of new industrial and trade policies and liberalization of economy. It also
 effected a reorientation of its programmes with the aim to make CSIR more responsive and move towards a self sustaining
 R&D institution. The cardinal feature of the Ninth Five Year Plan was the White Paper on CSIR focusing on its Vision and
 Strategy. Some of the reform process effected relate to re-engineering of the organizational structure; linking research to
 market place; mobilizing and optimizing the resources base; creating conducive and workable infrastructure and investing
 in high quality science that would be a harbinger of future technologies.
10.       As a result, CSIR stands today amongst the finest publicly funded scientific and industrial research establishments of
 the whole world. As the nation’s strongest holder of intellectual property rights (IPR), it leads the way in protecting
 traditional knowledge strength while adding to the new IPR capital.    CSIR today ranks second amongst the major PCT
 applicants from developing countries at USPTO.
11.       CSIR has also promoted excellence in science and is the only S&T organization which had nurtured and supported
 human-tech from 16 to 65 years of age through numerous schemes on human resource for scientific research.   CSIR’s
 mission is to provide scientific and industrial R&D that maximizes the economic, environmental & societal benefits for the
 people of India.
12.       The Committee was informed that the guiding principle for CSIR during the Tenth Five Year Plan would be to
 provide scientific industrial R&D that maximizes the economic, environmental and societal benefits for the people of India
 and accordingly, the Tenth Five Year Plan of CSIR and the Annual Plans have been formulated keeping in mind 8% growth
 rate envisaged by the Planning Commission and Government policy to invest 2% of GDP on Science & Technology. 
13.       CSIR seeks to foster the organizational values of: Excellence in science; Global competitiveness in technology based
 on high science; Local relevance in tune with socio-cultural and economic ethos of the people; and Innovation ranging in all
 the spheres of activities from science to technology and from management to financing.   These principles coupled with
 detailed analysis on strength, weakness, opportunities and threats carried out by CSIR laboratories were taken into
 consideration in deriving the opportunities for CSIR in the market place as well as for socio-economic development.
14.       The other factors which have a bearing on CSIR programmes for the Annual Plans are responsibilities on CSIR
 arising out of International Intellectual Property Rights arena, continuous training and re-training of CSIR staff,
 advancement of knowledge through enlarging the scope of fellowships to trans-disciplinary areas and supporting basic
 research that dovetails with its own requirement and expansion of S&T to proliferate CSIR technologies to the masses.

 been advising and assisting other organizations to take up computerization and the use of information technology but it has

 major unsolved problem of wastewater management by making a breakthrough in reducing TDS to 10 per cent by using
 biotechnological approach.
74.       The Committee is strongly convinced that environmental biotechnological research of the institute can prove to be a
 boon particularly for environmental management and control and disposal of municipal market waste, wastewater treatment
 and management, treatment and monitoring of Effluents, for TDS reduction and BoD and CoD estimation for monitoring
 pollution load in waste water.
75.       The Committee would therefore, like to recommend the Department of Scientific & Industrial Research to explore
 the possibilities of working jointly with the Ministry of Environment & Forests to develop a comprehensive waste
 management programme including both municipal market waste, management of waste water and control of bio-pollutants
 concentration in ambient air in the country so that the entire issue of waste management and control could be given a new
 dimension.
ENVIRONMENT FRIENDLY PLASTICS
76.       Plastic being xenobiotic is not degradable and in recent years search is being made for producing environment
 friendly plastic particularly biodegradable plastic like bacterial plastic. Since plastic are non-degradable, they have become
 a serious environmental threat.   Developing expertise and state-of-the-art know how for environment friendly plastic i.e.
 bacterial plastic production has been identified as a major challenge before environment friendly researchers.  In the post
 genomic era, where more than 100 bacterial genome have been sequenced, the Committee is, happy to know that IGIB has
 combined the power of bio-informatics tools to the genetic engineering tools to show that soil bacteria can degrade many
 biological fibers/polymers.  The plastic is also a sheet of synthetic fibers.  In fact, strategy has been applied at IGIB to
 search novel hydrogen producing microbes through bio-informatics tools using genomic databases; novel metabolic
 pathways have been identified by IGIB for developing know how to produce environment friendly plastics from cheap raw
 materials like bio-wastes. IGIB is also trying to train bacteria to take up the wastes from environment and clean the
 atmosphere.
77.       The Committee feels that in view of its environment friendly importance further effective research should be
 undertaken for production of such plastics by IGIB so that new areas of knowledge for production of environment friendly

R E P O R T 
  
            The field of biotechnology world over, as in India, has moved with spectacular speed towards 
developing a better understanding and insight into  life processes and addressing many problems
concerning humankind.  Its impact in the domain of health, ag riculture, environment and industrial 
sectors has given a new dimension to  our development process.  Ther e is a paradigm shift in basic 
research in modern biology; scien tists are moving closer to the f undamental secrets of life and the
application of the knowledge generated.   
2.         The Department of Biotechnology (DBT), under the Ministry of Science and Technology was set 
up in February 1986 to give an imp etus to the development of bi otechnology in the country.  The 
objectives of Department of Bi otechnology include the developmen t of products, processes and
technologies whose large-scale appl ications would result in societal and economic benefits.  The 
biotechnology programmes are implemented thr ough a number of autonomous and statutory
institution/universities by giving  them grants-in-aid. 
3.         Work on transgenic, coupled with pros pecting for new genes from our rich biodiversity, is 
poised to pay rich dividends in terms of new products and technologies for improved production and
enhanced nutritive quality of food, fruit and vegetable crops and reduce post-harvest losses.  Application 
of biotechnology to animal health and productivity  including our marine bi oresources will yield
attractive dividends.  India bei ng a global mega biodiversity hub, c onservation, characterization and 
sustainable utilization this natural wealth through the application of biotechnology assumes priority.   
4.         New generation of vaccines, diagnostic kits and therapeutics, are likely to lead to a major shift in
the healthcare strategy for preventi on, early detection and treatment of  diseases that impose the highest
burden.  Stem cell research has emer ged as a cutting edge area of enormous potenti al for application in 
cancer, autoimmune deficiencies, cardio-vascular and neurological disease and other disorders.  
5.         India is likely to require high quality human resource in the biotechnology sector, as industry and
public sector-driven R&D expands to propel the country into a global power in this sector.  The creation 
of infrastructural facilities, promotion of biotech parks and incubators are some of the programmes taken
up during the year, which have contributed significa ntly to the speedy progress.  The importance o f 
bioinformatics has also increased manifold and the best-performing centres are being upscaled as centres 
of excellence.  
6.         Biotechnolo gy-based programmes for societ y es pecially women, weaker sections and rural

GREEN COWS 
59.       The Committee would like to suggest that a section of resear ch in Biotechnology should 
concentrate on the br eeding of special cows that naturally produce low-fat milk that boost immune 
system which may be termed as ‘g reen cow’ and which are specifi cally engineered to produce less 
methane to help stem global warming.  Green cows  generally deliver low fa t milk that boosts immune
system, improve lactose utilization a nd relive diarrhoea.  Recent adva nces in Biotechnology as what the 
Committee has been given to understa nd have identified gene for milk  fat synthesis th at may one day
allow scientists to selectively breed cows that naturally produce low fat milk.  This will also 
considerably improve the efficiency of the milk production of the cows.  Si nce the green cows are
environmentally cleaner cows they produce less si gnificant amount of methane, which is a majo r
contributor to green house effect, in the atmosphere, second, only to CO2 which generally contributes to
global warming.  Green cow can alter cattle digest ion either by removing microorganisms from thei r 
stomachs that produce methane or by creating microor ganisms that can pr oduce metabolic products
other than methane.  The Committee also feels that  if DBT makes a concentr ation on such type o f
research, the emphasis on food safety  will increase and by increasing the body’s defence mechanism, a 
great section of population could be saved from constant attacks of common incurable diseases.  
  
BIO-TERRORISM 
60.       The Committee recommends  that the Department of Bio-technology should take steps to ensure 
bio-security without  hampering legitimate re search or free flow of information in the field 
biotechnology, first, there must be an increased awareness of risk of Bio-Terrorism among scientists and 
scientific leaders.  In order to  augment awareness about security, the committee woul d like to suggest
for arrangement of training and accr editation programmes that would in crease considerable awareness
and stimulate better communications between scient ific and national security communities.  The 
Committee feels that any Bio-secu rity policies must take a ‘botto m up’ approach by including direct 
involvement of working scientists.  The security provisions should wo rk hand in hand with the progress 
in biological research.  It is th e categorized opinion of the Committee th at the strategies that block the 
publication of certain research mate rials would deter the free flow of  information, impede careers o f
scientists in the field of bio-t echnology and discourage new incumbents  in entering the field of research
in Bio-Technology. 
            The guidelines should, therefore, be developed to allow researches to publish their work without 
providing information that would be useful to Bio-Terrorists.  Universities and other scientific 
institutions as what the Committee feels should deve lop the procedures to monitor scientific activities
and design full proof action plan to prevent any strategic inform ation leakage relating to Bio-
Technology to bio terrorists who w ould in turn adversely utilize th ese information for creating Bio-
Terrorism thereby throwing considerable threat on the very existen ce of human communities by waging
biological warfare. 
            Biological weapons pose a strategic threat mirrored by no other form of attack other than nuclear
weapons.  The Committee feels that as there is no simple solution to bio s ecurity, the Department o f
Bio-Technology must construct a syst em of checks and balances need ed to assure that the growing
power of life sciences is only used to protect life and not to destroy it.

R  E  P  O  R  T 
  
            Oceans have always influenced the life and history of mankind. From time immemorial, man has
been using oceans in several ways. According to our mythology, the Gods and Demons churned the
ocean and extracted amrita, the elixir of life. Even in the presen t ages, we get mineral, food and energy 
resources from the oceans. 
            The oceanic part of the world has an area of about 361 million sq km  (that is 71% of the globe),
an average depth of about 3,730 m, and a total volume of about  1,347,000 million cubic km.  The 
deepest part of the oceans is the Mariana Trench (11,516 m) in the Pacific Ocea n.  Compare this with 
the 8,849 m above sea level of the highest peak, the Mt.Everest.  Because of its vastness and interplay of 
processes, oceans control the atmosphere and global climate besides being a vast storehouse of resources
necessary for sustenance of life on  earth. Appreciating the importance of the subject, Government o f

understanding of the oceanic regime of the northern and central Indi an Ocean and also to develop
technology and technological aids  for harnessing of resources a nd understanding of various physical,
chemical and biological processes.  The Ocean policy statement was also enunciated in 1982. 
2.         The Department of Ocean Developmen t is the nodal Department for organising, coordinating 
and promoting development activitie s relating to ocean development in  the country.  The national level 
R&D laboratories, educational institutions and industries assist the Department in carrying out its multi-
disciplinary plans and programmes of national importa nce.  Further, marine research and capacity 
building is one of the key areas of the Department to promot e basic research in marine science for self-
reliance. Hence, the activities of the Department are targeted toward s scientific research and technology

has also the mandate towards inte rnational programmes arising out of  international obligations and

POLAR SCIENCE (ANTARCTIC RESEARCH) PROGRAMME 
11.       The objectives of the Antarctic Research Programme are to identify and initiate programmes o f
scientific and economic significance besides establ ishing infrastructure.  The Antarctic Research 
Progamme has been designed to ta ke advantage of the unique locat ion and environment of the icy
continent for understanding the key global processes which are manifested and controlled by this pola r
cap.  Antarctic is a pristine and natural laboratory, which enables th e scientists to study, detect and 
monitor global phenomena, such as th e atmospheric patterns and ocean circulations.  Glaciological and 
geophysical research provide s a clue to the geologica l history and evolution of  the earth.  In addition, 
Antarctica provides a singular platform for conducting studies on so lar terrestrial interaction, adaptation
of organisms, including human beings in the cold  land isolated conditions .  During 2004-05, the XXIV 
Antarctic expedition is proposed to be launched.  This expedition will ca rry out research in the fields o f 
atmospheric, geological, biologica l, environmental, medical and engineering sciences and global
change. 
12.       The success of the Antarctic Programme and sustained capabilities in Antarctic science and 
logistics prompted the Depa rtment to establish the first polar res earch lab of the country at Goa namely
the National Centre for Antarctic Ocean Research (NCAOR ) in 1998 which is res ponsible for carrying
out all the activities relating to Antarctic expediti ons. The research on polar science and expeditions to
Antarctica was being planned, executed and launch ed annually on behalf of the Department by the
Centre.  The Centre has a specific  R&D mandate in the realm of pol ar science and to coordinate an d
launch Indian Antarctic expeditions.  The Centre ha s a unique laboratory for lo w-temperature research 
on ice cores retrieved from  Antarctica and the Himalayas.  It w ould also have the facility for the 
application of remote sensing tec hniques aimed at understanding the s ea-ice-atmosphere interaction in 
the Polar Regions.  It would also have an Antarctic museum and a database repository on polar sciences.

22.       Although the Committee is happy with the contents and perf ormance of projects under Poly 
Metallic Nodules programme of Department, it is, however, scep tical about the Department’s 
assessment about the preservation of environmental norms for optimal sea ecology at the mining site.   
            The Committee is of the opinion that  before a comprehensive pla nning is undertaken for on-site 
mining of nodule, the Department should prepare an experimental chart about the precise disturbance of
the sea floor at the mining area to  assess its geological and ecologi cal conditions.  The Committee feels 
that while organisms would be de stroyed in the mined area undisturbe d areas would remain because o f
the complex terrain of sea bed which could serve as  biological reservoir for recolonizing the destroyed
section.  
23.       The Committee is of the opinion that dangers arising from the release of underlying heavy metals
when the upper sediment layer is removed, could change or disrupt geochemical systems that has been
stabilized over geological time, possibly creating zones of reduce d oxygen where life would become
impossible. 
            The Committee, therefore, feels that  before mining is initiated, Department must examine the
effect of mining on local animals at the site caused by dragging of plough across the bottom to stimulate
the effects of nodule mining on the se a bed, including the rates at whic h animals of the same species
returned to the disturbed area.  The study should be  done in this respect on mega fauna animals large 
enough to be seen at the ocean botto m.  The Committee is of the opinion  that the effects of mining will 
be greatest on the sea sponges that liv ed directly on the nodules because their habitat will be completely
destroyed.  Other free swim ming species will suffer a considerable  reduction in numbers due to serious 
disruption in food supply.  The Committee, therefore, is of the view that from emerging picture above 
the evaluation of bio-threat exposed by sea bed mi ning is indispensable to  be addressed thoroughly 
before venturing into mining operation and the Commit tee feels that any such evaluation is difficult
without better knowledge of the orga nisms living at the mining site a nd the eco-system in which they 
function.  It is quite appa rent that animals at the site area woul d be killed by the im pact of the mining
vehicle and by resettlement of the se diment cloud that impact of the mining vehicle will raise from the
sea floor.  
            Another potential effect of mining on the ocean floor is the bri nging up of unwanted materials 
during a mining operation i.e. sedi ments, trace metals from nodule waste and cold and nutrient rich
bottom water into the upper ocean. Owing to this probl em, the Committee feels that deep or mid ocean
level will be most desirable area for discharging of  miners waste as it would not be harmful to the
environment.  
24.       The Committee further feels that burial sens itivity of sea bed organism s i.e. the consequences o f
dumping a layer of sediment on t op of them as a direct reperc ussion of mining should be studied
thoroughly by Department as lesson for Environmental Impact Assessm ent of sea-bed mining.  The 
Committee feels such studies c ould be undertaken by the Depart ment through Remotely Operated
Vehicle (ROV). 
            The Committee, therefore recommends  that Department should undert ake critical assessment o f 
different mining technique s and their subsequent effects on Geochemistry  and Ocean Biology and
Department should generate relia ble data for determining the optimal mining techniques i.e. ideal
extractive metallurgy to minimize environmental impacts.  
            The Committee, therefore strongly recommends for constant assessment of environmental 
impact of deep sea-mining by Depa rtment before venturing into ac tual mining operation keeping the 
following into consideration for a meaningful assessment of the impact:- 
(a)                Biodiversity, species ranges and rates of gene flow in the nodule areas;

DRUGS FROM SEA 
26.       Worldwide researchers believe that oc eans hold the key to a w hole range of new drugs fo r
chronic pain, epilepsy and Parkinson’s disease.  The current attempt to reap a chemical harvest from the 
seas is just a continuation of the bio prospecting that the big drug co mpanies have been doing in jungles
for the past few decades.  The National Project on Drugs from Sea is a multi-institutional project aiming 
at developing potential drugs and chemicals from the marine flora and fauna. This project has led to
identification of five marine orga nisms showing potent activity as anti- diabetic, anti-viral, anti-fungal, 
anti-cholesterol and spermicidal ag ents for developing new drugs. Th e exploratory attempts will be
continued in an intens ive manner during the 10 th plan period. The Department has fostered the search

OCEANOGRAPHIC RESEARCH 
58.       The Committee is pleased to note that the Depa rtment is mainly using two Ocean Research 
Vessels, namely Sagar Sampada a nd Sagar Kanya for deep sea rese arch.  These vessels are using 
remotely operated vehicle (ROV) and Autonomous Underwater vehicl e (AUV) to study about deep sea
life forms at considerable depth.  However, the Committee feels that scope of deep sea research could be
more challenging and informative if machineries could dive be yond a depth of 6000 meters.  The 
Committee is therefore of the opinion that for a r eal deep sea study Advanced  Tethered Vehicle (ATV)
is needed by Department which is  an unmanned vehicle equipped with  latest advanced technology and
which can easily undertake researches beyond a dept h of 6 thousand metres.   The most striking 
advantage for using the ATV for underwater research is that it is extremely helpful to make researches at
extreme depth where it is dangerous  for divers to venture.  The Co mmittee is given to understand that 
such vehicles are cost affective and can be used in oc ean abyss with much flexibility.  It is observed that 
the vast majority of the ocean depths are bone chilling cold, completely dark and have ambient pressures
equivalent to the weight of the hundreds of atmosphe res. The exploration of th e deep sea is, therefore,
impossible without a subs tantial investment on la test technology.  The Comm ittee therefore strongly 
recommends that the Department may use Advanced Tethered Vehi cle (ATV) for the purpose of deep
sea research in view of its deep sea advantages and cost effective a pplications.  This vehicle will be 
extremely helpful for researches at  ocean benthos where gr eater variety of biotic  and abiotic elements
are available and a study of which could add consid erably to the store house of human knowledge about
ocean depth.
