microflora from wild ungulates. Its recolonisation in the rumen of domestic livestock has already
been done. A 1200 lit. capacity reactor  has been desi gned for solid state ferm entation and associated
processes for large scale bioconversion of lignocellulose residues to animal feed. Programmes have also
been supported for selection an d improvement of lignin degrad ing microorganism and Genetic
manipulation of microbes for enhanced ligninase expression. Efforts  would be made to develop specific
programme on identifying microorganism or to de velop recombinant microor ganism that can produce
useful  metabolic  products other than methane. 
  
Comments 
            The Committee notes the steps take n by the Depart ment in initiating research in the area o f
producing animal products that selectively suit human needs. The Committee is of the opinion that since
India is basically an agri cultural country with lo t of cattle population and hence milk production, the
concept of ‘green cows’ holds a lot of promise, especially for the ru ral population.  Further, since ‘low 
fat milk’ has a lot of market poten tial, it can prove to be a boon for the agricult ural and cattle rearing
community. The Committee therefore recommends that the de partment should initia te research in the
aforesaid areas at the earliest and spread the know ledge thus gained among th e cattle rearing population
of the country. 
  
BIO-TERRORISM 
Recommendation 
            The Committee recommends that th e Department of Bio- technology should take steps to ensure 
bio-security without hampering le gitimate research or  free flow of inform ation in the field o f 
biotechnology. First, there must be an increased awareness of risk of Bio-Terrorism among scientists 
and scientific leaders.  In order to augment aw areness about security, th e Committee would like to
suggest arrangement of training and accreditation programmes th at would increase considerable
awareness and stimulate better  
communications between scientific  and national security communities .  The Committee feels that any
Bio-security policies must take  a ‘bottom up’ approach  by including direct i nvolvement of working
scientists.  The security provisions should work hand in hand with the progress in biological research.  It
is the categorized opinion of the Committee that the strategies th at block the publication of certain
research materials would deter the fr ee flow of information, impede car eers of scientists in the field o f
bio-technology and discourage new incumbents in entering the field of research in Bio-Technology. 
            The guidelines should, therefore, be developed to allow researchers to publish their work without
providing information that would be useful to Bio-Terrorists.  Universities and other scientific 
institutions as what the Committee feels should deve lop the procedures to monitor scientific activities
and design full proof action plan to prevent any strategic inform ation leakage relating to Bio-
Technology to bio terrorists who w ould in turn adversely utilize th ese information for creating Bio-
Terrorism thereby throwing considerable threat on the very existen ce of human communities by waging
biological warfare.  
            Biological weapons pose a strategic threat mirrored by no other form of attack other than nuclear
weapons.  The Committee feels that as there is no simple solution to  bio security, the Department o f
Bio-Technology must construct a syst em of checks and balances need ed to assure that the growing
power of life sciences is only used to protect life and not to destroy it.   
                                                                                                               (Para 60) 
                                                                                            
Action Taken by the Department 
The Recommendations of the Co mmittee that the Department  of Biotechnology should take
steps to ensure bio-securit y without ham pering legitimate research and free fl ow of information in the

awareness of risk of bio- terrorism amongst scientists and scientif ic leaders.  The whole issue of bio-
security would be looked into from the viewpoint of bio-safet y, bio-security and information
dissemination and if necessary St andard Operating Procedures w ould be developed. The Department
would set up a small group, which would look into the details of  the recommendations of the

Comments 
            The Committee is of the opinion th at an expert group consisting of eminent scientists and

security keeping in view the security threat posed to the country on account of biological weapons.

November 2004. 
The Committee’s Recommendation, action taken thereon and comments of the Committee on the
action taken by the Department of Scientific and Industrial Research  are set out in the succeeding
paragraphs: -

Recommendation 
  
         The Committee appreciates the Departme nt for carrying out research  in many frontier areas o f
science and technology.  It is true that science is one of the areas, which can bring leadership and meet
the kind of objectives that India ha s set for itself.  However, the Co mmittee is of the opinion that the
Department should make efforts fo r transfer of technologies to in dustry and also strive for wide r
dissemination of technologies to raise funds from  Industry by having a greater interface between
Industry & R&D laboratories.                                                                                                                
(Para 27) 
  
Action Taken by the Department 
  
The suggestions made by the Committee are well taken. CSIR has been proactive in reaching to
the industry. CSIR is the only orga nization which involves industry fr om early stage of development
with a view to build an organic linkage with the industry. Recognizi ng the diversity of activities and
complexity of marketing R & D outputs, CSIR has adopted and put in place a decentralized approach
for marketing the entire knowledgebase generated at  different locations. The laboratories maintain
database of industry relevant to th eir sphere of activities. The laborat ories also make special efforts to
constantly maintain interactio ns with the industries to di sseminate the knowledgebase through
conventional as well as non-conventional approaches, including the print and electronic media. In each
of the laboratory a dedicated group inter- alia acts as a window for the marketing of the entire
knowledgebase of the laboratory. 
  
Comments 
         To realize the full potential of  the efforts involved in  the research and development in the CSI R 
laboratories, the Committee hopes th at a close contact with the i ndustry may be maintained. The
Committee recommends that a special cell may be set up to coordinate and pool the knowledge gained
in the CSIR laboratories and thereaf ter disseminate it through  direct interactions  with the industry o r
through the print and electronic media.

RESEARCH SCHEMES, SCHOLARSHIPS AND FELLOWSHIPS 
  
Recommendation 
           The Committee notes with satisf action the efforts made by Depart ment for stimulating interest 
and awareness among students for sc ience. The Committee recommends that the fellowships be given
for basic sciences as fewer student s are showing interest in them. It  is hoped that individual record o f
progress of scholarship  holders is being
maintained.                                                                                                (Para 32) 
Action Taken by the Department 
             CSIR provides fellowships to br ight young men and women in th e form of Junior Research
Fellowship (JRF), Senior Research Fellowship (S RF), SRF (Extended) and Research Associateship to
do research under the expert guida nce of faculty members / scient ists working in universities,
laboratories/institutes in various fields of scie nce and technology.  CSIR conducts CS IR-UGC NET 
Exam for Junior Research Fellowsh ip to do PhD and eligibility for l ectureship in five basic sciences
subject areas viz life, chemi cal, earth, physical and mathemat ical sciences. About 2000 Junio r
Research Fellowships are given each  year. Furthermore, about 450 Se nior Research Fellowships and
100 Research Associateships are provided to me ritorious science student s to do Ph.D and Post
Doctoral Research, respectivel y. Recently, CSIR has introdu ced Shyama Prasad Mukherjee
Fellowship Scheme to identify and nurture budding young scientific talent in  basic sciences from
amongst top 20% of the CSIR-UGC  NET qualified students. Indi vidual record of progress o f
scholarship holders are being maintained & based on progress report, their fellowships are extended /
upgraded. 
Comments 
             The Committee notes that most of the schlorsh ips/fellowships are provided to students at the 
higher level i.e. PhD/ Research levels. The Committee recommends that schlorships/fellowships may
be provided at the entry level i. e. graduation level and may be incr eased for students in Post-graduate 
level to stimulate interest am ong the new generation towards basi c sciences. The Committee also
recommends that the number of fellowships/scholarships should be increased over a period of time.

Recommendation 
          The Committee commends the Depa rtment for emerging as a pi oneering institut e to achieve
number one position in Indian & Foreign patent filings. The Co mmittee hopes that the Department
would maintain its position. The Committee hopes th at CSIR will remain vi gilant to safeguard ou r
age-old indisputable ri ghts over our traditional 
knowledge.                                                                                                                      (Para 38)

            The Department is emboldened with the encouraging remarks of Hon’ble Committee and CSIR 
will continue to make all efforts to maintain its dominant position in Indian and Foreign patents filing.
450 Indian and 500 foreign patent a pplications are expected to be  filedduring 2004- 05.  CSIR would 
also proactively protect value adde d traditional knowledge generated fr om integration of our tradition
knowledge system with scientif ic methods and modern medical  knowledge.  CSIR would also
continue to safeguard India’s interest in its traditional knowledge. 
Comments 
           The Committee appreciates the st eps taken by the CSIR to safegua rd the country’s interests, 
specially keeping in view the ef forts made by foreign organisations  to encroach upon our traditional
base. The Committee hopes that CSIR   would augment its efforts to safegaurd and assert our right to
own our traditional knowledge. In this direction, the Committee recommends that CSIR should initiate
contact with the rural people who possess a lot of informati on regarding our traditional
knowledge.

           The Committee feels that the Department should take utmost care to closely monitor and assess 
all ongoing projects; and initiate cr itical assessment of the complete d projects for thei r up-scaling and 
further advancement, if any. Besides, it should organize evaluation of ne w projects to be taken
up.                                                                  (Para 43)

           The projects in CSIR are being monito red at multiple levels to ensu re that the set target and
milestones are achieved in the prescribed time peri od and corrective action if any are taken at the mid
term stage.  The new projects in emerging areas are continuously evolved and taken up.

           The Committee notes with satisfaction the step s taken by CSIR to monitor the existing and 
evolving new projects. The Committee is of the view  that timely completion of all projects may be
made a prerequisite before initiati ng any project and all out  efforts should be, made to achieve the set
targets. At the same time, pro posals regarding projects in emer ging areas should be examined and
taken up at the earliest. 
INFRASTRUCTURE RENOVATION AND REFURBISHMENT 
Recommendation 
              The Committee feels that to face the chal lenges coming from rese arch initiatives from 
developed countries, India needs the state-of-art infrastructure and laboratories. The infrastructure 
should be seen as a st rategic national resource and funding shoul d be given on a long-term basis so 
that the modernization becomes a continued process for effectivene ss, improvement in  our scientific
growth.  The Committee is of the vi ew that the university laboratories need to be upgraded so that a
world-class infrastructure is provided for research in under-graduate and post-graduate level so that the 
interest for further research is sustained in young students. This in the l ong term would facilitate
advances in the scientific research.            (Para 48) 
Action Taken by the Department 
             CSIR provides financial assistance to promote research work in  the field of  S&T including
agriculture & medicine by wa y of research grant to Professors / Scientists working in Universities,
IITs, and recognized R&D laborator ies etc. Funds are provided for one or more JRF, SRF and RA,
contingencies & equipments . CSIR has discipline wi se research committees to  consider the research
proposals and make recommendations with respec t to quantum of gran t sanctioned under various
heads including equipments.  
              Besides, UGC, over the years, ha s launched several schemes for upgradation of infrastructure
viz. Development grants to unive rsities; Grants under various res earch scheme like Assistance fo r
strengthening of Infrastructure  in Science and Tec hnology (ASIST); University with potential fo r
excellence; Research funding council  for supporting research scheme; National Institute of Science. 
These are with a view to strengthe n the infrastructure as well as  undertaking acade mic research in
emerging areas of sciences. 
Comments 
               The Committee commends the steps initiated by the CSIR and UGC in promoting research at
the university level. 
  
TECHNOLOGY PROMOTION, DEVELOPMENT AND UTILIZATION PROGRAMME 
  
Recommendation

              The Committee feels that the scientific bodies in  India need more inte raction with industrial
houses and if the industrial and sc ientific communities work in tandem  both stand to benefit from the
other's expertise. In the presen t age of competition there should be  proactive approach from the CSI R
to reaching to industry for finding sponsor for rese arch instead of waiting for industry to approach
them.                                     (Para 56)

               The suggestions made by the comm ittee are well taken.  As me ntioned at Sl.No. 1  CSIR is
the only organization which involves industry from early stage of development with a view to build an
organic linkage with the industr y. Specific understandings are reache d with industry associations to
make known CSIR developm ents to their members.  CSIR ma nages a new innovative scheme - the 
New Millennium Indian Technology Leadership Initiative (NMITLI), which proactively looks beyond

synergising the best competencies of publicly funded R&D institutions, academia and private industry.

                The Committee hopes that the CSIR would ma ke sustained moves towards building a bond 
with the industry so that the technical expertise of the CSIR is transferred the industry.

Recommendation 
               The Committee commends the efforts of th e company for giving emphasis on indigenous
technology. But the Committee feels that the Department should make efforts to see that the company
continued to pursue the programme  of Development and Promotion of Technologies appropriate fo r
rural areas.                                           (Para 61) 
Action Taken by the Department 
              NRDC has been pursuing developm ent and promotion of technolog ies in rural areas. Rural
Technology Demonstration-cum Traini ng (RTDT) Centres are set up in association with NGO's in
various part of the country to de monstrate the utility of the rural technologies and ensure their faste r
dissemination through the network. The Corporation ha s so far set up 57 RTDT Centres in different
parts of the country.  Also, a new RTDT Centre has been opened on 23 rd  August, 2004 at Faridaba d 
under the auspices of the Centre of Technology for Sustainable Development (CTSD) and proposes to
set up 2-3 RTDT centres in 2004-05. It is also proposed to introduce 5 Simputers in the RTDT Centres

participated in one exhibition on ru ral technologies in Guwahati and proposes to participate in 2 rural
exhibitions in 2004-05. A proposal for setti ng up the National Rural & Household Technology
Demonstration-cum-Training Centre at IlT, De lhi with funding from Rural Development Ministry is 
under consideration. A propos al has been submitted to Director, Rural Development Ministry and
secretary, Science for society at DST for funding a programme for di ssemination of rural technologies
through a scientists Technology Caravan. 
Comments 
              The Committee feels that the bene fits of new technologi es rarely reach the rural areas. The
Committee hopes that the department  would increase its in teractive sessions with  the rural people to
ensure faster and wider dissemin ation of technologies suited for ru ral areas. All pending proposals in
this direction should be speedily followed up and initiated at the earliest. 
DEVELOPING NEW GENERATION FUELS & LUBRICANTS

(DAE) on the recommendations cont ained in the One Hundred Thir tieth Report of the Department
Related Parliamentary Standing Committee on Science & Technology, Environment & Forests on the
Demands for Grants (2004-05) of the Department of Atomic Energy  which was presented to Rajya 
Sabha and laid in Lok Sabha on 26 thAugust, 2004. There were twenty-f ive recommendations contained 
in the Report and the Department of Atomic Energy has furnished the action taken note in case of all the
recommendations. 
Action Taken notes on the recommendations of  the Committee were received from the
Department of Atomic Energy on 29th November, 2004.

Action Taken by the Department of Atomic Energy are set out in the succeeding paragraphs. 
BUDGETARY ALLOCATIONS FOR 2004-05 
Recommendation 
  
The Committee is happy to note that in X th Plan, out of total outla y of Rs. 23,283 Crores fo r
Nuclear Power Corporation of In dia Limited (NPCIL), Rs. 21569 Cr ores (92.6%) is for schemes fo r
which the Government has alrea dy accorded financial sanctions.  The work on these schemes has

project that is being undertaken  through a newly formed PSU na mely Bharatiya Nabhikiya Vidyut

the Department. The project execution and management experience gained by NPCIL is also being very

Action taken by  the Department  
  
            Disposal of vitrified high level wast e in geological formations has been adopted as a third and
final step of Indian strategy for management of radioactive high le vel waste (HLW) in our three step
approach. The first two steps of this strategy are 
  
1.                  Immobilisation of high level waste in solid form with the objective of  volume reduction 
and reducing the possibility of migration of radionuclides. 
2.                  Interim storage for a period of about 30 years to cool the waste a nd ensure integrity o f
conditioned waste package  by continuous surveillance. 
  
Many of  developed countries in  the world are also following the above three step strategy fo r
management of high level waste.  
  
Disposal of vitrified high level wa ste in deep bore holes or the se a bed is not planned due to the
following reasons. 
  
1.                    Disposal in deep bore holes (about 3000 me tres) is being considered basically  fo r 
disposal of spent radiation sources in  countri es where geological dis posal facility is not 
being planned due to either small size of their atomic energy programme or absence of it. 
In this concept, deep bore holes are planne d and waste is proposed to be disposed and 
sealed with no provision of retrieval. 
2.         In disposal in deep sea bed, there is  a large possibility of loss of control of the disposed
waste and, hence, it is not being considered now. 
  
We agree with the recommendation of the Co mmittee and share the vi ew that disposal o f
vitrified high level waste in deep bore-hoes or in the sea bed would be very costly.

            For minimizing the high level nuclear waste volume for pe rmanent storage and eventually
determining what happens to the ma terial when it leaks out of th e tank, the Committ ee feels, it is

Action taken by the Department  
  
The practice of decreasing the volume of high le vel waste by evaporation is being followed in
our  spent fuel reprocessi ng plants as well as in high level waste vitrificati on facilities. Evaporation by
concentration in specially designed thermo-syphon evaporators is an integral part of the basic flow sheet
of all these plants. We are, thus, able to reduce the waste volumes substantially. 
  
As regards the storage of HLW in  the liquid form, this is done in high integrity stainless steel
storage tanks with cooling and instrumentation provisions. Our experience of HLW storage in tanks over
last more than three decades  is excellent from safety point of view with not a single instance of leakage
of any of the tanks. 
  
In order to avoid transportation of HLW, care  has been taken during the plant design by co-
locating reprocessing and vitrification plants. Transfer of waste among reprocessing plant, waste storage
tanks and vitrification plant is done through underground shielded piping system to avoid radiation
exposure to operation personnel. 
  
Thus, aspects of volume reduction of  HLW, its safe storage and tran sfer are an in tegral part o f
the design of our facilities and their safe performance has been demonstrated during last more than three
decades of operations.

Recommendation  
  
            The Committee has been given to understand that  the Universal Extraction, or UNEX, process 
which is being studied in USA by Idaho National Engineering and Environmental Laboratory (INEEL)
engineers which is a subsidiary of US Department of Energy has developed the first demonstrated
technology of its kind capable of removing multiple radio active elements from high level nuclear waste
in one step.  Just a sprinkling of radioactive el ements turns volume of a largely harmless waste into
‘high level radioactive waste’ subject to rigorous and expensive storage standards.   
  
            Such waste is a byproduct of nucle ar energy and weapons developm ent and usually contains a
mixture of intensely radioact ive fission products like Stront ium-90, Cesium-137 and long lived 
radioactive elements like plutonium and Americiam plus hazardous and toxic materials. Separating most
of the radioactive elements  from the other materials can shrink volume of high-leve l waste, reduce the 
total disposal cost and minimise potential harm to the people and the environment surrounding it.  The
Committee is of the opinion that an extractant is required that works in one step and removes radioactive
strontium, cesium and other Actinides at once. 
  
            Using the UNEX process, trimming th e volume of high level waste at least twenty fold, each
gallon of waste shrinks to less than a cup and the twenty fold vol ume reduction leads to a corresponding
reduction in disposal costs.  The ma jority of the waste left over afte r a   UNEX sepa ration is far less
expensive to treat and store than the highly radioactive portion. 
  
            The Committee would like to suggest that this unique UNEX process of squeezing the volume of
enormous nuclear waste to  size less than a cup should be studi ed to depth by DAE and Atomic Energy
Regulatory Board (AERB) so that the benefit of the reduction of disposal cost could be enjoyed by the
Department as an economy measure for treating, managing and storing all types of radioactive waste e.g.
low level, intermediate level and high level nuclear waste etc., and a subsequent  feasibility report could
be submitted before the Committee for perusal and examination, partic ularly keeping in view the cost
effectivity aspect  of the project. 
( Paras 70, 71, 72 & 73)
  
Action taken by the Department 
  
In various countries several solvent extraction process have been developed for the separation o f
long-lived radionuclides, Stront ium-90 and Cesium-137 from acidic radioactive waste solution. These 
processes use different types of solvent employing solvent-extraction equipment of different designs.  
  
Universal Extraction (UNEX) process being studied by Idaho Nati onal Engineering and
Environment Laboratory (INEEL), USA employs a large number of  centrifugal  contactors  in a cascade
manner. In this process,  a universal solvent containing Ch roninated Co balt Di carbollide (ChCoDic) 
with polyethylglycol (PEG) to remove 137-Ce sium and Strontium-90 and C arbamoylmethyl Phosphine 
Oxide (CMPO ) to remove long-lived radionuclides is used. 
  
India has developed extens ive expertise during last  four decades in extr action  of uranium and
plutonium from acidic solutions gene rated during spent fuel reprocessi ng. The solvent used is 30%  tri-
butyl phosphate (TBP) + dodecane  in pulse agitated  columns. Plants  based on this solvent extraction
technology are in o peration at Tromba y, Tara pur and Kal pakkam from 1965 onwards. Presentl y,

REPORT 
        The Report of the Committee deals with the Action Taken by th e Department of Ocean
Development on the recommendations  contained in the One Hundred Twenty-e ighth Report of the 
Department-related Parliamentary Standing Co mmittee on Science & T echnology, Environment &
Forests on the Demands for Grants  (2004-05) of the Department of Ocean Development which was

Committee were received from the Department of Ocean Development on 27thDecember, 2004 
        The Committee’s recommendations, Action Taken thereon and comments of the Committee on the
Action Taken by the Department of Ocean Development are set out in the succeeding paragraphs:—

Recommendation

Committee feels that the Departme nt should have foreseen the re asons advanced by it for the non-

POLAR SCIENCE (ANTARCTIC RESEARCH) PROGRAMME 
Recommendation 
        Exploration of the icy continent is a challenging task before the Department. The Committee feels 
given the extremity of the prevailing situation in this continent of ice, Department has taken the real pain
to embark upon a formidable task of initiating scientific experi ments in extreme conditions. Although
the Committee is fully convinced about the quality of  the research work undertaken till date in this
uninhabited and inhospitable mass of ice land, it feels the following areas of research should be given
more attention due to their global, social, medical, scientific and economic importance: 
           (a)    Studies on evolution of Antarctic Glaciology; 
           (b)   Studies on ozone hole issues; 
           (c)    Studies in geological and geophysical investigation of the Schirmacher Oasis 
and Orwin and Wolhthat mountains; 
           (d)   Studies about Antarctic microbe s specially cynobacteria with  special reference to thei r
survivality rate in extreme co ld situation so that any ne w knowledge about the process o f 
biological withstanding of extreme low temperat ure could be utilized for Indian defence 
personnel staying in Siachen Glacier; 
           (e)    Studies in Antarctic pollution; 
           (f)    Studies in Krill biology; and 
           (g)    Studies in auroral phenomenon. 
        The Committee while strongly recommending basic and in depth research es in these fields urges
the Department to uphold its commitment to pr otect the pristine nature of the Continent.
                                                               (Para 17) 
Action Taken by the Department 
        The Indian Research Station is bei ng maintained according to protocol on Environmental
Protection to Antarctic Treaty, wh ich states that the waste management strategy is worked out in
accordance with the various recommendations of An tarctic Treaty Consultative Meeting (ATCMs) and
also on the principles as agreed by the Consultativ e Parties. The station is equipped with a treatment
plant and incinerator. 
        Further, regular cleaning in and around Mait ri is carried out under the supervision of Leader and
designated Environmental Officer. The solid waste collected is segregated and brought back for prope r
disposal and recycling as applicab le. The station is regularly insp ected by a team of  international
inspectors and the last repo rt of the inspection in January, 2001 stat ed that the site had a very orderly
appearance and the personnel showed dedication and commitment. 
        Research in the areas/fields suggested by the Hon’ ble Committee has al ready been/is being 
conducted as per the mandated/approved Antarctic programme.

Comments 
        The Committee finds the reply of the Department evasive, as nothi ng in detail has been mentione d
about the areas of research suggested by it. The Committee would, therefore, like to know the views o f
the Department on its suggestions. 
Recommendation 
        The Committee hopes that sustained efforts of the Department in the direction of setting up new
station will yield positive results. However, notwithstanding different surveys involved, some target date
should be fixed for comple ting the task undertaken. In the absence of any time frame, it may lose the
importance and urgency that is called for.              (Para 18) 
Action Taken by the Department 
        The location of new site as proposed af ter preliminary survey carri ed out during XXIII Indian
Antarctic Expedition in early 2004 is near Latitude 69° South and Longitude 76°  East. The Department 
is in the initial stages of survey of the selected site, which is required to be  assessed for environmental
parameters as mandated under the Envi ronmental Protocol of the Antarcti c Treaty and also for logistics
and scientific considerations. The Department is working in a planned way, keeping in view the logistics
constraints and pre-requis ite of Environmental Imp act Assessment (EIA) etc.  for obtaining necessary 
approvals of the ATCMfor establishing the new station. 
Comments 
        The Committee notes the reply. 
POLYMETALLIC NODULES (PMN) PROGRAMME  
Recommendation 
        Although, the Committee is ha ppy with the contents and performance of projects unde r 
Polymetallic Nodules Programme of Department, it is, however, s ceptical about the Department’s 
assessment about the preservation of environmental norms for optimal sea ecology at the mining site. 
        The Committee is of the opinion that be fore a comprehensive planni ng is undertaken for on-site 
mining of nodule, the Department should prepare an experimental chart about the precise disturbance of
the sea floor at the mining area to  assess its geological and ecologi cal conditions. The Committee feels
that while organisms would be de stroyed in the mined area undisturbe d areas would remain because o f
the complex terrain of sea bed which could serve as  biological reservoir for recolonizing the destroyed
section.                                                                                                        (Para 22) 
Action Taken by the Department 
        Noted. The Department is undertaki ng a well-defined component on Environmental Impact 
Assessment (EIA) pertaining to th e mining of polymetallic nodules from seabed. The experiment o f
precise disturbance on the sea fl oor has been conducted in a si mulated environment and various
geological, ecological and biologica l parameters are being monitored vis-a-vis the pre disturbance 
environment. A chart for monitori ng the parameters has been prepar ed and recolonisation studies are
also being carried out as a part  of EIA study. The study is being c onducted by scientists from National
Institute of Oceanography, Goa. Furthe r, there is an identified refere nce area which is not disturbed to
monitor the natural conditions. 
Comments 
        The Committee notes the reply and is  of the view that efforts to  extract polymetallic manganese 
nodules from deep sea bed be assessed from the point of view of  its impact on the ocean environment.
Besides, the Department should ensure that all guidelines for envir onmental improvement as
recommended in Environment Impact Assessment (EIA) are strictly implemented. 
Recommendation 
Page 5 of 17138th REPORT OF COMMITTEE ON SCIENCE AND TECHNOLOGY
7/16/2008http://10.21.217.2/book2/reports/science/138threport.htm

        The Committee is of the opinion that dangers arising from the re lease of underlying heavy metals 
when the upper sediment layer is removed, could change or disrupt geochemical systems that has been
stabilized over geological time, possibly creating zones of reduce d oxygen where life would become
impossible. 
        The Committee, therefore, feels that before mining is initiated, Department must examine the effect
of mining on local animals at the site caused by dragging of plough acr oss the bottom to stimulate the
effects of nodule mining on the sea bed, including the rates at which animals of the same species
returned to the disturbed area. The study should be done in this respect on mega fauna animals large
enough to be seen at th e ocean bottom. The Committee is of the opinion that the effe cts of mining will
be greatest on the sea sponges that liv ed directly on the nodules because their habitat will be completely
destroyed. Other free swimming spec ies will suffer a considerable re duction in numbers due to serious
disruption in food supply. The Committee, therefore, is of the view that from emerging picture above the
evaluation of bio-threat exposed by sea bed mining is indispensable to  be addressed thoroughly before 
venturing into mining operation and the Committee feels that any such  evaluation is difficult without
better knowledge of the organisms living at the mining site and the eco-system in which they function. It 
is quite apparent that animals at the site area would be killed by the impact of the mining vehicle and by
resettlement of the sediment cloud that impact of the mining vehicle will raise from the sea floor. 
        Another potential effect of mining on th e ocean floor is the bringi ng up of unwanted materials
during a mining operation i.e. sediments, trace metals from nodul e waste and cold and nutrient rich
bottom water into the upper ocean. Owing to this probl em, the Committee feels that deep or mid ocean
level will be most desirable area for discharging of  miners waste as it would not be harmful to the
environment.   
                                                                                                                                               (Para 23) 
Action Taken by the Department 
        Noted. Comprehensive study on biodivers ity of meiofuna, macrofauna, megafauna has been
undertaken in the entire nodule area in the Central Indi an Ocean Basin to assess their distribution and
their association with the nodules. This will help in  predicting the potential impact and in devising
methods for their conservation a nd recolonisation. Also, the studies  on environmental variability
associated with nodules deposits are being undertaken to address the problem of heavy metals, dissolved
oxygen etc. 
Comments 
        While the Committee notes the reply, it would appreciate sustained ef forts on the part of the
Department to review the performance of studies being undertaken by the Department. 
Recommendation 
        The Committee further feels th at burial sensitivity of sea bed organisms i.e. the consequences o f 
dumping a layer of sediment on t op of them as a direct reperc ussion of mining should be studied
thoroughly by Department as lesson for Environmental Im pact Assessment of sea- bed mining. The 
Committee feels such studies c ould be undertaken by the Depart ment through Remotely Operated
Vehicle (ROV). 
        The Committee, ther efore recommends that Department should undertake cr itical assessment o f
different mining technique s and their subsequent effects on Geochemistry  and Ocean Biology and
Department should generate reliable data fo r determining the optimal mining techniques i.e. ideal 
extractive metallurgy to minimize environmental impacts. 
        The Committee, therefore strongly reco mmends for constant assessm ent of environmental impact
of deep sea-mining by Department before venturing into actual mi ning operation keeping the following 
into consideration for a meaningful assessment of the impact:- 
           (a)    Biodiversity, species ranges and rates of gene flow in the nodule areas; 
           (b)   Burial sensitivit y of dee p-sea animals and their res ponse to the t ype of disturbance cause d

7/16/2008http://10.21.217.2/book2/reports/science/138threport.htm

when nodules are scrapped from the sea floor, as well as  recovery of marine organisms in space and
time; 
           (c)    Impact on ocean column by rising unwanted materials from mining operation located above
a mine site; 
           (d)   Natural variability in deep ocean ecosystems over space and time; 
           (e)    Access to sea bed data wh ich may be generated by Cent ral Data Repository under the
control of Department for accurate assessmen t of environment for determining the choice o f 
correct mining technique; and 
           (f)    Month to month, year to year and place to place ch anges to be invest igated as a furthe r
means of understanding the environmen t in which deep sea mining will 
operate.                                                        (Para 24) 
Action Taken by the Department 
        Yearly monitoring of the site which wa s experimentally disturbed is underway of which three
observations have been completed and further observations are propos ed to be carried out in the
forthcoming year at the disturban ce as well as at the reference si te to evaluate the processes o f
restoration and recolonisation of the seafloor environment and also the natural changes. This is projected
as a part of 10th Plan. Further studies will be planned on the basis of data collected and the observations,
if required. This data will be made available for designing the mining system and deciding the
operations. 
Comments 
        The Committee notes the reply.  
Recommendation 
        The Committee also recommends that apart fr om the mining of Polymetallic Nodules, the 
Department should also thoroughly assess the potentials of mining Hydrothermal Polymetallic Sulphides
and Cobalt-rich ferromanganese crusts from the Ocean bed keeping in view the export potentials of such
metals in the international market.  (Para 25) 
Action Taken by the Department 
        Noted. A project has been initiated for the study of Cobalt-rich crusted seamounts in the northern 
Indian Ocean. 
Comments 
        The Committee notes the reply and desires that the project should be regularly monitored. 
DRUGS FROM SEA  
Recommendation 
        The Committee notes with sati sfaction that under the Drugs from the Sea Programme, the
Department is in the process of doing a commenda ble work. The Committee is happy with the fact that
various steps have been taken by the Department for identificati on of numerous marine organisms
showing enormous potential for extraction of such drugs as are anti-diabetic, anti-viral, anti-fungal, anti-
cholesterol and spermicidal agents for developing new drugs.                   (Para 28) 
Action Taken by the Department 
        Two marine compounds are in advanced  stage of drug development with special emphasis on
safety pharmacology and toxicologi cal studies. An anti-diabetic co mpound has already entered into 
phase-I clinical tr ial in two hospitals under the coordinati on of Central Drug Research Institute, 
Lucknow after necessary approval of  DCGI. The coordinator and Dire ctor, CDRI, Lucknow is working
for involving pharmaceutical industry in the venture for successful foll ow-up and transfer of technology 
for commercialization of drugs from the marine resources with the assi stance of Department of Ocean
Development. 
Page 7 of 17138th REPORT OF COMMITTEE ON SCIENCE AND TECHNOLOGY
7/16/2008http://10.21.217.2/book2/reports/science/138threport.htm

        The Committee for the Purpose of Cont rol and Supervision of Experiments on Animals (CPCSEA)
has now given clearance for conducting chronic toxicity  studies in monkeys for the anti-hyperlipidemic 
compound. The study is in progress as per the schedul e and expected to be completed in March, 2005.
The safety toxicity study would provide another drug from the marine resources. 
Comments 
        The Committee appreciates the efforts being made by the Department in a ugmenting its efforts in
collection, identification and bio-evaluation of marine flora and fauna from Indian Coast. 
Recommendation 
        The Committee, however, feels that despite these initiatives by the Department, there is still enough
scope left for extraction of potentially anti-cancerous drugs from the depth of the ocean. The Committee
is of the opinion that pharmaceutical uses of mic ro-algae which are a grea t source of unexplored 
chemical compounds, are ex tremely beneficial for a possible s ource of noble drugs. Micro-algae are 
primitive single celled organisms th at live in a variety of environm ents and have a high potential fo r
producing noble chemical structures . The Committee is given to und erstand that bulbous yellow soft
coral that disrupts erratic cell divi sions in cancer cells and ocean mo lds that live in sea grasses also
contains sufficient virus killing proteins. Apart from this, the sea sponges are also a real source fo r
extraction of anti cancer drugs. Other cancer drugs like Didemnin -B isolated from Sea squint, 
Bryostatin-1 that could be isolated from Bugula, Dolestatin-10 that could be de rived from Indian Ocean 
Mollusk and Dolabella, a Sea hare, are also sources of potential drugs  for the treatment of cancer and
other incurable diseases. Apart from this, severa l pain killer compounds could be extracted from
horseshoe crabs from the depth of the Ocean. The Commit tee feels that if the department takes
comprehensive action to study the extraction of these drugs, the entire system of curative medicine could
be revolutionized on its path of treating and curing life threatening ailments like cancer and AIDS. The
Committee would, however, like to lay down that during the extraction of these drugs particularly from
the sea coral enough precaution shoul d be taken by the Department so  that ecological and biological
damages done to such coral surroundings should be reduced to the minimum so that scientific researches
in the field may not stand on the way of preserva tion of holistic sea-ecol ogy with a preposterous 
consequences.                                    (Para 29) 
Action Taken by the Department 
        Participation of few more institutions unde r the “Drugs from Sea” progr amme is being worked out 
for extraction of potentially anti-cancerous drugs from the depth of the ocean including micro-algae. It is 
of further interest that 14 new marine extracts  have been identified for follow-up work. Thei r 
bioactivities, namely, antidiabetis, dyslipidemia, antifungal etc. have been reconfirmed and bioactivity is
being localized in the fractions and pure substances. 
        Further, the sea moulds are being st udied under this programme along with seaweeds, sponges,
corals for extraction of various bi oactivities. The details of Didemn in B - Sea Squint, Bryostatin-1, 
Bugula, Dolestatin-10-Indian Ocean Mollusk & Dola bella, Seabella, Sea ha re present a source fo r 
potential drugs for treatment of cancer and other incurable diseases. The focus from the year 2005-06 
would be strengthened to take comprehensive action to study the extraction of drugs for cancer, pain etc.
As recommended, the Department is concerned to preserve the marine biodiversity for sustainable use of
marine organism including coral reefs and its ecology. 
Comments 
        The Committee notes the reply of the Department. 
COASTAL OCEAN MONITORING AND PREDICTION SYSTEM (COMAPS) 
Recommendation 
        The Committee observes that the efforts of the Department to monitor pollution in the coastal areas 
need to be continued vigorously. The Department should identify lo cations for periodical monitoring
alongwith sti pulated parameters for diffusion and dis persion characteristics. Be sides, the stations fo r

collection of nea r-shore samples must be planne d with a view to reflect th e pollution load that was
occurring there and the data collected should be pr ocessed and forwarded to State Pollution Control
Boards for taking remedial measures.                                                                                       (Para 32)  
Action Taken by the Department 
        The Department is monitoring the health  of coastal waters of India under COMAPS programme by
collecting data systematically on 25 parameters related to physical, chemical, biological, microbiological
characteristics of water and sediments including pe sticide residue from the marine organisms. The
programme is in operation at 82 locations along the east and west co asts of India including islands. As
observed above, the Department has identified 13 hotspots for intensive monitoring. Besides, models are
being developed for the evaluation of assimilative capacities of coasta l marine areas for mitigating the
adverse impact of pollution on marine environment so as to enable  the coastal State Pollution Control
Boards to prescribe appropriate disposal standards, water quality criteria, etc. 
Comments 
        The Committee observes that ther e is a need for greater coordi nation between the Department an d
respective State Pollution Control Boards for a continued monitoring of marine pollution levels and data
generated through Geographical Inform ation System (GIS) must be util ized to the fullest extent to
achieve desired results. 
Recommendation 
        The Committee also observes that the land- based pollutants effect the marine and coastal 
environment, including estuaries and inshore coas tal waters, which are th e most productive areas.
Therefore, it recommends that  a well-planned and we ll-managed marine wate r quality monitoring 
system is required to predict change s of trends in the qua lity of a particular marine water body so that
curative or preventive measures can be taken to restore and mainta in ecological balance in the wate r
body. Monitoring is needed to ensure that standards and criteria set by the regulatory agencies are met
for the protection of marine wate r
quality.                                                                                                                           (Para 33)  
Action Taken by the Department 
        The COMAPS programme has been collect ing data on 25 pollution para meter at 82 locations (72
since 1990, which was enhanced to 82  since 2002-03). The data collected are regularly forwarded to the
State Pollution Control Boards for taking remedial action. The programme also includes a component on
prediction of changes in seawater quality trend of particular water body/sea area. Integrated Coastal and
Marine Area Management Project Directorate of Department of Ocean Development is engaged at
present in this task and a decadal database fo r this purpose for all locat ions monitored under the
COMAPS programme is being developed. During the current year, the trend of changes in water quality
will be determined at least for 4 priority locations. For remaining locations, the efforts will be continued
during the 10thand 11th Five Year Plans. 
Comments 
        The Committee notes the reply. 
MARINE RESEARCH AND CAPACITY BUILDING  
Recommendation 
        The Committee feels that for strengthening ocean research centers, the Department should focus its 
efforts in assisting Universities  to create infrastruct ure facilities and build ing up a skilled human
resource base in marine sciences. Moreover, marine  science teaching on the su stainability of ocean
space and its resources should be strengthened at all levels, from primary to adult education; in curricula
at university level; in adult e ducation programmes for ocean users (fishermen, seamen, workers in oil
industry, coastal engineers) and for managers of ocean affairs.                                           (Para 36)

for identifying, developing and using the properties of living things to make  products or services, it

different parental source s, uses chemicals and radiation to cr eate mutant strain s or genetically

        The Committee is also happy to not e that two other ocea n coastal research vessels namely Saga r
Purvi and Sagar Pashimi are main ly being used by the Department  of Ocean Development for the
assessment of sea pollution within the Exclusive Economic Zone of India. 
        The Committee would like to suggest that  since the assessment of th e sea pollution and subsequent
action plan for dealing with the de nsity of pollution is extremely impor tant from the point of view o f
maintaining an optimal sea ecology, it is necessary  that indepth research through these two vessels
should be undertaken for a complete monitoring of the ocean pollution and initiating subsequent steps to
control them. The Committee acco rdingly, would like to advise th e Department that biogeochemical
pump, which are micro-organisms at the sea surface and which take CO 2 from the atmosphere an d 
convert it via photosynthesis into the organic carbon of  their cells should be st udied in minute details.
When these Micro-organisms die s ubsequently or consumed and excr eted, some portion of that carbon 
sinks to these floors where it is buried. As the entire world is conf ronting the threat of the global
warming, understanding this concept of biogeochemical pump is essential because  it could extract huge
amount of excess heat trapping CO2 from our atmosphere. A key clue lies in the tiny interface where sea
water meets sea floor and this cr itical chemical reaction determin es how much car bon dissolves bac k
into the water and how much remains in the sediments. This is known as carbon flux.

be more challenging and informative if machiner ies could dive beyond a de pth of 6000 metres. The
Committee is, therefore, of the opinion that for a real deep sea study Advanced Tethered Vehicle (ATV)
is needed by Department, which is an unmanned ve hicle equipped with latest  advanced technology and
which can easily undertake researches beyond a de pth of 6 thousand metres. The most striking
advantage for using the ATV for underwater research is that it is extremely helpful to make researches at
extreme depth where it is dangerous  for divers to venture. The Co mmittee is given to understand that
such vehicles are cost affective and can be used in ocean abyss with much flexibility. It is observed that
the vast majority of the ocean depths are bone chilling cold, completely dark and have ambient pressures
equivalent to the weight of the hundreds of atmosphe res. The exploration of th e deep sea is, therefore,
impossible without a substantial i nvestment on latest te chnology. The Committee, therefore, strongly
recommends that the Department may use Advanced Tethered Vehi cle (ATV) for the purpose of deep
sea research in view of its deep sea advantages a nd cost effective applicati ons. This vehicle will be
extremely helpful for researches at  ocean benthos where gr eater variety of biotic  and abiotic elements

PERSISTENT ORGANIC POLLUTANTS  
Recommendation 
        The Committee feels that Persistent Organic Pollutants (POPs) are the most common sea pollutants
which are constantly affecting the Ocean environm ent and optimal marine ecology. The POPs usually
gets generated in the deep sea envi ronment from the dead biotic orga nisms. When the particles of this
organisms get sink in the sea bed, a degradation of organic matrix occurs a nd consequently POPs get
released in the surrounding water. Under anoxic conditions, sediments containing organic carbon
releases contaminants into the surrounding water. POPs not only aff ect microbial food chain but also
coastal environments which are the most productive  areas of the sea. PO Ps are also ubiquitous.
Accordingly, it is an extreme th reat towards maintenance of opt imal sea ecology and it has high
exposure to humans also. Keeping the gravity of the situati on into active consideration, the Committee
feels that Sagar Purvi and Sagar Paschimi, two ocean research vessels, which are monitoring research on
ocean pollution may also direct a major chunk of their study towards the understanding of POPs
behaviour and subsequent control of the same from spreading on the sea benthos so that the entire biotic
community of ocean flora and fauna could be effectively preserved from environmental pollution. 
        The Committee also feels that two of th e main POP group namely dioxi n and furans which are the
principal threat to humanity should also be studied as a part of th e pollution control programme by the
Department.

            I, the Chairman of the Departme nt-related Parliamentary Stan ding Committee on Science & 
Technology, Environment & Forests, having been authorised by the Committee to present the Report on

Committee on Demands for Grants (2004-2005) of the Ministry of Environment & Forests.

Forests on the recommendations contai ned in the One Hundred Thirty-f irst Report of the Department-
related Parliamentary Standing Committee on Scie nce & Technology, Envir onment & Forests on the
Demands for Grants (2004-2005) of the Ministry of Environment & Fo rests which was presented to the
Rajya Sabha on 26th  August, 2004.

RESEARCH 
  
The Committee feels that the cont inuous and sustainable developm ent of forestry would depend
on research inputs in crucial areas, solving problems and expanding knowledge.  Therefore, the scope of
forestry research should cover not only biological and technology as pects (forestry, forest products,
conservation, wildlife), but also a wide spectrum of economic, envir onmental, sociological and policy
research. Moreover, Universities providing forest ry research should be given grants-in-aid for 
strengthening their infrast ructure and technical capabilities. O pportunities should also be provided fo r
furthering the academic advancement of foresters/scientists/academicians in the field of forestry. 
(Para 12)

Report, Forest Survey of India 2001) 
  
            The Committee may also be pleased to note that the focus of the forestry management has shifted
from State-controlled production to sustainable management with people’s pa rticipation in the past two 
decades. The Ministry of Environment and Forests vide letter no. 6.21/89-PP dated 1.6.1990 outlined the 
principles of Joint Forest Manage ment (JFM) and conveyed  to State Government s for creating massive
people’s movement through involvement of the vill age communities in the protection, regeneration and
development of degraded forests on “Care and Share” basi s. Further, through it s letters No. 22-8/2000-
JFM (FPD) dated 21.2.2000 and 24.12.2002, this Ministry issued the gui delines for strengthening of the
JFM programme. These letters provided the framework for the Stat e Governments to ensure meaningful
participation of women in JFM programme, extension of JFM in good forests areas, dovetailing o f
village-level forest management microplan under JFM with the Work ing Plan of the forest division, and
formalizing relationships with local village  community by way of signing of Memorandum o f
Understanding (MoU) for JFM.    
            As on date, all 28 State Govern ments have adopted JFM as their key policy relating to
conservation and development of forests.  As per available in formation on 10.9.2003, there were 84632
JFM committees in the country looking after 17.33 million ha. of forest lands (except Meghalaya, which
adopted JFM after 10.9.2003), which is approximately 23% of the total forest area of the country.  
            Tribal and women are the special focus groups under JFM. Almost 60percent of the forest cove r
in the country as per assessment by Forest Survey of India 2001 is availa ble in the tribal districts of the
country, and the tribal families ar e automatically covered in the JFM programme in these areas. As on
10.9.2003, approximately 8.4 million fa milies were involved in JFM programme out of which
approximately 2.7 million were Schedule Tribe families.  
            To ensure participation of wome n in the JFM programme, the guidelines issued vide this
Ministry’s letter dated 21.2.2000 st ipulate that 50% of the member s in General Body of the JFM
committee at the village level shoul d be women and in the Executive  Body their representation should
be 33%.  
            As per this Ministry’s Guidelines issued vide letter dated 1.6.1990, the beneficiaries of JFM are
to be given to a share in usufructs,  like grasses, lops a nd tops of branches, minor  forest produce, and a
portion from the sale of trees when they mature, to  the extent, and subject to the conditions prescribed
by the State Governments in this behalf. Each State Government has prescribed these shares to suit local
conditions. For example, the Madhya  Pradesh Government has provide d 100% share of the net profit o f
the harvesting of timber and ba mboo to the Joint Forest Mana gement Committees. The Policy
Guidelines issued by Government  of India vide letter dated 24.12.2002 also stipulate the signing o f
MOU by the State Forest Department with the JFM committees  to inter-alia, include roles and 
responsibilities of the two sides and the details of usufruct sharing.  
            In order to support JFM programme , this Ministry is implem enting National Afforestation
Programme (NAP) Scheme in the X Plan which starte d as a Pilot Scheme, i.e., Samanvit Gram
Vanikaran Samridhi Yo jana (SGVSY) Scheme, in the latter half of the IX Plan.  This Scheme is

Action Taken by the Ministry 
  
The National Forest Po licy, 1988 envisages one-third forest a nd tree cover in the country.  The 
cover should be two-third in the hills and in mount ainous regions.  In pursuan ce of this Policy, this
Ministry has requested all State/ Union Territory Governments to unde rtake necessary steps so that the
existing forest cover is maintained and enriched, a nd necessary additions are made on an increased rate
in the forest and tree cover.  The 1988 Policy stipulates a national targ et, and it may not be practically
feasible to breakdown the target to the state le vel because of several geographical and climatic
constraints, e.g. occurrence of snow-bound areas, glacial regions, water courses and water-bodies, stony/ 
rocky areas, deserts, etc.  in some States.  
                        In view of the abov e, those States/ UTs which are fo rest rich, e.g., Arunachal Pradesh,
Chhattisgarh, Manipur, Me gahalaya, Mizoram, Naga land, Orissa, Tripura, but  have the potential fo r
further increase in forest and tree cover have been requested to strive  for the same irrespective of thei r
present situation vide this Ministry's letter no. NAEB 1-5/2003-BI dated 1.9.2003 (Annexure-II).  While 
fixing the annual tree planting targets under 20-Point Programme, this Ministry also takes into account
all related factors, e.g. existing fo rest and tree cover in the State/ UT, the extent of potential lands
available as depicted by wa steland statistics, the past performance of the State/ UT with respect to tree
planting, etc. 
Comments 
  
            The Committee while notin g the reply of the Ministr y is of the view that the Ministr y will
have to make concerted efforts in coop eration with the States/UTs in achievin g the ambitious
target with re gard to forest/tree cover envisa ged in the Nation al Forest Polic y, 1988.  The
Committee would appreciate if it is kept informed of the pro gress made in this re gard,  on a year
to year basis.

Recommendation 
The Committee has observed that given the present state of Wild Life Conservation in India,
there are a lot of work to be done in the field to gi ve the word ‘Conservation’ a real meaning.  Over the
years, the Committee has noted that  the basic requirements for conserva tion of wild life have not been
fulfilled to its best by the Minist ry of Environment & Forests and neither much importance has been
attached for the preserva tion of endangered species of animal and flora which constitute the heart o f
nature in India. 
            In order to give a thrust to the real  understanding of the meaning of  the term ‘Conservation’, the 
term Wild Life will have to be interpreted in a different perspectiv e in the broadest sense possible to
include scientific work, field wo rk, planning and manage ment, control of poach ing and illegal trade,
awareness, education and extensi on of work, eco-development, captive breeding and zoo management 
etc. 
            In order to give a more thrust  on the crux of the above definition, the Committee feel that
following priorities for wild life conservation should be designed by the Ministry during the current plan
period:- 
1.                  Control of poaching and illegal trade in wild life and wild life produc ts made of wild life
parts; 
2.                  Development of protected areas network.; 
3.                  Welfare measures for wild life staff; 
4.                  Eco tourism; 
5.                  Wild life conservation outside protected areas; 
6.                  Prevention and reduction of damage to wild life;  
7.                  Establishment of second home for the Asiatic lion in Gir. 
So long as the Asiatic lion population remains restri cted to a single location, it is at constant risk
from catastrophic natural events li ke forest fire, flood, earthquake et c.  Accordingly, efforts should be
under way to establish a second population of this enda ngered species in a suitable animal habitat.  As
per the Committee’s categorised opi nion, Palpur –Kuno in Madhya Prades h could be identified as the 
most viable alternative for this purpose. 
(Para 25)
Action Taken by the Ministry 
As recommended by the Committee, this Ministry has already initiated the establishment of the
Wildlife Crime Bureau for intelligence gathering for the prevention of poach ing and illegal trade in
wildlife and wildlife products. In  addition, as per the decision take n by the National Board for Wildlife

region where there number is inadequate and al so to ensure all round development and bette r
management of existing protected areas.

Legal Protection against Wildlife Poaching and Trade  
  
            Govt. of India enacted a comprehensive legislat ion “Wildlife (Protection) Act, 1972”with the 
objective of effectively controlling poaching and illegal trade in wildlife and its derivatives. This has
been amended in January, 2003 and puni shment an penalty for offences  under the Act have been made
more stringent.  
Offences pertainin g to huntin g of endan gered species and alterin g of boundaries of protected
areas. 
  
            For offences relating to wild an imals (or their parts a nd products) included in schedule- I of part 
II of Schedule –II  and those relating to hunting or altering the boundaries of a sanctuary or national park
the punishment and penalty have been enhanced, th e minimum imprisonment pres cribed is three years
which may extend to seven years, with a minimum fine of Rs. 10,000/-. For a subsequent offence of this 
nature, the term of imprisonments shall not be less than three years but may extend to seven section (51-
A) has been inserted in the Act, making certain conditions applicable while granting bail: 
            When any person accused of the commi ssion of any offence relating to Schedule I or Part II o f
Schedule II or offences relating to hunting inside the boundaries or National Park or Wildlife Sanctuary
or altering the boundaries of such parks and sanctuaries, is arrested under the provisions of the Act, then
not withstanding anything containe d in the Code of Cr iminal Procedure, 1973, no such person who had
been previously convicted of an offence under this Act shall be released on bail unless- 
            (a)  The public Prosecutor has been given an opportunity of opposing the release on bail; and  
            (b) Where the Public Prosecutor oppos e the application, the Court is  satisfied that there are
reasonable grounds for believing that he is not guilty or such offences and that he is not likely to commit
any offence while on bail.  
            In order to improve the intelligen ce gathering in wildlife cr ime, the existing provision fo r
rewarding the informers has been increased from 20% of the fine and composition m oney respectively
to 50% in each case. In addition to  this, a reward upto Rs. 10,000/- is also proposed to be given to the 
informants and others who provide assistance in detection of crime and apprehension of the offenders.

Recommendation 
  
The Committee is of the opinion that the destruction and depletion of forests will not only lead to
loss of our vegetation but will also result in wi despread deterioration of  environment with fatal
consequences to the very existence of all forms of life.  The problem ca nnot be overcome unless a
consciousness is built among the people that they are integral part of  the forests and forests belong to
them.  Besides the feeling of alienation among the  tribals and local popul ation should be removed.  The
Committee, therefore, feels that the local populati on (including tribals) resi ding in the forest areas
should be actively associated with the management of forests a nd allowed to share its products, without
in any way compromising the preser vation of our national forests.  The active involvement of people in
the development of forestry sector has to be further strengthened.  In addition of all th ese measures, the
Ministry should also devise step s to inculcate among them a sense of belonging and commitment to
forests.

ZOOLOGICAL GARDENS IN THE COUNTRY 
  
Recommendation 
            The Committee is not satisfied w ith the manner in which the zoological gardens are being
maintained in the country. The facilities availabl e within the zoo for cagi ng animals, preserving thei r
ecological surroundings, the basic cl eanliness, the supply of food patt ern for the animals etc. are not
either significantly congenial or  are not conforming to the ethos  and requirements that an ideal
zoological garden. Zoos neither fulf ill the requirements for emanation of  the idea of conservation of the
wild life in an effective manner amon g the civil population nor do the y carry message of ‘think green’
Page 36 of 48139th Report of Committee on Science & Technology, Environment & Forests

among the visitors. The Committee feels that the entire  issue should be perused in a different frame o f
perspective to bring out the following in a holistic manner:   
The mission of an ideal zoological  garden should be to conserve , exhibit and interpret a living
collection in order to promote public recreati on, understanding of the relationships between man
and animal and action to sustain the environment we  share. In order to give a perfect thrust to
drive home the crux of the above definition, the zoo should be organised in such a manner that it
should talk about a sustaina ble relationship between the bu ilt environment and natural
environment and the same should be interpreted in a functional manner to the public. The basic
structures of the zoos should be designed in such a manner that th ese could be used as a vehicle
for education for the public combined with en tertainment. A “Think Gr een Logo” should be 
positioned from the very entrance to the deep interi or of the zoo so that it can constantly infuse
environmentally sound themes combined with en ergy efficient performa nce of the building, o f
the animals, water conservation a nd use of natural sun light as light source coupled with careful
selection of basic building materials in the zoo that minimize adverse impact on the environment.
In order to infuse a real thrust to the pict ure, the Committee feels that poly steel insulated
concrete forums could be used which are environmentally sensitive and friendly for construction
of animal confinements. 
            In a few words, the Committee w ould like to summarise the objective of an ideal zoo as
follows:- 
            “Demonstrating awareness towards the environment and to extend the zoos    conservation ethic 
to the community through education and action”. 
            The Committee, therefore, would like to suggest that massive holistic reform programme of zoos
in the country should be planned by the Ministry to bring out the above idea in an effective manner even
by providing all basic welfare measures and amenities to zoo workers and officials.

PROTECTION OF TAJ MAHAL 
Recommendation 
The Taj Mahal at Agra is  one of the most important monuments  of not only in India but also the
whole world.  In recent years owing to  growth of satellite industries, the ambient air quality particularly
within the Taj Trapezium Area (TTZ) has become more and more vulnerabl e to severe pollution
generating a serious threat to the qua lity of white marble stones of this  remarkable structure. This most
celebrated monuments viewed from  a distance, looms on the banks of  a stinking river almost always
enveloped in a haze of dust and smog from be lching smokestacks and exhaust fumes from the
surrounding industries.  The Committeefeels with a painful heart that this soot and fumes will eventually
turn the gleaming white building black. 
It is, therefore, obvious from the above, that in the recent year s the corrosive impact of the
polluted air on Taj Mahal ha s become a matter of grave concern.  Accordingly, the committee feels that
corrosive impact of pollutants and emissions from surroundings industrial conclave and running vehicles
within the vicinity of the monument is required to be addressed on extreme priority basis. 
(Para 82)
Action Taken by the Ministry 
For improvement in the environm ental quality in Taj Trapezium Zone(TTZ) and  particularly 
around Agra where the World famous  monument of Taj Mahal is lo cated, various steps have been
initiated,  which inter-alia include the following : 
 In pursuance of the Vardarajan Committee Re port on the Environmenta l Impact of Mathura 
refinery,  the thermal power plants  have been closed and Dieseliz ation of Railway yard was taken 
up;  
 TTZ was declared covering an ar ea of 10,400 sq. km. for prohibiti on of establishment/expansion 
of polluting industries;  
 In compliance with the order of the Hon’ble Supreme Court dated 10 th May, 1996, approximately 
450 brick kilns have been closed and the license d brick kilns are locate d beyond 20 kms. radial 
distance from Taj and other significant monuments;

 Natural gas, LPG and Propane is being used by industries in Agra;  
 The Petha industries, which are presently usi ng coal,  have been directed by District

Yojna is also proposed;  
 For reducing noise levels from  DG sets, an Action Plan is under preparation and all 
commercial/industrial DG sets above 15 kVA cap acity have been taken up for installation o f 
acoustic enclosures;  
 Project Planning and Development team of Gas Authority of I ndia (GAIL) have  studied and 
collected details for preparation of feasibility report on establishm ent of CNG facility in Agra.  
GAIL  has proposed setting  up of tw o main stations and five subsid iary stations. IOC has already

Comments 
            The Committee is happy to not e that various steps have been initiated for improving 
environmental quality in Taj Trapez ium Zone (TTZ). But what is more important is the final outcome
and success of these steps. For in stance, District Administration ha s directed the Petha industries to
switch over to use of Liquefied Petroleum Gas (LPG) at the earlie st. However, the Ministry has not
informed whether they have actuall y switched over to LPG. The Comm ittee is of the view that the
compliance of administrative order in right earnest is more important  than its issuance and therefore a
periodical review by the Ministry of its steps would act as a deterrent against the polluters. 
            The Committee has expressed its se rious concern over the hazardous effects of pollution on the
Taj Mahal in its previous Reports but only now, Gas Authority of India Limited (GAIL) has been asked
to prepare a CNG feasibility repor t. The Committee recommends th at the proposal prepared by GAIL
should be earnestly examined within a limited ti me-frame stipulated  by the Ministry and be made 
operational to avoid pollution engulfing the entire area. 
  
Recommendation 
            The Committee has been given to understand that Ministry of Pe troleum and Natural Gas has
launched a 10 point progra mme which is primarily aimed at re ducing air pollution for protecting this
national monuments from the cancerous effect of pollutants. The Committee, therefore recommends that
this 10 Point Programme should be implemente d on a war footing basis by a Joint understanding
between the Ministry of Petroleum and Natural Gas and Ministry of Environment  and Forests by setting
up of a basic task force for joint monitori sation for purposeful implementation of the
same.                                                                              (Para 83) 
Action Taken by the Ministry 
  
            All the issues raised in the 10- point progr amme had been considered by the Committee o f 
Experts under the chairmanship of Dr. R.A. Mashel kar, Director General, CSIR, constituted by the
Ministry of Petroleum and Natural Gas  in September, 2001, to recomme nd  an Auto Fuel policy for the
country along with a road map for its implementation. Th e final report of the Committee detailing an
integrated action plan was submitted on 25.9.02 and accepted by the G overnment on 3.10.2003. The 
Auto Fuel Policy gives a roadma p for achieving various vehicular emission norms over a period of time
and the corresponding fuel quality upgradation requirements.

            The 10 Point Programme inter alia pr ovides for supply of LPG to al l households within the Taj

outlets to running vehicles should  also be implemented within a set period of time.  Preferential
allocation of LPG to select industrial and commercial establishments within the TTZ area should also be
monitored without any further delay. The sale of high lead contained petr ol should altogether be

memory for long in the future.

7. The Committee, however, did not f eel satisfied with these arguments . It was clearly visible to the
Committee that even during the ye ars 1991-92 and 1992-93, the Department  had not been able to fully 
utilise the funds allocated for di fferent projects/scheme s. For example, duri ng the year 1991-92, the 
utilisation was Rs. 123.10 crores ( both Plan and Non-Plan) as agai nst the allocation of Rs. 137.25 
crores; and in 1992-93, it was Rs. 87.12 crores against Rs. 104.61 crores. In so far as the year 1993-94 is 
concerned, the same trend of under utilisation of al located funds appears to be continuing, though signs
of marginal improvement are there.  The reasons given by the Department  for the shortfalls in expendi-
ture in most of the cases are th at the saving was due to insufficie nt number of R&D projects of the
requisite quality (which the Committee found to be very surprising, cons idering the contrary situation in

promotional attitudes towards R&D in the Department) or release of less funds owing to delay in getting
approval of the competent authority (which again th e Committee found to be su rprising, considering the
powers available to scientific depa rtment). The Committee feels that in some of the cases there may be
genuine reasons for non-utilisation or under-utilisation of allocated f unds, but if this becomes recurring
feature in respect of use of budgeta ry allocations every year, it does not portray the Department in a
good li ght and will surel y result in some kind of hesitation to provide enhanced allocations in

28.  The Department of El ectronics has not only to make an anal ysis of the problems and define the

that the Committee has gathered in its discussion is more of efforts of an administrative nature, as would
be expected from a regular Governme nt department concerned with i ndustry rather than with science
and technology. There is need to cha nge this approach. The Department  also does not have a full time
Secretary in contrast to the earli er period when this area had a high powered Electronics Commission.

29. The Department has allotted the re sources available to it significantly on infrastructural facilities
rather than on R&D and links with  sectors powerful in electronics like DRDO , ISRO, Department o f
Atomic Energy appear to be wea k. The Performance Budget does not i ndicate in clear terms the actual
utilisation of allocated funds which would give a picture as to how the money has been spent and results
achieved. It gives just details of the project and does not highlight the actual physical targets laid out and
achieved. The Department of El ectronics aims at India becomi ng a significant global player in
electronics. The Committee does not see in the progr ammes of the Department  presented to it, any
integrated approach to achieve this. In the absence of such a vision  and major self-reliant strength in the 
country progress towards this is unlikely. The Commit tee would urge Government  to lay greater stress
on this area of opportunity.

REPORT
 
The Department of Scientific and Industrial Research (DSIR) is a part of the Ministry of Science and Technology with
 the mandate of indigenous technology promotion, development, utilization and transfer. Establishment of the Council of
 Scientific & Industrial Research in 1942 was a landmark event in the quest for using science and technology for national
