 Cyclotron becomes operational, production of radioisotopes and radio pharmaceutical (SPECT & PET) for advanced
 medical diagnostic purpose would become easily available therefore this programme may be accorded high priority for
 early completion. The Committee hopes that the enhanced allocation in 2005-06 will be fully utilized in installing the
 Medical Cyclotron Facility and other projects at VECC, Kolkata.
(Para 24)
8.         The Committee welcomes the idea and feels that this advanced fuel will reduce the cost of production of electricity
 through FBR and not only that by reducing the capital cost of production of electricity the plant life span will also increase
 by incorporating better safety features for these reactors.  Faster the breeding, quicker will be the rise in the FBR’s capacity.
 Other nuclear fuels for FBR and PFBR (Prototype Fast Breeder Reactor) like oxide, nitride and carbide fuels may now take
 the back seat for being used as fuels for FBR.
(Para 25.1)
9.         The choice of fuels for breeder reactors, the Committee feels, is a choice between doubling time versus the cost of
 production. The Committee, however, feels that oxide fuel with a ratio of 30% plutonium oxide and 70% uranium oxide is a
 well-proven fuel world over.  In India, however, mixed oxide fuel (MOX) could be used for prototype Fast Breeder Reactor
 (PFBR).
(Para 25.2)
10.       The Committee, on the other hand, feels that carbide fuel is very difficult to fabricate on a large scale as it is highly
 pyrophoric and is highly susceptible to oxidation and hydrolysis.  Moreover, reprocessing of spent carbide fuel is difficult
 as it is difficult to dissolve in nitric acid and leaves behind organic complexes.  Apart from this, the carbide fuel  has low
 burn up value in comparison to oxide fuel. The fuel ‘burn-up’ in a nuclear reactor refers to the amount of energy extracted
 from the fuel before it is discharged for storage or reprocessing.  Higher the burn-up, lesser will be the fuel cycle cost.
(Para 25.3)
11.       The Committee understands that cost of power production comes down with increased burn up value.  Also oxide
 fuel is easy to fabricate as it is not pyrophoric and hence needs no inert atmosphere during fabrication.  The Committee is,
 therefore, of the opinion that use of oxide fuel would be more vital for making a foray into fast breeder power plants.
(Para 25.4)

 The Ministry’s mandate also includes  environmental management to promote health considerations, to focus on poverty

 and wildlife and protection of environment.
The tasks assigned to the Ministry are achieved through environmental impact assessment, eco-regeneration,
 assistance to organizations implementing environmental and forestry programmes, promotion of environmental and
 forestry research, extension, education and training for capacity building, dissemination of environmental information,
 international co-operation, creation of environmental awareness among all sections of the country’s population.  These

 protection of environment.  Some of these are the Wildlife  (Protection) Act, 1972, the Water (Prevention and Control of
 Pollution) Act, 1974, the Forests (Conservation) Act, 1980, Air (Prevention and Control of Pollution) Act, 1981, the
 Environment (Protection) Act, 1986, National Forest Policy, 1988 the Public Liability Insurance Act, 1991, a National
 Conservation Strategy and Policy Statement on Environment and Development, 1992, a Policy Statement on Abatement
 of Pollution, 1992, the National Environment Tribunal Act, 1995, the National  Environment Appellate Authority Act,
 1997, the Prevention of Cruelty to Animals Act 2001. The Bio-Diversity Act 2002 has been passed and Rules 2004 have
 been finalized.

POLLUTION FROM COAL BASED METHANE AND CLEAN COAL TECHNOLOGIES
 
11.       Among the fossil fuels, coal has acquired the dubious distinction of being the dirtiest one.  Such an attribute is on
 account of severe environmental damage and acute pollution problems caused during mining operation, processing of the
 mineral till its end use and pollution arising out of coal based wastes.
 
12.       Land subsidence in underground mines, ugly scars of land in abandoned open cast mines, emission of fly ash
 during combustion of coal and huge quantities of ash generated from boilers of coal based power plants and industrial
 units are among the hosts of multi-facial problem associated with handling and subsequent productive use of coal. 
 Emission of carbon dioxide, an important component of green house gases (GHGs) and global warming is another
 emerging concern linked with the burning of coal.
 
13.       The Committee is of the opinion that although the coal constitutes a major source catering to the country’s energy
 needs, possibly with proper technologies and new initiatives for better management, it is possible to reduce the hazards of
 coal production which is being otherwise caused due to extraction of this mineral without proper planning.  Through
 scientific mining practices followed by land reclamation, beneficiation for ash reduction at source, improvement in
 combustion methods, use of efficient electrostatic precipitators, bag filters for trapping of fly ash emission and effective
 management of ash including its utilization for bricks, cement and such other purposes, many of the problems can be
 prevented and controlled.
 
14.       The Committee feels that Central Pollution Control Board should lay down the environmental guidelines for coal
 mining activities prescribing the use of beneficiated coal with lower ash content in power plants and lay down specific
 norms for emission and effluents from coal combustion system.
 
15.       In India out of the total land area of 3.29 million sq. km., only 0.45% area, that is, about16,000 sq. kms. is coal
 bearing  and out of this coal bearing area, active coal mining area is about 2500 sq. kms.  The Committee feels that
 maximum land degradation in coal mining is caused by open-cast mining.  Since the productivity is higher in open cast
 sector, this pace of growth cannot be sustained for long since the stripping ratios will increase the mining operations
 which may consequently run into  land access and other environmental problems.

16.       Air pollution in coalmines is chiefly due to the fugitive emission of particulate matter and gases including methane,
 sulphur dioxide and oxides of nitrogen.  The mining operations like drilling, blasting, movement of the heavy earth
 moving machinery on haul roads, collection, transportation and handling of coal, screening, sizing and segregation units
 are the major sources of such emissions. Underground mine fire is also a major source of air pollution in some of the
 coalfields.
 
17.       High levels of suspended particular matter increase respiratory diseases such as chronic bronchitis and asthma
 while gaseous emissions contribute towards global warming besides causing health hazards to the exposed population
 
18.       Methane emission from coal mining depends on the mining methods, depth of coal mine, coal quality and
 entrapped gas content in coal seams.  The proper management of methane emission should be one of the important factors
 which should be handled by the miners and mining authorities to reduce its emission into the atmosphere.
 
19.       The major source of water pollution in the coal mines is the carry over of the suspended solids in the drainage
 system of the mine sump water and storm drainage and in some of the coal mines acidic water is also found in the
 underground aquifers.  In addition, waste water from coal preparation plant and mine water are other source of water
 pollution which requires immediate control.
 
20.       The main sources of noise pollution, are blasting, movement of heavy earth moving machine and drilling and coal
 handling plants and the effective monitoring of all these issues are necessary for reducing noise pollution.
 
21.       Subsidence of surface takes place due to extraction of coal by underground mining.  Subsidence is exhibited by
 cracks on surface and lowering of land in the worked out areas compared to surroundings.  The surface is rehabilitated by
 dozing and sealing  of cracks followed by plantation of trees.  The subsided areas with medium sized depressions are ideal
 for developing water pools and sustain green vegetation and also to meet the water needs of local people.  The Committee,
 therefore, recommends that the mined areas, which are backfilled, should be rehabilitated for development of vegetation. 
 In the quarried areas water reservoir is developed for water harvesting.  The big voids created by open-pit mining can
 cause land degradation which, the Committee feels, could be gainfully utilized to serve water reservoirs which will
 provide moisture for vegetation in the surrounding areas and the water could be used for domestic supply after necessary
 treatment.
 
22.       It is understood that major coal projects are required to obtain Environmental Clearance from the Government. 
 Mitigative/control measures are identified to reduce the adverse impacts on environment.  It helps to integrate
 environmental considerations into mining and related operations right from the planning stage.  For this purpose, the
 project proponent needs to prepare an Environmental Impact Assessment Report and an Environmental Management
 Plan.
 
23.       The Committee is of the opinion that for abatement of the pollution problems associated with the coal mines, the
 Central Pollution Control Board needs to develop National Environmental Standards and Code of practice for coal mines
 which should be given due consideration by the Ministry of Environment & Forests and given a legal framework.
 
24.       The Committee is of the opinion that supply of  high ash laden coal to power plants not only poses environmental
 problems but also causes poor plant performance and high cost for ash disposal. The Committee, therefore, strongly
 recommends that Ministry of Environment and Forests should evolve a mechanism for suggesting measures for improving
 the quality of coal supplied to the power plants.
a)         Particularly power plants located beyond 1000 kms. from pit head; and
b)         Power plants located in critically polluted areas, Urban sectors and in ecologically sensitive zones.

26.       The Committee has been given to understand by Regbional Research Laboratory that most widely studied
 microorganism for removal of pyritic sulfur from coal is Thiobacillus ferrooxidans, a Gram-negative, acidophilic,

OPTIMAL HYDRO-CARBON ENERGY MANAGEMENT THROUGH CLEAN DEVELOPMENT
 MECHANISM (CDM)
 
27.       In the wake of implementation of Kyoto Protocol in February, 2005 stabilization of greenhouse gas concentrations
 in the atmosphere at a level that would prevent dangerous anthropogenic interference with the climate system appears to
 be one of the challenging subjects before the country in the current global environment scenario.  The Committee would,
 therefore, like to invite the attention of the Ministry of Environment and Forests in conjunction with the oil sector
 that investment in low emissions technologies is the demanding need of the hour and the problem should be
 addressed in such a fashion that long term national emissions reduction should be made one of the priority areas.
 
28.       In order to give an effective implementation of the above proposal of the Committee, the following model may be
 considered by the Ministry of Environment & Forests:
·
        The solubility of additional carbon dioxide in the ocean surface water decreases with rising concentrations. 
 Thus, the relative oceanic uptake of carbon dioxide is reduced at higher concentrations.
·        The land vegetations may serve as an additional medium term sink for anthropogenic carbon emissions.
·        The radio-active greenhouse forcing grows only logarithmically with increasing carbon dioxide and Green
 House Gases (GHG) emissions.
 
29.       The environment friendly performance objectives and mechanisms for tracking progress in achieving the prime
 objective of the aforesaid model for the growth of the oil industry on the one hand and socio-economic sustainability on
 the other, the implementation of socio-environmental policies involving oil companies and the Ministry of Environment &
 Forest requires combination of technological advances and innovative approaches.
 
30.       The Committee is of the opinion that for addressing the key issues pertaining to the transition of a carbon based
 economy to a hydrogen economy, the Ministry of Environment and Forests needs to promote the following:
§
         Promote more rapid dissemination and use of efficient, existing commercial technology in strategic and
 environmentally sensitive areas of the country.
§         Encourage the development and use of innovative, currently non-commercial technologies.
§         Enhance the ability of all oil sector companies to achieve and utilize advanced and efficient technologies, and
§         Improve scientific understanding by addressing well-known uncertainties, in the adoption and implementation of
 efficient technologies.
 
BOTANICAL SURVEY OF INDIA: METHODS OF CONDUCTING SURVEY AND
 STRUCTURE OF SURVEY REPORT
 
31.       The Committee has been intimated by the Botanical Survey of India, Dehradun, that the main objective of
 conducting botanical surveys is to collect plant samples from different regions/ecosystem for documentation of plant
 diversity of these regions/ecosystems . The surveys are conducted in different seasons of a calendar year matching the
 flowering and fruiting of herbs, shrubs and trees of the region.  In certain specialised ecosystems, like cold deserts in the
 Himalayas, where the growing season is limited to 2-3 months in a calendar year, the survey is conducted during June-
September only.  In case of algae, fungi and pteridophytes (fern and fern allies), the surveys are conducted during
 monsoons, whereas for bryophytes and lichens, post monsoon season is ideal.  For documentation of plant diversity, BSI
 adopts random sampling method following linear transacts in different directions.  Along with the collection of samples,
 the information on life form of the species (herbs, shrub, tree, liana, climber, etc.), locality, altitude of the collection site,
 habitat (terrestrial epiphytic, epiphyllous, saprophyte, parasite,  aquatic etc.) local name uses, if any, abundance and such
 features which will not remain in herbarium specimens  as colour of the flower/leaf, bark, etc., fragrant, height/girth and

 FOREST CONSERVATION, DEVELOPMENT & REGENERATION
35.       This is an on-going programme to check indiscriminate deforestation and diversion of forestland for non-forest
 use.  For ensuring effective forest protection many schemes have been identified. One such scheme is the strengthening of
 forest protection force. The Ministry is of the view that adequate protection mechanisms have to be exercised on grazing
 of cattle on forestland and removal of fuelwood from forests. People have to be provided with adequate fuels to remove
 their dependence on forests for fuelwood.
 
36.       Under Forest Conservation, Development  & Regeneration Programme, Integrated Forests Protection Scheme
 (IFPS) has been formulated for implementation during the 10
th Five Year Plan by merger of the two schemes namely
 ‘Forest Fire Control and Management and ‘Bridging of Infrastructure Gaps in the forestry sector in the North Eastern
 Region and Sikkim’ which were being implemented during the 9 th Plan period. The main components under the scheme
 are:-
(a)    Forest Fire Control and Mangement – Under this component, assistance is provided for taking preventive and
 control measures for forest fires, assistance to Joint Forest Management Committees, monitoring and
 evaluation etc.
(b)   Infrastructure Development for Forest protection – The main activities being assisted under this component are
 Survey and Demarcation, Working Plan preparation, Enumeration, forest road, vehicles arms ammunitions
 wireless sets etc.
 
37.       During the year 2002-03 the Scheme was operated as 100% Centrally Sponsored Scheme. But funding pattern was
 changed to sharing basis (75.25) during the year 2003-04 in respect of all the States/UTs.  But North Eastern States
 expressed their inability to provide for 25% of the State’s share due to poor resource position.  Therefore, the matter was
 taken up and the funding pattern for the North Eastern Region including Sikkim and other special category States was
 modified to (90:10) sharing basis during the year 2004-05.  It continued to be (75:25) in respect of other States/UTs.
 
38.       The Committee was informed by the Secretary, Ministry of Environment and Forests during the course of meeting
 that Integrated Forests Protection Scheme (IFPS) is the only scheme of the Ministry under which assistance is being
 provided for protection of the existing forests, however in the current financial year i.e. 2005-06 the Planning Commission
 has decided to transfer this Centrally Sponsored Scheme, to the States. Therefore, this scheme that has a proposed outlay
 of Rs.445 crores out of Rs.800 crores outlay for Tenth Planstands excluded from Ministry’s Annual Plan for 2005-2006.

 facilitating focused, concerted management of ecotypical reserves in various states, constituted on a ‘core-buffer’ strategy
 through funding the technical support, including site-specific inputs to elicit local community support for conservation.
 Initially, the project was launched in nine tiger reserves, covering an area of 16,339 sq. km. which has now increased to
 28 tiger reserves, ecompassing 37761 sq. km. of tiger habitat distributed in 17 States.
 
45.       The Committee expressed its serious concern over the news of disappearance of Tigers from the Sariska Tiger
 Reserve and requested the Ministry to furnish a status note on the poaching and disappearance of Tigers. In response, the
 Ministry has informed the Committee that there has been considerable media coverage recently speculating a country
 level decline in tiger population in the wake of claims that tigers have not been spotted in recent months in the Sariska
 Tiger Reserve of Rajasthan.  Based on field visits by senior officials of the Ministry of Environment & Forests, the
 Rajasthan State was asked to carry out an intensive search for tigers in and around Sariska, apart from ensuring
 compliance of directives issued from Project Tiger for protection, regulation of tourist visitation inside the reserves and
 systemic  improvement.  Though no direct sighting of tigers or pug marks were seen during the search, the State has
 reported collection of some indirect evidence like droppings.  The State has been advised to send the collected samples to
 the Wildlife Institute of India for species identification.  The Wildlife Institute of India has also been directed to carry out
 a detailed ecological study in the Sariska Tiger Reserve for an appraisal of the status of tiger, prey animals, the

46.       The Ministry also expressed some concerns and observations based on the field visit, which are as follows:-
(a)        Non-compliance of Government of India Guidelines/Directives.
            Despite guidelines and repeated requests from the Ministry of Environment & Forests, there appears to be a general
 lack of will on the part of the State for compliance, which would have otherwise ensured the desired degree of protection
 in the Sariska Tiger Reserve.  From the middle of June, 2004 to mid September 2004 there was no Deputy Director
 functioning in Sariska, since the incumbent proceeded on leave.  The DCF level officer (Deputy Director) is the cutting
 edge, as far as field implementation of Project Tiger is concerned.  Therefore, this absence has also contributed to the
 collapse of the day-to-day administration and protection within the reserve.  Further, the CF & Field Director of Sariska
 also proceeded on leave in September and a junior officer of the level of ACF was made responsible for management of
 the reserve during the said period.  The State Government could have entrusted this task to a trained senior officer.
(b)        Disturbance caused to the Reserve by heavy vehicular traffic and the human influx:
            There is a State Highway (No.29) passing through the Sariska Tiger Reserve which links Sariska to Dausa.  The
 vehicular traffic on this road during day time has gone up considerably, especially during the free entry days earmarked
 for Hanuman (PANDU POL) temple visit twice a week (every Tuesday and Saturday).  The vehicular traffic during the
 free entry days has increased from 14706 in 2002 to 27982 (April, 2004 – January, 2005).  Likewise, the pilgrim visitation
 inside the reserve has also gone up from 138342 to 177580 during the period.  The influx of pilgrims on annual meal day
 in the month of ‘Sawan goes considerably high toughing as high as 30000 on a single day.  This is the major cause of
 disturbance to wild animals and no initiatives have been taken to regulate this traffic of vehicles as well as human beings,
 despite clear directives from the Ministry of Environment & Forests for containing the visitation within the carrying
 capacity.  The State highway 13 (Alwar-Jaipur), carrying a very large traffic of goods vehicles, was reported to have been
 diverted to the new road built with a central assistance of Rs.3.5 crores to avoid road hits of wild animals on the old route
 which passes through the core of the Reserve.  However this still remains to be implemented.
(c)        Heavy human and cattle population
            As many as 196 villages are situated in and around the Sariska Tiger Reserve with a cattle population of 275414. 
 Further, 28 villages are located within the Tiger Reserve itself with 11 villages in the core of the Reserve. The State has
 hardly taken any initiative for relocating these villages despite the fact the funding support for such initiatives are
 provided under the Project Tiger.  It is noteworthy that the people who were relocated earlier in 1976 from the Kraska
 village have returned to their original settlement area.  Likewise, some families of another earlier relocation (village
 ‘Karnakavas’) have also returned to the fringe area of the Reserve.  No effort seems to have been made by the State to
 redress the situation.
 
47.       The Ministry submitted that forests and wildlife being state subjects, the field implementation of the project,
 protection and management in the designated reserves is done by the project States, which also provide the matching grant
 to recurring items of expenditure, field staff/officers, and their salaries.  The Project Tiger Directorate of the Ministry of
 Environment & Forests is mandated with the task of providing technical guidance, funding support, overall coordination,
 supervision, monitoring and evaluation of the project, apart from facilitating the states to carry out the All India
 Estimation of tigers periodically.

PROJECT ELEPHANT
51.       Project Elephant was launched in February, 1992 to assist States having free ranging populations of wild elephants
 to ensure long term survival of identified viable population of elephants in their natural habitat.  The Project is being
 implemented in 13 States, viz Andhra Pradesh, Arunachal Pradesh, Assam, Jharkhand, Karnataka, Kerala, Meghalaya,
 Nagaland, Orissa, Tamilnadu, Uttaranchal, Utter Pradesh and West Bengal.  States are provided financial as well as
 technical assistance in achieving the objectives of the Project.  Help is also provided to other States with small population
 of elephants for the purpose of census, training of field staff and mitigation of human elephant conflict.
            The main activities of the project are as follows :-
i)
                    Strengthening of measures for protection of wild elephants from poachers.
ii)                   Development of scientific and planned management for conservation of elephant habitats and viable
 population of wild elephants in India.
iii)                 Ecological restoration of existing natural habitats and migratory routes of elephants of elephants.
iv)                 Promotion of measures for mitigation of human – elephant conflict in problem areas and moderating pressures
 of human and live stock on crucial elephant habitats.
v)                  Eco-development and veterinary care.
vi)                 Research on issues relating to elephant conversation.
vii)               Public education and awareness programme and capacity building  of field staff, mahouts and veterinarians.
 
52.       The Committee feels that Project Elephant is a major project of the Ministry but getting less importance. The tusk
 is as precious as tiger skin and not immune from Poachers. Therefore, the Committee recommends that Elephants should
 also be protected from the poaching and effective strategy should be evolved for their preservation. In view of decline in
 Tiger population in Sariska, the Committee suggests the Ministry to undertake an evaluation of Elephant population and
 take corrective measures accordingly.
 
53.       The Committee recommends that sufficient allocation must be provided to various States for habitat management
 mitigation of human-elephant conflict, payment of ex-gratia relief for loss of human life and crops caused by wild
 elephants, strengthening of anti-poaching measures, capacity building of the field staff, registration of domesticated
 elephant using microchips etc.
 
54.       The Committee recommends that endangered species need to be preserved while the population of other animals
 should be sustainably managed.  The Ministry should generate data and information on maintaining a sustainable
 population of each animal for their scientific management.  Research initiatives in the field of sustainable use of wildlife
 products are needed.  The Ministry should cover not only wildlife research and training but also the socio-economic
 aspects of wildlife conservation.
 
55.       While the Committee is concerned about the protection of wildlife in the Protected Areas, it feels that wildlife
 should also be protected outside the Protected Areas and sufficient allocation should be made for the purpose.

 adjoining lands through systematic planning and implementation, in a cost effective manner. The Ministry should also

 population and expansion of townships and the success of the scheme depend on continuous efforts to be made by all
 these agencies.  The present approved cost of NRCP is Rs. 4688 crores out of which GOI’s share is Rs.3994 crores  Of
 this Rs.928 crores has already been spent during IXth Plan.  This leaves a balance of Rs.3066 crores which is required to
 clean the rivers as per the present approvals under NRCP against an outlay of Rs.1417 crores for X Plan.  Moreover, the
 present approved cost of projects does not cover the full pollution load of even major rivers like Ganga, Yamuna, Gomti
 etc.  Thus in order to achieve the target of cleaning of major rivers by 2007, huge amount of funds are required and given
 the position that we are in the midst of the Plan, it is most unlikely that the target would be achieved.  So we may have to
 extend this target to XIth Plan. 
 
76.       Regarding strengthening the process of approval of projects and monitoring and evaluation mechanism in the
 Ministry, the Committee was informed that the projects of River Action Plans were initially considered by the Govt. on
 the basis of pre-feasibility report (PFR) estimates prepared by the State Govts.  After the project was approved in
 principle, detailed project reports (DPR) with firmed up cost estimates for various sub-components were prepared by the
 State Govts./Project proponents.  These DPRs were appraised and approved by the Ministry following which
 Administrative Approval and Expenditure Sanctions were issued.  On the basis of these sanctions, the State
 Govvernments/implementing agencies awarded contracts according to their own policy and rules.
 
77.       As projects sanctioned on the basis of Pre-Feasibility Reports submitted by State Governments were not based on
 firm cost estimates, it was seen that often there was a wide variation in costs when detailed project reports were prepared
 resulting in to large savings or cost escalations leading to delay in implementation of projects.  This delayed release of
 funds by MoEF in a number of cases.  It was, therefore, decided that in future only projects based on firm cost estimates
 in DPRs would be considered for approval. 
 
78.       The Ministry has submitted that it is most unlikely to achieve the target of cleaning of major rivers by 2007 and it
 may extend the target to XI Plan.   On this submission of the Ministry, the Committee express its serious concern on the
 tardy pace of execution of river cleaning project and recommends that all causative factors for the slow progress of the
 project be identified and sorted out expeditiously and all out efforts be made to accelerate the momentum required to
 achieve the stipulated targets within their scheduled time limit and cost estimates.
 
NATIONAL LAKE CONSERVATION PLAN
79.       The National Lake Conservation Plan (NLCP) was initiated in June, 2001 with approval of 3 lakes,  namely, Powai
 (Maharashtra), Ooty & Kodaikanal (Tamil Nadu). Initially the scheme was approved as 100% Centrally Sponsored
 Scheme(CSS). However,   w.e.f. 2002, the funding pattern was changed to 70:30 cost sharing between Central and State
 Governments.
 
80.       The objective of the scheme is to restore and conserve the polluted and degraded urban lakes of the country.  To
 begin with, NLCP proposed to  cover urban lakes of tourist importance especially those not covered under the wetland
 programme of the Ministry.  The scope of work under NLCP has, however, been expanded during the Xth Plan to include
 rural water bodies.
The activities covered under NLCP include the following:-
i)
                    Prevention of pollution from point sources by intercepting, diverting and treating the pollution loads
 entering the lake.
ii)                   In situ measures of lake cleaning such as Desilting, Deweeding, Bioremediation, constructed wetland
 approach etc. depending upon the site conditions.
iii)                 Catchment area treatment and lake beautification which may include bunding fencing, creation of
 facilities and public recreation and entertainment(children park, boating etc.)and public area.
iv)                 Public awareness and public participation.

98.       The Committee is of the view that 90% of the country’s medicinal plants occur in forest habitats.  The most
 important strategy for conserving the medicinal plant gene pools is to establish a nation wide network of forest gene banks
 (average size 200-500 ha in tropical forest and 50-100 ha in high altitude forest) across the different forest types and
 altitudinal range in all bio-geographic regions of the country.  In view thereof, the Committee recommends that Ministry
 should urgently initiate programmes or in-situ conservation of genetic diversity. The Committee also feels that
 conservation of genetic diversity and documenting the entire traditional medicinal plants should be undertaken in such a
 manner so as to plan for development of traditional medicinal plants.  Besides, the Ministry, in collaboration with CSIR,
 DST, DBT and Ministry of Rural Development, should support community owned enterprises based on medicinal plants. 
 
TROPICAL BOTANIC GARDEN AND RESEARCH INSTITUTE, (TBGRI), THIRUVANTHAPURAM
 
99.       Tropical Botanic Garden and Research Institute (TBGRI) with its mandate for conservation and sustainable
 utilization of tropical plant diversity is recognized as a National Centre of Excellence in ex –situ conservation of tropical
 plants.  TBGRI also functions as the National Gene Bank for medicinal and aromatic plants of peninsular India and has a
 Bioinformatics Distributed Information Centre.
 
100.     TBGRI is the only organization in India, which maintains a 300 acre conservatory garden for the wild tropical plant
 genetic resources of India, besides a well integrated multidisciplinary R&D system dealing with conservation,
 management and sustainable utilization of tropical plant resources.  The Institute is ideally located at the foothills of the
 Western Ghats.  The institute has 121 acres of forest land with hills and hillocks, portions of evergreen, decidous, marshy
 and riverine vegetation in addition to grass lands and rocky areas.  All of them to large extent provide different
 microclimatic conditions for different species.  The Institute also have a well-organized Arboretum, Palmetum,
 Bambusetum, Orchidarium, Medicinal plant garden and Field Gene Bank of wild plant collections to which new additions
 are being carried out from the topical areas of the country.  The Institute has about 20 major projects at operational stage
 on survey and inventory conservation and sustainable utilization of plant genetic resources in India.  TBGRI is accredited
 to UNCED and enjoys the membership of Botanic Gardens Conservation International.  The Institute is the coordination
 and National Database Center for All India Coordinated Research Project on Ethnobiology sponsored by the Ministry of
 Environment and Forests, Government of India.  TBGRI also harbours a well-established herbarium of vascular plants
 and fungi and a group of well-trained taxonomists.
 
101.     Keeping in view above the facts, the Committee considers it as an institute of national importance and, therefore,
 recommends that the TBGRI should be elevated to a national institute under the administrative control of Ministry of
 Environment & Forests.

 the country should be left with the junior officers.
 
(Para 50)
29.       The Committee feels that Project Elephant is a major project of the Ministry but getting less importance. The tusk
 is as precious as tiger skin and not immune from Poachers. Therefore, the Committee recommends that Elephants should
 also be protected from the poaching and effective strategy should be evolved for their preservation. In view of decline in
 Tiger population in Sariska, the Committee suggests the Ministry to undertake an evaluation of Elephant population and
 take corrective measures accordingly.
(Para 52)
30.       The Committee recommends that sufficient allocation must be provided to various States for habitat management
 mitigation of human-elephant conflict, payment of ex-gratia relief for loss of human life and crops caused by wild
 elephants, strengthening of anti-poaching measures, capacity building of the field staff, registration of domesticated
 elephant using microchips etc.
(Para 53)
31.       The Committee recommends that endangered species need to be preserved while the population of other animals
 should be sustainably managed.  The Ministry should generate data and information on maintaining a sustainable
 population of each animal for their scientific management.  Research initiatives in the field of sustainable use of wildlife
 products are needed.  The Ministry should cover not only wildlife research and training but also the socio-economic
 aspects of wildlife conservation.
(Para 54)
32.       While the Committee is concerned about the protection of wildlife in the Protected Areas, it feels that wildlife

 should also be protected outside the Protected Areas and sufficient allocation should be made for the purpose.
(Para 55)
33.       The Committee is of the opinion that the destruction and depletion of forests will not only lead to loss of our
 vegetation but will also result in widespread deterioration of environment with fatal consequences to the very existence of
 all forms of life. Therefore, the Ministry should evolve mechanisms for ecological restoration of degraded forest areas and
 adjoining lands through systematic planning and implementation, in a cost effective manner. The Ministry should also
 restore fuelwood, fodder, timber and other forest produce on the degraded forest and adjoining lands in order to meet the
 demands for these items and local population including tribals should be allowed to share its products without 
 compromising the preservation of our national forests.  In addition, the Ministry should also create general awareness and
 help foster a people’s  movement for promoting afforestation and eco-development with the assistance of voluntary
 agencies, non-governmental organizations, Panchayati Raj Institutions and others and promote participatory and
 sustainable management of degraded forest areas and adjoining lands.
(Para 59)
34.       The Committee is also of the view that the Ministry should formulate an effective strategy to consider all activities,
 current and potential,that can influence forests and related social, economic, and environmental outcomes.  More focussed
 interventions are required that address issues relating to opportunity, empowerment, and livelihood security of the poor
 people who depend on forests in different ways.  A broader livelihood approach, covering productive capacity,
 institutional and legal structures, market access and tenure must be adopted that puts forests into the broader context of
 rural development.  The focus should be on improving governance (especially correcting major distortions in incentives
 and markets that are reducing the value of the forest resource), and the development of efficient markets and encouraging
 competitive private sector participation in the sector.  More focused interventions are required for maintaining natural
 forests for eco-system protection and sustaining the global and local forest values.
(Para 60)
35.       The Committee recommends that the Ministry should have taken the initiative for strengthening Environment
 Education in the formal educational curriculum and for this purpose, it should vigorously interact with the University
 Grants Commission (UGC), the National Council for Educational Research and Training (NCERT), the Ministry of
 Human Resource Development, All India Council for Technical Education (AICTE) and the State Education Department
 to ensure integration of environmental concept into the curriculum. Moreover, talented persons should be encouraged with
 remunerative schemes and attractive pay scales to do research on environment related issues.
(Para 63)
36.       The Committee also recommends that to promote and awareness among the students, the scientists, planners,
 policy makers, etc., and also for exchange of information and knowledge on different aspects of ocean science and
 technology, the Ministry should sponsor, organize and conduct seminars/workshops/symposia, etc.  These measures will
 help the Ministry in building up a skilled human resource base in environmental science, besides augmenting existing
 infrastructure facilities.  
(Para 64)
37.       The Committee recommends that National Mangrooves Afforestation Programme should be designed so that new
 research projects on the priority areas of mangrove and coral reef conservation for supplementing Management Action
 Plan of strategically identified mangrove areas is accorded importance.
(Para 70.1)
 
38.       The Ministry has submitted that it is most unlikely to achieve the target of cleaning of major rivers by 2007 and it
 may extend the target to XI Plan.   On this submission of the Ministry, the Committee express its serious concern on the
 tardy pace of execution of river cleaning project and recommends that all causative factors for the slow progress of the
 project be identified and sorted out expeditiously and all out efforts be made to accelerate the momentum required to
 achieve the stipulated targets within their scheduled time limit and cost estimates.
(Para 78)
39.       The Committee feels that lakes are critical in sustaining the environmental health of our country.  Acting as a huge
 reservoir, they not only provide water but also recharge and replenish the ground water and prevent floods.  Besides, their
 importance from the point of view of beauty, and aesthetics are well acclaimed. But the Committee is not satisfied with
 the lackadaisical approach of the Ministry in undertaking the lake conservation schemes.  They are moving without any
 specific targets and objectives.  The Committee is anguished to note that even after repeated recommendations of the
 Committee, the Ministry has not come out with any specific targets to be achieved during a particular period.  The
 Committee expresses its serious concern and recommends that the Government should formulate short-term and long-
term plans on lake conservation with specific targets and should proceed further in that direction as per those targets. 
(Para 84)

40.       The Committee made an on-the-spot study visit on 3 rd February 2005 to have a first-hand assessment of the
 Pollution caused by M/s Oswal Chemicals & Fertilizers Ltd., Paradeep.  During it’s study-visit, the Committee was
 apprised by the management of M/s Oswal Chemicals & Fertilizers Ltd., Paradeep that with such a huge operation where
 production of 6840 TPD of di-ammonium phosphate was involved it wasn’t possible to close the operations of the Plant
 as ordered by Orissa State Pollution Control Board (OSPCB). Now the Central Pollution Control Board, New Delhi after
 examining all aspects related to Pollution, has referred the matter to OSPCB for their views, and the opinion of OSPCB
 are still awaited. The Committee therefore, recommends that as the industry was asked to carry out process, safety and
 environmental audits of the plant through a reputed firm, therefore it should  be given adequate opportunity to carry out
 these procedures and thereafter adopt suggestions made by the Environmental audit. To enable the process, safety &
 environmental audits, Engineers India Limited, New Delhi requires the Plant to run in a steady state of operation
 therefore, the Committee is of the view that the plant should be in a steady state of operation so that the process by
 Engineers India Limited, New Delhi is completed and corrective measures  suggested in right earnest.
(Para 94)
41.       The Committee also notes that as huge production of fertilizer by the Plant is involved, mere closure of operations
 would send wrong signals to the business community besides diminishing the benefits to a larger section of population
 primarily the farmers. However, every effort must be made to impress upon the Industry to comply environmental norms
 for a safe and smooth functioning of the Plant.
(Para 95)
42.       The Committee also expresses its dismay that the issue has now been pending quite long and recommends that the
 same may be sorted out without further delay.
(Para 96)
43.       The Committee is of the view that 90% of the country’s medicinal plants occur in forest habitats.  The most
 important strategy for conserving the medicinal plant gene pools is to establish a nation wide network of forest gene banks
 (average size 200-500 ha in tropical forest and 50-100 ha in high altitude forest) across the different forest types and
 altitudinal range in all bio-geographic regions of the country.  In view thereof, the Committee recommends that Ministry
 should urgently initiate programmes or in-situ conservation of genetic diversity. The Committee also feels that
 conservation of genetic diversity and documenting the entire traditional medicinal plants should be undertaken in such a
 manner so as to plan for development of traditional medicinal plants.  Besides, the Ministry, in collaboration with CSIR,
 DST, DBT and Ministry of Rural Development, should support community owned enterprises based on medicinal plants. 
 (Para 98)
44.       TBGRI is the only organization in India, which maintains a 300 acre conservatory garden for the wild tropical plant
 genetic resources of India, besides a well integrated multidisciplinary R&D system dealing with conservation,
 management and sustainable utilization of tropical plant resources.  The Institute is ideally located at the foothills of the
 Western Ghats.  The institute has 121 acres of forest land with hills and hillocks, portions of evergreen, decidous, marshy
 and riverine vegetation in addition to grass lands and rocky areas.  All of them to large extent provide different
 microclimatic conditions for different species.  The Institute also have a well-organized Arboretum, Palmetum,
 Bambusetum, Orchidarium, Medicinal plant garden and Field Gene Bank of wild plant collections to which new additions
 are being carried out from the topical areas of the country.  The Institute has about 20 major projects at operational stage
 on survey and inventory conservation and sustainable utilization of plant genetic resources in India.  TBGRI is accredited
 to UNCED and enjoys the membership of Botanic Gardens Conservation International.  The Institute is the coordination
 and National Database Center for All India Coordinated Research Project on Ethnobiology sponsored by the Ministry of
 Environment and Forests, Government of India.  TBGRI also harbours a well-established herbarium of vascular plants
 and fungi and a group of well-trained taxonomists.
(Para 100)
45.       Keeping in view above the facts, the Committee considers it as an institute of national importance and, therefore,
 recommends that the TBGRI should be elevated to a national institute under the administrative control of Ministry of
 Environment & Forests.
(Para 101)

POST-TSUNAMI ASSESSMENT OF CORAL HEALTH IN ANDAMAN WATERS AND   INDIAN OCEAN
Recommendation
The Committee has been given to understand that massive influx of seawater borne by Tsunami on 26/12/2004
 severely affected several section of coral population in Andaman & Nicobar and in certain strategic areas of Indian Ocean. 
 The Committee has been further given to understand that four research vessels, namely, Sagar Purvi, Sagar Paschimi, Sagar
 Sampada and Sagar Kanya of the Department of Ocean Development were commissioned in these waters to undertake,
 interalia, a detailed assessment of destruction inflicted by Tsunami on the coral health of these regions.
The Committee, however, finds that assessment with regard to the impact of Tsunami on coral reefs in Andaman &
 Nicobar Islands is somewhat contradictory.  As per the Annual Report of the Department for 2004-05, coral reefs have been
 severely affected by Tsunami whereas Secretary of the Departmentin his presentation before theCommittee on the 1
st April,
 2005, maintained that by and large coral reefs were unaffected.  The Committee, therefore, feels that a detailed physical
 verification of coral health is necessary to assess accurately the status of their health in post-Tsunami scenario.  The
 Committee would like to have a factual note in this regard, inter-alia, giving the future contingency plan in case of such
 natural eventuality.
(Para 10)
Action Taken by the Department
            The activities relating to the assessment of the damages caused to the coral reefs in Andaman and Nicobar islands
 including undertaking coral reef habitat restoration projects etc. fall within the purview of the Ministry of Environment and
 Forests (MoEF).  The Department of Ocean Development (DOD), under the Integrated Coastal and Marine Area
 Management Programme, has taken up only mapping of coral reefs using GIS, mainly to demonstrate the use of the GIS

 technique in coral reef mapping and monitoring in Andaman & Nicobar and Lakshadweep Islands.
Point raised by the Committee
What are the procedure and benefits of Coral reef mapping and monitoring in    A&N Islands and Lakshadweep
 under the Integrated Coastal and Marine Area Management (ICMAM)? What are the actual benefits derived therefrom?
Clarification by the Department
The Department of Ocean Development, under the ICMAM Programme, has proposed to demonstrate the use of GIS
 in mapping of coral reefs in Andaman and Nicobar Islands and Lakshdweep.  The procedures for coral reef mapping and
 monitoring include qualitative and quantitative analysis of coral reefs using Line Intersect Methods (LIT) with the help of
 SCUBA diving equipment.  During the survey, accurate position of investigating area is recorded using the sophisticated
 GPS equipment namely Arc Pad.  The data collected is brought into GIS Environment with the help of Software called Arc
 Info and Arc View.  The plotted data with respect to coordinate indicates the status of the corals at the time of
 Investigation.  This technique is useful in monitoring the health of the corals in the subsequent years by the local
 authorities.  The ICMAM Directorate has already developed this technique for Andaman and Nicobar Administration and
 Lakshadweep Administration through training programmes so as to facilitate them for continuously monitoring the health of
 the corals.
Comments
            The Committee notes the reply.
Recommendation
The Committee apprehends that certain branching corals like Acropara Cytherea also known as stag horn corals
 which are common in Andaman waters might have been affected severely by the Tsunami onslaughts.
The Committee is, however, of the opinion that unless comprehensive planning is made, neither proper and deep
 assessment of the heart of coral in these areas could be made nor any critical measures could be designed to remedy the
 health of these corals in the affected areas.  The Committee, therefore, understands that in order to have a very successful
 picture of the entire assessment scenario, the following measures need to be considered by the Department before
 undertaking major audit of coral health in these areas:
i)
                    Norms of audit through symbiotic studies of coral health will have to be mapped.
ii)                   New insights into the role of cell suicide and apoptosis in bleaching of corals should also have to be
 developed.
iii)                 A detailed mapping of coral stress tolerance is necessary to be assessed and mapped.
iv)                 The Behavior of coral reef fish is needed to be assessed on a comparative pilot-scale basis in coral areas
 which are severely affected by Tsunami and areas which are less affected or are not affected at all by the
 Tsunami onslaught.
v)                  Since reef bleaching and mortaity are highly co-related, the study of coral bleaching in detail is also
 necessary since this could be linked to global climate change specially elevated sea water temperature and
 high solar irradiance.                                                                                                      (Para 11)
Action Taken by the Department
            The Department of Ocean Development (DOD) under the Integrated Coastal and Marine Area Management
 Programme has taken up only mapping of coral reefs using GIS, mainly to demonstrate the use of the GIS technique in
 coral reef mapping and monitoring in Andaman & Nicobar and Lakshadweep islands.  However, the subject of coral reefs
 pertains to Ministry of Environment and Forests (MoEF) and all the recommendations made by the Committee are pertinent

 to the activities that are being undertaken by MoEF at present.
Recommendation
The Committee feels that successful restoration and management of coral health require a more realistic and
 historically informed understanding of the ecology of near-pristine condition of coral reefs that can only be obtained by a
 combination of retrospective analyses, modeling and intensive studies of eco-systemstructure andfunction of the very few
 isolated reefs that have escaped intensive exploitation by Tsunami onslaughts.  The Committee understands that studies
 based on an index known as DI, i.e., comparative Deterioration Index of community for corals will have to be undertaken
 for deriving a comparative picture of analysis of the health deterioration of different corals groups in these regions.  The DI
 values can show the likelihood of some of the corals getting rehabilitated early and some corals more at a later stage which
 is proportional to the destructive index of each coral communities following the Tsunami onslaughts.  The training should
 be given to surveyors  for fast yielding of elaborate data based upon deterioration index of these coralcommunities so that
 relatively accurate picture could be framed for the subsequent restoration.  Moreover, the DI approach can serve as an
 efficient tool for Marine Protected Areas (MPAs) Selection and Management.  The Marine Protected Areas (MPA) is the
 primary form of protection in the marine coastal zone and could be used as a spearhead for marine conservation including
 the restoration of coral health.  The MPA could be directly linked with DI index and the coefficient of the DI picture can
 give details for restoration of the marine protected areas.  Apart from this, identification of new Heat Shock Protein (HSP)
 of marine invertebrates is expected to enable rapid and accurate quantitative monitoring of short term and long-term
 fluctuations in marine eco-system. The expression of specific stress proteins present in certain coral community can be
 identified as early warning system for future changes in coral communities following Tsunami disturbances and also the
 ability of reef eco-system to withstand global changes could also be
 assessed.                                                                                                                                                    (Para 12)
Action Taken by the Department

Recommendation
The Committee recommends that the Department should study the icy continent’s atmospherics and ozone
 depletion.  Besides ongoing activities, it should also plan to undertake studies on lake biology, Antarctic microbes, and
 relation of the Antarctic plate with the Indian plate, telemedicine, clean energy technology, micro and molecular biological

Action Taken by the Department
Studies on ozone hole, ice core and climate changes
Studies undertaken by the India Meteorological Department (IMD) and National Physical Laboratory (NPL) have
 provided insight to understand the temporal and spatial dynamics of ozone hole phenomenon. Analysis of ice cores obtained
 by Indian Scientists have provided insights into the changes in the earth’s climate during the past two centuries.  A high-
tech Ice-core laboratory has been established at NCAOR, Goa under its long term ice-core-drilling & research programme. 
 Palynostratigraphic studies of lake sediments have thrown light on the nature and dynamics of paleoenviroments.  Satellite
 imageries and GPS based studies are included to expand the scope and dynamics of Antarctic ice sheet and sea-ice. 
 NCAOR, Goa has recently published an Atlas on Antarctic Sea-Ice using satellite data over a period of two years.

Relation of the Antarctic plate with the Indian plate.
Premier organizations like Geological Survey of India (GSI), National Geophysical Research Institute (NGRI) have
 undertaken studies on the relation between the Antarctic plate and India plate.  There are strong evidences suggesting that
 the Indian Eastern Ghat Mobile Belt (EGMB) and Enderby Land, East Antarctica shared a common Mesoproterozoic (1100
 Ma) evolutionary history.  The east Gondwana Land, then comprised of India, part of East Antarctica and Australia while
 the west Gondwanaland comprised a small fragment of South India, Africa, South America and central Droning Maud
 Land, east Antarctica (area in which Indian Antarctic Station, Maitri is located).  Indian earth Scientists have been working
 in the area of exposing rocks which have been involved in the Pan-African orogeny.  The Indian base has offered a unique
 opportunity to study the processes that were responsible for amalgamating east and west Gondwana. This, in turn, has also
 helped them to understand the processes involved in the evolution of continents through geological past with co-relatable
 implication on the evolution of Indian subcontinent.  Geochronological studies have helped to trace back the chronology of
 tectonometamorphic events.

REPORT
 
The Report of the Committee deals with the Action Taken by the Department of Atomic Energy on the recommendations
 contained in the One Hundred Forty-Fifth Report of the Department Related Parliamentary Standing Committee on Science
 & Technology, Environment & Forests on the Demands for Grants (2005-2006) of the Department of Atomic Energy,
 presented to both the houses of Parliament on 25
thApril, 2005. There were twenty-seven recommendations contained in the
 Report Action Taken note on those recommendations was received from the Department on 25th July, 2005.  The
 Committee considered the draft Action Taken Report in its meeting held on 18th November, 2005 and decided to seek
 clarification/additional information on certain points contained in paras 20, 25.1to 25.9, 27 to 32 and 39.  The Department’s
 clarification/additional information on the points was received on  1
st December, 2005.  
            The Committee’s recommendations, Action Taken thereon  by the Department of Atomic Energy, points raised by
 the Committee (wherever necessary ), clarifications by the Department and comments of the Committee thereon are set out
 in the succeeding paragraphs: -
 
PLAN OUTLAY 2005-06 (DEMAND NO. 6-NUCLEAR POWER SCHEMES)
Recommendation

The Committee notes that there has been an increase of Rs.933.19 crore in BE  2005-06 (Rs.4700.00 crore) over RE 2004-05
 (Rs.3766.81 crore) in respect of Nuclear power Corporation of India Limited (NPCIL). This increase is further narrowed
 down to Rs. 659.99 crore as a Supplementary Grant of Rs.273.20 crore that was obtained for Russian Credit during 2004-
05.  This is on account of KK-1&2 project which has now entered advanced stage of expenditure on account of delivery of
 equipment from Russian Federation. The credit utilization accordingly has grown from Rs.1445 Crore (RE 2004-05) to
 Rs.2004 crore (BE 2005-06). However, in Bhartiya Nabhikiya Vidyut Nigam Ltd. (BHAVINI), BE 2004-05 could not be
 utilized because of slow pace of work.  The Committee, therefore, recommends that NPCIL should make all efforts to
 ensure that there is no delay in execution of the projects on account of increased Internal and Extra Budgetary Resources 
 (IEBR) from  Rs 1496.00 crore to Rs.2696.00 crore during the year 2005-06 and fully utilize the budgetary provisions made
 during 2005-06                          (Para 14)                       
Action Taken by the Department
Nuclear Power Corporation of India Ltd. (NPCIL) will have to borrow from the market in addition to the utilization of
 internal reserves to meet the requirements of funds. NPCIL, being a AAA Company, has been able to obtain funds from the
 market at attractive rates. All the projects being executed by NPCIL are currently progressing as per schedule. A monitoring
 mechanism to monitor the physical and financial progress of work and take corrective measures, if necessary, at several
 levels periodically is in place. NPCIL is confident that funds will not be a constraint for the execution of its projects.
An amount of Rs.253.30 Crores was approved in BE 2004-05 for Prototype Fast Breeder Reactor (PFBR).  Since the
 financial sanction for PFBR was accorded in September '03, the BHAVINI was formed in October '03 and Certificate of
 Commencement of Business was received in November '03, action for awarding of various contracts could be started only
 after November '03.  Since it was felt that the full approved budget provision would not be spent during 2004-05, while
 preparing RE 2004-05 an amount of Rs.165 Crores only was requested for.  Out of the amount of  Rs.165 Crores also, an
 amount of Rs.41.25 Crores which would have been drawn by BHAVINI sometime in January '05 in the normal course
 could not be drawn because of  "TSUNAMI" which struck Kalpakkam on 26.12.2004,  has affected the construction work
 very badly.  Large quantity of sea water, muck and slush entered the pit while concreting on Nuclear Island Connected
 Building (NICB) raft was going on.  Work could be re-started only after complete removal of the water, muck and slush and
 cleaning of the pit and after getting the regulatory clearances.  The pit was made ready to reconstruct the raft within a short
 period of 4 months.  Re-concreting of the raft was started on 27.04.2005. 
Comments
            The Committee notes that the work on the Bhartiya Nabhikiya Vidyut Nigam Limited (BHAVINI) was greatly
 hampered by the onslaught of the ‘TSUNAMI’.  The Committee hopes that the reconstruction work would progress as per
 the new schedule and would be completed at the earliest.  
Recommendation
The Committee also recommends that measures like ensuring availability of designs and clearances in advance of the project
 financial sanction, advance procurement of long delivery and critical items, completion of pre-project activities and
 essential infrastructure works, use of modern CAD tools for design and project management coupled with adoption of the
 concept of execution of large supply-cum-erection
 packages would not only lead to reduced gestation periods of the projects
 under construction but would also reduce the financial cost component of the capital cost, thereby increasing the normative
 capacity factors. The Department should devise strict monitoring and a phased-wise completion schedule for BHAVINI
 which should be strictly adhered to.                                                                                                             (Para 14.1)               
Action Taken by the department
BHAVINI is already implementing the measures recommended by the Committee.  The action, for procurement of long
 delivery and critical nuclear steam supply system components was taken in advance of the project financial sanction.  Pre
 project-activities like excavation, geo-technical investigation and construction of Site Assembly Shop (SAS) were started
 well in advance and completed.  The advanced software tools are planned to be procured for design, erection and
 construction.  The concept of supply cum erection packages are being envisaged for systems like Turbine Generator (TG)
 equipment, Switch Yard, Cabling, Piping and I&C system.  Project planning tools like Prima Vera software is used for
 monitoring of the activities, resources and rescheduling.
Comments
The Committee appreciates the measures taken by the Department to ensure timely completion of the projects.  The
 Committee recommends that such advance measures be undertaken in all the projects under the jurisdiction of the
 Department to ensure time bound completion of the projects.         
Recommendation
The Committee finds that the pace of expenditure by the Department of Atomic Energy has not been uniform and the
 reasons attributed are more of administrative nature. The Committee, therefore, recommends that the Department should
 formulate strict monitoring mechanism with proper planning and co-ordination of projects/programmes for regular infusion
 of funds in various projects/schemes in all quarters of the financial year to ensure total utilization of plan allocation and
 avoid surrender/shortfall of funds  in the last quarter of the financial year.

CHOICE OF FUEL FOR FAST BREEDER REACTOR (FBR)
Recommendation
The Committee welcomes the idea and feels that this advanced fuel will reduce the cost of production of electricity through
 Fast Breeder Reactor (FBR) and not only that by reducing the capital cost of production of electricity the plant life span will
 also increase by incorporating better safety features for these reactors.  Faster the breeding, quicker will be the rise in the
 FBR’s capacity. Other nuclear fuels for FBR and PFBR (Prototype Fast Breeder Reactor) like oxide, nitride and carbide
 fuels may now take the back seat for being used as fuels for FBR.                     
(Para 25.1)
The choice of fuels for breeder reactors, the Committee feels, is a choice between doubling time versus the cost of
 production. The Committee, however, feels that oxide fuel with a ratio of 30% plutonium oxide and 70% uranium oxide is a
 well-proven fuel world over.  In India, however, mixed oxide fuel (MOX) could be used for Prototype Fast Breeder Reactor
 (PFBR).                                                                                                                                             (Para 25.2)
The Committee, on the other hand, feels that carbide fuel is very difficult to fabricate on a large scale as it is highly
 pyrophoric and is highly susceptible to oxidation and hydrolysis.  Moreover, reprocessing of spent carbide fuel is difficult
 as it is difficult to dissolve in nitric acid and leaves behind organic complexes.  Apart from this, the carbide fuel  has low
 burn up value in comparison to oxide fuel. The fuel ‘burn-up’ in a nuclear reactor refers to the amount of energy extracted
 from the fuel before it is discharged for storage or reprocessing.  Higher the burn-up, lesser will be the fuel cycle cost.          
                                                                     (Para 25.3)
The Committee understands that cost of power production comes down with increased burn up value.  Also oxide fuel is
 easy to fabricate as it is not pyrophoric and hence needs no inert atmosphere during fabrication.  The Committee is,
 therefore, of the opinion that use of oxide fuel would be more vital for making a foray into fast breeder power
 plants.                          (Para 25.4)
The Committee understands that breeder technology works on the principle of self-sustenance and ability to produce more
 plutonium than it actually consumes to produce power.  The breeding ratio, which is 1.1 in case of oxide fuel, is 1.2 – 1.4 in
 case of carbide and nitride fuels.  While it is maximum in case of metallic fuel i.e. 1.4 – 1.5 and hence doubling time       
 (i.e. surplus plutonium produce to start a new reactor) is shortest in case of a metallic, carbide and nitride fuels respectively
 in comparison to oxide fuel.                                                      (Para 25.5)
The Committee, therefore, is of the opinion that doubling time becomes paramount when the country goes on
 commissioning new reactors.  Hence, the stress on using advanced fuel is necessary.  The Committee feels that making
 technology available for producing power at cheaper cost may gain more public acceptance, which is vital to breeder
 programme.   (Para 25.6)
 
            The Committee is of the opinion that lower burn up by using carbide fuel is not economical since fabrication and
 reprocessing would increase cost of power production.  However, the Committee feels that long-term strategy calls for fuels
 with shorter doubling time.  Sometimes it is felt that nitride fuel seems to be more preferable due to its easier reprocessing
 and improved performance.                                                                                                        (Para 25.7)
 
The Committee recommends that the Department of Atomic Energy may like to consider the following choices:-
i)          High breeding ratio and shorter doubling time
ii)         High burn up value and less fuel cycle cost
iii)         Faster breeding and quicker capacity of fast breeder reactor
iv)        High burn up value and low production cost of power; and between
v)         Easy fabrication and reprocessing and low cost of power production before ending itself finally by choosing the most
 ideal fuel for its FBR and PFBR programme.                                                             (Para 25.8)
 
The Committee feels that without choosing the best options from among the above series, the choice of fuel for future
 reactors of the Department of Atomic Energy may not be optimally fulfilled unless maximum efficiency in power
 production is derived at least possible opportunity cost.

Action Taken by the Department
 
The 40 MWt Fast Breeder Test Reactor (FBTR) at Indira Gandhi Centre for Atomic Research (IGCAR), Kalpakkam uses a
 Pu-rich U-Pu mixed carbide as the fuel. The choice of this fuel was necessitated by the non-availability of enriched uranium
 and the technical problems expected with the use of oxide fuel with high percentage of Pu  ( about 70 %  PuO
2). The
 carbide fuel was indigenously developed and has performed exceedingly well at FBTR, having attained a burn-up of
 140,000 MWd/t without any fuel pin failure.  The Reprocessing Group at IGCAR has also successfully demonstrated the
 capability to reprocess mixed carbide fuel of 50,000 & 100,000 MWd/t burn-up.
However, it is to be noted that the reprocessing technology for carbide fuel has not been established on a commercial scale
 in any country. Also, since the carbide fuel is air-sensitive, difficulties are envisaged in the large scale manufacture of
 carbide fuel. On the other hand, the performance of mixed oxide fuel in fast reactors has been proven in other countries and
 sufficient technical data is also available in published literature on their properties. Also, the fuel has been fabricated and
 reprocessed on a commercial scale in other countries. Considering the difficulties associated with fabrication and
 reprocessing of carbide fuel on a commercial scale as well as the lack of international experience on carbide fuel cycle, the
 well proven mixed oxide fuel with lower PuO
2  content ( 21% PuO2  in inner zone and 28% PuO2 in outer zone) has been
 selected for the 500 MWe PFBR.
 It is envisaged that in addition to PFBR, 4 more FBRs of 500 MWe capacity are planned to be constructed by the year 2020
 as part of DAE Vision 2020 Programme.  Since the main objective of these reactors is to prove the techno-commercial
 viability of the FBR technology when multiple units are constructed, mixed oxide fuel has been considered for these
 reactors also. However, through the use of better materials and design, it is aimed to improve the burn-up of the oxide fuel
 as well as the breeding ratio in these reactors.
It is realized in the department that the rapid growth of fast reactors is only possible through adoption of fuels and fuel
 cycles which would ensure higher breeding and consequently, lower doubling time. It is therefore necessary to switch over
 to fuels like metallic fuel, which has higher breeding ratio. It is at the same time recognized that a good amount of R&D
 efforts is required to establish a reactor and fuel cycle based on metallic fuel, since the experience with respect to metallic
 fuel is also limited.
IGCAR has therefore taken up the planning of necessary R & D to establish the fuel cycle, carry out test irradiations in
 FBTR and gain sufficient experience with respect to the metallic fuel with the long term goal of establishing fast reactors
 with metallic fuel. The core configuration of the later 500 MWe FBRs will be chosen in such a way that the metallic fuel
 can replace some of the oxide fuel bundles.
             Thus, the approach in the Department is to proceed with oxide fuel for the next four 500 MWe FBRs and then
 switch over to metallic fuel to get lower doubling time.  This approach gives continuity in the programme and also adequate
 time to generate necessary data on the utilization of metallic fuel.
During Mid-Term Appraisal (MTA) of Plan Projects, a new Scheme has been introduced for initiating advance action in
 R&D activities to be taken up for development of metallic fuels.  The said project is already sanctioned.  All efforts are
 made to begin with the development of metallic fuel for FBRs, in the X Plan itself, so as to achieve the long-term goals.

FOOD IRRADIATION
Recommendation
The Committee, therefore, feels that some precautionary measures should be taken by the Department of Atomic Energy
 while irradiating foods so that the possible health risks involved before consumption of irradiated food could be effectively
 dealt with. In this connection, Radiological Safety, Microbiological Safety, Nutritional adequacy and Toxicological Safety
 measures may be kept in view.                                                                                              (Para 35)
Action Taken by the Department
The safety and nutritional adequacy of the irradiated foods have been thoroughly studied for past several decades. Perhaps
 no other method of food processing has been subjected to such a thorough assessment of safety as the radiation processing.
 The various aspects of wholesomeness and safety of radiation- processed foods have been studied in great detail. These
 include investigations on Possibility of induced radioactivity, Microbiological safety, Safety of chemical changes,
 Nutritional adequacy, Animal feeding and Human trials.
Only after studying the results of the above and decades of research, the technology has been approved for commercial use.
Comments
            The Committee notes the reply.
Recommendation
The Committee also feels that long term effects of irradiated food should be studied thoroughly from the point of view of the
 fact that how ionizing radiation alters chemical structure of food material.  This could be managed if a monitored safe label
 of exposure of food to radiation is laid down by the Department of Atomic Energy.                                              (Para 36)
Action Taken by the Department
The changes that take place in food material as a result of processing by radiation have been thoroughly studied. The long-
term effects of consuming radiation-processed foods have been studied in multi-generation feeding trials on animals. Human
 volunteers have eaten irradiated foods for long periods without any side effects. Astronauts and cosmonauts have been
 eating irradiated foods during space flights.  At the energies of the gamma rays from cobalt-60 (1.3 MeV) and those
 recommended for using X-rays (5 MeV) and accelerated electrons                  (10 MeV), there is no induction of
 radioactivity. The microbiological aspects of radiation- processed foods have been studied in detail. None of these studies
 have indicated that foods preserved by radiation pose any special problems in relation to microflora. It has been found that
 there are no unique radiolytic products formed and free radicals in the system disappear depending on the nature of the
 commodity and its post-irradiation storage and treatment. In fact, the chemical differences between radiation processed
 foods and non-irradiated foods are too small to be detected easily. Though rough composition of food remains largely
 unchanged, some losses in vitamins may be encountered. However, these losses are often minor.
In 1980 a joint Expert Committee on Food Irradiation (JECFI) consisting of Food and Agricultural organization
 (FAO)/Internal Atomic Energy Agency (IAEA)/World Health organization (WHO) reviewed the extensive data on
 wholesomeness collected up to that time and concluded that irradiation of any commodity up to an over all dose of 10 kGy
 presents no toxicological hazards and introduces no special nutritional or microbiological problems. An Expert Group
 constituted by WHO in 1994 once again reviewed the wholesomeness data available till then and validated the earlier
 conclusion of JECFI. In 1998 another Expert Group constituted by WHO/FAO/IAEA affirmed the safety of food irradiated
 to doses above 10 kGy. Codex Alimentarius Commission that sets standards for food worldwide and the World Trade
 Organization has also recognized the technique.   In addition, a number of scientific bodies and associations have also
 endorsed the safety of radiation-processed foods. These include naming a few:
American Medical Association
The American Gastroentrological Association
American Dietetics Association
American Meat Institute
Institute of Food Technologists

Comments
            The Committee appreciates  that necessary laws have been enacted to control the irradiation of some vegetables,
 spices, fish and for quarantine treatment.  However, the Committee feels that the scope of the laws can be enlarged to
 include in its ambit other eatables like agricultural and poultry products. 
Recommendation
The Committee feels that high voltage electron beams generated from linear accelerators which could be a better alternative
 for food irradiation technology than application of Cobalt-60 and cesium 137 because the penetration depth of gama
 irradiation is not there and with shorter exposure time, the food could be safe with this method.  With all other existing
 methods of food irradiation, the Committee feels only low efficiency could be maintained combined with high cost of
 production of irradiated foods.                                                                         (Para 37)
Action Taken by the Department
It is possible to use both machine sources (accelerated electrons and X-rays) as well as radioisotope sources (cobalt-60 and
 cesium-137) emitting gamma rays. Both have their advantages and limitations. The choice of the source would depend upon
 several product and process parameters.  In case of electrons, the depth of penetration is a major problem, that can be solved
 by their conversion to X-rays. However, the conversion of electrons to X-rays is not economical.  On the other hand, cobalt
 sources are very rugged and reliable.
Comments
            The Committee notes the reply.
Recommendation
The Committee feels that in order to make the food irradiation a success, the following factors for judging the bactericidal
 efficacy of a given dose of irradiation may be adopted:
Kinds and species of organism composing the food.
Numbers of organisms present because the dose of radiation should be proportional to the number of organism present in the
 food.
Composition of the food.
Presence and absence of oxygen
The physical state of the food during irradiation including moisture content and temperature.
Condition of the organism, that is, its age, temperature for growth etc.          (Para 38)

            It is a well-known fact that exact prediction of earthquake is not possible and the science of earthquake prediction
 has not reached a mature stage as yet, though seismologists all over the world are working hard in this area.  It will be a
 great service to humanity if the seismologists succeed one day in their efforts and save the humanity from great devastations
 from time to time.  Till then, we may try to minimize the effect of this natural catastrophe. This can be ensured by enforcing
 suitable building laws in the country, especially in the areas which are more sensitive seismologically.  It has to be ensured
 that all construction activities are undertaken with due regard to earthquake.  As regards the existing structures, the
